title: The Power of God and the Nature of the Word
english: We have a discussion concerning God from the Scripture and from common understanding that He is unchangeable, and that He is immutable. For He who is not at all subject to quality does not turn, nor is He altered; for no alteration is anything other than a change according to quality. Not every change is an alteration, but the one according to quality. There are indeed also other changes, since there are also motions. That which becomes changes, but this motion is not an alteration. That which grows changes, but this is not an alteration; for such a motion is addition and increase. But when someone becomes lazy from being diligent, or lazy from being diligent, he is altered according to quality, just as when one comes from sickness to health and again.

But the words, regarding the meaning of the thing about which they are spoken, we understand. God was not composed of parts, since He is not composite; therefore, sitting upon Him, rising, walking, turning of the face, or illumination of the face, pass by. But in these things, regarding those arranged about Him, it is necessary to grasp the meaning in a God-befitting way to preserve faith. For some, through the words and their fluidity, subvert the things signified. Indeed, some have even dared to run into such a prosperity or impiety, so as to think the God human-shaped because of the manner in which they are written. And they say that God has hands, limbs, and feet, and appearance, and the rest. But if we know this always, regarding whom these things are said and from whom, we are able to lead the things to what is signified, to what is made manifest. If we do not grasp them in a God-befitting way, we are not able to have a pious conception concerning them according to each of the [words].

The prophets. For this one, in a certain place, says: 'Are not his words beautiful and rightly proceeding with him?' If they are not with him, according to his intention, they are not beautiful. If you hear—behold—sleep and wakefulness and repentance, and you do not receive such things according to his intention, then the things said about him do not rightly proceed with him.

But when you receive such things with him, the words proceeding rightly with him, being filled with spirit, have neither shadow nor sketch. This is what the Savior said in the Gospel: 'You wander, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God' (Matt 22:29). You wander, saying that he does not make things from non-being; for they say this: 'To do is later than to be; for there must exist something underlying. Those who are dead are without hope of resurrection.' Since, therefore, they do not receive these things through the power of God, because of this they stumble. God is able to bring from non-being into being and to transform corruptible bodies.

He says, then, to the Sadducees. He who thinks he knows the Scriptures wanders when he is ignorant of the power of God which is spoken concerning Him and by whom they are spoken. For whose sake these things have been spoken to me, I will say, apart from the deed about to take place. The Savior and our Lord is both God and man; God always, but not always man; for before the creation he was God, but not a man. And this also was destined to happen for the sake of salvation. And the becoming man has a cause, but being God is not because of a cause, but because of his own existence and the essence of his offspring; for thus I heard: 'I live because of the Father' (John 6:57) of mine. He does not say this because the Father makes me alive, as the Eunomians wish, but he says this, as...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Distinction of Divinity and Humanity
english: If someone says: 'For this reason I am rational, because I have a rational father; and for this reason I am mortal, because I have a mortal father,' it is true; for the 'because' is a demonstrative cause. Since, therefore, he lives because of the father, what is being said is not a life named from life, but as a fountain of life and as one giving to all; for we say that the living one has life, but we also say that the life is not one named from life, for life does not participate in [something else], but it is life itself. Thus, he does not live through the father.

A human, therefore, [lives] because of something, but God [is] not because of something. Yet both have run together regarding the arrival of a season. I do not say the arrival is entirely according to the flesh; for many [seasons] He desired; He is always arriving. And thus I have drawn out what is in Micah: 'And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, you are small. Out of you shall come to me the ruler, and his exits are from the beginning' (Micah 5:2). For it is not that he came from the father just now previously, from which the need of the administration of saving things [comes]. The need of his exit is always happening and happening wherever. For this reason, he said not one, but many exits. 'For this reason He will give them until the time of birthing.'

The last exit, that of the birthing of Mary, is a certain 'until the time of birthing'; for the Scripture does not praise those [plural] birthing, but says one birthing, signified by the word. And 'birthing' in the strict sense is not one who took in seed and conceived and formed and surrounded, but she herself gives birth. For this reason, he came from a woman. No one of the others [comes] from a woman, but all [come] through a woman; yet all [come] from men; for the woman comes from the man, and the man through the woman. And this must be said: that genealogies are made casually, scientifically, and piously when they are descended from fathers; for the genealogy from women is slandered. Therefore, only this one has given birth without a man. And for this reason the Savior came from a woman, not through a woman, even if many others are made [to be said] not 'from Mary,' but 'through Mary.' So many will seem to be ambassadors [speaking thus]. And God is from the Father and not because of something, but the human...

Regarding the descent from David and Mary and for what reason: for the sake of the salvation of the world he has come, to abolish death, to do much for mortals who had cast [themselves] away through their own negligence. Why do I say these things in grace? The things said about the Savior declare his divinity. And all the things reported concerning divinity are incomparable to any other; for he is the only-begotten. But the things said about the man touch upon human faults, just as they do those of the dying. The zealous become imitators of the man. But they do not imitate the divinity—for this is an unreasonableness—they imitate the man. Whatever is said about the man could also be said about the angels and about perfect men. But whatever is said about the divinity, neither about angels nor about holy men will be said. I do not say that any of the created things is wisdom, or a radiance of glory, or a character of the divine essence, or the only-begotten Son of God.

But whatever is said as being about the man, it could be said, for example: 'You seek to kill me, a man,' being 'one who has spoken the truth to you, which I heard from God' (John 8:46). And many others, having learned the truth from God, spoke the truth. Not this one more, but this one more, this one incomparably. And again: 'But because I tell you the truth, you do not believe me' (John 14:11). And others speak the truth: for if we grant that no one spoke the truth except Christ himself, we give in to the anonymous heresy. That is, an anonymous heresy that seems to overturn [the truth] or to have come from the books. And many have books and compositions, and they say this too: that the truth never came among men except upon the appearance of the Savior; for 'grace and truth came through Jesus Christ' (John 1:17). And see where the argument leads them: because they want the old scripture to not be from God, nor the prophets, they say that the truth never came to men except after the appearance having happened. And saying these things, they divide the one divinity, and they say that the one who was the Creator was before the appearance, and they seek another father for Christ. But we do not say this, that ever the truth...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Eternity of Christ's Reign
english: It has been hidden. It always sends out its own testimonies. Among men, however, it is a matter of either seeing it or not seeing it. And just as it happens to the perceptible sun that those with clouded eyes cannot see it, and we do not immediately say that the sun does not exist, so also we do not say that truth has never existed among men, lest we should disparage the Scripture.

And I say to you: if you bring me two different kinds of fruits, such as figs, because you divided them from the matter, it is necessary that other plants and other things also be. Therefore, it is impossible for the Gospel instruction to have made the truth into men, nor for the one called the old before the advent to have been enlightened according to the truth. They necessarily approached from different fruits and different qualities; not because there is a different divinity, but because of their strange beginning, this followed.

If, therefore, the Savior says: 'I am the truth' (John 14:6) and Shepherd and Door and the others, these names and what is signified by them are unshared from the natural ones. But if he says that 'I am a man', if it is said about him that he is righteous—'you killed the righteous one,' says Peter (Acts 7:52)—these names run together for both men and angels.

Take the same manner for me regarding a king; and since a king is something of a nature with the kingdom of the Word, unable to be either taken up or cast off, that itself is kingdom. And just as one is not called righteous because he possesses righteousness, but being righteousness itself, so also a king is not from appointment, but the king himself is from the King, as God is from God. He also has an acquired kingship, which he desired to have by appearing, so that he might also bring down those warring against the human race and bring them themselves into a lawful dominion, so that he might rule lawfully.

If, therefore, he says: 'I have been established king by him upon his holy Mount Zion' (Psalm 2:6), he is not speaking about the innate and eternal kingship, but about that which he received for our sake. And teaching is a kingship upon God. Thus, there was the teaching before the advent, which they said was spoken by him as a Word like God, and there is another for the sake of some. This, therefore, has a beginning and an end. For it has been said in...

To the twelve prophets: 'and the Lord shall reign from Zion from now and until the age'. The 'from' and 'until' signify time. But if it is said concerning a man that he reigns from this time and until that, it signifies a limited [reign]; for before the time from which his kingship began, he was not king, and at the end of the kingship, he is no longer king.

But concerning the Savior we do not say this, rather he reigned from the time from which he received authority through ordination, and he is no longer reigning when this reaches an end; for that [end] is through him. Just as divinity does not come to him through another, so neither does the kingship nor the holiness. 'God is our king before the age' (Ps 89:3). And the kingship before the age is through him.

Again: 'your kingdom is the kingdom of all the ages' (Rev 11:15). This is said of the Word God. The Word has neither a beginning having kingship nor an ending; for 'Lord' [means] 'reigning for the age and upon the age and yet more'. He was at a loss to signify [the difference between] time and age, and said 'and yet more'. We take 'yet more' thus: even if you take another age, he reigns yet more; even if another, yet more; even if all [ages], yet more he reigns; from which it is shown that his beginning is without end; for the kingship which he had according to [human] kingship has sometimes ceased and has taken a beginning; but why is [this kingship]? Because of the salvation of the world, because of the removal of 'the sin of the world' (John 1:29).

And just as a physician is always a physician from the time he has the art, and as far as he practices it, he has a beginning and an end of being a physician, and for the one suffering, there is a beginning and an end of that physician being 'yet more', when he reaches a possible health and a possible recovery, so also you will say concerning teachers. There is a certain teacher from whom one has received knowledge. He becomes a teacher of this [one] when he comes to him; and when that one has been instructed and has fully taken up the knowledge like the teacher, he ceases to be his teacher. And it is a kind of virtue for a teacher to sometimes cease to be a teacher of this [one]; for having perfected them, he is no longer [their teacher]. But if he remains always a teacher of this [one], no one is perfected according to the teaching of him. Therefore, hearing such things, those not understanding the Scriptures in this way—for example:
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Kingly Joy and Reward
english: "When the kingdom is handed over to God and Father," he no longer reigns in the same way; not that he ceases to reign entirely, but he no longer reigns thus. There, he is called both king and kingdom; for "Lord, the king shall rejoice in your power" (Ps 21:13). If we take this word regarding the Word of God, he himself is found to be both king and power; for "Christ is the power of God" (1 Cor 1:24), and "the power of the Most High"—who is this?—"overshadowed" (Luke 1:35) Mary, so that she might conceive and become the mother of the temple. Therefore, if we wish to receive power from the Word of God, we look for the king, the Lordly man. He rejoices in the power of God.

Has the success not occurred in those things in which it is necessary to rejoice and be glad? These successes have not happened by the power of the man, but from the power to the man. Likewise, Paul says the resurrection of the Savior happens in this way: "He was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God" (2 Cor 4:10). We do not say the life is living by the power of God, nor the power is living by the power of God. "Having been put to death in the flesh, he was made alive in the spirit." He is put to death in the flesh, not put to death in divinity. We understand these things said about the man because: "the king shall rejoice in your power" (Ps 21:13); for even if he has prevailed over wars and subjected them and "given authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions" (Luke 10:19), this has happened by power; for this power strengthened the existing temple and the king himself to become the "author of salvation" (Acts 3:15).

"You put to death the author of life" (Acts 3:15). He is first in all things; for he says, "so that he might become himself first in all things." He is second to no one, nor is anyone equal to him in common things. I say, then, that the affairs of the Lordly man and the holy men are common. But no one is equal to him, nor is he second to anyone; therefore he is called the leader. "Lord, the king shall rejoice in your power" (Ps 21:13). And this could be said of each individual queen according to God. Abraham was a private person regarding his immediate life, yet it is said he was a "king by God." Thus, he had another kingdom: to save the divine laws and the spiritual [things].

For he who reigns thus, even if he does not rule others, rules himself; first himself, then others. Again: 'You have reigned without us; and it would have been better if you had also reigned, so that we too might reign with you.' Do not think, O Corinthians—for they were self-willed in this and thought greatly of themselves—he says: do not think that we envy you if you reign. We do not reign for your sake. God does not wish to complete us without you; for this reason we do not reign because you are not yet reigning. If, therefore, you reign, we are ready to reign.

Just as if certain people, being great men, were called to a banquet by the king. The philanthropy of the king called also those inferior to those present. He says: 'Let us not eat without them, so that they might not be left out, those coming later, to be feasted.' They also have those who arrived beforehand and were feasting previously. This also is said in Psalm 1: 'The righteous shall wait for me, until I repay them in kind' (Psalm 1:5). No one is said to wait by chance among those expecting to wait, but rather the one who has received [the call], having a purpose to enjoy these things.

Every one of the saints, therefore, is a king. And they were saying that what is fitting for the Savior also fits the righteous, even if in a diminished and lesser way. He says therefore also concerning each saint: 'Lord, in your power the king shall be made glad.' And he did not say 'he rejoices,' but 'he shall be made glad.' When the time of gladness is, then he shall be made glad.

4 Therefore, this can also be said specifically concerning David and concerning his human and sensible kingship, that having ruled the kingdom well, he shall receive a reward upon it; for each one, when he has been entrusted with what, if he endures well, has a reward upon them. Becoming faithful over a little, he enters 'into the joy' (Matthew 25:21) of the neighbor and of God. 2 Lord, in your power the king shall be made glad. He speaks of the saving power that makes the king rejoice, according to how God is the Word. Previously it was said that the words must be taken just as the underlying things are, and not to force the things toward the meaning. With us, the name of power is being worn down. It signifies many things; I say power as equal to strength. I do not say thus the Savior of God...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Kingship and the Distinction of Terms
english: To have power. I say power means capacity. Someone might think that this is not contained in the Scripture. But it is contained: 'God is faithful, who will not let you be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation he will make the way of escape to endure' (1 Cor 10:13). He speaks of capacity; for they say equal to equal. And thus the adversary has the power to endure and to receive the outcome of victory. See then, it is contained.

And again: 'the power of sin is the law' (Rom 7:7). The law is able and to be transgressed. It does not have it by actual operation. And well and timely the apostle has used this expression: 'the power of sin is the law'; for he wants us to be in the capacity of sin and not in the operation. If it had been said: 'the power of righteousness is the law', we would not have been righteous by operation, but in capacity. And being in capacity, we were unjust by operation. Thus the apostle set down the auspicious word; since it also has the power equally for both, for guarding and for transgressing; but because of what is advantageous.

And power also signifies capacity. And the king's camp also signifies it: 'he cast Pharaoh's chariots and his power into the sea' (Ex 15:1). 'A king is not saved by much power,' by much hand and camp. The Savior, therefore, apart from these things signified, is called the power of God; for by what word the Father is able, not having this from power, but from essence, and his essence, according to which he is able, might be called power, so also the Son. He says therefore: 'he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God' (Rom 6:9). As far as it reached human weakness, he underwent the cross. Therefore this God was not able to undergo it, but man was able to suffer this. And indeed he has suffered, but by the power of God he lives. The power, therefore, of God is Christ, as he is God. 'In the power' therefore 'the king rejoices' (Rom 16:20). And the king was spoken of in more ways. We have said.

Kings are to be understood historically as David, by upward leading as the man from Mary, and by imitation and following as those who imitate him. And we have presented, from the epistle to the Corinthians, another kingship besides the immediate one.

'Lord,' therefore, 'in your power the king shall rejoice.' This is said either from the spirit-bearing man or from the Holy Spirit himself who happens to be in him; for when the Holy Spirit says 'Lord,' he says this not only of a man who is already released, but also when he prepares someone to be spirit-bearing. He is therefore the one saying, as in: 'the Lord says to my Lord' (Ps 110:1). And the Savior says: 'If in the Holy Spirit he said Lord, how is he his son?' (Matt 12:42). If he is his son, how is he a slave, and if a slave, how is he a son? He thus shows a certain relation and disposition; for even if the Savior says: 'the Lord created me' (John 10:36), he says it at the right time; for he did not say: 'the Lord begat me'; for to beget belongs to a father, but to create belongs to a lord. When he speaks concerning his own divinity, he does not say 'Lord,' but: 'I am in the Father and the Father in me' (John 10:30). 'I and my Father are one' (John 10:30). And 'Lord' and 'Father' are different things.

Often when we speak concerning a quality, we attribute the things of the quality to the quality, and the things of the quality to the one possessing it. I say that knowledge is to know. It is a falsehood to say that knowledge is ignorant. Opposites are found co-existing, knowledge and ignorance. And I say that the one who knows is knowing. Furthermore, many people often say that a physician ought not to be a lover of money. Then they say that medical science knows how to abstain from greed. He says the habit not apart from the one having it, nor the one having it apart from the habit. Therefore such things are common to both the one having and the one being had. And we have often presented from the teaching of the Apostle, that he calls 'love' the one having love; for when he says: 'love never behaves unseemly' (1 Cor 13:5).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Desire and Petition
english: He calls the one possessing it by the name of possession. And I say indeed also concerning the one possessing love that it benefits. And it benefits by that benefit which love provides. If therefore I say that the holy one says this, such as the hymnodist, not separating the Holy Spirit from the one possessing it, nor do I say that the one possessing it says these things apart from the Holy Spirit. If then 'David in the Holy Spirit calls him Lord' (Ps 37:4), so also it is as a partaking, not being severed from the partaker, just as knowledge is not without the knower.

And 'he will rejoice exceedingly in your salvation' (Ps 103:5). The king, just as he is gladdened by power, so also rejoices exceedingly over salvation. And salvation and power are the same, being understood according to one or another conception. Power is that which sustains all things and leads all things thus as it thinks. So also it is salvation; for what he does, he does for the sake of salvation—what he does in men, he does for the sake of the salvation of men.

You gave him the desire of his soul. You know that the word 'himself' denotes authority, not merely the things adjacent. The desire of the soul is bad when, assuming a bad soul, one says 'soul'. But when I say that the soul itself has desire, I speak of its essential desire. The one using desire in this way sees nothing of the bad things, but of the good things; for he received the desiring faculty and the desire, so that he might pursue the beautiful things, so that he might enjoy the profitable things. If, therefore, it happens that he is a lover of silver of wealth, he did not receive the desire of his own soul, but the desire of the lover of silver. Great, therefore, is the happening of the desire of the soul, without adding 'the bad' to it. Indeed, in another psalm he also says: 'the one filling your desire with good things' (Ps 144:11). He speaks to the soul. It has been said to us many times in other places that adjacent words do not make an antithesis. If I say, 'the desire of the soul is good,' and again I say, 'the desire of the righteous is good,' the adjacent words do not make an antithesis. But if I say, 'the desire that is shameful, the desire that is evil, the desire of the unrighteous,' an antithesis is made. That desire is not simply of the soul, but of such a soul. Therefore, the adjacent words sometimes agree, and sometimes they contend and make an antithesis. Thus indeed it is said: 'every desire of a righteous man is good.'

There is no distinction between the desire of a righteous soul and the desire of a soul without addition. And he did not withhold the will of their lips, and this appears even regarding the sensible. If I say now: 'so much as a father desires his children to live well', because I have made a memory of a father, I want them to live well. But if I say: 'an evil father wants his children to do such things', I have removed paternal compassion. 'With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you' (Luke 22:15). And the 'with desire' and 'I have desired' is in such a way as: 'rightly I pursued the righteous', the worthy of being desired. And there is sometimes to desire and also the unworthy of being desired, as it says: 'passion, an evil desire'. An evil desire is not a thing to be desired, just as a pseudo-good is not called heretical, even if some call it so.

3 And he did not withhold his lips' petition from him. If the word is about [the one] from Mary, it is clear that he brings a petition for those for whom he has come to save. You have indeed: 'wherefore also he is able to save to the perfection, always living to intercede for them'. 6 He always lives in interceding. And take 'always' thus: as much as they need, entreating and mediating. 'And if anyone sins, we have a counselor toward the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous' (1 John 2:1). And since the others also run to the teacher with this haste, they also want to intercede for those for whom they were entrusted, not setting their own prior intercession, but following the justification of the one calling them to imitation. According to all the rewards of the king, it is necessary to be careful not to be deprived of his petition. For example, when we speak about the one ruling sensorially, saying that the petition of his lips was not withheld, but it happened in the outcome, we signify his praise. Even if we speak about the saints—for they too are called kings—and there is great praise for them, it is when their petition is well-received. For 'the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears to their petition' (Psalm 34:15), and: 'he hearkens to the prayers of the righteous' (Psalm 34:17).

3 Dipsalmos. 10 The 'dipsalmos' is found nowhere, neither in the Hebrew scriptures, especially in the Psalms. But this also lies in the song of Habakkuk. Those knowing the dialect are able to say what it means.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Precious Stones of Virtue
english: However, we speak of what has come to us. Those who say that it signifies a change of face are lying; for we have found changes of faces in the psalms even without the diapsalma. Again, they say that the diapsalma signifies a certain interval—for example, saying 'he ceased and at another time he began'—and this diapsalma signifies a chronological interval. But we cannot say this; for it is not laid down that he spoke these verses of the psalm after another time.

But those who have conversed with the Hebrew readings say that this is a musical rhythm, just as they say rhythms and melodies in musical matters. Therefore, these things are not for us to know, but for those who have conversed with the dialect. In every dialect, indeed, it is possible to be appropriate to music. Nor is there music or a rhythm of sounds when they are arranged unharmoniously. Sometimes I think I know letters and to comment on readings. And if we see something in a garden, which is named by a farmer because we do not know it, we learn from him, and not already, not devaluing learning, we remain uneducated from this. So, even if we do not know the Hebrew dialect, we have heard that it signifies a musical rhythm according to the Hebrew dialect.

'For you have preceded him in blessings of goodness' (Psalm 21:3). God has preceded the king in all interpretations in blessings of goodness. The 'you have preceded in blessings' is equal to: 'While you are still speaking I will say: behold, I am here' (Psalm 40:2). For example, suppose a certain prayer is being sent up concerning living well, concerning having virtue; it says: 'while you are still speaking,' not yet having fulfilled the word of the prayer, because of the giving, I say I am present.

The 'of goodness' we take here as 'of kindness'; for often we take the 'good' as if toward slander: 'evil characters make the conversations bad,' instead of the pleasant, the kind. And the pleasant itself is taken even regarding praise, when someone has a good character, and regarding the pleasant. Likewise also the innocent: 'for through the good-speaking they deceive the hearts of the innocent.' And also: 'the innocent believes every word.' 'You have set upon his head a crown of precious stone.' If this is said concerning the Lord's man, this crown is that which is placed upon the head...

A crown is woven from his precious stones, that is, from virtues or those possessing virtues. Within the weaving of this crown lie those stones being built up with gold and silver upon the foundation, Christ. It is clear, however, that neither gold, nor silver, nor the stones are taken according to physical sense.

Even regarding each king, such as Abraham was, or as the other saints are, we say this: just as the ruler of Tyre, when he lived well, was placed among the Cherubim in the holy mountain of God, when it was a 'seal of likeness' and a 'crown of beauty,' he was not bound by perceptible stones; rather, one is crowned from such stones. For instance, Joseph contended regarding temperance. Temperance is a precious stone. These [virtues] crowned him, as well as Susanna and the martyrs. And since virtues follow one another, and he who has one has all, the woven crown is not a single stone. Therefore, 'from a precious stone you placed a crown upon his head.' The 'precious' pertains to that which the precious thing is. We call these stones here, such as pearls and hyacinths and the others, precious, because they are also stones distinct from those. Since, therefore, these great stones are kinds of virtue, behold, these stones are precious and surpass all those appearing to be so in the world.

And that the disciples of the teachers are crowns, Paul taught: 'my joy and crown,' addressing the church that discipled him. 'On that day the Lord of Sabaoth will be the crown of hope.' The material of this crown is the Lord of Sabaoth; for 'the Lord of Sabaoth will be the crown of hope.' And since anyone being there cannot yet have a perfect participation in God, but this will happen when 'God becomes all in all,' becoming a fire perfected in all, in the final desired one; for this reason he called it a crown of hope. For if we are to know Him then, when we see Him as He is, and when we see Him by seeing Him as He is, when we have reached the end, this crown is of hope. It is of end-hope, it is that which we await. 'She sought life from you, and you gave it to him.' We say that the Savior [acts] according to the man—if indeed
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Blessed Life
english: I say 'according to man', do not divide him from the Word—because he is a 'Paraclete' 'towards the Father' (John 14:16). Neither is the Word without the man, nor the man without the Word, but the one joined from both becomes a Paraclete and 'living always to intercede on their behalf' (1 John 2:1) intercedes. Therefore he asks for that life which he wants to be made alive by. And through him the life-giving happens; for he was 'slain in the flesh and made alive in spirit' (Romans 8:11). And the soul of Jesus is not life, but has the living by God measuring and granting it; and all the other souls, as to say each one: 'my soul lives by him'. The soul has a value according to immortality. But 'to live toward God' bears fruit from that which is upon us, just as living again by sin is from that which is upon us.

Length of days into an age and into the age of the age. Again, the length of days we are not able to take up explicitly. But 'into the age' he says 'and into the age of the age'. And these days which are given and become by the sun, are called in this one age only. And it has been said also: 'when will these things be, and what is the sign of your presence and the consummation of the age?' (Matthew 24:3); and: 'until the consummation of this age'. And 'in the days' of the age, if the Scriptures say, they say the days of the age. This one who asked is great and did not send a prayer about a small and indifferent thing, so that even his prayer is remembered, nor about these days which pass by the sun and moon. Otherwise, therefore, these things are to be considered. And it is owed to note that in the Scriptures many times such things fall away and seem as impossible.

'Honor', he says, 'your father and your mother, so that it may go well with you and you may be long-lived on the earth' (Exodus 20:12). But not always the one honoring parents remains for many years in the land. Many younger ones are transferred. For it has been said in the Wisdom of Solomon about such things: 'he was snatched away, not by wickedness, but his understanding changed or deceit deceived his soul' (Wisdom 4:13). And he says that: 'having been perfected in a little while, he filled long ages'. And he says that prudence is great and old age is an uncorrupted life. But if uncorrupted life is old age, it does not consist of days, but of virtue; differently it must be taken.

the days. Therefore, 'he asked you for life' is not so that he himself might live, but so that those for whom he offers the prayer might. Concerning life, we are not speaking of the common kind, but that which is according to virtue. He who has not known sin, nor even done it, nor even held a guile in his heart, did not have a mortality extending toward the blessed life. Therefore, asking for life, he did not ask for himself, but he wants that to be given to them for whom he offers the petition; for he is 'living always to the point of encountering' those who are to have life through him.

Therefore, 'he asked you for life, and you gave it to him.' He says this to God, either the psalmist or the Holy Spirit within him. And it is a great testimony when, having sent up the prayer, he receives the requests. So you gave it to him, 'length of days for ever and ever unto the age of ages.' The saints do not wish at all to have a long-lasting common life in this life. For instance, he says, 'it is better to dissolve and be with Christ' (Phil 1:23). And again: 'Woe, that my sojourn has been lengthened' (Ps 119:18). 'I am a stranger in a land' (Gen 23:4).

He who is 'a stranger and a sojourner' has a longing and a goal to depart from the sojourn, in order to dwell in the appropriate place. Just as the life indicated there is not a common life, which even impious men and irrational animals live, so also 'length of days' does not mean a long-lasting life, but 'length of days,' just as he who honored his parents will be long-lasting and long-lived. And in Deuteronomy it is said: 'This is your life and this is the length of days,' of 'loving the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul' (Deut 6:5). Behold, even the length of days is [that of] one loving Him with all the soul and all the power and all the longing.

Therefore, 'length of days unto the age.' These things can be taken regarding the blessed life in this way: for there is a life which is the same as the knowledge concerning God. When it was being said: 'And this is the eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Him whom you sent, Jesus Christ' (John 17:3), this life is the knowledge concerning the Father and the Son. And again: 'He who believes in me has eternal life' (John 6:47). He who believes in the Savior does not have a common life. The impious are often found to be more long-lasting than the diligent. They...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Continuity of Knowledge and the Eternal Light
english: They desire this long life, because they consider no other good than such a state. Just as life now is praiseworthy and forthcoming, so also 'length of days' for this age, so that each doctrine of truth may be known and illuminating, having great light. A praiseworthy day is each practical virtue being made straight.

Since, therefore, just as perfect and complete knowledge will receive here the partial knowledge, so also regarding practical virtue, those who have been proven righteous through practical virtue from there—for they have righteousness now and forthcoming—will be differently eager for 'length of days' for this age, not this common one, but the one capable of having come into being, about which they say: 'This is the day which the Lord has made' (Ps 118:24); for they are pointing to it. But no one points to the future, but to that which is already present and has established itself. The future, when that time comes through which it comes, is no longer future. Again, that too will fall under pointing.

Thus, if you take the king, and even the holy man, and even him who has come forth from Mary, they do not pray about that life or length of perceivable days, but about those already spoken of. They receive long-age life and offer thanks concerning this. And the long-age life is not the life of one age. Appropriately, each age receives life, sometimes as beginning and introductory, sometimes as intermediate, and sometimes as complete.

But after all these spoken days—each doctrine illuminating the soul, being shone upon by the sun of righteousness (Mal 4:2), we have called a day. After these, there is a certain complete state of light in the flashes of progress. That day is not interrupted by night, nor does it become a multitude of days. And it is possible to receive it thus; since the virtues have affinity with one another—for each is luminous—one length of days...

It happens from their following, and it is not interrupted. I say: each scientific principle is separated from the others; for the scientist knows many things. For example, as if it were in medicine, a surgical principle or a dietary one; as if it were in grammar, this or that. When someone is perfected, he no longer possesses these different things; for now it is perhaps more possible to possess the surgical, and less the dietary. But when he presents to me a perfect physician having all the principles perfectly and without excess, they are no longer poured out [distinctly], nor do they have difference even in matter.

Suppose for me a man having complete health according to the body. He no longer needs diet alone, nor incision. He has cast away those things for the sake of which he needed these, and instead he has health that no longer produces anything else. And for his sake all these things are labored for. And the maintenance of it is labored for with a certain desire; for they are just as if they were producing health, so also things protective, such as the gymnasium or such food.

That long day, therefore, is uninterrupted; for it will be a long time before that time is fulfilled: 'The Lord will be to you an eternal light' (Isa 60:19), when the sun no longer fails, 'nor shall the rising of the moon light the night' (Rev 21:23). And these things are not said about the sensible luminaries; for 'immediately' 'after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light' (Matt 24:29). But these lights will no longer give [light] to those who are friends of this [world]; for the sun will be sevenfold and the moon like the sun. Generally, it is said concerning the heavens that 'they shall be changed.' And when he says heavens being changed, and the stars and luminaries in them, just as, if we speak concerning the earth: 'all the earth worships,' we say those dwelling in the earth. 'Sing to the Lord, all the earth' (Ps 96:1). 'Great is your glory in your salvation.' If we receive the glory truly, we do not call the most pleasant state glory. For example, we do not call a human beginning glory, nor a dignity; for all these things are...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Greatness of Christ's Glory and True Splendor
english: Glory is small for men of little thought and little goodness. Thus, physicians who bring health to those who are well seem to take glory for themselves—it has been thought rather that the healthy person is more glorious than the one suffering—but the glory is not great. Similarly for a pilot.

In the salvation of God, therefore, there is 'great glory'; for this salvation touches the mind and the soul. And of all that is in us, the mind differs and the soul from the body, even if it does not seem so to others. And it is possible even to call the Savior himself 'salvation', as he is found in many places: 'All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God' (Ps 95:3). 'And all flesh shall see the salvation of God' (Isa 49:6), instead of 'every man' or 'every sensitive soul'. In this salvation, therefore, is 'great glory'.

Even if the death which he received seems to be without honor—for 'cursed is everyone hanging on a tree' (Gal 3:13) according to the law—yet this seeming dishonor was able to receive such glory from the purpose of salvation, because salvation has become not of food, nor of men simply, but of soul and mind and spirit, as Paul writes: 'Your whole spirit and soul and body' (1 Thess 5:23). The seeming dishonor is therefore a glory surpassing all.

I wish to remind you of a thought. When I was speaking concerning the Gospel, concerning that place: 'He who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do, and greater than these he will do' (John 14:12), to others this interpretation was also given: if you consider the analogy of the one doing, the great things are small; as they are small compared to God. For the apostles did not perform sensible works greater than those of the Savior. The Savior raised Lazarus, already on the fourth day being in death and near to decomposing and already having reached the point of stinking. The apostles did not do anything of this kind. Jesus brought the blind from birth to sight. If, however, you consider these works of the Savior, they are small compared to having performed the rational essence, the heavens, the souls. And the works of the apostles, even if they were greater than those of the Savior, since their power is [from Him], are rather called greater than those which the Savior did; for they were not able to do greater than these. But Jesus both did and always does. And the apostle says: 'We see the one being humbled'...

Jesus [was humbled] through the suffering of death. He was humbled through the suffering of death, but he was crowned with "glory and honor." The humbling led to glory, and indeed it led to the greatest. I reason that "the sufferings of the present time are not worthy of the glory that is about to be revealed" (Rom 8:18). And those sufferings of Christ are those which his imitators suffer, having first suffered as he did. Great, therefore, is his glory. Even if it be a cross, even if it be death, if you see the goal of salvation and the Savior, what greatness is there? Not great is the glory of others. For indeed there are times when they had glory, and yet the glory departed even while they were living.

Thus also I have heard what is said in Isaiah: "and of his peace there is no limit" (Isa 9:7). "Justice and an abundance of peace rise in his days until the moon is taken away." Observe the peace that they caused to rise; for it holds until the completion, for nothing else signifies the taking away of the moon except the completion, when "the sun will be darkened and the moon will not give its light" (Matt 24:29). Peace is not in one nation, nor on earth alone; for he "made peace" through "the blood of his cross" (Eph 2:14), not only "the things on earth," but also "the things in the heavens."

6 Glory and splendor shall be laid upon him. Glory and splendor are laid upon him along with this great glory which exists in his salvation. And splendor consists of things and endeavors in which there is what is becoming. Works done from virtue become fittingly. Many things seem to men to be becoming, but they are not truly becoming; just as I have said concerning glory, that there are honors and dignities which are not such things as men think them to be, but they were supposed by them to be such. Splendor, therefore, they call—take the meaning from the literal sense, from history—such as are gladiators, and if they are small-spoken, they diminish the contests and the expenses from a small intention, and they seem to do what is becoming for the athlete, but they do it little, and they are called these "small-splendid" ones; for they are not found to be surpassing, being less than nothing in the becoming, compared to the gladiators before them. This, therefore, is called splendor, when in...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: True Magnificence vs. Vanity
english: Let there be a size that is appropriate. But it is most especially magnificence when it is for the sake of the appropriate itself, and not for the sake of anything else.

Let it be said: if one, being rich, spends great things on small matters and small celebrations, he is not magnificent. It is an excess of magnificence, just as we say that rashness is an excess of courage and impiety is an excess of piety. For example, if someone provides a feast for his drinking companions and spends as much as no one else spends at weddings, he is not magnificent. It happens for the sake of vainglory. But magnificence does not happen for the sake of vainglory.

Let us come from being led by the sensible things to the things about which the word is: the Savior worked the appropriate in great things. And the righteous man shows the appropriate in great things toward men. What is greater than saving the inhabited world, and making peace not only of the earthly things, but also of the heavenly things? What is greater than rectifying that by which the heavenly, the earthly, and the subterranean things bend the knee to the Savior for the glory of God the Father? This glory is magnificence, and it has a kinship with propriety. And concerning Him, the God, it is said: 'The Lord has reigned, He has put on propriety' (Ps 96:10). This propriety and magnificence are the same.

To whom did it befit to save the men, or he who did not have sin? He did not have sin, knowing that it is beautiful to abstain from sin, to have righteousness, that it is beautiful to not retaliate against one who insults, and not to defend those who behave wickedly. 'The one suffering,' He says, 'did not threaten' (Ps 21:1). Not only did He not do what was deserved, but He did not even threaten. A threat is a prior announcement of fearful things. But when it is no longer a prior announcement, but happens by the outcome, it is no longer a threat.

'Glory and magnificence You will lay upon him' (Ps 103:2). And it is good also to say 'You will lay upon.' In another text, this is also attributed to Him: for not only now when He arrived, did He begin to place this glory and this magnificence in the rational [things], but always and everywhere, as He was able, He did this. And the glory and magnificence through His arrival have become an addition, such as through the cross. For 'You will give him a blessing unto the age of ages' (Ps 21:7). Thus, as we have said concerning life: not so that He himself...
unto the age of ages
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Hope and Scientific Expectation
english: "of the Most High". See: it seems here to have been sent from the Father and the Holy Spirit. Others, however, read it this way, and this reading is better: "and the Lord, the Lord, has sent me; and his Spirit also has sent" (Ps 2:7); the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. The former version says this: that the Father and the Holy Spirit sent the Son. Each person receives the reading according to his own appropriate understanding, as has already been said. And here, therefore, there is a person of the Lord being spoken of here. And the Son is his image, "the character of his substance."

Concerning the one having taken on a face by the Savior and every righteous man, it is said: "rejoice him in joy with your face" (Ps 2:11), for when the Son and the Father come, and someone has seen the character immediately and the one of whom the character is: "he who has seen me has seen the Father" (Ps 2:12). Rejoicing happens by God and of his own face. And it is also possible to take it this way: "rejoice him in joy with your face." Therefore, this is said concerning every righteous man: for your face, through which "in image and likeness" (Gen 1:26) it has become, shall be revealed of him.

And I say: things that have happened, even if they are separate, often exist together with substances; for example, color: for the body is not first created, and then it is colored; it is created having been colored, and nevertheless we say that color is in certain things among those things that happen and un-happen. I added "in certain things," since among sensible things, it neither comes upon nor goes away from the snow; nor does moisture come upon or go away from water; for it is essential. Since, therefore, the rational is good from the beginning, it is not good in the same way as God; for it is not good according to substance, but according to a state and a disposition. Even if man has become "in image and likeness" (Gen 1:26), this thing which has form is separate, being cast off and being taken up. However, when God saves, every image will be destroyed. But this shall be revealed in the one having been saved.
For the king hopes in the Lord (Ps 20:7). This king hopes in the Lord. He hopes that there will be salvation for those for whom he has come to suffer. The end of the one striving is not in doubt.

But he hopes unchangeably; for 'in the mercy of the Most High he is not shaken' (Ps 56:3). Therefore his hope does not fall. And I offer a paradigm, though it is perhaps a violent one: no one hopes for things present. The healthy man does not hope to be healthy, nor the rich man to be rich. It is of things to come. Hope and expectation are the same. Expectation is a genus of hope; for hope is indeed the expectation of good things from God.

Of things to come, the former [the possible] has an existence such that it is able to happen or not to happen as it may turn out, but the latter [the certain] will certainly happen; for example, what I say scientifically, by way of an image: that after such a period there is an eclipse of the sun. Only the expert hopes for this; for the other person does not know at all whether it happens or does not happen. It is good to remind of this that there are four problems: two simple and two compound. Simple are 'that it is' and 'what it is.' Then compound are 'how it is' and 'why it is.'

It is therefore for the expert to expect these things which will certainly happen scientifically. For he knows both that an eclipse is, and what an eclipse is, namely a running-to-meet of the moon. And how it happens: that, when the moon becomes in opposition under the sun, an eclipse happens. Behold, the 'how it happens.' And the 'why it is so': because the sun, revolving, moves in varying intervals. And under the solar circle is that of the moon. Therefore it does not always happen in opposition. It is as if there are two circles. If it happens thus and again into the lower [one], the lower thing happening hides the upper. They say, therefore, that an eclipse is the opposition of the moon toward the sun.

It is therefore for the expert to know this unpassable expectation. And of things happening by chance, let them expect, I say, rain or good fortune. But many dispute these things. He says, therefore: 'Rejoice in him with joy; for the king hopes in the Lord' (Ps 21:14). The king is the one hoping. And his hope and expectation are unpassable. And he says: 'In the mercy of the Most High he shall not be shaken' (Ps 56:3). He being shown mercy by the Most High is not shaken; for then he is shaken, when the subjects are found unworthy of his kingship. And he abandons them, he turns away from them. And to hope is as to be persuaded by God, in this way.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Hand and the Right Hand of God
english: We receive according to the intention. 'Of the Most High' means to bless the rational things, just as also: 'Glory to God in the highest and on earth peace' (Luke 2:14). 'May your hand be found against all your enemies, and may your right hand find all those hating you' (Psalm 86:15). Just as also regarding the body there is a difference between the right and the hand; for the right is a hand, but not every hand is a right. We also have here a hand and a right named concerning God.

And concerning David the true, of the seed of David, in another psalm it is said: 'And he shall set his hand in the sea and his right in the rivers' (Psalm 146:7). And see that in the sea the hand is simply placed; for the right is not in the sea, but in his rivers. And again: 'Your hand has destroyed the nations' (Psalm 18:44). See: 'hand' is said many times, and also the military power of a king, and the hands of judges are the executioners. And the devil therefore knew that it is a harmful hand; for he did not say: 'Send your right', but 'your hand, and to grasp all that he has'. 'May your hand be found against all your enemies' (Psalm 86:15). Your hand will be revealed, the one punishing your enemies.

Thus also I hear of: 'But the face of the Lord, to those doing evil, to destroy their memorial from the earth' (Psalm 7:9). Those doing evil think that there is no providence, that there is no vengeance against whom they transgress. But when they receive experience of some wrongdoing, sometimes becoming aware, they see the face of God; and the face is thus: they recognized that God is within. And just as 'from the greatness and beauty of the creatures we observe the Creator by analogy', so from the greatness and the complexity of the administration the Judge is perceived. We have found therefore also Pharaoh despising, then being struck, grasping the understanding of God. For he says at one time: 'The Lord is righteous' (Exodus 9:16). He who says before this: 'I do not know the Lord' (Exodus 10:2), now confesses even to know Him and that He is righteous. 'But I...'

Even if the people are ungodly, if the face of God has become one doing evil in Pharaoh, the hand is found; for they must at some time know that He is a judge, even if not in this life, but when the time comes. Therefore it is said: 'May your hand be found.' 'May your right hand find.' But the hand is found against enemies, and the right hand finds those who hate. And those who hate may be slightly less evil than the enemies. Not every hater acts as an enemy, but every enemy hates.

And just as it was said regarding the sea, that the hand of God should be placed to make the surge and the salt-spray cease by driving them back, the right hand is in the rivers of the Savior—and these are those having a life according to the Spirit, 'from whom flow rivers of living water' (John 7:38). 'The rivers, Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voices' (Ps 68:2)—in this way the saving, lifting-up right hand of the Savior is found, according to what was said: 'The right of the Lord, lift me up; the right of the Lord has made strength; I shall not die, but I shall live' (Ps 118:8-9).

You have set them as a furnace of fire for the time of your face. Concerning the enemies alone can it be said of those being handed over to punishment. But if even concerning both, thus interpret what is written: See, those building upon the foundation, the Christ, if they are gold or silver, they are only burned, but they are not annihilated, nor are they consumed even if found by the fire (1 Cor 3:12-15). But if 'wood, hay, or straw,' they are annihilated and laid down like a furnace of fire, for they are like smoke. And the smoke is a follower of the beneficial energy of the fire.

Therefore, when wood and hay and straw are 'for the time of the face' of God—for it will be a time when a judge shall be shown, as it lies—those called wood and hay and straw do not be annihilated so as to no longer exist—and it is impossible to be annihilated in this way—but as they are hay, they are annihilated; for this fire of punishment does not work upon essence, but upon states and qualities. The fire consumes...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Divine Counsel and the Face of God
english: These are not creatures, but such states or dispositions. And teaching does the same: it takes the ignorant and makes him vanish, not as a man, but as an ignorant person; for it makes his ignorance vanish. In this way, righteousness makes the unrighteous vanish, not so that he no longer exists, but so that he no longer exists as unrighteous.

Lord, in your wrath confound them, and let fire devour them (Ps 53:3). Someone is confounded when he begins to waver and repent. And 'let fire devour them' means so that they no longer are such. 'You shall destroy their fruit from the earth and their seed from the sons of men' (Ps 53:10). The 'seed' is a homonym. When contrasted with fruit, it denotes the seed of a plant; but when contrasted with children, it is the seed of a man; for we have in the Scripture many times the 'seed' named after children. It is about the difference of the words that is now to be said.

This says: being upon the earth and having drawn near to the earth, they were stuck to it. Instead of the pure soul, the works of the flesh bore fruit. This is 'you shall destroy the fruit from the earth.' The earth is the good and beautiful thing, which, receiving the seed of Jesus that is cast, bears fruit. But the same earth, as a subject, is this one that bears thorns. And the receptive one is a rational substance of seeds. And from ourselves, this earth receives the difference.

'And their seed from the sons of men' (Ps 53:10). He sowed into the sons of men, not into the sons of God; for they are unfit for these. 'From the sons' therefore, 'of men you shall destroy their seed,' so that also the fitness toward the worthless fruit is lost. If someone has virtue by operation, the seed of wickedness is prevented, and the fitness and the power are [there], so that it seems to be destroyed.

'Because they turned to you for evil' (Ps 53:12), to you, having made them straight. Their choice turned toward the evil. You know that regarding sensible creations and idols, the one who has worked the evil work receives mockery, but the one who has done what is right receives praise. For it is said in Sirach: 'The work of a craftsman shall be praised' (Sir 38:33). ... if someone turns away from the 'according to the image.' How much then it reached to them, they judged evils toward you. 'They consulted plans' (Ps 53:12), which he would not be able...

To stand. And so that, having been led again by history from history—as if by a mere history, though I do not know if it is history—those who wished to build a tower, having the head up to the very limit, deliberated and were not able to stand. Indeed, they scattered. God perfects counsel when it is deliberated rightly and according to his will. He who pursues this 'does all things according to his counsel.' By this counsel, God brings a completion.

"You shall set them at their heels." It is often said of those concerning God that his body is [the church]; "you are the body of Christ," and in this body eyes, ears, and hands are found. Therefore, "you shall set" "them at their heels." You shall arrange these behind your body. This can be understood thus: the preceding things are called the face of God, and these created, sensible things are behind; for they are with him. Indeed, just as Moses at the end was not able to behold the face of God, God passes by with his glory and shows him the things behind. Indeed, he immediately wrote down the generation. Therefore, he shall set them at their heels; for the face is set toward the saints according to the prayer they offer up: "let your face shine upon us and we shall be saved." "In your remnants you will prepare your face." The remnants are the other saints besides those who "hate," those who were left over in the destruction. And it is well that it is "you will prepare" and not "you will give." It holds it ready so that everyone wishing to see it is able to see it.

"Be exalted, O Lord, in your power." We shall sing and indeed chant your mighty acts. For you do all these things powerfully. And after the beginning of the chanting, the power of God is praised: "Lord, the king shall rejoice in your power." The power that rejoices the king and performs all the things spoken of is exalted, not rising from a low place to a height, but no longer being thought of by men as lowly, but high as it is. And if we say, "I will exalt you, O Lord," we do not mean that we are lifting you up from the low to the height. To exalt is to confess him; that is the height. Therefore, he sings triumphantly—for power is spoken of a king alone, and of this king there are powers—things that can be done kingly. Toward the end, on behalf of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Psalm as the Voice of the Savior
english: The morning perception; a psalm of David. It is a spiritual day being made by the 'Sun of Righteousness,' about which much is laid down in the Scriptures, and especially in the New; 'as in a day,' he says, 'let us walk decently' (Ps 90:12). You know that even according to the literal sense, those doing something shameful do so in darkness, and especially then, when many good people were present. He who is, therefore, in ignorance of the existing good, is in darkness and does many things bringing shame. But when one is illumined by the light of the true one, 'walking in the day,' that is, progressing—for walking signifies progress—he does and thinks all things decently, nothing of those bringing shame.

The prophet Isaiah also presents this state, saying: 'My spirit cries out to you, O God, in the night' (Isa 26:9). This, therefore, is the morning perception; for even if we have illumination and the beginning of the day, we beg for the light to be present, so that the day may not fail, so that it may not be unable. 'Unto the end,' therefore, 'for the morning perception'; for having begun the day according to the perception of God, if the one perceiving remains in the same intention toward the one helping, he remains in that perception until the whole day; for if he perceives something in the beginning having only a little light, he perceives much more when it becomes midday. You find many such things lying in the Scriptures. God appeared to Abraham at no other time than at midday; for then the light had become at its peak. Moreover, the sun is at its zenith as if to be a shadowless thing to the air around us. But he says these things more allegorically, since even the literal sense leads to this.

This is also what the bride says to her own bridegroom: 'Tell me, whom my soul has loved, where do you graze and where do you gaze at midday?' (Song 3:1-4). At the beginning of the day, by which you graze, I have become. But I seek the midday time, when the light is at its peak. 'Where do you graze, where do you gaze?' so that being there as a companion with you, I may work the work; for I too want those sheep, which you graze, to graze. And the holy women who were shepherds, such as Rebekah, bring a symbol of such a state. 'For the' 'morning perception.' But who has the morning and the...

Is it possible to say at the beginning of the day, 'the night has passed, the day has approached'? For this reason also the women seeking Jesus, when he was crucified, did not see him at the midday hour (Matt 27:45), but from early morning. You know therefore also that the history concerning the Savior truly holds in general regarding everything significant, in which his works shine more than human things as light. We say that it happens in the morning time, when it takes hold of illumination so as to say: 'early I will stand before you and watch.' Such is also this: 'for you were darkness, but now in the light of the Lord' (Eph 5:8). 'Unto the end,' therefore, since the expected thing attained its end, which the economy of the Savior established and perfect virtue.

Listen then: this psalm is single-personed. That which says 'person' from the beginning until the end is the same. And there occur often in psalms and in prophecies shifts of persons, both of those speaking and toward what is being said and concerning what is being said; for everyone who speaks carries the person of the one announcing. And since he does not speak as it happens, but speaks to certain [people], there is also a second person: the one hearing the speaker and the matter concerning which he announces. The speaking [part] therefore is one person here.

And many things were taken from this psalm in the New Covenant, as if spoken from the person of the Savior, the one the psalm is said to be. Entirely this is so: 'the God, my God' (Ps 22:1); the Savior, encountering the cross, said this voice. And 'they divided my garments among themselves' (John 19:24) was also said by the Savior, having been said in the Gospels. And 'I will announce your name to my brothers' (Heb 2:26); Paul in the Hebrews wrote that this was said from the person of the Savior. Since, therefore, three testimonies lie here from the psalm, that the speaker is the person of the Savior, the whole psalm must be received as having been announced from his person.

And I say this necessarily—and I have also inserted it in those [works] concerning the Incarnation—since they always present to us words as if concerning the body of the Savior having existed, such as: 'but a body I have prepared for myself,' and: 'Christ suffering in the flesh for us,' we say that: if it were appropriate 'only': 'but only a body I have prepared for myself.' There is sometimes to wear more garments. If someone says concerning someone, 'look, I have a cloak, I have a tunic, a garment...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The distinction between reality and the concept of error
english: Let him not add 'only', for he is not forbidden to have the others. Again, let one have, bring, a shield and a sword and a helmet and a breastplate. If it is necessary to say that I have a shield, let him not add 'only', for it is not denied that he has the others. We have here said by him concerning the person: 'Save my soul from the sword.' Even if in another place he says, 'I have prepared a body for me', and there was no memory of the soul, and here there is a memory of the soul, and not yet that he says, 'Save my soul from the sword', he has spoken concerning the soul of himself alone.

2 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1). The name of the forsaking, when spoken literally, does not reveal becoming being in darkness. For the martyrs, indeed, were not forsaken, though they were cast into the boiling pot. But those who sacrifice, even if they suffer nothing, were forsaken. When someone asks not to be forsaken, he asks this so as not to fall from his purpose. It seems that falling into abandonment does not happen to one suffering nothing, but sometimes it happens to him through malice, as I said, of the sacrificers. Abandonment, therefore, is the turning away of God from the one being forsaken.

Which Saul experienced: 'You have not listened to me,' he says, 'nor even in sleep' (1 Samuel 28:6); and he went toward the medium. If ever, therefore, you see a rich Christian having everything well, but having haste toward astrologers or toward necromancers or toward such things, these were forsaken. And if you see a poor man having fallen from wealth, but possessing God, such as Job was (Job 1:1), this one was not forsaken.

Since, therefore, the Savior came to a cross, and it seems to men to be abandonment to fall by such a death, he says this toward their assumption: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1). Perhaps he also speaks of abandonment as if of his own body; for the Hebrews were a body to him before this. Therefore, that people was forsaken. And he speaks of his own abandonment, since he was their head. 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1); he demands the cause and the end of the abandonment, for what it is. 'For what reason have you forsaken me?'; he is demanding an end, not so that it might be known to him, but so that [it might be known] to the body.
His, to his own men. Far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions.

Here, so that we do not begin to mythologize, we are compelled to grasp a deeper theory. A thing and the concept of that thing are not the same. Many know the sensible things, but do not have a concept of them. It is a great thing to have a concept of realities. For in this way we separate a thing from the concept of the thing. And I mentioned color and appearance. But color is one thing and appearance is another, though they are inseparable from one another. Therefore, we separate them by concept. Color receives the more and the less. But appearance does not receive the more and the less, so that the color of the appearance is something different, even if it is never separated from it, even if it never exists without it. These things are said by those having a demonstration by subtraction. We subtract by concept this from that; it will not be sensed, it will not exist. When, therefore, we say that a line is a simple length, the sensible one is not simple. It certainly has width. But we subtract by concept.

I say: those who have transgressions that they will sense and that will exist do not know their concepts; for if they had known that it is harmful, that it turns toward destruction, they would not be acting them out. But there is having the concept of a transgression; for example, let it be a transgression being done against the law of God, such as to murder a man somehow. But when some judicial authority, serving the righteous law, puts to death the one worthy of death, just as Agag was murdered by Samuel (1 Sam 15:33), Elijah had the concept of a transgression, not a transgression, and Samuel. For the Savior says according to the man: for he himself is the one who has lost hope, the one saying these things: "Far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions" (Ps 38:13). Not "are far from my salvation"; for he did not know sin, he did not do it. But I have it by concept; I know what sin is. And therefore the words of transgressions were far from my salvation. Let my salvation not take a mixture so as to be darkened. For sometimes someone is saved because of something inherent in him as good; if it is evil, his salvation is diminished. Many, indeed, have often asked: if someone does many evils, but does a few goods, does he perish? To say that he perishes is a subtraction of the hope of the persons.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Manifestation of Mercy in Day and Night
english: It signifies. I have said many times toward this point: that the punishment is diminished. Let it be said: let more people have done injustice; from these, some did not do injustice, but showed mercy. His punishment is diminished, and these things have not been done to him sluggishly. When someone previously sinned, he has the works 'going before him to judgment'. They run ahead of him, leading him on to the judgment. But other sins follow. When someone, while acting, does good and a few sins, these follow. 'Likewise', he says, 'also the good works'. As I have said concerning sins, so also concerning good works I will say. However, no one having done good remains without fault above. From it, his punishment is diminished. And he who 'did not know sin nor did it' (1 John 3:5) and the words of the lapses, has far from himself his salvation; he has his salvation pure, neither sin nor lapse being left to it, but not even this, the word of a lapse.

3 O my God, I have cried days to you, and you do not listen, and night, and it does not come to my mind (Ps 142:2). The state of the life of men is diverse. It has some profitable aspects, and it has some dark aspects. And in these human things there are days, which are called 'day', and dark things, which are named 'night'. This therefore he says: and in the pleasant and bright things toward you I cry, and you listen, and in the night I do this, and it does not come to my mind; for after your departure and the dark things no longer being unclear, it has become manifest to me. He listens to our crying in the days; and at night, that is to say, 27 being in the dark state, we have him helping, and in the matter we have received knowledge that he helps; for this is: 'and at night, and it does not come to my mind'. And even if it were to others that this were the case, if this were 'the man before God', he was abandoned, this was not to his mind; for he came to this voluntarily: 'I will go to myself toward the mountain of myrrh' (Song of Solomon 1:4). Myrrh...

His body has journeyed to the mountain, because on behalf of all those who were myrrh-soaked, he accepted death. As for why it is so, let us learn from another psalm: that the dark things are ignorance and night; 'by day,' he says, 'the Lord commands his mercy, and by night he will make it known' (Ps 92:2).

When we clearly and readily see men being pitied, God has commanded his mercy by day. And 'by night' he 'will make it known'; for if you know that God also punishes and hands over in order to make his mercy known—for he does not hand over men to punishments crudely—in this night, the dark one, he will establish it, and the mercy of God will be made known. And by day he commands the mercy when his mercy is manifest, and by night; it is possible [to manifest it] through the darkness of the state of those being punished. However, even if they also despair, he himself will make known even in the night his mercy.

'And not unto oblivion of me' (Ps 16:11); I do not cry out in ignorance at night, I do not cry out in ignorance that you listen. 'But you dwell among the saints, O praise of Israel' (Ps 67:35). See what he says: you who dwell among the saints and are the praise of all those having pure hearts and seeing you—for such people are Israel—you have not abandoned me; for if you dwell among the saints, and the saints suffer something, they were not abandoned; for how could you be in them, and not simply, but the praise of Israel?

And it is also possible that 'but you dwell among the saints' means this: even if you have surrounded some with a pitiful death and it seems to [one] that you have withdrawn from me, yet in the saints, in those I teach, in those I think upon, you dwell. If you are in these, I have not been abandoned. And it is possible for the holy things to be taken also upon the blessed logical beings, and upon the holy men, and upon the mysteries of the kingdom of the heavens. For God, being present everywhere, is found in such things, and all such things are his temple, a multi-purpose temple. Therefore, [you] are a praise in Israel; for he truly...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Distinction of Universals and the Meaning of the Head
english: The visionary one, possessing the mind of Christ and seeing God within, is not troubled. You are the praise of Israel; 'in you we shall be praised all day long' (Ps 145:1). Our fathers hoped in you (Ps 22:4). Our fathers, having hoped in you, were heard 'and were not put to shame' (Ps 22:5); for always receiving their prayers, you brought them to a state of favor, even if they should die through afflictions. For that which hears them when they cry out is not that which makes them be outside of the afflictions, but that which is outside of the harm brought by the afflictions; thus also it was interpreted: 'do not bring us into temptation' (Matt 6:13). Even if the holy ones praying seem not to be heard, all the more they are heard, because by remaining in afflictions they are proven as athletes. For what a failure it would be if one praying should turn away from the afflictions? Furthermore, 'our fathers' is in the presence of the Savior; you know that he counts himself in many ways according to the human manner. They hoped, and you saved them; they cried out to you and were saved. Not by leading them into nothingness, but by overcoming through afflictions. 'They cried out to you.' Having cried out, they were saved. And the cry we take to be the stretched-out prayer; for we do not cry out with a laughing voice, for thought is the word of the soul, and voice is the sound of the inner man.

They hoped in you and were not put to shame. I am a worm and not a man (Job 25:6). The fathers, having cried out to you, were not put to shame; for they have attained that of which they expected, that of which they hoped. Here he teaches blindness: 'I am a worm and not a man' (Job 25:6). The man does not deny being a man, but [he teaches] that the man is such, since he does not even perceptually call himself a worm. I am not therefore that man about whom it is said: 'for where there is strife and jealousy among you, are you not men?' (Jas 3:16); but I have the same disposition toward them, drawing everything for their sake. And this too can be understood: since his body did not come from the casting of a man's seed, but from the mere matter taken from the womb, according to this he calls himself a worm; for the worm does not come from a union, but from simple matter. And here, from the simple matter subject to the female, the body arose for him. 'In it' indeed 'has been born' and 'has been born from it.' But the other bodies are said to be 'through women' [by way of] the washing...
