To receive. Since therefore this one did not have her birth from the seed of a man, it did not happen through her, but from her. A reproach of men and a disgrace of a people. I am a reproach not simply of men, but of the 'men'. All those who, looking at me, mocked me.

Some wish to falsely make the universal many times; for the universal is sometimes cut and becomes universal in another way. If I say, 'All men are mortal,' I say this universally. But if I say that 'all the grammarians,' I speak of certain men, and the universal has come from the grammarian, not from the man. 'All the diligent are righteous.' I do not say this that 'all men [are righteous].' So also here: not all those looking at him mocked him—for indeed the apostles, looking, did not mock him—but all those looking at him in this way as a disgrace of a people, as a reproach; for the others did not look at him in this way.

They spoke with lips, they moved the head. If they had spoken from the heart, they would not have moved the head. They spoke with lips to many. And it is not a wonder if they said these things concerning the one who suffered and was seen hanging. And God himself blames them, saying, 'This people honors me with their lips' (Ps 51:17). Therefore all the hypocrites, when they rejoice with the holy and the righteous, speak only with lips. And those who indeed boast grandly about the Savior were doing this: 'But [he said] the one destroying the temple and in three days building it up' (Mk 14:58).

Furthermore: to move the head? Perhaps even regarding history; they did this by cutting corners. And often the head signifies the mind. When anyone thus speaks against the Savior with lips without having seen him as he ought to be, he has a shaken mind, he has a wavering mind. Because the head signifies the mind: 'I have given their paths into [their] heads' (Ps 101:8), and this head did not possess anything of itself. 'And from thence he will come out, and your hands shall be upon your head; you will say, I have not sinned; for behold, I am judged against you' (Zech 10:5). And coming out of this life, you will have your deeds upon your head. And also: 'His pain shall return upon his head' (Job 34:31). But also praiseworthily: 'The eyes of the wise are in his head' (Prov 2:10). And he who, being not wise, has become wise, does not have [them] being carried around.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The progression from milk to spiritual strength
english: The eyes are moved to another place. Thus he says that the insight of the wise man is in his head according to Christ; for 'his head is the Christ' (Ps 22:1). He hoped in the Lord; let Him rescue him; let Him save him, because He wills him. Mockers say so. He said that men have also been accustomed to say such things concerning the righteous who are afflicted: 'If he is willed by Him, let Him save him'. And He will rescue him, not because they say this, but because he is willed by Him. He executes His own economy. He came to fulfill the will of the Father; for 'I have come down from heaven not to do my own will' (Jn 6:38). If therefore he does the will of his Father, He wills him.

For 'you are the one who burst me forth from the womb' (Ps 22:9). And regarding the history, something plausible might be said. Mary received 'the Holy Spirit coming upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowing her' (Lk 1:35). And just as God Himself forms bodies in the womb—as He formed Jeremiah and this body in the womb of Mary. Since therefore the same purity and cleanness were regarding the body, He Himself burst it forth from the womb. He did not do something great in this, but just as having formed Adam he showed him to be a man, so having formed him he brought him forth.

'My hope is from the breasts of my mother' (Ps 22:10). Even while still nursing you showed yourself, that you are my hope, having called the Magi—for while still an infant he mastered magic. In receiving milk I was not acting like an infant as other infants are ignorant of God, but I held hope in you.

'Upon you I was cast forth from the womb' (Ps 22:9). He, not having done sin nor having deceit in his heart, he who 'before knowing calls father and mother' (Ps 22:11) took 'the power of Damascus and the cunning of Samaria', he who 'before evil things came forth' chose 'the good'; for this shows that he neither did sin nor knew it. All men, after the choosing of the evil, choose the good. This one, before evil things came forth, chose the good. And this is that he is sinless, that he did not know sin, because even not according to childhood age he sinned, which things are not very difficult, yet they are presented as preceding virtue. This might also be said concerning every saint, through this same thing becoming so in life. He became...

“Behold the man, sent from God, his name John.” “And he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from the womb of his mother.” (Luke 1:13-15). Each of these is able to say these words to that: “Upon you I have called from the womb,” that is, “From the womb of my mother, my God you are.” But if concerning Samuel it is said: “And Samuel before knowing God” (1 Sam 3:7), it seems to contend with the things previously said. Therefore let us see more wisely how the word is the will of God.

Job says: “And even if I have eaten my morsel alone and have not shared with the orphan, except as a father guided them from the womb of my mother” (Job 29:15); for how was he able to provide for and care for orphans from the womb of a mother? Thus, therefore, I take it: a praiseworthy practice is a continuous progression; then the practice takes its beginning when the word is fulfilled. I am able, therefore, to say this: he says that I have done good things not after the evil things, but the word having been fulfilled in me, it began from the praiseworthy things; so that we may leave those things entirely, having been brought from elsewhere this state which is “pleasing to God.”

Since, therefore, there is another generation besides the one at hand, and that generation is in a certain way a mother, someone is torn from a womb, from this womb; for not by God alone can a man be brought from this womb into light. And from the breasts which are suitable with milk, which they receive, beginning now to be God-fearing, from those breasts they have hope toward God. And often milk signifies something else: “those turned away from milk; hope upon tribulation they received.” Not he, having ceased from milk just now and having been torn from the breasts of the mother, is able to receive hope upon tribulation.

Often the infant is said to be in relation to the perfect man, with the intermediate ages being passed over in silence: “When I was an infant, when I have become a man” (Ps 22:10, 71:17). And he has become a man not by a first and single change, but by many changes. Therefore, bearing the state of an infant and having a weaker disposition, he is given milk. But when he is able to become someone great, then he is torn from the milk and then he is prepared for athletic power, to pursue and achieve “tribulation upon tribulation and hope upon hope.” “For indeed, owing to be teachers because of the time, again you have need of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Unity of Essence and Distinction of Persons
english: To be taught, and you have become in need of milk, not of solid food. You see, that the middle parts were passed over, and the extremes were taken. Often indeed such things are said when the middle parts are passed over.

11 From the womb of my mother, my God, you are (Psalm 22:2). As from the womb of a mother, according to the former explanation from the womb of a mother, Job guides orphans; that is to say, from the womb of a mother, that is to say, from when I began to have knowledge, I served no other god, not my own womb, nor mammon. Or if it is the other, that in this way they descended having God, possessing God. But we do not say this about everyone, but about those who are proclaimed in the Scripture that they have never almost existed in sin, such as John and Jeremiah.

'For you are the one who burst me from the womb.' He said 'to burst' and according to the former probable thought that: since the member of Mary in which she gives birth did not have an exit, she gave birth through the cooperation of God. 'My hope is from the breasts of my mother.' I did not begin to hope after completion, but from the breasts of my mother I had hope in you. If it is understood concerning the holy, we say: the upper Jerusalem is the mother of the saints. From the breasts of this one hope is taken by those who hope, from those who have been discipled by them; for often the breast does not signify the member, but the milk itself.

'Upon you I was cast from the womb, from the womb of my mother, my God, you are' (Psalm 22:9). Upon you I was cast; not toward another was I cast, and then after that toward you. This is given, that from when I began to know piety, I perceived you, I served you. And according to the deeper meaning, that in this way I came to have God with me, just as John. The 'yet shall be filled'; for 'yet' is not said concerning that which has not existed at all.

12 Do not depart from me, for tribulation is near (Psalm 22:10). He speaks concerning the passion. And I need your presence. But when these things are said from the person of the one who was anthropized, it is not said privately toward the Father nor toward the Son, but toward God—one divinity of Father and Son—we say. If, therefore, we say that: 'Christ is the head of every man, but the head of Christ'—he did not say 'the Father', but 'God'; for he receives Christ now as High Priest and as King. Therefore, the head is the divinity.

For if 'the Father' has spoken, he excludes the Son; if 'the Son' has spoken, he overlooks the Father; for he has spoken 'God', since there is one divinity of Father and Son, and one God: indeed, God is one, but Father and Son are not one. Abraham and Isaac are one man, but one is the father and the other the son. Therefore, they are not one according to relation, but one according to essence.

For there is no helper. No one else is able to help. It can also be understood thus: 'for there is not'—I did not cast my care upon another helper. And it can also be: 'for there is no helper to me,' since all are against me, there is no one now, as far as human reasoning goes, who helps. Therefore, do not turn away from me. And it is possible also to say: not even an angel is able to help the one so far off. He does not dare to help because you, being greater than all, that is, the divinity, are present with him, and no one else is of such a kind as to help in this matter.

Many bulls have surrounded me, fattened oxen have enclosed me. Consequently, he speaks of the various factions of the Jews: Pharisees, Sadducees, and the others called Jewish Scribes; for these, in thinking greatly of these animals, are compared to them, especially since these animals are also tillers of the earth. And it is possible to call them bulls, and the fattened oxen are those acting as such, for example: 'the peoples labored in vain' (Ps 106:36)—these are the bulls. 'The kings of the earth stood up' (Ps 2:2). But we do not always perceive kings and rulers; for even a single king, being small and no longer having a kingdom, has been overtaken by the remaining Roman authority.

But Paul interpreted who the rulers are: those who became the cause of the Lord being crucified, of whom he says there are many wisdoms. And he says: 'If they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory' (Acts 4:28). If they had known that they were bringing about the destruction of their own [order], they would not have dared to do this. As we previously said prophetically regarding 'he who touches you touches the apple of his eye' (Zech 2:8): they, having laid hold of the Savior, destroyed themselves; and they rushed to kill him, thinking they would end his rule. On the contrary, it turned out for them: they themselves were destroyed. Fattened oxen have enclosed me; they opened upon me...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Scattering of the Disciples as Poured Water
english: Their mouth is like a roaring lion snatching and roaring. They were prepared to be like oxen. But they changed into ferocity, as if to open their mouth against me, according to the roaring lion; for then especially it harms greatly, when it roars. Therefore, their wildness and their mocking attitude against the Savior signifies—for he says, 'as a roaring lion, they opened their mouth' (Ps 35:23)—that they are no longer quiet, no longer intending to be quiet. These then, who seemed to be quiet by meditating on the law of God, were oxen, until they desired to open their mouth against me and to say: 'Crucify, crucify him; we have no king but Caesar' (Jn 19:15), according to the lion that was not satisfied, they have done this.

But was the passion not yet? All these things are said prophetically. Things that are possible before they exist, before they come into being by energy, in a state of possibility they both may come to be and may not. And no one has the power to guarantee whether it will happen or not; for toward both sides the weight is equal. But when someone having foreknowledge, or God himself, foreknows that of the possible things this shall be, as it happens to us, when it already exists; for upon the existing and the having happened already, we have the power to say which is true and which is false, whether it has happened or has not happened. But upon the future things, we do not have the power to say this, but only to say that the other will be, but not this. Since therefore even here a divine eye fore-grasped the future, it is no longer to him as possible things. Because of this he says: 'They laid hands on my hands and my feet.' If another were speaking, he would not have said this, but 'they will lay hands' or 'they will not lay hands.'

Like water I was poured out, and all my bones were scattered (Ps 22:14). He speaks of the scattering of the body here, of them, of the disciples, when all were scandalized and it is filled: 'all you will be scandalized' (Mt 26:56). And the hour will come when all you will flee, you will go to your own, and you will leave me alone (Jn 13:38). Just as the water that is being poured out.

It always runs and does not stand still; so also here, 'as water they were poured out' (Ps 22:14). He did not say 'they are being poured out,' for they do not remain in such a state always. What he says concerning himself, he says concerning himself regarding the body which is the sum of the faithful of the church. 'My bones'—the support of my body; for the apostles were more supportive than those who believe. And these were scattered. My heart became like wax melting in the midst of my belly (Ps 22:15); were his bones scattered? This occurred when the disciples were stumbled. This poured-out water, unless it becomes an obstacle, is always carried along. And the disciples, therefore, were scattered, as if they were poured-out water. When they were around him, they were gathered like river water, being a spring. But when they went out from him, it happened at a certain time, like the water that is poured out. And the water will stand one day; for it is not always carried along. So also the disturbance and the stumbling of the disciples will immediately cease, which has already happened.

My heart became like wax melting in the midst of my belly (Ps 22:15). The heart of this body, which is composed of the sum of those having believed, is the spiritual part. And these, therefore, became like melting wax, those who are the heart of him. However, even if the wax melted, it did not happen outside of his belly; for they are within his belly, so that they may be formed again. After the disturbance, indeed, those who had experienced it were shown again to be sons of the Savior. But what kind of disturbance? It was a passion extended for a little while, not so as to remain. And the melting of the wax does not happen always, but when it melts, it changes into some vessel or some other use, and again it is gathered, not far from the belly of the one producing this heart. But for what purpose the belly? It is the very power of the Savior, through which he forms and begets. If he again produces the procreators of the body, Paul, being of the body, was saying: 'through the gospel I have begotten you' (2 Cor 5:19). And: 'those whom...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Honey, Wax, and the Shell
english: I suffer pains until Christ is formed in you. They do not become outside of the belly; they are not orphaned. Moreover, 'has my heart become like melting wax?' (Psalm 51:7). I said that what is said about it according to the human might be said also about everything righteous. His heart, when it is not light, but has something material mixed in, melts. But toward the beautiful, the melting happens; for the melting wax does not become outside of the one having it. 'In the midst' therefore 'of my belly.'

Concerning the intelligible, different names signify the same thing. I call the sheep an intelligible thing which is under the true Shepherd. This sheep is also called light in another way. Indeed, having once been asked by a philosopher whether I have something to say from the Scripture that the soul is incorporeal, I said these things: every name of a body signifies only that alone by which it is called. For example, the sensible vine is nothing other than a vine, and the stone which is so named bodily is nothing other than a stone. But when many dissimilar things are spoken of concerning the same essence, it is evident that that essence is an intelligible one. So also we speak concerning God that He is incorporeal, since He is also named light and fire and spirit and spring. These things cannot be anything bodily, but according to an intention. And such intentions concern the intelligible.

If, therefore, the man or the soul is called light, and is also called a sheep and a plant—for it is indeed called both a plant and a sheep—it cannot bodily be all these things, so that it is an intelligible essence. If, therefore, you hear [it spoken] concerning the soul, you hear [it spoken] concerning a heart, an intellect, a belly, a spring; and for it is indeed called both a plant and a sheep, do not take it according to sensation. The vessel, therefore, of the soul, in which it receives spiritual nourishments, is called a belly. Furthermore, since it is also generative, one possesses this belly both as receiving nourishments and as giving birth. You know that the wax is a follower of the honey. The composition of the honey existed previously, and because of the honey [there is] the wax, not because of the wax [there is] the honey. And just as regarding a plant, the fruit is not because of the leaf, but the leaf is because of the fruit—for it is a protector of the fruit—so the wax is not something preceding, but a follower. If, therefore, the soul...

If it possesses the preceding virtues, it is honey. But if, along with those, it has something of matter mixed in, it is wax. For this reason, he says that the sinners melt like wax 'from the presence of fire'. Honey, however, is praiseworthy; it is a preceding substance, and it signifies sweetness. Just as to sweeten is to have a healing quality. Therefore, the 35 preceding things of the soul—which are good both in movements and in activities—resemble honey; but the second things, having something of the sensible and material mixed in, are wax.

Thus a man sometimes melts; the material sometimes falls away from the intellect and the heart, so that the mind no longer has anything entangled with it, but is entirely incorporeal, just as it surpassed the beginning. 'My strength has dried up like a shell' (Ps 101:7). My strength has cast off all moisture and all liquidity, as if it had been thrown aside like a shell. And it can be said otherwise: that which is muddy in us—and you know what that is—if it remains mud, it is dissolved by the passing of moisture. But when it takes on dryness and casts off all the moisture from without from the matter, it dries up according to the shell.

Each of the examples taken is taken according to something. This is often said; for if it were taken from everything, it would not be an example, but that very thing which we wish to show. Therefore, the shell is often mocked in this way: a vessel made of shell, if broken, they say, does not receive [liquid], nor can it be glued. I say in another way: that which is made from clay, when it is hardened by fire and a kiln, casts off the soft and the easily broken. Thus 'my strength' 'has dried up like a shell'. We take it in both ways: it no longer has any moisture, nor a muddy state. It can also be taken otherwise: it has cast off all bitterness from the much approaching affliction.

'And my tongue is stuck to my jaws' (Ps 118:13). It is the custom of Scripture to speak of the sticking of the tongue to the throat to mean silence. Since my sweet things are no longer present, and since those concerning me and my listeners are no longer present, lest I seem to carry the word in vain, I have been silent: 'my tongue is stuck to my throat'. But it is not stuck when we are conversing. Through the movement of the tongue, the word is carried forth. But when it is stuck to the throat, it is silence.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Body of Death and the Nature of Christ
english: But this silence does not come from the one being silent, but from those who are not succeeding as listeners. For he says in one of the prophets in Amos: 'Many are the fallen in every place, I will cast down silence' (Amos 8:11). If they flee, I cast down silence, so that I may not be honored to bring forth the teaching. And this indeed is one of the aids.

For instance, in Isaiah, he commands the clouds not to pour rain when the vine bears thorns instead of grapes, when, having remained [unfruitful] of the one watering in order to make righteousness, he makes iniquity. The grape is righteousness, and iniquity is the thorn. And since, being watered, he has not produced suitable fruits, but anxieties and worldly pleasures, he no longer speaks; for most often the wicked rub themselves against the words concerning virtue, learning to despise them. Sometimes, indeed, he endures the rain. And the rain and the voice mean the same thing here; for it reveals the divine teaching. Just as it no longer rains when good fruits are not being borne, so he no longer speaks nor converses when those listening have [thoughts] concerning other things. And this he speaks to men.

According to the intention of the teacher, the listeners are called disciples, but when he is the shepherd, they are sheep. And since they are no longer sheep nor men, but have become scorpions according to that which was said: 'Son of man, in the midst of scorpions you dwell' (Ezekiel 2:6). 'Many' therefore [is] 'the fallen in every place, I will cast down silence.' But it is read differently; for the wording is ambiguous. It is possible to take it thus: 'Many is the fallen in every place; I will cast down silence'; in every degree; for here the place signifies the degree, as also in others. Concerning Judas, indeed, it is said that he strayed from the place of the ministry which was entrusted to him. 'Many' therefore [is] 'the fallen in every place.' In every rank of those owing to be sober and vigilant and to speak of the things of virtue, 'the fallen is many,' except not all. 'I will cast down silence.' And it is possible also to divide the verse thus: 'Many is the fallen. In every place I will cast down silence.'

I do not only keep silent from the mystical things, but also from the ethical things; for in every place in which it was necessary to stand and be established and to be ready for a listening, a fall has occurred, and everywhere I cast down silence. Therefore, the sticking of the tongue to the [palate] signifies silence.

...the larynx. "If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my tongue cling to my larynx, if I do not remember you" (Psalm 137:1). If I do not remember you (Psalm 102:3), let me take silence. 16 And you have led me into the dust of death. Even if the voice were in the presence of Jesus, even if it were in the presence of the holy men who knew [God], having become like the wicked in the place of affliction, having been humbled—"you humbled us in a place of affliction" (Psalm 102:3). For the ones saying [this] are holy, as the conjunction signifies of the psalm. "Body of death" (Psalm 49:14) is said of that which surrounds us, and it is also said "dust of death" (Psalm 49:14). It is not "dust of death" in essence, but because those being forced from the life outside the body come into this, the body is named death. "Into the dust" therefore "of death you have led me" (Psalm 49:14). If it were life, it would have been led upward; for to be led up is to be brought into life and blessedness and an immortal state. Even if the Savior therefore says this, this: the light "into the dust of death you have led me" (Psalm 49:14). They descended into a body so that I might die on behalf of all, so that "by the grace of God above all" (1 Cor 15:10) I might taste "death."

Differently, therefore, from other men, it is said "dust of death" and "body of death" for the Savior; for if the body becomes death when the one using it sins, and Jesus did not sin, he came into the dust of death being able to undergo death. Therefore, those who stumble, saying that he is either merely a man or a heavenly body having endured [nothing], and attributing death to him, are mistaken. It is not so. Divinity, without such a thing, does not undergo death; for it is immortality. And just as for God, being light according to truth and essence, this is not darkness to him, so also in life there is no death. It is impossible for life to receive death. But he took upon himself something capable of undergoing death and division, and this is called death essential to it; for many other things are said of some things as not being essential to them, such as "garment, my footwear." In this way, the body is not essential. If, therefore, he says life receives death, he says receiving according to the outside. And I will say something paradoxical: just as the body receives death, so life vivifies the body. And this common life, the entanglement of the soul with the body, provides the vital movements to the body. How much more then, life itself or the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Dogs and the Assembly of Fornicators
english: A soul having been made alive by the preceding and blessed life; and it is good also to say: 'You have led me into the dust of death' (Ps 22:14). It was not He who descended into the dust of death, nor did the soul descend into the dust of death. But this happens to those being incarnated through wickedness.

Since He himself, for the sake of the economy and the salvation of all, received a body and God prepared a body for Him, He says: 'to be led by God into the dust of death.' But when men were, who confessing say: 'our belly has been joined to the earth' (Ps 79:10). When anyone does not nourish himself with the heavenly breads, the heavenly food, but the earthly—not the earthly sensible, but the opposite of the true bread—this food binds the soul being nourished to the matter, and it becomes a humiliation into the dust of the soul.

Here, however, the soul was not humiliated by Jesus into the dust, but was led by God. He came to this in an economical manner; for He had by no means committed sin, even though He was receptive; for if he were not receptive, he would not be praised at all. The abstaining therefore from sins brings praise to the one who has refrained when he was by nature prone to act.

Now, is dust and death the same thing? No; for He did not say: 'and into the dust of death You have led me.' If dust and death were the same, He would have said: 'into the dust of death You have led me'; but: 'into the dust of death.' The mortal body, which is able to be dissolved from the essence carrying it, is 'the dust of death.' And perhaps also by a second sense it is the dust of death, because it brings death to the flesh-loving soul.

'Many dogs have surrounded me; the body of the saints is dead'—for 'always they carry the death of Jesus in the body' (2 Cor 4:10). But the dead body does not have desires; for how is it possible? Is the mortal living? And it lives then when it is entwined with the soul. Then it has desires. Having died, it does not have desires. Having killed the members which are on the earth, it does not have desire.

Now, is the soul found to be the cause of sin? The soul of the one sinning is the cause of the sin; for nothing else is sin except the disobedience of a commandment, the transgression of a law. The body is not under a commandment in order that it might also transgress. The soul, transgressing, leads the body into...

To serve the sinful eyes; it is like an instrument. We do not say that the sword that sheds blood is a killer, but rather the one using it? For how is it possible? If we do not attribute sin or righteousness to a rational animal having a soul, do we attribute these things to the soulless body? By its own logic, the body is soulless.

'For many dogs have surrounded me, a company of fornicators has enclosed me, they have gripped my hands and my feet' (Psalm 22:17). Thus write: 'For many dogs have surrounded me, a company of fornicators has enclosed me,' because of this 'they have gripped my hands and my feet.' The 'for' is a causal conjunction. It is not attached to those following: 'You have led me into the pit of death,' 'for many dogs have surrounded me.' No, but: since 'many dogs have surrounded me and a company of fornicators has enclosed me,' because of this 'they have gripped my hands and my feet.' Humans remaining would not have done this.

But he says 'dogs' here to mean men having a dog-like manner. And he slanders the movements of the dog in many ways. They are entirely base toward filth. Thus, it has become customary to call the lawless and the women 'dogs' in this sense. Indeed, even the law also, suggesting this meaning, counted the dog along with the prostitute: 'You shall not substitute a dog for a change, nor a prostitute's hire' (Deuteronomy 23:18). He did not say a change of a donkey or a horse; for these changes were being brought into the house of the Lord.

And it is both shameless—'and the dogs are shameless to the soul'—and flattering. Therefore, men who have such movements are called dogs in judgment. These, then, surrounded the Savior. When they were sheep of God, they were at least outside the dog-like state. But when the people had become lost sheep, the loss did not turn them into non-existence, but into a dog-like, deficient, and scorpion-like state. And all this was said regarding the Hebrews: 'And all dogs are inward, knowing how to bark' (Psalm 22:16).

When the Israelites thought against the Savior, then they became dogs. And the being a 'company of fornicators' followed their becoming dogs; for when they were sheep, they were a divine flock. So they became dogs around me and a company of fornicators. Because of this they cast me to the cross; for the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Garments of the Word
english: The striking of the hands and feet of the Savior signifies nothing other than the cross. Therefore, consider the things just mentioned: is this assembly, which is not shameless for souls that are unbridled and lustful—those who lust through insults, who hate the one who made the resurrection of the dead and the sight of the blind and the healing of lepers, and who wish to subject them to death—is this not an assembly of fornicators? But there is a praiseworthy assembly.

They struck my hands and my feet (Psalm 22:16), and regarding this history, some have said this: many shepherds became like irrational animals, and it was never recorded that a fold was placed upon a fold, nor a dappled mare upon a dappled mare, nor a flock upon a shepherd, nor horses upon a horse-breeder. Only men placed rulers, and history brings many rulers, and those of good character and earnest mind, to be removed by those ruling. If they remained sheep, they would not have been led away. So when dogs became prevalent, and even humans became dog-like in manner, life, and disposition, they were called an 'assembly of fornicators.' To be 'fornicators' means to rise up against the benefactor, to stand up against the shepherd.

All my bones were numbered (Psalm 35:10). Whatever was in them, they subjected my bones to numbering, even though they were not countable. Therefore, it weaves together the mind. It also rises up according to history, the dividing of his garments and the casting of lots around the weaver's whole cloak (John 19:23-24). In a certain way, the word in the present Gospel text struggles; for the soldiers did this. But the soldiers were not Hebrews; for altogether a Jew was not permitted to serve in the military; but since they in a certain way became the cause of him being handed over to the soldiers as well, they apply the utterance to themselves.

But they understood me and had mercy on me (Psalm 35:11). How? Having understood, they had mercy on me? — Having perceived, they saw the scattering of my bones. And 'to show/pity' is often said regarding the fault-finders.

And the powers of his teaching can perhaps be called bones. 'They divided my garments among themselves' (Psalm 22:18). For this reason, we no longer wish to remain here regarding the historical [sense]; for it has already been said that even the soldiers divided them into four parts, having made them, and cast lots upon the tunic woven from top to bottom of all.

I say: just as the sum of the believers was called the body of Christ according to a certain figure, as the apostolic testimonies signified, and we used to say that the joints of this body are the useful parts, so again we say that this very God-breathed Scripture is the body of the Savior, but the useful meanings of this body are the contemplations concerning the other superior meanings. And the words are garments; for the Word according to the understanding is clothed by the words.

Even if, therefore, I have enumerated its bones, they were not divided; they only saw them as if they were not; for if they had seen them as they are, they would have been empowered in them and would have made them their own, as it is said: 'All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like you?' (Psalm 35:9). For these are not sensible bones that say this.

Therefore, the garments of the Word are divided by all those who hold different opinions, those who hold false doctrines. They drag the words toward what they want and make them their own, such as: 'The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways' (Proverbs 8:22). The word is a garment of the 40th contemplation. The Arians drag it as they wish and consider it their own. The ecclesiastics, again, receive it as being worn by Wisdom who says this, and others receive others. And it is possible to find the same words almost by all the heterodox being handled differently and differently. So they divided them, they stripped the words of the Word and dragged them naked of the Word toward their own will. 'And upon my clothing they cast lots' (Psalm 22:18). No one, having possessed any lot, casts it upon it, but when he is able, he casts something into many...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Single Divine Operation and Christ's Victory over Death
english: They come as partners, and concerning them a lot is cast. If someone leaves an only-begotten son and appoints him as successor, all the things belonging to the deceased are his, and no lot is cast. But when many come upon the true heir saying, 'We too are children of him,' a division of his garments occurs. But they are not divided, only the words; for the same word does not lie with the same mind differently according to heretics. Each one pulls the word toward his own mindset and will. Therefore, the diligent and truly faithful one possesses the whole robe of Jesus, not having it torn; so he does not cast a lot; the whole is his. For even if they cast a lot and use the words, they do not become his, they do not become masters of them; for a wise man according to Christ comes into the midst and shows that what he thinks is his is not his.

And what about garments and clothing? The garments together are called clothing, but each one by itself is not called clothing. And just as many sheep gathered together at once are called a flock, but each one is not called a flock, and people who have come together into one are called a people, but each one is not called a people. 20 'But You, Lord, do not delay Your help' (Psalm 70:5). If they exerted themselves in these things, even if they bring tribulation upon me, I have entreated You not to turn away, 'for tribulation is near' (Psalm 70:6). And the tribulation, if it has become near from those surrounding me like calves and bulls, from those scattering my bones, from those becoming causes to me such that my tongue is stuck to my throat, but You, do not delay Your help. Immediately then the resurrection of the Savior occurred, and immediately those who were scandalized turned back to Him. So the help has not been far.

And these things, according to the intention of man, Jesus says: 'Do not delay Your help.' The help which is required happens from no one else but from God. And I said that, when 'God' is said, it does not always signify the Father, separating the Son, nor the Son dividing from the Father; for the divinity is one. And because it is thus, we call the help the resurrection from the dead. Where it is said that He has delivered Himself and has been raised, and where the Father is said to be...

He has given [life] and has raised [him], from which it is shown that the one resurrection and the one work being done by Father and Son happens through only one divine energy. Even if the Father does [it], as God working this, he works it; even if the Son, he does this as God.

20 Pay attention to my understanding. For if you pay attention to my understanding, the help is not far from me, but being near, it worked; for he says previously these things concerning the men: for he did not come so that previously he himself might die and rise, but through others. 'By the grace of God he was raised above all death' (Rom 6:9). All died on behalf of them. This one by the grace of God was raised above all. 'The love of God holds us together, judging this thing to be that if one died on behalf of all, then all died' (Rom 6:10), so that those having died might no longer be dead, 'but live by that one who died on behalf of them and rose' (Rom 6:10). Some human power is able to give [life] on behalf of another, and some reproach is able to be received on behalf of another, and a rebuke. But death, no one is able to receive on behalf of another. And behold: he was raised alone, he was not swallowed by it, nor did it consume him. But he who is being swallowed by death swallows it himself. 'Death, having prevailed, swallowed [up]' (1 Cor 15:55). This one swallowed death, the one having been laid under it. And since Jesus 'did not commit sin,' and through the seizing of sin death is swallowed and swallows the one sinning—therefore he was raised above all; indeed, he was raised. And he has given the reason: 'so that through death he might render powerless the one having the power of death' (Heb 2:14). In death he destroyed death.

28 Save my soul from the sword (Ps 54:23). Jesus is also the one saying this verse, and he is able to say this also concerning his own soul, which he had the power to cast out and take back, and concerning every soul made his own. Just as it is said each of the saints is not merely a man anymore, but a man of God, so a soul desiring to please God is not merely a soul anymore, but a soul of God. Thus, in either way, he says these things concerning his own soul and that which he received, and concerning every soul made his own. And the sword sometimes signifies punishment; as if it is said: 'in the sword all sinful people of the people shall perish'; for it has never happened in history.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Sword and the Unity of the Person
english: So that the whole people might be cut down by the sword. Some of them died, but not all. He says this: all sinners will be tested by execution. He sometimes reveals both an evil power and the devil himself; for when it is said regarding Mary, 'and a sword will pierce your own soul' (Luke 2:35), he speaks of the adversary. When he casts thoughts upon someone or wishes to cast them, if that soul does not receive them, they pass through it, like the fifth arrow of the Psalm (Ps 42:5) when it is sent not at the mark, passing through the archer.

He cast [it] into Judas; he acted against Judas. He did not secure himself, he did not guard against it: 'do not give place to the devil' (Eph 5:11), and he did not pass it by; for it entered into him. And he who says, 'I did not know the evil one passing away from me,' had the sword passing through. To not know here does not mean ignorance, but not having been tested. Thus, even those who despise to say something, even if it is present, even if it is, say: 'I do not know.'

Regarding 'save': the 'save' certainly means all this: 'save me, having seized me and being under it.' Save me so that I may not suffer anything from it. Regarding: who is speaking? They wish to say this: 'if he speaks about the soul himself, who is the one speaking? It is a body that is speaking.' But those saying such things stumble.

In composite things, each of those in the composition is said of the whole composition. 'Your whole spirit and soul and body.' Is the spirit something else from the men, and the soul something else, and the body? Therefore they posit [them as separate]. We often speak about a city, saying it has a bad city, a bad ruler, a bad people, bad laws, not right ones. What is the city apart from the bad rulers, the counselors, and the people? And just as we speak about the human body, saying a head of the body, a face of the body, a hand of the body, feet—is the body something other than these, while each is something else beside itself? Those who have done the logical things well understand these things easily. See: everything having sensation and soul is an animal, and I say that the animal is not a man, nor a horse, nor an ox. But I say this: that man is not the whole genus, nor is he the whole animal. And I say each...
composite human
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Humiliation and Exaltation of the People and the Son
english: He has souls; but this one he has as unique, for it is unshakeable. And I say unshakeable in this way: not being turned; for that which is called unshakeable in a completed sense signifies the unchangeable. When I say that the righteous man is not turned toward injustice, I say the righteous is unshakeable in the measure that he possesses righteousness; for the unshakeable does not turn. But not everything that does not turn is unshakeable.

Therefore, this soul is unique to him among the others, because it alone possesses the capacity to be always with him. No reasoning, no impulse, no disturbance can separate it; for even if it is disturbed, the disturbance stands only as a pre-passion. For this was shown through the 'now', seeing that the 'now' does not signify continuous time, but the significant moment, the non-existent time. All time has three divisions, but this 'now' has none, for it is the boundary of time.

"He began to be terrified and to be in anguish" (Ps 22:16). Until the beginning, one cannot receive a pre-passion instead of cowardice; for pre-passion is a testing of nature, not making a quality bad or serious, unless it takes on the following things so that it is no longer a pre-passion. Often these things have been distinguished for us as being four: pre-passion alone releases an inclination, it does not subject one to an inclination; but passion is with a moderate inclination; and the disposition is then malice; and much more is the action once taken up.

"Save me from the mouth of the lion" (Ps 22:20). Here he can also call the devil a "lion", for he attacked in the time of the passion. Indeed, when it was said in the forty-day temptation that "the devil departed from him", it is adjacent in the Gospel to "until a time" (Lk 22:36). Then again, it came when the passion was. And since I was saying that the attacks are brought to the man of the Savior himself and to his own, when Peter says or the Savior says to Peter, "Behold, Satan has demanded you" (Lk 22:31), in a way he wanted to devour the members of the Savior by attacking against the Savior. He says, therefore, "Save me from the mouth of the lion". He can also call that people a "lion", for "it became [said] my heritage is to me like a lion in the thicket" (Ps 22:10). May I not suffer these things which they want to dispose me toward. He says these things because every rational essence, even if it is perfect, needs the alliance from God. "Save me from the mouth of the lion."

And 'from the horns of the unicorns my humiliation' he can say here, referring to the multitude of the Jews, the people of Israel; for he said in Jeremiah: 'I have forsaken my house, I have left my inheritance. My inheritance became to me like a lion in a forest' (Jeremiah 12:7). Having been a people whom I placed in Paradise, where there was much fruit, when they had turned into wildness, then consequently they nest in fruitless trees—for the forest is nothing other than a place of fruitless trees. Therefore, they encamp there. And my inheritance, which I had so that it might be a people and a portion of the Lord, was so provoked against me as to be thrown upon a lion, not a lion being tamed—for often lions come into human places being tamed—but as in a forest, as a wild beast.

And it can also be said concerning the devil; for we say this also, that after the temptation in the wilderness it is said: 'He has departed for a time.' 'And from the horns of the unicorns my humiliation' (Psalm 92:10). The unicorn is a strong animal. It is not subject to man, it is not tamed by man. 'From the horns' therefore, 'the humiliation of the unicorns,' the cross and death saying his own humiliation. 'He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross' (Philippians 2:8). My humiliation, therefore, then, flows from these unicorns—and these are also some evil enemies—then, when I rise from the dead; for 'the kings of the earth and the rulers were gathered together' to surround him with death. Then God delivers him from his humiliation; he rises from the dead. And all these things are spoken concerning the man.

Therefore, without delay he immediately brought forward: 'I will declare your name to my brothers' (Acts 13:34). 'I will proclaim your name to my brothers; and again: behold, I will be trusting in him, behold, I and the children whom God has given to me.' And again: 'Wherefore he ought to have been made like his brothers in all things' (Hebrews 2:17). Not only according to the body, but according to all things. According to his divinity, the only-begotten Son of God does not have a brother; for if he had a brother, he would not be only-begotten. But to have brothers is opposed to being an only-begotten one. The only-begotten has no brothers. The one having brothers is not only-begotten.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Firstborn and the Unicorn
english: Only-begotten. He says 'brothers' referring to the apostles and all those from the circumcision who believed in him; for many believed from among the Jews. And the twelve and the seventy were among them. According to the flesh, therefore, those were his brothers.

But they become his brothers again according to the Spirit, those partaking of the 'spirit of adoption' (Rom 8:15); for if 'he who does righteousness is born of God' (1 John 5:1) and 'he who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God' (1 John 5:1), some are sons of God. These, however, are brothers again, not only-begotten, not according to the divinity, but according to the one who became man. The apostle, therefore, using the word in this way, applied it to the man: 'for which reason he is not ashamed to call them his brothers'; for he left nothing of what is required for a man to be a man. Since if he does not have all things, he is not a man.

I have said many times that there are certain mixtures, like hydromel. If water is removed, it is only honey; or even if it is mixed with something else, it is not hydromel. If, therefore, he had body only, he would not have been made like the brothers in all things; for the appetitive soul is irrational. A soul without intellect is irrational, not even subsisting as a principle, unless it be in the composition; for the appetitive souls are joined to the bodies of which they are souls. Therefore, 'in all things he was made like the brothers', not in some things, and not in others.

The apostle says again: 'so as to be the firstborn among many brothers, whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to them' (Rom 8:29). You see that being the firstborn among many brothers was a matter of acquisition, when he became man, when he took upon himself to be a man from among brothers. But if he says 'firstborn' here, say 'more honorable'. And so also the 'church of the firstborn' (Heb 12:23) is so named. It is not possible for all to be firstborn, yet it is possible for all to be honorable. For this reason also Jacob demanded the birthright (Gen 25:31) from Esau, the honor of the firstborn. Therefore, firstborn is in...

He is like many brothers, as the 'firstborn from the dead' (Colossians 1:18). He is the first of every dead person; for when he rises, someone else is able to rise. Therefore he says to proclaim the name of the Father, that is, to make it manifest. And when they know the Father and know the name of the Father, then they have the knowledge of the Son being brought in together with it; for these things bring in one another successively. And I speak according to being and according to knowledge. It is impossible for one knowing one thing to not know the rest regarding that thing.

'And from the horns of the unicorns.' It is also called a rhinoceros. And in the eighteenth Psalm this is so: 'And the beloved as a son of unicorns' (Psalm 18:25). This animal is said to have a size not less than a large calf. But it is very coiled, it is thick, and it has a horn above the nose, and the animal is very strong, and when it is angry, its horn becomes so much the strongest as to be harder than an elephant's. But when it is not angry, it is soft as flesh. And sometimes, when there is heat, it throws large stones so that it may place itself in that place, being cool. This animal, then, as I have said, when having become angry, has the horn very hard. But when being calm, it does not have it.

Therefore they are tested to take its horn; for it is precious. Since, then, they want such a thing, they do not shoot at it without foresight; it does not fall to a beast, nor is it wounded by a polecat or any other. But they throw at it with a bow. So when it is angry, then they shoot at it with the dart. But: toward what kind of person do we take it? Toward Christ? —if it be taken praiseworthily. And it is taken praiseworthily in the eighteenth Psalm: 'And the beloved as a son of unicorns' (Psalm 18:25). It signifies having an only-begotten kingdom. The kingdom of the Savior, therefore, does not have duality, but is simple, like the presence of God. And because of this, it is called one-horned. But when it is taken mockingly, it is taken because of the wildness, not because of the horn. Some say as in...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Supremacy of the Fear of the Lord
english: The phrase 'from the horns of the single-horned ones' is a mystery, for the upper ends of the cross had the shape of horns. 'I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise' (Ps 22:22). He who sings to God in the midst of the assembly is one who offers hymns with boldness and decorum. It is necessary for the one singing to God to be righteous; for 'praise is fitting for the upright' (Ps 33:1), and 'there is no beautiful praise in the mouth of a sinner' (Ps 68:3).

Just as we say that the divine Word is spoken 'in authority'—when someone teaches about temperance while being temperate, he has the Word in authority; but if he is uncontrolled and filthy, he does not bring it forth fully. His conscience trips him up. Just as the one who carries out appropriate works and has the practical life conforming to the contemplative life has the Word in authority, so the one who sings to God in the midst of the assembly is one who lacks no hesitation. For example, if one teaches about temperance so that he may be temperate, then he sings to God in the midst of the assembly; likewise, one teaching about almsgiving should be such, and one speaking about courage should be such. Therefore, when you see someone speaking about courage while being a coward, he is not doing this in the midst of the assembly. For the 'midst' signifies boldness, and this is to be learned from another psalm: 'He did not dwell in the midst of my house, practicing arrogance' (Ps 129:6). No one wished to appear arrogant to me. He did this in a corner, withdrawing, [of] the red ones. Thus, the Savior sings to the Father in the midst of the assembly. And when I say the Father, listen to the Son as well. He sings to God, and the divinity is one of Father and Son.

'You who fear the Lord, praise Him' (Ps 115:11). It is not the one who happens to praise God, but the one having fear toward Him. But not every fear is of God; for there is a fear of punishment. This is not of God. Furthermore, regarding 'perfection' toward God, 'love casts out fear' (1 John 4:18). The one having love toward God from all heart and all mind does not have a passive fear. In this way, the disciples of Jesus were called by the Savior to be outside of passive fear, saying, 'Do not fear those who kill the body' (Matt 10:28). And those saying, 'The Lord is my helper, I will not fear; what can man do to me?' (Ps 118:6). They cast out the passive fear; for the fear of God is not passive, it is not of punishment, but...

Regarding reverence. 'The fear of the Lord surpassed all things' (Ps 33:8); nothing is second to it, not even love itself. And: 'There is no deficiency to those fearing him' (Ps 34:9). 'All the seed of Jacob, glorify him' (Ps 115:12). It can also be said explicitly that: since that people from the patriarchs was called to hymn and to serve God, it appropriately stands over all to do this.

For since many have become sinners from them, we take 'all the seed of Jacob' not to mean the evil one—for it was said concerning him: 'evil seed'—but when it is outside of all wickedness, as he himself is whose seed it is. And we take here Jacob the patriarch and say that: since this one has become a wrestler and from this deed he received the appellation, all those wrestling, being surrounded by evil, of the opposing powers, of the evil adversaries, these are Jacob; for in his exploits Hosea arranged this, saying: 'In the womb he wrestled with his brother and prevailed with God and was able' (Hos 12:4). To prevail with God and to be able is a great exploit. Thus indeed he counted the one who wrestled with his brother in the womb.

And the Savior was also said in Isaiah: 'Jacob my servant, I will take hold of him' (Isa 41:9). And Matthew said that this word is fulfilled by Christ. 'Let all the seed of Israel fear him' (Ps 115:12). Not passive fear is glory, but the fear of God, which after much [effort] comes to those who have strived to have it. 'Son, if receiving the word of my commandment you hide it with yourself, your ear will obey wisdom, but if you direct your heart toward understanding' (Prov 2:1). And shortly after: 'And if you seek it as silver and as treasures you search for it, then you will understand the fear of the Lord' (Prov 2:4-5). Behold, after many rectitudes and perfect virtues. But how we say simply: if you know the exploits and the excellences and the achievements of Elisha, you will see what kind of person the one fearing the Lord is, not a random one.

All the seed of Jacob, glorify him (Ps 115:12), because he did not make nothing of nor disregarded the prayer of the poor. Here he calls the Savior who came among us 'poor' because he became poor for our sake. And just as it did not become a curse simply, but...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Paraclete and the Prayer of the Poor
english: “so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations”—and a blessing that is productive is not, in reality, a curse. The productive things of the good are good. The productive things of those pleasing to God are themselves pleasing to God. And the name of the curse signifies the cross, just as the apostle himself, having written this voice, demonstrated. He said: “For it is written: cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree” (Gal 3:13), and just as he became dead, in order to show and make the dead alive, and he became [dead] in death, in order to destroy death and to set free those held by it; so also he became poor, in order that through his poverty they might become rich for whom the poor became [poor].

And behold the difference: “know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that being rich he became poor for your sakes” (2 Cor 8:9). To become poor for us, is not to be rich for us; for it has not been said to become rich just as it has been said to become poor, but “being rich he became poor for your sakes.” And just as having the form of God and being in the form of God, having taken the form of a slave of God, he did not cast away the form of God, so he, becoming poor for the sake of others, did not cast away the wealth; for we do not say of his wealth as if it were the virtues of holy men; for he himself is the provider of the virtues, he is the one in whose participation the virtues exist. Thus, remaining rich, he became poor. But he became poor for the sake of others, so that they might become rich.

And when we remain in the prior poverty and do not hasten to take up that wealth which his poverty grants, that which is for us, he remains poor; for if for the sake of others, so that they might become rich, he became poor, when they become rich, he is no longer poor. He became poor by becoming flesh. When we behold “his glory, a glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), we have become rich from the poor, and he himself was shown to be rich from the poor, he did not become rich. For his glory has become manifest, that “as an only-begotten” he is “from the Father, full of grace and truth.” “He did not disregard nor make void the prayer of the poor”; for he was interceding for the salvation of all. “And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the...”

righteous, so that he might forgive us our sins. Truly, insofar as we are in sins, we have him as a Paraclete. But when we cease from having sins, he no longer pleads at all concerning this. Therefore also he is able to save to the full those who approach God through him, always living to intercede for them.

If he intercedes for them so that they may live, when they live, he no longer brings up this prayer concerning them, but rather pleads concerning its preservation, concerning its remaining. This, therefore, the prayer of the poor, he neither despised nor disregarded the one bringing it. 'Nor did he turn his face away.' A person turns his face away from one praying when God is not favorable, but also when he prevents the prayer from being sent up. He prevented Jeremiah at one time from praying for the people. Why? For ambassadors and Paracletes ought to bring an embassy for those having repented and no longer sinning.

For he says: 'Do you not see what they are doing? Their fathers' [they] searched through, being filled with idolatry, and they do not remain. So also the face of Samuel was turned away, when he heard: 'How long will you grieve over Saul, while I have rejected him?' (1 Sam 15:11). But the face has boldness for those interceding, if those for whom they intercede run together with his will. For he neither despised nor disregarded the prayer of the poor, nor did he turn his face away from me.

The poor man himself says concerning himself. A change of face has occurred. The writing Spirit says: 'He neither despised nor disregarded the prayer of the poor.' Then that same poor man, whose prayer was not loathed, did not turn away, says: 'Nor did he turn his face away from me, and in my crying out to him, he heard me.' And in my crying out to him, he heard me. Great is it to say this. This is not said in mere words, but when it is shown that the thing for which he prayed exists.

And so this happened: 'My praise shall be in you in a great congregation' (Ps 18:3). Behold, the work of the cry I have accomplished; I have established it as a congregation of peace for me, 'glorious, having neither blemish nor wrinkle or anything of this kind' (Eph 5:27). My praise, therefore, is this, that he accomplished this. Just as indeed not...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Perpetual Seeking of Wisdom and God
english: It is a great thing to praise the perfect one in whom wisdom is spoken, rather than to milk; thus it is not a great thing for one having an excessive life. He is not praised for such things, nor for other deeds, but for having made the whole church—and not just any, but a great one—stand upright. And this is possible: my standing upright is a great praise to the church.

"My praise is from you; in a great church I will confess to you; I will pay my vows in the presence of those who fear him" (Ps 50:23-24). Vows are paid regarding those who are thankful and who have already acted. A prayer sent up to God is called a petition. But when it is sent up with a confession, saying, "if these things shall be to me, I will pay these," this prayer is a supplication and a vow. Even Jacob said: "If God will give me bread to eat, of all that he gives me, I will give a tenth." This is a vow. No one, having prayed for something and not having received it in due time, will say, "I will pay my vows," or "in the presence of those who fear him"; rather, [he says it] so that they may be benefited, for they themselves will also learn the vows which they pray to pay. And it is possible [to do it] "in the presence of those who fear," not in addition to those sacrificing—for those sacrificing cannot know which thanksgiving has been fulfilled or which vow has been paid—but in addition to those who fear.

"The poor shall eat and be satisfied" (Ps 106:9). "Being rich," he has become poor because of our poverty. Therefore, he not only freed these poor people for whose sake he suffered what he has said, but he also showed them being satisfied from those who were starving; for he is indeed the "bread of life," and his flesh is incorruptible food and his blood is a divine drink. When therefore the rich, having become from the poor through his poverty, partake of these, they eat and are satisfied. Similar to this is: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied" (Matt 5:6); not ceasing to eat the bread of life, but in chewing and having it sensuously. To him who is to be formed, that which is said in the Wisdom of Sirach seems to oppose; for Wisdom says there: "he who eats shall hunger again, and he who drinks with me shall thirst again." It does not mean the unfulfilling here, but the craving of the drink and the...

The one eating wisdom is never satisfied, but is always in a state of hunger. And the one drinking it as a divine water or wine harvested from the true vine thirsts again; that is, he always desires. Therefore, the desire to place it again and to crave it is to be filled.

The difference between a pauper and a needy person has been said many times: he who has come from wealth into poverty, that one is called a pauper. And you have this from the Scripture: 'the rich have become poor and have gone hungry' (Ps 34:10). But a needy person is one among the needy, who always provides the necessities while toiling. Thus they differ by another and another thought, since they are alike insofar as they are left behind from the abundance of those who crave.

And those who seek Him will praise the Lord, as it was said concerning wisdom, because being drunk, it prepares those who have drunk to thirst again; and divine food—for food is also the breathing of air. When we live, we breathe; we do not live by having been breathed into. Thus it is with the divine food and the holy drink: in being approached and being supplied, it prepares the benefit. And those who seek Him will praise the Lord.

I say: God is always in the state of being sought; for even if someone finds Him, it has been said: 'He is found by those seeking Him' (Ps 105:4). There is, therefore, a certain way of being always in the state of seeking. Even if Eunomius rages, it is possible to find Him according to partial knowledge and according to partial prophecy, and again, He is in the state of being sought. And the seeking of God itself is beneficial. To be entirely in the state of seeking God is perfection.

Even if Eunomius rages, saying that we know God as He knows Himself. He who knows God as He knows Himself, God knows, not by parts; and those who have said, 'we know by parts,' are lying. He who knows God as He knows Himself is not in the state of seeking Him, for he had him and has him. Therefore, those thinking thus speak lies. When, therefore, we know Him in the age to come, or after all the ages in the desired end, we know Him as it is possible.

'Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet been made manifest what we shall be. We know that when He is revealed, we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is' (1 John 3:2). Not as He is, but as it is to know in perfection. However, even if...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Knowledge of God
english: As far as is possible for his nature and generation to present himself for discovery, we have grasped what is known of him, 'because the known of God is manifest in him' (Rom 1:20), not simply himself, but the known. We recognize him: that he is creator, that he is providential, that he is unshakeable, and unchangeable. And I wish to grasp a logical theorem.

Demonstrations are scientific theories; for there are two kinds of syllogisms—forgive me now for remembering the eristic and the sophistic—the dialectical is among the more glorious, which they call the argumentative. This demonstration comes from what seems to men, not from the nature of things. The demonstrative [one] from these things themselves is not from the judgment of men, but from the existence of the subjects concerning which we wish to take scientific theory. It is therefore impossible for an irrefutable demonstration to come from opinions.

Demonstrations are from assertions; for if I wish to demonstrate that man is a rational being, I say something: he is not without soul; for many other things are without soul, and the irrational. I must therefore demonstrate this: man is receptive of sciences. Everything receptive of sciences is rational. Therefore, man is rational.

And even if we have knowledge concerning God, even if it were perfect, we have it from assertions, saying that he is incorporeal. But the incorporeal is an assertion of a body [the absence of body]. It is immortality, without beginning, and unchangeable. Even if a perfect knowledge concerning God should exist upon the perfection of things, it is not that [knowledge] which God himself has concerning himself; for he will not negate the generated, knowing himself to be ungenerated, as the Eunomians themselves desire; for he will not deny death, knowing himself to be immortal. We, by the deprivation of what we know, know what is immortal.

And we do not have, according to scientific knowledge, the power to impose upon that which is said to be contrary to death, and we call him the deprivation of death, and everything, such as invisible; we do not learn him to be invisible according to any assertion, but because we know what is visible, having sensation and having sight, by the deprivation of this state we take the invisible. I say these things because of the Eunomians, that it is impossible to have the same knowledge of God as God has concerning God. It is not that [knowledge] which God himself has concerning himself.

And another thing: our knowledge is a disposition of the soul. But dispositions receive the more and the less. But the knowledge of God, which he has, whether concerning himself or concerning some other, is not a disposition; it is essential. And just as I say 'hot' and I say 'fire', and I say 'the heated water', but the water...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The distinction between essence and accident in knowledge and soul
english: It accepts more and less. Therefore, it can sometimes be cast away and sometimes taken up. But that which is hot in fire does not accept more and less, for it is not essential. The knowledge of God is essential, so it is incommensurable with knowledge according to disposition. And the incommensurable things do not accept likeness.

These things are not said in vain; for since the Logos constructs the Son to be consubstantial with the Father and [establishes] the same divinity through the being known by the Father and knowing the Father, they wish to share his knowledge with ours, saying: 'Just as we know God, and he knows, that we know him perfectly, as he knows himself. And the Son likewise has the knowledge concerning him. Therefore he will not rule us.' 27 Their hearts shall live unto ages of ages.

Often things that have happened are called homonymously by those to whom they have happened. We say that there is an essence of the soul; when God says, 'Do not fear those who kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul' (Matt 10:28). Thus the name 'soul' denotes essence. And when he says, 'Spirits and souls of the righteous, bless the Lord' (Ps 146:20), it denotes essence. For the name of the soul often signifies something that has happened to the soul; for when it is said in Jesus Wisdom: 'An evil soul will destroy the one who has acquired it,' it names the disposition and the intellect 'soul'; for the one who has acquired it, the soul, is the man. And again: 'Having reached those near, in the obedience of the truth.' From this it is also nicknamed, 'You, man, are equal-souled to me,' the one having the same choice as me. And again, if it is said: 'And eat grapes as much as you will fill the soul,' it speaks of the appetitive power as 'soul' in this way.

Not all then the things said denote the underlying essences, but there is also when it signifies things that have happened to them. And it has happened to man to know God. Therefore, it is not said 'knowledge' of the man, but 'knowing.' Here the thing that happened is not homonymous with the underlying thing. But the Savior is called both wise and wisdom, and having knowledge and knowledge, and righteousness and righteous; and I do not say here 'happened' and 'underlying,' but through two parallel names, the same.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Immortality of the Soul and Heart
english: It is signified: for if I say that the Savior is righteousness, I do not say him as a person, nor as a disposition; and if I say him just—'but you have denied the just one' (Matt 23:35)—I do not say the one who performs [it], but the righteousness. Thus also we say of God in general. I do not say that God is just in the sense of participating in righteousness, but in the sense of providing righteousness. And the soul according to essence does not receive the more or the less. But that soul, by which some are called beautiful-souled, does receive [it]. Therefore, the disposition is called 'soul' in the same way as the essence.

The heart and the mind mean the same thing; for when it is said: 'Where your treasure is, there also your heart will be' (Matt 6:21), there also is your mind. 'Blessed are the pure in heart' (Matt 5:8). Therefore, to say mind and heart is the same. Not concerning all things, however, but concerning men. See: the soul and the mind of man are immortal. If it is immortal, it is sought, or it is something else and another thing.

And the sinner, having an immortal soul, is never destroyed; for one should not pay attention to those saying that the souls of the wicked turn into non-existence, as the Stoics wish among the Greeks, and the Hieracites among the Christians. Therefore the soul is immortal and has a natural life according to which it is moved. And the sinner also has this life according to which he is immortal.

He does not speak now about this natural life saying: 'their hearts shall live' (Ps 42:5)—but according to that life which the believer has and the one knowing God has. If the hearts live unto the age of ages according to the blessed life, it is evident that they also remain always according to the essential life, which is common to sinners and to the diligent. And just as I say that everyone has sight when animals have sight, I say that the one seeing well previously had sight; for he would not have seen well if he did not have the seeing, and again he would not have seen badly if he did not have the seeing. Therefore both the soul and the heart have life forever, whether it be wicked or diligent. And natural life anticipates; for he would not have been able to live according to God and to live according to faith, if he were not immortal, if he did not have essential life. Therefore the hearts of these, those having eaten and having been filled, those fearing God and...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Eternal Life and the Return of the Nations
english: Those praising him shall live not for one age, but 'for the age of ages.' A multitude of ages is signified; for he did not say 'for one age,' but 'for the age of ages.' And just as 'Sabbaths of Sabbaths' is said and 'years of years' for those many years which are the days of a year, so he shall live 'for the age of ages.'

All the ends of the earth shall be remembered and shall turn back to the Lord. He prophesies concerning the salvation of all mankind; for it is necessary that that which is spoken of be brought to pass, about which this holy one says again in another psalm: 'all the nations, all whom you have made, shall come and worship before you' (Psalm 22:27). For God did not make the rational beings so that they might sin, by standing up against Him to worship these things, but so that they might honor God. And since this is the purpose of the Creator, but a purpose of those who have come to be has intervened, the purpose of God must prevail. Therefore, when He is remembered, we provide the cause for being remembered; for He remembers those who remember, as He knows those who are attentive. When we remember, then He remembers us and calls us into salvation. The 'they shall turn back' shows that no one is evil by essence, but by choice. If the evil was able to diminish the choice toward something else, the good will be able to call it back to its former state.

And all the patriarchies of the nations shall worship before Him. After the turning back, they worship. They do not worship first and then turn back; thus it signifies progress. And it is a great thing to worship before God. He who worships Him as is fitting worships before Him. Therefore, the reason: 'because' the kingdom is His. He says 'kingdom' here, not the beginning, but those who are being ruled, as it is said: 'in the gathering of peoples together and the kingdoms of serving the Lord.' If they were bad by construction, they would have been something else.

And He Himself is the master of the nations. Since the kingdom is His and He Himself has made the nations, He is their master. Therefore, they turn back to their own master. They do not enrich God by turning back; for they are His.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: From Elementary to Perfection
english: in essence

Let us be brought to the state of 'we carry the nature'. Let us leave the elementary word, for it is the beginning of the teaching of Christ. Let us be led forward to perfection, so that having become perfect in this way, we may be able to be perfect hearers of Christ; for 'we speak wisdom among the perfect' (1 Cor 2:6).

Sometimes the soul is called, as I have already said, a sheep. When it is a sheep, it grazes on pasture, not on flesh, not on the flesh of Jesus, nor on bread. It is not yet able to have desire for these foods or to manage them, even if they are presented to it. It grazes on herbs; and herbs are spiritual. Sometimes it is also called a plant and needs rain; it grazes on the art of agriculture, so that having grown, it may bring forth perfect fruit somehow; 'but I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God'. And here, therefore, the sheep-like state, which is as it were more irrational, along with gentleness and stability, signifies through the saying: 'The Lord is my shepherd, and I shall not want' (Ps 23:1). I am without wandering, and without wandering as a sheep. Just as even a baby says: 'The nurse feeds me, and I shall not want', making it clear that it is of infantile foods.

The interpreter says: 'Into a place of pasture, there He pitched His tent'. There is a pasture-like teaching suitable to sheep. And perhaps this is no other than this voice of Christ; for He says: 'My sheep hear my voice' (John 10:27). The disciples of Christ, having become perfect according to His training, being no longer sheep, do not hear a voice, but they use Him as Teacher; for 'you' 'call Me' the Lord and the Teacher, and you say well: 'I am'. Therefore, 'into a place' 'of pasture, there He pitched His tent'. Not 'He dwelt', but 'He pitched His tent'.
