And the tent signifies progress; 'I shall pass through to a place of a wonderful tent until the house of God'. The one making progress has a portable dwelling, which is virtue itself. But when he reaches the goal and the end of it, he no longer pitches a tent, but dwells. This one, the holy man, knowing the greatness and the progress...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Twofold Nature of Justice
english: He says: 'One thing I have asked from the Lord, this I will seek: to dwell in the house of the Lord' (Psalm 27:4)—not to reside temporarily—'all the days of my life.' This applies to the one entering life, the one progressing, and the one being perfected. Therefore, many know life when saying: 'Better is your mercy than life' (Psalm 104:15); for in whatever way I become life, I am held and helped by your mercy.

2–3 He nourished me by waters of rest, he restored my soul (Psalm 23:3). He led me upon paths of righteousness (Psalm 23:3). Water is appropriate for the sheep. Those who are being led to pasture and are being fed are watered, not with wine; for where there is bread, there also the wine is named. 'Bread sustains the heart of man'—and a perfect food is indicated through the bread—'and wine gladdens the heart of man' (Psalm 104:15). Therefore, where there is pasture, there is also water, and where there is bread, wine is also found. And the perfect Eucharist is fulfilled from bread and wine; for the sheep-like state is aided by pasture and water.

The 'water of rest' can be said because the one drinking it does not grow weary; for 'the one drinking' (John 4:14) 'from the water which I will give' (John 4:14) will have 'a spring leaping into eternal life' (John 4:14). The water is not moving downward, but it comes toward the drinker by leaping itself. Hence it is 'water of rest.' This water serves for nourishing and for cleansing. And since the soul being cleansed casts out sin—for this was compared to a 'talent of lead'—the water provides rest. It casts out both thirst and filth.

Furthermore, since he remembers about shepherding and pasture and water, he immediately moves to the inner man, the Word, and says: 'He restored my soul' (Psalm 23:3). In the restoration, the change is indicated. I no longer remain a sheep, I am no longer under a shepherd, I do not have a craving for water. 'He restored my soul' (Psalm 23:3). And what has happened by my soul having been restored? God 'led' it (Psalm 23:3) 'upon paths of righteousness' (Psalm 23:3). The paths of righteousness are, in appearance, virtues or the acts of virtues. Often in the divine teachings, the name of righteousness signifies virtue in general; for there is also a specific virtue called so, justice. If we say that there are four general virtues: courage, justice, temperance, and prudence, one of the virtues...

It is signified through 'justice'. And when it says: 'and you, masters, equality and justice', here justice according to merit is signified. And when it says: 'just weights and a just scale', it mentions the distributive aspect of justice. And from it, it distinguishes the justice that is distributive according to merit and that which is, as they say, restorative; for justice is said in two ways, either restorative or distributive according to merit.

This, therefore, is called just which is restorative, and in order that I may demonstrate it from the Scriptures: the law protects, 'tooth for tooth and eye for eye' (Exod 21:24). One who has come by violence and cut out his eye, is defending himself against an enemy with pleasure. The one whose eye was taken is grieved, or the tooth. God gives law that the one who has acted wickedly should suffer the same. And from his pleasure, a removal occurs, and there is added to the one suffering because of the things happening to him, and equality is made. This, therefore, is called just which is restorative.

The distributive is not seen in the equality of the nature of the thing, but in the proportion of the distribution. Thus, the paths of justice that are well-trodden, walked upon by many, are the paths of justice. And the practical activities of justice can also be paths of justice; for justice is most especially suffered and worn down when it is practiced. Since practical virtue is signified by this name of justice, this is confirmed by this: 'walking blamelessly and working justice, speaking truth in his heart, who did not deceive with his tongue and did not do evil to his neighbor' (Ps 15:2-3). And with a little more: 'he who does these things shall never be shaken for ever' (Ps 112:3).

You see that having gathered all the kinds of virtue together, he spoke of it generally as justice. 'Lead me therefore' (Ps 23:3) 'upon the paths of justice'. And those before the written law observed this justice. Concerning Abraham, it is said that 'he kept all the judgments and commands' of the Lord. Even though they had not yet been given, but he kept them, and lived according to them. And Abel, therefore, is testified to be upon justice. The return, therefore, of the soul is the journey that leads onto the paths of justice, so that it may no longer be a sheep.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Divine Evils and the Shadow of Death
english: He led me on the paths of righteousness because of his name (Ps 23:3). This was not so much because of my own worth, but because of his own designation he provided this for me; for even if someone runs toward good things and has a desire for them, if God does not show mercy, the things being striven for are not achieved.

Likewise also in the 118th Psalm it is said: 'I have run the path of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart' (Ps 118:32). Because you enlarged my heart and gave breadth to my understanding, I have run the path of the way of your commandments. Therefore, through God, the things being striven for are always achieved. For he created the rational beings so that they might share in his designation.

And by designation I mean not a collection of syllables joined together, but a designation showing the quality of the one named; for a definition of a name is given thus: 'A name is a principal designation representing the specific quality of the one named.' And this is especially true of a nickname. One is called 'wise' from wisdom, and it does not have a mere designation, not one consisting of syllables joined together, but one declaring the quality which wisdom provided to the soul. A principal designation is therefore the name that is primarily representing the quality of the one named.

So if you say 'man,' it is representing the quality of a man—and by quality here I mean the specific identity—for you have said the specific quality of the one named. And the specific quality of a man is manliness; for if you were to say another quality, others would share in it; it would not be specific. Let it be said that someone is a disciple of a physician, but he knows nothing of medicine; he does not have the quality of medicine, and he is a reproach to the one who taught him medicine when he knows nothing of it nor practices it.

For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will not fear evils, because you are with me (Ps 23:4). Since 'because of his name' he 'restored my soul' (Ps 23:3), he is with me. And since he is with me, driving away every evil, not even the shadow of death approaches me.

But 'evils' is said in two ways in Scripture, and perhaps also in common usage. The opposites of virtue, the kinds of wickedness, are called evils; as if one says: 'In the laughter of a fool, he does wrong,' and: 'Turn away from evil and do good.' But they also call unpleasant things evils, since men call pleasant things good.

The good things. And even if they are good things for men, they are not truly good. For this reason, even toward the rich, Abraham said: 'You have taken the good things for yourself.' If he were speaking about the 61 virtues, he would not have said: 'the good things for yourself.' 'The Lord will give good things to those asking him.' He did not say: 'their good things.' For when Job says: 'If we have received good things from the Lord, shall we not also receive evil?' (Job 2:10), he says 'evil' regarding the plague, the most pitiable death of children, and other things.

But it appears most clearly from Isaiah, the prophet saying thus concerning God: 'And he himself was wise to bring evils upon them' (Isa 59:21). Even for a wise man it is not [easy] to bring the kinds of evils that are the 40 evils, how much less for God. Indeed, even the wicked, when they pretend virtue, do not say: 'we are bringing evil to someone.' But it is said concerning God that as a wise one he brings evils. He speaks of things that are harmful. And he views the end of the bringing of evils: 'and his word shall by no means be set aside.'

On account of his word not being set aside, he brings difficult things; for they heard by a commanding word what they must do and what they must abstain from, but they despised this word, and as much as reached their misery, was set aside; so he brings evils, so that his word might not be set aside. And medical surgery and cauterization, bringing health to the one suffering these things, are not evils.

But he speaks here of a shadow, not that one which we say the law has—'for the law has a shadow of the things that are to come' (Col 2:17)—but here he speaks of a shadow standing in the way of death. And sin stands in the way of death. And now I say death, not the common one. See: the painters, before the images and the forms, draw in shadow. And that shadow is the beginning of the image. Therefore death has a shadow, namely sin. And this prefigures and demonstrates death.

For if I become in the midst of the shadow of death, I do not fear it. Such as Joseph, how much, at the exhortation desiring to seduce him into immorality, he became in the midst of the shadow of death, and he did not fear evil, and that did not seize him. But: is the shadow the one in the midst? Since the word is not concerning common death, neither was it necessary to think of its shadow in this way; for just as that which you say is a prefiguration, being a certain sensible thing, shall be seen.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Banquet of Wisdom
english: The underlying meaning implies that what follows the shadow is both perceptible and visible; so it is here, since the shadow becomes a matter of the soul, and death touches the soul. 'Sin'—which was a shadow—becomes a mother when 'completed,' meaning it brings about and produces death. 'If I walk in the midst of the shadow of death' (Ps 23:4). Has this happened to those in affliction? Yes, if one were terrified, he was sinning. Is 'in the midst' meant as being in sin? I do not say this. I do not say the shadow of death is the act of being afflicted, but rather the sense of dread and cowardice arising from affliction. For the martyrs were in the midst of the shadow of death, but not in death itself. They were afflicted, but they did not succumb to the tribulation that was promised to follow. A similar thought is expressed in: 'Do not bring us into temptation' (Matt 6:13). For they do not say: 'Do not let us be afflicted.' If that were the case, the apostles would never have spoken, saying: 'In all things being afflicted' (2 Cor 4:8). Therefore, not entering into temptation means not being seized by the will of the one testing. 'I will fear no evil, for you are with me' (Ps 23:4). Having you with me, I fear nothing of those intending to harm. 'Your rod and your staff, these have comforted me' (Ps 23:4). You see that he was not inexperienced with the shadow of death. Your staff, becoming my support, and your rod, disciplining me, comforted me; they brought me out of death, even if I have become within its shadow, even if I have entered into the midst of its shadow. The rod and the staff of God are taken both for discipline and for support: 'He who brings wisdom from the lips, strikes a heartless man with a rod' (Ps 32:9). He named the disciplinary and corrective word a rod. And Paul writes to the Corinthians: 'What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?' (2 Cor 10:2). And it is taken for support: 'The staffs are in your hands; and you received it with haste; it is the Lord's Passover' (1 Cor 11:33).

He prepared a table before me in the presence of those afflicting me (Ps 23:5). We connect the present things to the prelude; for because of them it has happened, when we said that after the drinking of milk, 'solid food' is given, being the wisdom of God spoken of in the perfect (1 Cor 3:2). And even here, after the beastly conduct, even if it was occurring with stability and gentleness, having been shepherded by you...

I remained late; for the table had received the feast. We had the condition of a sheep; we had need of feasts resembling lessons and having the power of water. But when I advanced, my soul being turned back by you toward the paths of righteousness (Ps 23:4) so that I might be comforted by your rod and your staff, I have become a man. For this reason we did not prepare a feast, but a table, and you revealed to me before me its beauty, its nourishment, its deliciousness. Your wisdom has prepared this table for me.

She has laid upon it 'having slaughtered her own victims' (Prov 9:2). And she has laid upon it 'her own wine' (Prov 9:5), 'mixing' it with this table, and she calls all to eat and drink from this table. And we call here the table of wisdom the divine [one] for children. And sacrifices are laid upon this; for when we perform the sacred rites and slaughter the doctrines of piety, so that we may make them ready for food, then the sacrifices are laid upon the table. And no one else offered them except Wisdom herself, who 'prepared her own table' (Prov 9:2); for she did not simply say, 'she prepared a table,' but 'her own.' And the table of Wisdom does not have other delicacies laid upon it except the wise teachings.

Furthermore, she 'mixed her own wine' (Prov 9:5). She took water to it, so that we, being unable to receive it unmixed, might take wine already mixed. There are certain unspeakable words, which are not let to be [called] wine. When anyone is able to lead these into explicit teaching, she mixed, adding to them a perceptible gift: the examples of the Scripture, the words announced in parables. Again, since God is the Word and Wisdom is [the Word], but we were not able to take the Word unmixed, she mixed it with the Incarnation, and we received, moreover, mixed wine from both the Word of the Incarnation and the majesty of the Only-begotten. 'And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory' (John 1:14). Behold the mixture. This was not the mixing of anyone else but of her own Wisdom. You know that the one mixing sometimes makes the mixture according to the capacity of the drinker. And so Wisdom mixed her own wine and does not give the same mixture to all, but what each can contain. Therefore, there are those who are sober, in whom this mixture seems more [potent]...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Table Set Before Opponents
english: To be more watery. The part of the humanization overflows. When someone 'beholds his glory, a glory as of the only-begotten from the Father' (John 1:14), the wine overflows. Therefore, he prepared this table not near the one being called, nor far from him, but before him and in front of those distressing him.

The apostle, turning this enigma to something clearer, writes: 'For a large and effective door has been opened to me, and many are standing against [me]' (1 Cor 16:9). When someone has a word and a door of a word strong and effective, he has many standing against him. And the devil himself stands against, wishing to prevent the benefit from the effectiveness of the word, as do sophist men and other evil men. Not so much, indeed, do they stand against, as having once attacked the one working well.

'In front of those distressing me' he prepared the table. He once said concerning that saying about the infant Jesus: 'For before knowing how to call father or mother, he will receive power over Damascus and the curs of Samaria in the presence of the king of the Assyrians' (Isa 7:6). It was not a great thing if the curs took [things] while the king of kings was absent, but in front of him, while he was present, they snatched what he had under himself. Or did he not plunder the magi in front of the king of the Assyrians? For they were in the act of practicing magic. They did not come to the child having previously repented, but while the demons were still active.

Such a thing, indeed, has been seen ecclesiastically, that those, having done their usual things in calling demons, not sparing them, recognized that the magic was dissolved from the child signified by the appeared star. Having come, therefore, to me, such a thing, these distressing ones were present, and in their very faces the things of the blessing happened. The 'in front of' can also be thus: they were present in opposition of will, wishing to prevent what is for them, or wishing to harm him. 'I anointed my head with oil' (Ps 23:5). You showed me Christ; according to what signifies...
my anointed ones
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Earth and its Fullness
english: "They drink intoxicatingly by night." In darkness and ignorance, these people drink. But those who drink, having taken a divine drink—that is, having been made glad—drink in a sober way. "Eat, drink, be intoxicated, brothers," the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs (Song of Songs 5:1). The "be intoxicated" does not mean this, not "be strengthened" from wine, but "be made glad."

And "your mercy shall pursue me all the days of my life" (Psalm 23:6). Your mercy is as if "I have anointed my head" (Psalm 23:5); it does not anoint my head for a little while, but always; since it is near to me, and thus every one of the anointed ones becomes a Christ eternally. Therefore "all the days of my life" pursues me; it does not allow me to become distant from it; for it is close by, since it is present to me, and thus every one of the anointed ones becomes a Christ eternally. It no longer dwells for a day or two, but for "all the days of my life." And "all the days of life" takes in the illuminations of the soul having come from the sun of righteousness.

A Psalm to David; of the first Sabbath. The superscription is appropriate; for it is for the one day of the Sabbaths. "One of the Sabbath"; the eighth following. This also is the first of the Sabbath. For since it is a beginning of a cycle of a week, it is also called the eighth; for the week is circumscribed up to the seventh, the seventh being an addition, that is, a day or a unit. The second begins again from a unit. This is called at one time the first of the Sabbath, that is, after the Sabbath, and at another time the eighth, so that the two weeks may be gathered together. In the giving of the holy part to the seven and the eight, the Jew alone has the Sabbath. They have neither the first of the Sabbath nor the eighth, having not at all considered the former week. Therefore, he alone, having the ecclesiastical opinion, who brings forth from his treasure new and old according to another comparison of the Gospel (Matthew 13:52), has the new of the Sabbath. Transcending the first week, he began the second, which is according to the Gospel. And this also is called the eighth in relation to the first week and the first of the Sabbaths.

The first verses of the Psalm can be understood both according to the word and the sense. But the fullness of the earth is to take in its world; for as Moses said: since plants and animals have come upon it, it is said: "it has been completed" (Genesis 2:1)...

The heavens and the earth. And God finished his works on the sixth day (Gen 2:2). We take this literally: that fruits and animals are the fullness of the earth. The apostle instructs, advising those from the Gentiles and the Jews not to be superstitious about foods, saying: 'Whatever is sold in the market, eat, without examining anything (1 Cor 10:25); for the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord (Ps 24:1).' Meat is especially sold in the markets, but also other things contributing to nourishment.

'The earth and its fullness belong to the Lord' (Ps 24:1) means the inhabited world and all who dwell in it. I said earlier that the earth was divided into its part for farming and its part for habitation. That which has the preparation for habitation is called the inhabited world, but that for farming and other things is called earth. God is the maker of both; for how could these be his, if he himself had not made them? Therefore, 'the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord' takes it in a general sense.

He established it upon the seas and prepared it upon rivers—that is, the earth or the inhabited world. The inhabited world is also the earth. What is said here is equal to what is said: 'He who made the earth stand upon the water,' and by Job: 'hanging the earth upon nothing' (Job 26:7); for if it is established in the sea, it does not have a hard and solid foundation, but in the waters it has the hanging. And every water has a ground beneath it. Since the sea has a ground beneath it, it must certainly have something underlying it. But nothing else is found except the liquid. For this reason, he says the earth is established upon the seas.

It holds itself by turning upon itself. It is not a hard ground supporting it as if so arranged, but it turns around itself. Indeed, even the Greeks say in their accounts that straight lines sent from a circle—and straight lines are not perceptible, but are considered by reason—hold it in the very center. And this is the hanging it upon nothing. This is the will of God; for 'you established the earth for its stability, it shall not be moved for ever and ever' (Ps 104:5). For how could the seat received by such a word of God be prone to falling? Since, therefore, the earth is upon the sea...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The misuse of reason and the metaphor of the soil
english: It has been founded, and a part of the earth is the inhabited world, and it itself appropriately has this seat by its moist nature. And he says regarding the rivers that it is prepared for them; not to be founded upon rivers, but to be prepared; for it is not possible to say that it has its foundation both in the sea and in the rivers, but it has been founded upon the sea, having been prepared for the rivers, so that it might be benefited by them, just as certain springs and channels flowing through it. Such bodies, if they do not have water sprinkled throughout them by which they can be held together, become fragments. And these things are [to be understood] regarding the literal sense.

But since the following things can no longer be taken historically: 'Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, and who shall stand in his holy place?' (Ps 24:3), it is necessary to say that the way of the ascent and the seat of the standing were not mentioned, but the answer is made to the one asking: 'Who is the one ascending and who is the one standing?' Thus: 'innocent of hands and pure in heart.' That being innocent refers to the hands, and that being pure refers to the actions. Then he says 'a divine character': 'innocent of hands and pure in heart, who has not taken his soul in vain.'

This is understood in two ways. 'In vain' refers to the foolish person taking his own soul, deliberating, choosing, and acting; for often these things—the unseemly, the sensible, the transitory—are signified by the name 'vain'; as if he were saying, 'and you will know where you were, when you were trusting in vain things,' meaning the transitory things. It can also refer to the sins themselves. 'In vain' he took [it], the one rising in the morning and drinking wine and staying late so as to be consumed by the wine; for 'woe to those who rise early and pursue strong drink and stay late; for the wine will consume them' (Isa 5:11). Again, they have haste to rise from dawn and hurry to the courts, in which injustice follows; this one 'has taken his soul in vain.' This is also consistent with what is said in Isaiah to certain people: 'Vain is the strength of your spirit' (Isa 5:12). Here, 'spirit' is the opinion. Similarly, this applies to what was said concerning the Virgin, that just as she is holy in body, so she is holy in spirit, in opinion and in mind. Therefore, 'vain' is 'the strength of your spirit.' If anyone, then, [uses] the mind...

His mind is also worn out by 'worldly cares' toward vain things; his strength is in vain. They exhaust the power of reasoning toward vain things. Indeed, one can see such people and even more wicked ones. They exhaust the whole strength of the mind toward these things.

A second explanation for: 'who has not received his soul in vain' (Psalm 39:9). God prepared man as a rational being, not merely so that he might possess reasoning and do nothing according to it; for this He made the rational being, so that he might receive virtue and exercise it. 'He has received his soul in vain' does not mean God gave it thus, but that he himself has taken it thus. As one might say, for example: He made man from soul and body, and there are certain movements of the soul, and there are also movements of the body. We have the activity of members: walking, doing something with the hands, seeing. If anyone, then, for instance, having feet, never walks, he has his feet 'in vain' in a certain way.

And for an upward leading: the following [words] force even the preceding verses to be led upward. 'The Lord' is that 'earth,' that 'good and noble heart' which received the one whom Jesus cast seed, and bore fruit a hundredfold, or a hundred and sixty and thirty (Matthew 13:8). Often I have said that the intelligible things can be taken in the same way through more various thoughts, when they were saying the soul is a sheep and a plant. Here, therefore, the same earth is both earth and inhabited world. When, therefore, it bears the practical virtues, it is an earth having fullness. But when it has the divine gifts of the Spirit, it is an inhabited world having inhabitants. It is not a desert; for He has not said, 'Come, and let us abandon it,' as it is said to the doomed inhabited world. And this is the assembly of the Jews.

And he extends this also to every soul having, at first, a dwelling, but leaving it by its own fault. Therefore, this is connected to: 'He himself founded it upon the seas' (Psalm 74:3). Sea and seas is the name given to the place of earth and the condition of those dwelling there. Having being in billows and in saltiness, I call the dwelling; upon these seas He founded it. And this sea takes the sting of Jesus, so that from it...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Integrity of Oaths and the Source of Blessing
english: Let the diligent catch good animals. But if these hunters are friends of virtue, they are said to be hunted from the sea so that they may come out of it, and in another way to be established upon the sea; for here they are established so that they may appear 'having been rooted and built up in love' (Eph 3:17). And 'upon the rivers' (Ps 46:4) of those flowing from the belly of the one having the Spirit, they are prepared, so that they may receive these rivers flowing from the belly of each believer. And the various gifts of the Spirit are the rivers.

For the one wishing to learn toward the one being examined: 'Who is he that ascends into the mountain of the Lord and stands in the holy place?' (Ps 24:3). An answer is brought: 'You seek who is ascending and standing? He who is innocent with his hands and pure in heart, who has not taken his soul in vain' (Ps 24:4).' This is the one ascending through progress. And progress is the ascent. And the standing is in the perfection. When someone becomes 'perfect as the Father in heaven' (Matt 5:48), he has stood in the holy place, unless indeed he surpasses the whole such state and takes the beginning of another; therefore also in the psalms it is said: 'I have seen the end of every completion' (Ps 37:36).

There are many ends, as it is in the learning of letters. One completes the task in the knowledge of the characters, and begins by syllabifying, and again, having attained the end of those, a different beginning becomes. For a circle, one cannot take either a beginning or an end. If, therefore, one recognizes from a sign the beginning of the circle, and completes the whole circle, he comes again to the beginning, as it is with the sun. In such things, ends are always brought according to the same pattern.

The Jews, therefore, perhaps say that 'to ascend to the mountain' means to ascend into the temple and to stand in it. The following things are gathered together by this thought. 3–4 Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord and who shall stand in his holy place? Innocent with hands and pure in heart, who has not taken his soul in vain and has not sworn in vain to his neighbor. It lies in the Decalogue: 'You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain; for the Lord will not cleanse him who takes his name in vain' (Ex 20:7). This must be grasped inwardly, perfectly, introductory, and appropriately by those beginning. Chiefly the...

The young man, being ready to receive the laws of God, 'does not swear at all' (Matt 5:37); therefore he does not take the name of the Lord in vain. He receives it not in vain, being satisfied with 'yes, yes' and 'no, no' (Matt 5:37). It is possible for those introducing this to say: it is not necessary to swear falsely; for he who falsely invokes the name of the Lord, as far as it reaches him, has received it in vain; since he is able to demonstrate even faith to the one disputing, and easily brings him to the oath without an oath. This faith through an oath they call unprovable.

And the external laws, when it was not possible to demonstrate, not through writings, not through witnesses—then also he does not cast himself upon swearing, but the judges, desiring to find every proof and not finding it, flee to this last resort. 'Who did not take his soul in vain' (Ps 15:4). And immediately he joined: 'nor did he swear upon deceit' (Ps 15:4); for everyone swears 'upon deceit' perversely; for he does not think he is swearing perversely. It rarely happens through ignorance. Often someone, forgetting, swears, and again there is an accusation, as regarding sins committed while unheard.

I say: some do not blame those who are drinking while saying what should not be said, and doing what is not necessary, saying that drunkenness is an unconscious state by which these things which they are blamed for happen after drinking; but drunkenness itself is voluntary; for it was necessary not to get drunk.

This one shall receive a blessing from the Lord. Having outlined who is the one ascending the mountain and standing in a holy place, and what follows such a person, he says: according to the one who ascended, he is in the mountain of God and standing in a holy place. And after the ascent of the mountain, so that the summit of the mountain may be the holy place, he says that 'this one shall receive a blessing from the Lord', 'a spiritual blessing, the one in the heavens'; for it is said: 'for indeed the Lawgiver will give blessing'. And the Lawgiver gives not to those transgressing the law, but to those turning toward it in deed. And again: 'Behold, thus', he says, 'shall be blessed the man who fears the Lord' (Ps 128:1). The cause of the blessing is reverence, the fear toward the Lord; therefore it is said: 'The Lord shall bless you out of Zion' (Ps 128:5). If God blesses such a person from Zion, because of virtue having preceded him and right understanding for him...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Desiring the Face of God and the Coming of the King
english: the diligent one

They want to make a child of you; but desires produce a child of the devil. Again, those having the same desires are one generation. It is thus also with: 'The generation of the upright shall be blessed' (Ps 112:3). Jacob was seeking the face of God. Everyone praying sincerely for the appearance of God prays to receive it, and this is to seek the face of God. The saints indeed send up a prayer saying: 'Let your face shine upon us and we shall be saved' (Ps 27:8).

And this is also possible because: we have received the inscription of the psalm 'into one of the Sabbaths', and we call the resurrection of the Savior 'the Lord's Day', sometimes as the eighth [day] and sometimes as the first of the week according to various thoughts. They 'seek the face' of the one about to arrive, having heard that 'bending the heavens, he shall descend' (Ps 18:13), because 'a Savior is coming' (Ps 98:1). For the heralds of the truth, those running ahead of the one arriving, hear: 'Say to the daughter of Zion: behold, a Savior is coming to you' (Zeph 3:14), and: 'Say to the cities of Judah: behold, our God comes with might' (Isa 60:1), to shake off evil, so that we may learn to strike down the adversaries, those working evil, 'the one working in the sons of disobedience' (Ps 2:9).

Finally, having enjoyed the economy—for 'still' 'it shall say of your word: I am present' (Ps 105:4)—immediately the ascent of the Savior is signified after the arrival; for the word says through the psalms: 'Lift up your gates, O rulers of yours' (Ps 24:7). Your rulers, lift up the gates. Or thus: your gates, O rulers, lift up, which you preside over, which you guard. 'And be lifted up, O eternal gates' (Ps 24:9). The word says 'and be lifted up', presenting the greatness of the one about to descend and enter through the gates. If you remain here, you will not be able to contain his ascent. To lift up and to lift up [further] can also mean to make them through the middle; for he who is the very distant King does not need an entrance. And again: 'And the King of glory shall enter' (Ps 24:10). The heralds, angels, [announce] the Savior.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Lord of Powers and the Gates
english: Taking these things up, they speak to the heavenly powers, to those dividing the heavenly gates. Then they inquire, 'Who is this King of Glory, whom you announce is coming, to whom the gates must be lifted and the eternal ones—not the temporary ones—the immortal ones, must be raised up?' Near to this is what is brought forward in Isaiah: 'Who is this coming from Edom, with garments stained red from Bozrah? Why are your garments red?' (Isa 63:1). And they inquire again.

Even if this body, being raised from the dead, and especially the one of the Savior previously, does not possess the characteristics of flesh having been transformed into spiritual, yet by the grace of the one ascending, traces were preserved for the recognition of where the one ascending comes from. And because of this: 'Garments stained red from Bozrah' (Isa 63:1). And just as having risen from the dead and appearing to the disciples, desiring to confirm to them that the body which he had has risen, he showed the marks of the wounds, he showed the side, not that the body possesses a side—for to bear a side is hard and prototypical—but so that he might be fully known as the one who rose, so that they might not think badly concerning the resurrection from the sign of the fullness of the resurrection, as if after the resurrection the raised body carries the characteristics of the corruptible, 'he entered through closed doors' (Luke 24:40); so also here, being taken up, immediately after the ascension, he showed the characteristics of the flesh, not so that they might remain; nor did those things which he showed, such as having eaten and the marks of the wounds and the others, remain with him having them. Not so that we might eat, for he ate after the resurrection, but so that they might see that he, whom he said, was himself the one who rose. This indeed Luke says: 'To whom he also proved himself alive after his suffering, by showing many proofs and by eating and touching' (Luke 24:39-43). Observe that he also proved himself alive after his suffering by eating.

Lift up your heads, O gates, and be lifted up, O ancient gates, and the King of Glory shall enter (Ps 24:7). Who is this King of Glory? They inquire: concerning whom is this said that he shall enter, so that we may open the doors for him and lift them up? He says: 'The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord, mighty in war' (Ps 24:8). He makes the answer from His works. As at the beginning of the ascent to...

The mountain of the Lord: 'and who shall stand' (Ps 24:7). And 'how many' was not used—not that Abraham or John [were meant]—but 'if anyone is innocent in hands and pure in heart', so also here he did not say 'how many', but by deed he showed the matter: 'the Lord is mighty and strong, the Lord is strong in war' (Ps 24:7, 8). As it began, these things were pre-proclaimed. But when he rose and was ascended, it is no longer said that 'he will come out' (Ps 24:8), the one who transformed the kingdom upon the earth, the one who destroyed the power of death, the devil; but he is 'mighty and strong, the Lord is strong in war' (Ps 24:8). Comparing that prophecy which has it thus: 'the Lord of powers will come out and will crush the war'. As it began, these things were pre-proclaimed. But when he rose and was ascended, it is no longer said that 'he will come out' another 'the Lord is strong in war' having brought down the tyrants.

The Lord is strong in war: 'lift up your gates, O rulers of you' (Ps 24:7). Since they asked who it is, and having said it, they asked 'which are the gates' and to open [them], they say: since the Lord is mighty and strong and strong also in war, do not hesitate, do not delay. And behold: to those in charge he says: 'lift up the gates' (Ps 24:7). And since the gates also are rational, and toward them he stretches out, saying: 'and be lifted up, eternal gates' (Ps 24:9). And 'be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory will come in' (Ps 24:10). Therefore he says: 'the Lord of powers, this is the King of glory'.

Often the armies are signified by the name of power. The Lord is of these powers, of the heavenly armies; for such powers appeared to the shepherds praising God when Christ was born. And altogether the Lord is of all these powers, of the thousands and myriads praising and ministering. And it is possible to take the powers thus: each rational substance acting as a power of holiness. Just as we say a musical woman and a grammatical woman, when she possesses these things, so the one participating in 'Christ, the power of God' (1 Cor 1:24), each is a power. Therefore, the Lord is of these powers. But the power is to be understood in two ways: either each rational substance participating in the power of him, the Savior, is called a power, or the army of the rational substances, the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Soul and the Flesh; Davidic Authorship
english: Thus they are arrayed for battle. Who is this king of glory? The Lord of powers, He is this king of glory. Do not seek who He is regarding what we say; for the Lord of powers, He is. And you also are powers, and each of you a power according to the second meaning. 'Lord' therefore; because with authority He said that 'He is the king of glory.'

Concerning this power and this manifestation, Paul also writes: 'The mystery of godliness is great, for He was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit' (1 Tim 3:16), and 'taken up in glory' (Acts 1:11). The one taken up in glory is the Lord of glory, He is the king of glory.

It is not to receive now a word ill-interpreted in an unseasonable way by some. They wish to say that 'the Lord of glory, having been crucified' is the God Word; for those denying the perfect humanity say that 'the one crucified, the Lord of glory' is the same God Word. And such is indeed the syllogism which those who err thus say, and the reasoning of Apollinaris the heretic, who says that 'the Word' became 'flesh' by a change of essence, and such syllogisms which Apollinaris set forth in his writings: Christ was crucified. The one crucified is the king of glory. Therefore, Christ is the king of glory.

And thus they hear the syllogism: 'Christ is the king of glory. Christ was crucified. Therefore, the king of glory was crucified.' And these people speak monstrosities. The cross is manifest; for it is a fixing down of a body; 'they pierced my hands and my feet' (Ps 22:16). He who says that the God Word was incorporeal being crucified allegorizes the cross. And when the cross is allegorized, the resurrection will also be allegorized. And when the resurrection is allegorized, all things that happened are as if they were dreams.

And these people say the same things; for even if they name [it] for the sake of some deception: body and body? And if you say 'yes', that very body is not other than the God Word. So they are two. So are we not saying two? For what is absurd, to say two, the temple and the one in the temple? For the body is called the temple of the Savior. And it is not said: 'who was manifested as flesh', but 'in flesh'. And again: 'having been put to death in the flesh'. It has not said: 'having been put to death as flesh'. 'Every spirit that confesses in the flesh' (1 John 4:2)...

and having come. Therefore, even if they do not wish, there are two: the flesh and the one seen in it. But we do not call the flesh without soul; for this flesh, having been produced, has become without soul, as it is evident to us. 'The flesh dwells in hope, because you will not abandon my soul to Hades' (Ps 24:14). If it had remained in Hades, the flesh would not have had the hope of resurrection. But previously they inquired: 'Who is this king of glory?' (Ps 24:8) and they heard an answer; then, since the king of glory is not a random person, they inquired with greater precision and a second time, and moreover they received another answer, no longer 'the Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord is mighty in war' (Ps 24:8); for perhaps it was possible to suppose that one of the powers had been chosen by God; and he says: 'The Lord of powers, he is the king' (Ps 24:10). Thus I call him the Lord of powers, not as a power.

A Psalm of David. The psalm is said to be 'to David'; for it is one thing to be 'of David' and another to be 'to David'. 'Of David' is said when he himself has composed or is singing. But 'to him' is said when it is brought to him. If, therefore, I say that this triumphal hymn is to the athlete, to the victor, then David has set a subscript. And the things said do not stand only regarding his own person, but also if another should be found according to him. Who then is this David? 'Who will do,' he says, 'all my will' (Ps 40:8). Let the psalm be said concerning everyone who does the will of God.

'To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul' (Ps 25:1). It is not for everyone to say: 'To you I have lifted up my soul, O God.' But he who is able to say: 'My soul lives to him' alone lifts up his soul to God. God is in highness; I do not speak according to a place—and often these things have been made clear to us—but in a highness of surpassing nothingness. When someone therefore tears away from the things below his own soul, from the devil and the causes of evil and of evil itself, he lifts it up to God, so that it may live to him alone, so that it may dwell with him, so that 'having been joined as one spirit' it may become to him. It is a great thing to say this voice, having an unknowable soul. 'If our heart does not condemn' (1 John 3:21), he says, 'we have boldness toward God.' When the heart is known, being checked by conscience, [it is not...]
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Shame and Hidden Sins
english: One is able to say such things about oneself. But such a person is rare, and because of the difficulty of finding them, they are perhaps thought by some not to exist at all. Furthermore, the rarity is shown by the proverbist saying: 'Who shall boast having a pure heart and shall speak boldly as being free from sin?' (Psalm 25:3). By saying pure, he means the heart being rightly disposed and thinking concerning piety. He who is persuaded according to the truth, that one has a pure heart. And he who is outside of practical sin speaks boldly as being free from sin.

Because the truth and those things thought truly purify the soul and the heart, Peter the apostle writes: 'having purified your souls in the obedience of the truth' (1 Peter 1:22). And James writes: 'Cleanse your hands, sinners, and purify your hearts, double-minded' (James 4:8). They cleanse hands, those making their actions crooked, and they purify their soul, those casting away all double-mindedness; 'and purify' indeed, he says, 'hearts, double-minded.' Most of all, those thinking wrongly are double-minded. Sometimes they are seized by glory and held by it, but when they look at things otherwise, they find them to be having [something else], and how they once remain in the grasping bad-glory.

Thus, one is presented as free from sin who has lived a life according to the right way. He has a pure heart, the one thinking the things of the truth, having taken 'the mysteries of the kingdom' (Matthew 13:11) in soul and having been initiated according to them. This one, therefore, lifts up the soul toward the Lord. It is not one who happens to do so who lifts [it]. To say [it] is perhaps easy for everyone, but to do [it] is either difficult or has reached the point of being nearly impossible, not because of his own nature.

And this, since according to the apostle 'no one says Lord Jesus, except in the Holy Spirit' (1 Corinthians 12:3). And these men themselves, when they call the God Lord, do not say [it] with voice alone, but with deed and disposition. When they act thus, disposed as toward a master, doing what he wills and commands, they are truly slaves; and since what is turned toward [him] is that of a truly slave, he is truly a master. 'My God, in you I have trusted; let me not be put to shame' (Psalm 25:2). Happy is the one having precise knowledge, having trusted in it, who converses with all and is not put to shame. He who has trusted in virtue is not [cut off]...

They act wickedly; therefore, they are not ashamed. For those committing sin are the ones undergoing shame. Some say, 'they shall rise up for reproach and eternal shame.' Thus the word prays for the unfeeling that shame may come to be for them: 'fill their faces with dishonor'—speaking regarding faults—'and let them be ashamed and perish and know that you are the Lord' (Ps 51:1-4). When they feel [shame], being such wicked people, they perish according to that state in which they are.

The one who is confident in his iniquities, if he knows that he sins wickedly, is ashamed and perishes as a wicked man, not as a rational substance. Because of this the apostles say: 'we have spoken the hidden things of shame' (2 Cor 12:7). We have not spoken only the manifest things producing reproach and shame, but also the hidden things. And it can be so: for some, the things of drunkenness are hidden. When they are intoxicated in wines, such as they were regarding whom Paul writes, 'whose glory is in their shame' (1 Cor 5:31), in whom it is necessary to be ashamed, they themselves wish to be honored. Indeed, one finds fifty men wishing to be honored through much variety.

But how are they hidden? I have spoken of the hidden things in two ways: sins are in thoughts. Therefore, not only does the diligent and the simple man refrain from practical deeds, but also from the hidden things, as he also sends up a prayer: 'cleanse me from my secret [sins]' (Ps 51:3). Otherwise, the unknown things are called hidden. Having been bold regarding all manifest transgressions, that they are forgiven him, the saint says: 'who will understand transgressions?' (Ps 19:12). He who understands transgressions is rare.

Since it is possible for me to be ignorant of them, 'cleanse me from these. Spare your servant from others' (Ps 51:3)—for they are foreign to me, to my essence, both they and those acting them against me. And furthermore he adds: 'lest they overpower me.' If the hidden things do not overpower me, 'then I shall be blameless.' And he adds: 'and I shall be cleansed from great sin.' We say these things are in thoughts, and to be so as to be unknown to the possessor. How then is the one being cleansed from these 'from great sin' cleansed? You know that the 'great' of [it] is in relation to what. As for the one desiring to be entirely pure, even the small things of sins seem to be great. And they once took such a pattern: if a garment many times...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Shame and the Universal Affirmation
english: If it has filth from elsewhere, even if someone touches it or handles it, it does not seem to have been defiled. But if it is immediately brought from a cooperage, and the touch of the fingers seems to be a flaw, it seems to make it something unclean. The entirely clean man considers even a brief thought a great sin. It is possible even to say that the mind is able to benefit all; regarding practical sin, that which is in thoughts is the shortest.

If someone saw a woman for desire and sustained the appetite until pre-passion, he has not committed the practical sin. If that pre-passion is removed, one is purged from a great sin; from practical sin he is cleansed. To such purity the one saying this has arrived, as if saying something certain: 'If I saw injustice in my heart, let the Lord not hear me' (Ps 140:3). Just as he brings upon himself a request and a punishment, if he has injustice in his heart. He says: 'For this reason God has heard me,' with the implication: 'For this reason God has heard me, because I did not see injustice in my heart.' If he saw injustice in his heart, let him not receive the prayer. Therefore, 'for this reason' [means] 'He heard me.'

They said this because the one having confidence in God makes all things right that are worthy of being made right; for I do not say that those things which God forbids are made right. They once took that: 'And let them be ashamed and perish' (Ps 106:45). But what follows being ashamed and perishing, except to know 'that the name is the Lord' (Ps 113:3)? For God indeed says to someone, after doing evils, to cease doing and thinking such things: 'Be ashamed and take your dishonor.' You have been cast into dishonor. You gave the pretext; for you did those things which bring dishonor upon you. Be ashamed therefore of what you have done, and take your dishonor, not saying: 'I have not sinned'; for he was saying to God: 'I have not sinned,' as if saying to God: 'Behold, I am judged against you in saying: I have not sinned.' And I am judged against you, not in order to condemn you, but in order to...

Having been shamed, let the dishonor cease. 2 Let my enemies not mock me. Then my enemies will mock me, when saying that having trusted in you, shameful things are being worked out. They are enemies to me, not I to them. For this reason also the Savior says: 'Love your enemies' (Matt 5:44). The addition seems to pass by; for it was necessary to say: 'Love the enemies'; but since the slaves of Christ ought not to have enemies, while others wish to be enemies, let them love those. That place by Aristotle, how it once seems to be well for civilization. Saying concerning the preceding and the following, he said: previously we want the just friends to be, even if they are far away. But by what has happened, we want the enemies to be just, so that they may not harm anything. For their own sake we also want this. But the apostles of Christ 51 do not pray for them so that they may not harm, but so that they might not be harmed. 3 For indeed all those waiting for you will not be shamed (Rom 10:11). The 'all' is often in the Scripture taken instead of the universal decision; for we do not even say this, that of those waiting, some are shamed and others are not, as the particular decision teaches, saying: not all men are just. Here therefore instead of 'no one': no one of those waiting for you is shamed. And continuously in the Scripture the universal decision is signified through the universal affirmation taken from transposition. And you know that the affirmation from transposition often follows the simple decision. 3 Let all those acting lawlessly be shamed for nothing. Hear 'to act lawlessly for nothing' thus: wickedness is worked out for nothing, not to bring glory, not for the promise. It is unstable, its being is in something else. If therefore the one having wickedness wishes to cast it away, it no longer exists. But some again, either through ignorance or more sophistically, say that virtue also is thus, that it too has its being in something else.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Injustice, Lawlessness, and the Two Ways of God
english: This is a falsehood; for the Trinity possesses goodness essentially. Humans possess the good and the just and virtue through participation in the Trinity. Even if they themselves turn away, it exists. It exists in God, from which they have the capacity to be excellent. But evil, if it is not active, does not exist at all.

For this reason, many scriptures teach that it does not exist; from which it is concluded that there are neither two opposing principles in essence, nor are men bad by construction, as many heterodox people also desire, claiming that no one will choose either good or evil. Much that is absurd and impious follows from this. See: if all existing things are such by construction, and the wicked are so in essence, all legislation passes away; for the law cannot make the good good, nor the evil good. And if the law passes away, all exhortation, all encouragement, all counsel passes away, and the reason of man is entirely refuted; for he who does not have choice and will is not rational. And the coming of the Savior is superfluous. Does he make the good good? It is such from itself. But does he make the evil good? It is not of a nature to receive the participation of good. Therefore, the one sinning sins in vain.

For it is written in another psalm concerning that great one, the devil, the cause of all evil: 'Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked' (Ps 74:6). We have said many times that the names lying against the opposing power are names of choice; for indeed, 'devil' is said, he is named 'Satan', which is 'the adversary', 'sinner'; and this name is a name of choice. And with the article, it is even more so itself: 'Behold, I have given you to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power' (Lk 10:19)—not of an enemy, but 'of the enemy'. And: 'Save us' (Mt 6:13)—not from an evil thing, but 'from the evil one'. And here: 'Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked' (Ps 74:6). Then it brings forth: 'His sin shall be sought, and it shall not be found through it.' Because of its own nature, it is not found. His sin is sometimes sought and is not found, not existing anywhere, not having moved to another place, but because of itself it is not found, since it does not have being by itself.

Unless in the one acting. And furthermore: 'and injustice lied about itself' (Ps 25:11). Here, to lie, we say in this way, as we often say the earth lies. Injustice therefore lies about itself, so as to no longer exist. It lied about itself because of its own nature. Thus, those who act lawlessly do so for no reason, not to gain something, but rather to be harmed. 'Make known to me your ways, O Lord' (Ps 25:4), those who act lawlessly without having experienced the law.

Now, concerning the written [word], regarding the law according to teaching, I say: for those not having received this are called lawless, as also in: 'blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven' (Ps 32:1). But sin after the law is not called simply lawlessness, but transgression: 'transgressions ensnare a man, and each one is constricted by the bands of his own sins' (Prov 5:22). 'Nor do the lawless persist before your eyes' (Ps 139:7). The lawless person never becomes an addition to God. Under the eyes of God, he does not become [so] except in a different way according to the word of providence. But according to the command of the diligent, they do not persist. They do not persist in the same way as the righteous, concerning whom it is said: 'the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous' (Ps 34:15). Therefore, by saying 'they do not persist', he shows that they once were, when they were guarding the law, but when they have become transgressors of it, then they have been cast out from the eyes of God.

'Make known to me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths. Lead me into your truth' (Ps 25:4-5). The ways of God are said to be twofold: either those leading toward Him, or those which He Himself walks, proceeding through all things, as is necessary according to the word of providence or according to benefiting and being in His receptive ones. For he says: 'I will dwell in them and walk about' (Ps 15:2). But he who walks about has paths, which He Himself walks. Thus, we call the ways of God either those leading toward Him—and these are the virtues—or those which He Himself treads according to His providence and judgment and administration and gift. It is therefore necessary to know the ways of God by Him making them known. 'And teach me your paths' (Ps 25:4). That is, those which those hurrying toward You [tread], or those which You tread, proceeding through the works of Your grace. If there are even more to say: you know that before teaching, something must be known; for from pre-known things come understandings and scientific proofs. Both...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Eternal Age and Repentance
english: Therefore make known to me your ways; for in this manner I shall learn your paths, following those who have worn them down, those who have proceeded in the good things or those who have proceeded because you proceeded, having a subscript and a pattern, 'that we may follow your footsteps' (Ps 25:4). Therefore, to know precedes to teach. Thus it is said that demonstrations and teachings come from things already known. It can be understood in this way: that common concepts are pre-known. And indeed, when we test a teaching, we say we are testing it in reference to common concepts.

For indeed, at times a teacher says something, and the common concept of the learner pre-perceives and knows whether he speaks well or not. You will find even in these human, scientific demonstrations, that sciences are not being led well if those listening do not pre-perceive what it is necessary to pre-perceive. For indeed, this has often been said to us: that when someone learns something that must be foreknown before the instruction, it is not right to speak to him through obscure words, since it is not familiar to him. 'Guide me into the truth' (Ps 27:11).

After the practical virtues and the guidance according to disposition, the guidance into the truth occurs; for, he says, 'desiring wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will supply it to you' (Ps 119:2). And wisdom and truth are the same. The Savior, indeed, is said to be both: 'Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God' (1 Cor 1:24). And he himself said: 'I am the truth' (John 14:6).

And teach me, that you are my God and Savior. You are my God, having created me; you are my Savior, willing that I should improve. Therefore, become my teacher. As Creator, so also [become] teacher. And I waited for you all the day. I waited for you all the time of my life, so that I might have you as teacher and Savior; for 'toward you' I 'lifted up my soul' (Ps 25:1), not toward another. I did not entreat another, so that you might make known to me your ways and teach me your paths, but I deemed you worthy to become teacher of these things to me.

Often the whole of our life's time is called 'a day', according to what has been said: 'for your sake we are dying all the day' (Ps 116:3), instead of what the apostle has made 'every day' (2 Cor 6:13). And 'a day' can be said to be the whole time of the life of the saints, because they are always in light, being illuminated by the tru[th].

The thin light of 'the sun of righteousness' (Malachi 4:8). This day is not interrupted by nights; it is continuous. For it is said in the Psalm: 'our age is for the illumination of your face' (Ps 36:9). And the life which is extended by the sojourn here is called an age; for it is said, 'there shall be to you a servant for an age' (Ps 119:9), and 'I shall not eat meat for an age' (Ps 119:119), instead of 'through life'. Since therefore the time of our life's day has come to illuminate your face—for we have come to pre-announce your presence—our whole age has become for the illumination of your face because of the illuminating and making manifest to men your visitation.

Remember your mercies, O Lord, and your compassions, because they are from eternity. For even if I have entreated and lifted my soul to you and desired other things to be present to me from you, I do not ask these things according to merit. You provide these things mercifully and compassionately in accordance with the one: 'not of the one willing nor of the one running, but of the God who shows mercy' (Romans 9:16); for even if we have done all things from ourselves, by the mercy of God we strive to attain their end. Hear me as a merciful one, and as a compassionate one receive my prayers. 'And your compassions, because they are from eternity'. For it is not yesterday and the morning that I began to be compassionate. You are eternal, you are eternally good.

Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances (Ps 25:7). You see that concerning former ignorances and sins one prays for mercy and the compassion of God; for there is no longer repentance sending back a prayer upon committed sins. Repentances happen upon things passed away. For it says: 'do not remember the sins and the ignorances of me' (Ps 25:7) which I have, and now I do not have, but those of youth. And it is possible even thus: whatever the age of the one ignoring and sinning may be, he is young in the youth of his mind, in the newness of his conduct. It is possible, therefore, to always find those who confess and bring words of repentance concerning sins passed away, doing this: 'we have sinned, we have transgressed, we have been ungodly' (1 John 1:8); for how is it possible? The one repenting asks for virtue. How then can one who is still in sins have or receive virtue? 'Turn away' (Ps 34:14) therefore 'from evil and do good'. According to your mercy, remember me. What about 'remember me'? It is a personal idiom of the Scripture instead of 'know me' (Ps 139:1).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Testimony and Divine Glory
english: Because of your goodness, Lord, not because of my own virtue do you remember me. The Lord is good and upright; he who is with uprightness is good. For often 'good' is taken in a sense of deception: 'bad associations corrupt good morals' (Prov 13:20). Thus, 'good' is not taken here in a praiseworthy sense, but in a sense of being easy or indulgent. Similarly with 'innocent': 'the innocent believes every word,' instead of meaning 'the well-disposed.' And regarding heretics, Paul writes: 'by flattering speech and blessing they deceive the hearts of the innocent' (2 Cor 11:14). Because of this, he establishes laws for those sinning in the way.

If he were abrupt, if he were not good, he would not establish laws in the way of salvation for those sinning, but would hand them over to be punished. Therefore, he establishes laws for those sinning in the way, so that having traveled this way, they may possess salvation. And observe: he does not say 'those who have sinned,' but 'those sinning.' And those still sinning, through exhortations, admonitions, and laws, he leads into the way. But how can the written word mean this, considering all the implications of the law?

He will guide the gentle in judgment. Having judged, he guides the gentle; for again, gentleness often signifies indulgence. But when they are guided having been judged, they possess a perfect virtue, which the Savior taught them to have, saying: 'Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart' (Matt 11:29). And 'in judgment' can also be understood thus: judging these gentle ones to be capable of being benefited, he guides them. And the first interpretation is most in harmony with the text: that having been judged, they come upon the way having God as a guide. Or does he not guide, he who says: 'Learn from me, for I am gentle' (Matt 11:29)?

All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. In many places of the Scriptures, mercy is joined with truth. How great is the truth, so that I might say, it is above men. And observe that all things rational, and all things transcendent, and all things above, require truth. Here, however, we require mercy, so that we may be able to know the truth. It has been said in the previous sections: 'Guide me in your truth, O Lord, and in your paths' (Ps 25:5). Therefore, the beginning of walking these blessed ways is from mercy.

It becomes a part of God, and an end from the truth. [This is] for those who search out His covenant and His testimonies, not for those who search simply, but specifically those who search out [them]. Those searching the Scriptures, they too are searching out the covenant of God. To search and to seek out are the same thing.

"And His testimonies": His testimonies are the words testified by Him. You know that what has been testified is irrefutable. Therefore, the irrefutable is often signified by the name of 'testimonies' regarding the divine instructions. What? That which He Himself testified? That which He Himself confirmed. And it is possible to call things irrefutable and unshakeable testimonies, not because they were testified by someone, but because their nature is such that they testify by the truth.

"And the witness," He says, "is faithful in heaven." Concerning God, if it is said that God testifies, we do not mean that the one testifying establishes Him. John came "that he might testify about the light" (John 1:7); for John, the one testifying about the light, did not provide faith and standing to the light. The one testifying shows himself to be knowing by his knowledge, and the one testifying is shown to be diligent by his virtue. So also those who have been well-pleasing and have struggled in persecutions are called witnesses as is fitting. They showed themselves to be lovers of truth, they showed themselves to be knowers of the truth. They did not confirm the truth, but they confirmed themselves. Therefore, those things worthy of the one testifying are often called testimonies.

"For your name's sake, O Lord. Not for the sake of our diligence or our life, but because of your name. This indeed is said in another psalm: 'Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory' (Psalm 115:1); for we are enriched by you and you were named our God, so do it for your name's sake. "And atone for my sin; for it is great." We say "it is great" in this way: if so many paths have been made known to Him, and He has been led to the truth, how much sin does He have? It has been said before [the next part]: "Cleanse me from my secret sins" (Psalm 51:2), because even a small stain is a great sin to the one who is entirely cleansed.
"Who is the man who fears the Lord?" Therefore, he asks: who then is the man who fears God? To this one "he will teach in the way in which..."
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Testament and the Eyes toward the Lord
english: God himself chose. It is not a random person who fears the Lord. Many of us think this way, and many times we say, 'I simply want to fear God.' But we do not know what we are saying; for 'the fear of God surpassed all things,' as the Scripture says. And further: 'there is no lack for those fearing him.' If the one fearing God has no lack, he is most full. The 'who is' can be both small and spiritual.

He will lay down law for him in the way in which he was chosen. God himself is chosen. But it is possible for the man to be chosen; for virtue is primarily called 'choosable.' Just as that which is worthy of being loved is lovable, even if no one loves it; and likewise that which is worthy of being hated is hateful, even if no one hates it; so the 'choosable' is choosable, even if no one chooses it. For even bad things are chosen, but they are not choosable. Rather, the opinion regarding these things is mistaken. 'He will lay down law for him in the way in which he was chosen.' That is, either the one laying down law or the one receiving law. Both are true.

His soul shall be delighted in good things. This man who fears the Lord has his soul being delighted in good things. And his seed shall inherit the land. 'His seed' is not necessarily the physical—for the bad sons of many holy men were shown to exist—but the seed being generated through instruction and the imitation of virtue.

The Lord is a stronghold to those fearing him. Therefore, he speaks of the magnitude of the one fearing God. Those fearing God have no other stronghold than Him whom they fear. He is their strength, he is their king, he holds them. 'And the name' of Him has become a particular possession of 'those fearing him.' It is not a particular possession of men, but of those fearing; for indeed He gave it to all, but it has become the property of those fearing. And His covenant is to make it manifest to them. Covenants, when they are sealed, are not yet manifest...

It is written to the heirs. Therefore, this testament does not remain forever sealed, but it shall one day be released, so that the inheritance may be given to those written down. Thus he will make it known to them.

And since he often calls the divine word a testament, both the old and the new, the one before the visitation and the one after it, this testament must be made known; it must be released. It is released then when the things foretold are fulfilled by the outcome, according to: 'so that what was said might be fulfilled' (Ps 40:8). For it becomes valid when the one who made the arrangement has died; for the release happens then. Even if it is not released in the sense of a contradiction, it is released by power; for when the things commanded are being handed over to those who have received them, the testament is released.

15 My eyes are toward the Lord always, because he himself will drag my feet out of the snare (Ps 25:15). Observe that, if we do not attend precisely to the words, opposites are found. It is no longer according to the one saying, 'Great is my sin' (Ps 51:5), but rather, 'My eyes are toward the Lord always' (Ps 25:15); for he who always keeps his eyes toward the Lord has no sin at all, he has a pure heart. In this way, he is also able to see God himself.

Therefore, when he does not see at one time, and perhaps not at another, yet having his eyes toward the Lord always, he says, 'But I am with you always' (Ps 73:23). And being with you, he does not sin. Unless someone becomes outside of God, he does not sin. 'Those who prolong' therefore 'will separate themselves from you' (Ps 139:7). And what about 'and his testament'?—the testament of God is made known when someone is proven worthy to receive the things promised.

The testament of God has something paradoxical compared to the other testaments; once, the testaments of men are released. But God [is] day by day. This, therefore, both makes the testament known to those coming and to those who are worthy. Just as in all other things the things of God deviate, for it was said that this sensible light, when it comes into the middle, illuminates the eye that has it; it does not provide comprehension to the blind. But the [thing] of...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Twofold Knowledge and the Eye of the Heart
english: The light of God is perceived at once, providing sight and enlightening it. To those who are blind and do not know Him when He rises, He grants even more: to have the eyes of the mind and to perceive the light. In this way, the covenant is not suddenly released; rather, if someone today makes himself worthy to be the son of the One who possesses and is an heir, then it is revealed to him. 'My eyes are continually toward the Lord' (Ps 25:15). Since 'the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous' (Ps 34:15), it is necessary that the righteous also have their eyes continually toward Him.

They do not see Him at all times, but sometimes [they see] one of the forbidden things; for just as 'no one can serve two masters' (Matt 6:24), so no one can have his eyes toward God and toward evil or the maker of evil first. God is a spiritual essence seen by the eyes of the intellect. When the eyes of the intellect are stretched toward Him alone, they see nothing else. And the physical hands are not able to see when we see God, just as one serving God is not able to serve Mammon.

And regarding 'is not able' I say this: he is not able to do justice while he is doing injustice; for I do not say as I say 'it is not possible for a man to fly,' but rather that as far as he is righteous, he is not able toward sin, and when he is a sinner, he is not able toward virtue. 'My eyes' therefore 'are continually toward the Lord' (Ps 25:15). I always see Him. And he who sees God does not sin; 'everyone who sins has not seen Him nor known Him' (1 John 3:6). And behold the piety of the saints; even if he himself chooses to direct his eyes toward the Lord, it is evident that he is not sinning; the achievement of sinlessness is inscribed by God: 'since my eyes are continually toward Him' (Ps 25:15), because of this I escape the snare which sin prepares; for 'He Himself will rescue my feet from the snare' (Ps 124:7).

I searched for some of the ancients, which is a fine thing to say, that sometimes the eye is named in the singular of the inner man, and sometimes in the plural. In the Song of Songs, for instance, it is said: 'You have made us one from your eyes' (Song 6:9). 'My eye brought forth tears.' 'My eye was troubled from my spirit.' But in the plural: 'I lifted up my eyes to the mountains' (Song 6:4); and in the present verse: 'my eyes...'

Because of all things toward the Lord. And 'having been enlightened the eyes of the heart' (Eph 1:18). We have a twofold knowledge; for then it is knowledge of truth, when the form of each thing being known is received into itself.

The works of God are both visible and invisible; and from the greatness of these and from their beauty, the one who constructed them is perceived. And our mind is an eye seeing the invisible, the pure heart, which also sees God. And we also have the sense of eyes. And if it applies to the visible works of God in this way, as they were constructed and possess nature, it is healthy. But when, I say, seeing the sun we think it is God himself, seeing the heavenly arrangement we regard as mere idle chatter, this eye does not see correctly; for it was necessary 'that the invisible things of God be seen through the works of the creation of the world' (Rom 1:20).

The invisible things of God are seen then, when we apply [our sight] to the visible creations of God and thus from the creation of this sensible world we see clearly the invisible things of God. We are not able to see the arts and the sciences in the minds of men except when the mind is invisible. And from the constructed works or scientific contemplations we receive the sense of the mind, according to what science or art has made it. Primarily, therefore, one perceives the science of the mechanic; he who is able to receive the principles of mechanical constructions into his own intellect. Similarly also regarding others; we call that one a physician who knows medical matters as they ought to be, as the science dictates.

When, therefore, someone sees the invisible as it ought to be—and by 'as it ought to be' I say, as it is possible—and sees also the invisible creations of God, of which the human soul is also [a creation], he has this eye seeing toward God and pure through all things. When he also correctly perceives the sensible creations and the providence concerning them, he has the sensory desire—not this I mean the one of the body, but the intellect of the sensibles, the visible—succeeding, and thus he has the eyes toward the Lord through all things.

As a slave speaks. And a slave is the one serving God, who both in disposition and in deed confesses the lordship, 'he who does the will of the Father in the heavens' (Matt 7:21). 'Because he himself will drag the feet out of the snare' (Ps 91:3).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Uniqueness of the Only-Begotten Son
english: Even if the trappers and hunters seek to catch my foot, as if to throw it into a trap, I do not suffer this because I keep my eyes toward the Lord at all times. For often the settings of the wicked snares are called the disciplines of the Divine: 'the foot was caught in that trap which they hid' (Ps 7:15). Frequently the enemies of truth prepare traps, and by catching others in these traps, they themselves are snared. And there is such a thing in history: Haman prepared wood in order to crucify the righteous Mordecai, and he himself was crucified upon it. And concerning this great man it is said: 'He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and he will fall into the pit which he made' (Prov 26:27). Even if these things do not happen in this life, they certainly happen in the life to come, caught in the trap which he prepared.

For many observe these sensory things and consider themselves to be escaping them, such as: 'all who take a sword will perish by the sword' (Matt 26:51). But this is not a contradiction; rather it says: those who take a sword will fall under punishment. In many places of the Scriptures the sword signifies punishment, as in: 'I will drink my arrows, and my sword devours the blood of the wounded' (Ps 11:6), and: 'my sword was drunken in heaven' (Ps 73:4); for it also touched those who sinned in Psalm 86 and drew them toward punishment in this way: 'our soul was snatched like a sparrow from the trap of the hunters' (Ps 86:7). And see the difference: perhaps some of those being hunted by these wicked hunters are taken entirely into the traps, while others only their feet.
