Therefore those saying: 'our soul was snatched like a sparrow' were caught entirely. You say immediately: 'the trap was broken, and we were snatched away.'

Here, since the saint has his eyes toward the Lord at all times, concerning more trivial sins he says: 'my feet became a trap.' Therefore, snap them out of there, so that having become otherwise unfooted, they may run the way of the commandments of God and say: 'I ran without iniquity and I directed my course' (Ps 119:45). 16 Watch over me and have mercy on me. When God watches, mercy comes to those being watched; for they are worthy of being seen; for the [one who...]

By sinning, one is distanced from the eyes of God and from His face. Adam, indeed, when he sinned along with Eve, 'was hidden from the face of the Lord God' (Gen 3:8). They do not endure being seen by the face of God when they most clearly realize to themselves that they have sinned. But Cain, acting impudently, led himself away from the face of God; for 'Cain went out.' And the one going out does so by choice. Concerning Adam and Eve, it is said: 'the Lord cast them out.' While they were still inside, He cast them out; for it was no longer permitted for them to be inside. Nevertheless, they were surrounded by desire. They are not as evil as the one who went out from the face of the Lord. These are those about whom it is written: 'lawless ones do not abide before your eyes' (Ps 119:19). But they go outside the eyes of God voluntarily; for the eyes of God, beholding, enlighten those who are looked upon. 'For I am poor and only-begotten' (Ps 31:6).

Aetius, the leader of the Eunomian heresy, says to some: 'How great a thing you grant by saying that the Christ is the only-begotten of God. And many other creatures are only-begotten. The sun, indeed, is only-begotten.' I say to him: it is not the same thing to be something 'only-begotten' and to be an only-begotten offspring or an only-begotten Son. Therefore, these things said to others as 'only-begotten' are not said with the addition of 'Son,' or 'from the Father,' or 'offspring.' But the Savior, if He is ever so named, is called with such an addition: 'and we beheld His glory, a glory as of the only-begotten from the Father' (John 1:14). And the one who is the only-begotten Son from the Father is the Father's only. And again: 'so God loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son' (John 3:16). I say: since there is an only-begotten Son, it is impossible for there to be another son belonging to that only-begotten Son. And nothing of the creatures is only-begotten; for even if the sun were only-begotten, it is not an only-begotten creature, nor an only-begotten work, but an only-begotten sun. So also among humans we say 'only-begotten child,' not because he is the only one that exists, but because he is the only one to that parent. And that: 'he who does not believe is already condemned, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God' (John 3:18). Since, therefore, he who says these things is not an only-begotten Son, let us observe how he is called otherwise; for even if [he speaks of] David the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Meaning of Only-Begotten and Tribulation
english: If you take a man, he was not an only-begotten. He had six other brothers. Therefore, it must be avoided to say 'only-begotten' in this way, as in: 'And I myself was left alone, and they seek my soul to take it' (Ps 142:4). By what logic they say the sun is only-begotten, by the fact that there is no other sun; so when the saint is made solitary and separated from other men by life and contemplation, he is only-begotten. 'Only-begotten' therefore means 'I am and [I am] poor.'

Yet he who is thus poor is rich; for he 'is rich' in every sense and in all knowledge. But toward the God who looks upon him and bestows gifts, he is poor; just as Abraham said: 'Since I have begun to speak to the Lord, I am indeed dust and ashes' (Gen 18:27)—for he did not say 'dust and ashes' all at once, but 'since I have begun to speak to the Lord'—so also Moses, though trained in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and possessing sufficiency regarding speech, called himself 'heavy-tongued and slow of speech' (Ex 4:10) from the time he began to speak to your servant. And this man, therefore, even if he is rich—for nothing is richer than he who has his eyes always toward the Lord—yet toward the one looking upon him and showing mercy, he saw himself as poor.

And it is also possible to say 'only-begotten' meaning 'I have only one soul.' This being caught, it escapes from the snare; for to me it is only-begotten. The tribulations of my heart have widened. Not in every case, I say, do tribulations widen, but for the one bearing them bravely. The apostle writes this: 'In all things being afflicted, but not in anguish' (2 Cor 4:8).

Those knowing the Hebrew dialect say that to be in anguish, when it is named after tribulation, signifies the intention of being afflicted, the being in anguish from not bravely bearing the afflictions, such as Job, who 'in all things being afflicted was not in anguish' (Job 1:21); for how could he be in anguish, he who says: 'As it pleased the Lord, so it happened; let the name of the Lord be blessed'? And the apostles coming out from the council, because they were dishonored for the name (Acts 5:41), were not being afflicted according to the disposition, but were rejoicing. And regarding sensible things, the one contending for the crown of expectation, seeing it lying before his eyes, bravely bears the wounds, and rejoices that, being struck, he does not falter. Therefore, the name of tribulation when...
distress
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Unjust Hatred of the Wicked
english: The world came into being in six days. He who does not surpass it is under necessity. This number is perfect. What he says is this: he who is contained by the world and its parts and thus lives is necessarily under necessity. But when he surpasses the world and ascends above it, in the seventh he sabbaths from the works of the world. And becoming in the seventh—which is led, pure, and left to the people of God—he becomes blameless.

To sin against this is to approach it and act it out. If, for instance, he says, 'It is good for a man not to touch a woman,' this does not mean that to touch a woman's body with evil is the only thing. 'Bring me out of my necessities' (Psalm 143:7). Since we have given to your judgment, look at what appears to me; I say, 'Bring me out of my necessities,' so that I may not be compelled by sin and become loose toward virtue. Then you bring me out of these, if you will give me forgiveness of sins. This too can be understood: the coming punishments, the additional and distressing necessities.

The afflictions of my heart have been enlarged (Psalm 137:7). Often regarding different readings we do not doubt. Now it is necessary to know that they 'were enlarged' and not 'were multiplied'; for he who is afflicted in heart is no longer serious but also foolish. It is not permitted to take the things before this verse and after it as foolish for him who says these things, he who has his eyes always toward the Lord. 'See my lowliness and my labor, and forgive all my sins' (Psalm 143:7).

He labors in this world, having reached a peak, 'the body of lowliness.' Along with this evil, it happens to be humbled; for often affliction is called humbling according to: 'You humbled us in a place of affliction' (Psalm 143:12). When we have come into the place of affliction, we were humbled. And it is possible also to say that: when the eyes...

He always had [the Lord] before him, seeing [Him], and then he saw himself humble, even if he is righteous, just as they say concerning Abraham: not always did he see himself as 'earth and ash' (Gen 18:27), but when 'he began to speak toward the Lord.'

'Behold my enemies, for they have multiplied and unjust hatred has hated me' (Ps 35:19). Unjust hatred is hated by one who hates for no other reason than that he is zealous. In this way, indeed, the disciples of Jesus were hated. Concerning these things he teaches to send up a prayer: 'Pray for those hating you, love those hating you' (Matt 5:44). It is not we who hate anyone; for it has been said: 'Do not hate any man, love every man' (Lev 19:18). But they hate.

And it is not our sin to be hated by some, but rather an accident, when we provide no pretext of hatred. Therefore he says: 'Behold my enemies, for they have multiplied and unjust hatred has hated me' (Ps 35:19). They do not hate me with righteous hatred. They hated me as an unrighteous man, as a covetous man. And since they hate me having nothing of these things, they hate me unjustly.

And such people multiply; for if the righteous man is hated because of virtue, he possesses all the virtues according to the many things said concerning the sequence of virtues. The unrighteous hate the righteous, the intemperate the self-controlled, the arrogant the humble, and in every way those in wickedness hate the righteous. The righteous man, therefore, is one, even if he has all the virtues; for wickedness divides those having them, for it is not possible to have all the wickednesses at once. Therefore the coward cannot be bold, the superstitious cannot be impious, the rogue cannot be foolish.

In one way, Egypt hated Joseph, making him a prisoner and a captive to be tested as an evildoer. This hatred was unjust. Jezebel against Naboth worked out death, and it was this hatred that was unjust. And Herodias, the wife of Herod, worked out death against John, [showing] pity, as much as was in her. Of those, therefore, unjustly...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Boldness and the Childlike State
english: Through the vote and judgment of providence, some things are made manifest and others are not. The [fate] of John became manifest after his death, but of others before death, such as Susanna and Joseph. Even if vengeance occurs here or not, no one seeks whether it is thus or not here; for the judgments of God happen this way; for 'his judgments are unsearchable' (Ps 18:25). Guard my soul and rescue me; let me not be put to shame, for I have hoped in you (Ps 94:19). If you guard my soul without harm or injury, I know that I shall be rescued; for indeed I am rescued from the evildoers or I receive a crown because of having been afflicted. The guileless and the upright clung to me, because I endured you, Lord. Not only did I profit myself by enduring, endurance which brings salvation—for 'the one who endures will be saved unto the end' (Jas 1:12)—but I profited many because I endured you, and I had many friends. But he speaks of the guileless here as those being crushed by malice, not the well-behaved. Thus the upright were joined with them. According to the reception of malice they are guileless, but according to the taking up of virtue they are upright. For example, one who turns away from evil so as to no longer practice it has become guileless. And since after the turning away from evil he receives the doing of good, the one who turns away from evil becomes upright. It is therefore possible to call the same people guileless and upright according to one thought and another. And it is also possible thus: those who are guileless according to practice being outside of malice, while the upright are those who think the things of piety.

Redeem, O God, Israel from all his afflictions. Since He Himself has attained the petition concerning Himself, He wills also for Israel—for every discerning one and possessing mind—to have the same salvation, to become outside of the afflictions through God having redeemed. It is not out of place, then, to take these things also concerning the man of the Lord. Beginning from where we began the psalm, if we have spoken, it is because the things said concerning the man according to the Savior are common to all the righteous, only His being His own in the theological [sense]. Judge me, Lord, for I have walked in my guilelessness. The voice is very bold toward God. But he has boldness toward God, whose heart does not condemn, as the great disciple and evangelist John writes in the epistle: 'if... (1 Jn 3:20)'.

"Our heart does not condemn us; we have boldness toward God." Thus the whole psalm is sent up from much boldness. He speaks of some things as if already accomplished, and of others as present and active, and some things signify a prayer of the speaker; for he says: "Judge me, Lord, for I have walked in iniquity" (Ps 51:3). He did not say "I shall walk," but "I have walked." And here "iniquity" means guilelessness. He who has turned according to the instruction of Jesus and has become as children, he has become in guilelessness, and such a person is perfect in mind, but a child in wickedness, as the apostle writes: "Be perfect in mind, and a child in wickedness" (1 Cor 14:20).

He who is a child in wickedness does not ignore it—for how could he be a child in it if he ignored it?—but he does not act upon it. This is indeed what he says: "In my iniquity I have walked." Thus, here it is different. In both cases the guileful means what was previously said, "turned according to the children." Therefore, he who has turned according to the teaching of Jesus and has become as children does not lack sense. He does not mean the foolishness of infants, but the immobility toward evils. It was said, therefore, that a child sleeping with a woman does not accept her desire. So when someone, having become perfect, has such a state of being without desire for debauchery, he is a child in guilelessness and has become as children having turned. For observe that these children, according to their age, are not such as to be foolish or easy-going. But the perfect one has become such that it is a matter of choice to be thus a child and thus without guile. Regarding infants, this does not appear; it is not a matter of choice, but of an age that does not permit having a perfect intellect.

The "I have walked" here does not speak of an interruption or a stopping, but that I began this way from a long time ago, or I began this way from the womb; for he says: "Upon you I have been leaned from the womb, from my mother's womb you are my covering" (Ps 71:6). And the saints, concerning whom it is said: "Whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son" (Rom 8:29), belong to this boldness. And hoping in God, I shall not be weak. He no longer says "having hoped," as with "I have walked." But the hope toward God makes one strong and very capable. Since, therefore, I hope in you, "I am not weak." Concerning this...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Sacrifice of the Soul and the Meaning of Kidneys and Heart
english: Weakness is often produced by the divine disciplines. 'He brought them'—he says—'them'—evidently the Hebrews—'in gold and silver, and there was no weakness in their tribes.' For when God leads anyone in gold, that is to say, in a pure mind, and in silver—a tested word—there is no weakness. Those led thus do not suffer weakness, but are strong 'in the one strengthening' them. And as the apostle says, 'I can do all things' (Phil 4:13), he who is able to do all things does not suffer weakness; so also each of the wise men who is strong does not suffer weakness. For how could he who says to God in Psalm 92, 'I will love you, O Lord, my strength' (Ps 92:10), suffer weakness? He who hopes in wealth will surely suffer weakness.

And even if the name of weakness signifies sickness—for it does mean—this is what it says: hoping in the Lord, I shall not be sick according to the soul, I am always being healthy; for 'the one keeping the commandment, this one is healthy.' This is not spoken concerning physical health; for many keeping a commandment suffer sickness, and many transgressing commandments are healthy. 2 Test me, O Lord, and try me (Ps 26:2). Behold the boldness; 'refine my kidneys' and see if there is injustice in me. No one is called to examine such hidden things, knowing the marrow, unless he has much boldness. Therefore, some people, because of the excess of the boldness of the one speaking boldly, take the psalm for the man of the Savior. And it has been said to us already many times, that the achievements of the Savior touch the man and all perfect men. 'Test me, O Lord, and try me.' Bring me into the contest. Just as a capable athlete might say to the contest-setter: 'Test me and try me, if I am such a man as I promise.'

To test God in this way means that he is worthy to happen to receive testing from Him. 'But just as we have been tested by God to be believed in the gospel,' 'we were pleased to share with you not only the gospel, but also our own souls' (1 Thess 2:8). Someone shares his own soul with someone when he prepares him according to the quality he possesses. Not only, he says, do we have the readiness to share the gospel with you, but also our own souls. If anyone becomes an imitator of the apostle and has all his disposition and practice, he trans[fers]...

The soul of the apostle is received. This can be grasped easily: for 'we are ready even to risk our lives' because 'he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for one another'. If we, when placing our lives for those we love, were placing some intellectual or allegorical soul, it would be different; but we do this by imitating Jesus, who truly laid down a human and not an allegorical soul.

“Purify my kidneys and my heart. For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have rejoiced in your truth” (Psalm 51:10-14). Behold that through all things he trusts in his own purity. Since these things seem to be beyond human power, he immediately says: “for your mercy is before me” (Psalm 51:14). I know that even if I propose good things, even if I hasten to run after them, if you do not show mercy, I will not be perfected. Therefore, “I have rejoiced in your truth” (Psalm 51:14). One need not be self-deprecating here when the subject is truth. I recall someone saying: if you are asked, “Are you a virgin?”, say: “Because of God, I have been a virgin until now, and I wish to remain a virgin until now through faith, and entirely.” He who rejoices in the truth of God has the mercy of God before his eyes. Having the one who cooperates and perfects before his eyes, he will speak boldly toward those who have already been made upright by him. Therefore I say: “Purify my kidneys and my heart, for your mercy is before my eyes” (Psalm 51:10-14).

The kidneys and the heart are joined together in many places in Scripture: “God tests hearts and kidneys” (Psalm 7:11). “And even until night my kidneys instructed me” (Psalm 16:7). And just as when we hear 'heart', it does not mean the part of the body, but rather the one who has it sees God; again: “Hear me, you who have lost your heart”, no one loses this bodily part in such a way—if not, if God casts out a stony heart and places a fleshy one in its stead, we understand the intellect. Along with this heart, the so-called kidneys are not parts of the body. It is said that the seminal women are first composed there, and from there they easily pass into the sexual organs. Therefore, the kidneys are procreative and ministers of seed.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: True Will and the Seat of Folly
english: Therefore there are also wombs, according to that which the soul or the mind brings forth; those he calls kidneys along with the named heart. 'You are near,' he says, 'to their mouth, but far from their kidneys' (Psalm 51:4). From these kidneys you are far, O God, not from the physical parts. Therefore I have directed my kidneys and my heart, test me (Psalm 51:6). I do not have seeds capable of bearing offspring, such as to become exalted children, destructive children, like those Judas had; for it is said: 'Let them be brought to destruction. Let there be no redeemer for him' (1 Samuel 2:9), nor a helper to his children, not concerning physical children. Perhaps we do not even know if he had children. He calls all the traitors of the truth his children. Just as Paul brings forth through the gospel, he brought forth through the betrayal of those from whom he came in order to hand over Jesus: 'What do you want me to give you, and I will hand him over to you?' (Matthew 26:25). Through this eagerness, he became the father of all the traitors of the truth. 'And I rejoiced in your truth' (Psalm 96:11). The one rejoicing in the truth of God is not ashamed of his words; for Jesus said: 'Whoever is ashamed of me and my words' (Mark 8:38). But if he himself is ashamed of the one being ashamed, the one speaking boldly and remaining in the truth and preferring it above all, he himself is a weakling; let him remain in him.

4 I did not sit with a seat of futility and with law-breakers, I will by no means enter. The evil and the good are not co-existing. The one having the good cannot partake of evil. The one having been set upon evil, insofar as he is evil, is unfit for virtue. And since abstaining from evil—when one, having a nature toward them, abstains from them by choice—the children do not have intemperance, but I do not say they abstain from intemperance. The soulless and the irrational do not have impiety; and I do not say they abstain from impiety; for abstaining is a volitional movement. In the first psalm, therefore, he blesses the man who is perfect according to the inner man: 'Blessed is the man who walked not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of scoffers' (Psalm 1:1). The sophist and deceiver can say that neither the child, nor the irrational, nor the soulless 'walked in the counsel of the ungodly and in...'

"He does not stand in the way of sinners, nor does he sit in the seat of mockers" (Ps 1:1). Denying the perfect man such things, he says: how can one abstain from these by having "his own will in the law of the Lord" (Ps 119:2)? For it is not possible for everyone to have "his own will in the law of the Lord." For those who think they do not sin by returning to the law only because they fear punishment, do not have "their own will in the law of the Lord." If indeed someone were to persuade them that there is no punishment, they would do everything that is forbidden. But he who has "his own will in the law of the Lord," even if a thousand trials and many punishments were hanging over him, does not depart from the will of the law. Such were the Maccabees, such were the witnesses of the truth among us.

Just as he does not previously say that the perfect man abstains from evils by having his own will in the law of the Lord, and having said the appropriate good things here, he then says what is forbidden and says: because I walked in integrity (Ps 26:4) and hoped in you, not having my mercy weak before your eyes, since I am such a person, "I did not sit with a seat of futility" (Ps 26:5). He did not distinguish the futility of the seat by anything other than being in such a life; for life is divided among men, not a place. Diligence divides the serious man from the base men, and knowledge separates the one who has it from the ignorant. So also here, the one who walked in integrity and having hope in God, and because of this being strong and not weak, "did not sit with a seat of futility" (Ps 26:5).

And here one might say: "the child and the irrational and the soulless did not sit with a seat of futility." But they did not sit with a seat of futility because of not being by nature, but because of walking in integrity and hoping in God. "And after those who transgress, I shall by no means enter" (Ps 26:6). I never consented with those who consult in vain and sit in council to do such things, nor did I enter after transgressors. I did not only not sit, but I did not even enter; for after the entrance, the sitting is that which is in the council. Jeremiah also was attaining to this choice and virtue, saying: "I did not sit with those playing, but I was reverent from the face [of God]" (Ps 26:6-7).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Disposition and the Mirror of Action
english: “from your hand; I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness” (Ps 26:4); for these things he says to the Pantokrator. To play and to counsel in vain are the same thing; for here the playing is not praiseworthy, but it turns out to be like that which the butchers had; for they “sat down,” he says, “to eat and to drink, and they rose up to play.” This way of playing turns out to be forbidden. “I did not sit” therefore “among those playing at the council.” And it has been shown many times that the superficial things of life, those harming rather than helping, the ungodly, are called vain. He who has concern with such people, even if he does not sit with them locally, is sitting in the council of vanity.

“And with law-breakers I will by no means enter” (Ps 26:5). He says “law-breakers” here to mean those transgressing the law, not those who have no law at all—for those are lawless and law-breaking—since he was far from such people. And what about: “I will by no means enter”?—instead of: I did not enter into lawlessness; for to enter with law-breakers, that is, to transgress the law, is just as to enter into virtue means to act according to virtue. I hated the assembly of adulterers and I will not sit with the ungodly. The adulterers are either the same as those sitting in vain, or they are not far from them. And perhaps those sinning in practical matters sit in vain, while those thinking false things and having heretical opinions are the assembly of adulterers. And it is good even to say “adulterers.” No one is said to be adulterating according to his nature, but rather he who is disposed toward acting thus, yet is able to be outside of that action.

“I will wash my hands in innocence” (Ps 26:6). He who says: “In my innocence I walked” (Ps 26:7), and saying: “Test me and try me, refine my reins and my heart” (Ps 26:2), says: “I will wash my hands in innocence.” We say this: the former achievements are spiritual.

They were a disposition signifying the one speaking boldly that he has no injustice in kidneys and heart, to walk in innocence, to hope in God, to speak boldly and say, 'test me and try me' (Ps 51:6). Since therefore I am thus according to the opinion, and I have pure actions. The disposition has washed my actions. 'I will wash' (Ps 51:7) therefore 'my hands among the innocent'; for I am not satisfied with disposition alone.

And I will circle your altar, Lord (Ps 51:2). And the priests according to the law, washing, circled the altar. And such a regulation teaches that the one officiating must have pure actions. Therefore, without fail, a basin was constructed for washing 'the feet and the hands' not from any other material but from mirrors. Moses took much gold and other vessels from the Hebrews to construct many of the temple's vessels, a lampstand, a table. And the silver ones, and the gold ones, but the basin he made from the mirrors of the women (Ex 38:8), teaching that someone, having washed his actions and the moving powers of the soul, ought to reflect himself.

For such a way is called a mirror, and James writes: the 'one having become a hearer of the word' (Jas 1:22) and not a 'doer of the work' says: 'he perceived his face in a mirror and immediately went away and forgot what he was' (Jas 1:24). He did not blame the perceiving of the face in the mirror, but the departing immediately. Just as the one looking in the mirror, when he turns away from the mirror, no longer sees himself, so the one returning to the law, if he is not a doer of the law, passes away according to the one departing from the mirror and takes forgetfulness of that according to... 'but we all, with an unveiled face, are being reflected the glory of the Lord' (2 Cor 3:18). In the basin, therefore, that which became from mirrors, and the apostle washed his hands and prepared others to this. To hear the voice of your praise (Ps 51:17). You see,
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Two kinds of destruction and the path of integrity
english: For after the washing of hands, there comes also the seeing of wonders and the hearing of the voice of praise. For virtue must not stand only up to practice, but also up to contemplation and praise, up to the knowing of that very good thing, the truth, and to narrating all your wonders. The hearing of the voice of praise happens toward the narrating of all the wonders of God. He does not have in his own word any other narration or that concerning the wonders of God.

Thus, the one saying these things is a priest, not one who priesthoods by succession according to the daily shifts of the law, but just as Samuel was always in the house. And each of the saints is able to say, 'I also am with you always.' And here it is said, 'My eyes are toward the Lord always' (Ps 84:10). He who has his eyes toward God always encircles the altar of God, remaining with Him always, always performing the sacred rites.

Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place of the tabernacle of your glory (Ps 26:8). What is the difference between a tabernacle and a house? It has often been said that the tabernacle signifies progress; for it is a house of travelers, a portable house. But the house is established in one place. It signifies perfection. 'And the place of the tabernacle of your glory I have loved,' when it was progressing. The glory of the tabernacle, that is, of progress, becomes virtue both in the practical and in the contemplative. Magnificent is this one who is able to say, 'All that we were useful to do, we have done.' This one is magnificent. Primarily, the fitting is well when it becomes virtue and godliness. He is beautiful who, through chastity, achieves 'how to please the Lord.' He who is 'holy in body and spirit' (1 Cor 6:19) has beauty. Therefore, I loved the beauty of your house, the perfection.

Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood (Ps 142:10). He does not say, 'Being righteous, do not condemn me with the ungodly, do not draw me toward them.' Rather, you do not join with me with the ungodly if you prevent me from entering into ungodliness. I am prevented from entering into ungodliness if there remain to me achievements of what I have confessed, if I remain walking in innocence, if hoping in you so as not to grow weak. I am perfect. And being perfect, I do not perish with the ungodly. No one is excellent with the wicked...

It is said. The type of destruction is twofold: do not punish me with the ungodly, and do not number me among those punished because of ungodliness. And second: guard me in piety, in pleasing with 'your truth'; for 'ungodliness does not save' those who are by it. Not saving him, it destroys him.

And 'with men of blood my life' (Ps 51:14). Let me not have such a life as those murderous men have. By an analogy: those who are arrogant, being great men, yet stumbling the little ones in the church, are 'men of blood'. Do not let such things happen to me so that I have life with them. 'This life and the length of days is to love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul' (Deut 6:5). He having this life does not have life with men of blood; he is dead toward the men of blood, but dead because he does not have the life which they have.

Of whom lawlessness is in [their] hands. Still in their own practices they have lawlessness. They do not possess [it], but they have [it]. And their right hand was filled with gifts. It is possible also to slander judges as bribe-takers. And even those who do not judge, many times we bribe when we show partiality to someone. And if he acquires pleasant things for himself, he bribes; he receives gifts from himself.

But I, in my innocence, went my way. No one of those bribing and having the right hand filled with gifts, no one of the lawless and men of blood, went in innocence. Such was Elymas the sorcerer, ungodly and walking in lawlessness and having the right hand full of gifts; for it seemed to be excellent at deceiving, and it is said concerning him: 'O full of all deceit and all trickery, son of the devil' (Acts 13:10). But he, being full of all trickery, is not able to say: 'In my innocence I went my way'.

Deliver me, O God, and have mercy on me (Ps 51:1). He who walks in iniquities, existing in the iniquities previously mentioned, says 'deliver me'. Even if I am in the most distant iniquities, and with your cooperation all the things of virtue are lifted up for me, yet you have still touched me, the 'body of humiliation', yet 'in the place of my affliction' I am; therefore 'deliver me'. For my foot has stood in uprightness. The same thing as standing in uprightness is the foot of the inner man and that in the rock according to what was said: 'You stood upon a rock' (Matt 7:24).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Divine Light and the Armor of Truth
english: "my feet"; for straightness is like an uncracked and continuous rock. My foot is therefore firm in my straightness. Standing in straightness is the same as standing in faith; for it says, "for indeed you have stood in faith" (Ps 118:137). Such a standing does not happen without Jesus. Those having this standing stand by him, as he says, "there are some standing here," meaning, here by me.

"I will bless you in the churches, Lord" (Ps 22:4). In the church I will offer thanksgiving hymns, not outside anywhere. He who promises to give thanks to God outside, contrary to the ecclesiastical opinion, does not bless in the churches.

Of David; before being anointed. The psalms before this were "to David"; this one is written "of David." He himself brought it forth by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. He sent it forth "before being anointed." Thirdly, David appears anointed; first, when he went to Samuel and was anointed, and Samuel to Jesse. Second, after Saul had finished; the beginning was preserved; for some were seeking David as king, while others [sought] Mephibosheth the son of Saul. After the son of Saul was betrayed by Abner because of the appearance of a woman, David was anointed over all the people in Hebron. Therefore, he was anointed a third time. Previously, the peak clearly belongs to a private person. Second, in order that he might rule a part of the people. After the death of the son of Saul, in order that he might also rule the rest of the people, he has been anointed again and again by all. We seek, therefore, regarding what kind of anointing he speaks here. One says that it is generally regarding every anointing; he says the psalm was spoken before being wholly anointed, and quite so; if before the first anointing, it is clearly also [before] the second and the third. If before the second, not necessarily before the first. If before the third, not necessarily before the first and second. But the psalm seems to have been spoken especially before the first anointing, which is before every anointing. Therefore, the psalm is "before being anointed."

"The Lord is my light and my savior" (Ps 22:1); whom shall I fear? If God enlightens me and saves me, whom do I fear? Neither man, nor an evil power, nor even the devil himself. And the "who" here is instead of "no one"; for this usage lies here continuously.

In the Scriptures: 'What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us?' (Romans 8:31) stands instead of 'no one.' 'Who shall bring a charge against the elect of God?' (Romans 8:33) stands instead of 'no one,' and furthermore: 'Behold, the Lord helps me; who can harm me?' (Psalm 27:7) because of many things signified by the word, as it has been said elsewhere, now the 'who' lies instead of 'no one.' Therefore, the word is not about sensible life and some sensible illumination; for by the divine light the mind and the soul are illumined. And life is always joined to salvation. This is the same: eternal life and eternal salvation; for 'Israel' is indeed 'saved by the Lord with an eternal salvation' (Psalm 116:8).

That life is always joined to the illumination, it is seen from many things: 'the life was the light of men' (John 1:4), and again this saint prays: 'enlighten my eyes, lest I sleep into death' (Psalm 139:24), signifying that he who is deprived of the illumination sleeps into death; not the common death, but the one opposed to the blessed life. Therefore, 'the Lord' is 'my light and my salvation' (Psalm 27:1). He himself guides me, speaks to me according to the hidden, enlightens me through which he speaks, and his word prepares to have salvation immediately. Since I said that the one having been illumined has life in every way—the Savior himself also says: 'I am the light of the world; he who follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life' (John 8:12).

He who has the light of life is not defeated by anything, especially since the truth of God itself becomes a shield fighting for him; for 'his truth shall surround you as a weapon' (Psalm 5:12). Therefore, it immediately reaches: 'The Lord is the defender of my life; from whom shall I dread?' (Psalm 27:1). The Lord is the defender of my life; from whom shall I dread? Who is able to make me afraid? I am clothed in 'the armor of God' (Ephesians 6:13), I 'have the shield' (Ephesians 6:16) of faith, extinguishing 'all the flaming arrows of the evil one' (Ephesians 6:16). If the shield of faith extinguishes the arrows of the evil one, it does much more for those of inferior archers; for there are also other worthless archers. For indeed, 'behold, the sinners have bent a bow, they have prepared arrows in a quiver to shoot at those upright in heart' (Psalm 7:12). I am not defeated by anything. The armor of God is unhurt and unstriking. His shield is truth. And no one is able against the truth.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The distinction between affliction and enmity
english: It is to happen; 'for we are not able,' he says, 'according to the truth, but on behalf of the truth.' It is an armor that protects the one equipped and keeps him unharmed. 'Lord' therefore [is] 'the defender of my life.' He does not say this concerning common life; for many of those reclining toward God and having put on his armor have died the common death, so that I may not say 'all'; but also many violent ones stood by, of whom Naboth is [one] and many apostles. Isaiah indeed was afflicted. 2 In the approaching of those intending to harm me to eat my flesh. Those intending to harm the soul eat flesh. If anyone is found having flesh, he has strong enemies against him. The flesh is his food. And the flesh, about which Paul says: 'for the mindset of the flesh is enmity toward God' (Rom 8:7), and: 'we are not in the flesh' (2 Cor 5:3); if he were speaking about the sensory flesh, his word would be false; for all the saints, being in the flesh, pleased God while still surrounded by flesh, and they are not able to say: 'we are not in the flesh.' But when someone kills the flesh and casts down its works, he is not in the flesh. Therefore it is said: 'those of Jesus Christ have crucified the flesh with its desires' (Gal 5:24) and they have it having been made dead, no longer acting. The one being crucified has his hands free to do and his feet to go wherever he wills. Therefore those having been crucified with Christ crucified the flesh with its desires, they left it dead, as if to carry the death of Jesus remaining in their own flesh: 'always we carry the death of Jesus' (2 Cor 4:10). 'Lord, defender of my life; from whom shall I dread? In the approaching of those intending to harm me to eat my flesh' (Ps 27:1-2), since they did not find that which they desired as food, 'they grew weak and fell' (Ps 27:2). See then what this signifies.

2 Those distressing me and my enemies, they themselves grew weak and fell (Ps 27:3). They had come to tear me into weakness, to treat me badly. But for them the passion has happened which they intended to inflict on me; for if they had found 'flesh,' they would have devoured me into weakness and consumed me into sickness. But since they did not find 'flesh,' 'they themselves grew weak and fell' (Ps 27:2), having been subjected to famine. 'Those distressing me and...

"My enemies themselves have grown weak and fallen." Not every one who afflicts is an enemy; the good person also afflicts. For many enemies, intending to afflict and surround those against whom they are hostile, are not able to do this unless God permits it. But many also afflict without being enemies. For instance, parents afflict while disciplining children, and masters afflict slaves, and they are not enemies at all.

It can indeed be said that both groups—the afflicters and the enemies—have grown weak and fallen. And this is possible: the afflicters themselves are also enemies, for they do not afflict for the sake of exhortation and instruction. They are not such as it is said of: "He who brings forth wisdom from his lips, strikes a man without heart with a rod" (Prov 26:3), and: "What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod or with love?" (1 Cor 4:21); these afflicters are not enemies.

But there is a time when the enemy also afflicts; and not by necessity. But what kind of "killing" [is meant]?—this is not living according to evil activities. He who carries the killing of Jesus does not live licentiously; he has been killed toward licentiousness, he has been killed toward making his belly his god, he holds his members inactive regarding fleshly desires; he does not allow them to be autonomous, for he has purified desires. For it has been said: "Let not sin reign in your mortal body to obey its desires" (Rom 6:12).

If an ambush is set against me, my heart shall not fear. Therefore, how it does not fear nor tremble is explained by saying: "Whom shall I fear?" and: "From whom shall I tremble?" (Ps 56:3), since the expression "whom" seems to exceed [the scope of the question]. Even if a whole ambush of evil men and powers is set against me, my heart does not fear; even if they kill the body, the heart remains unshaken, my mind is not struck. If a whole camp with great generals comes against me, I have a fearless heart, my mind does not fear. For the multitude of armies is called by this name: Jacob, when he was returning from Mesopotamia and was about to meet Esau, saw an ambush of angels; for how could there not be an ambush regarding one who was about to go against an enemy who was rushing and hating him? And Elisha similarly: an ambush.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Progressions and the Single Request
english: He was stationed like Elisha of Syria. A divine encampment has happened around him, not according to history, but according to the spiritual sense. The soul is led by the mind and is yoked to it. If someone wishes to take the will as well, it is possible. The name of the spirit of the heart in Psalm 101 sometimes signifies the will, but the mind is to be taken here.

If war rises up against me, in this I hope (Psalm 27:3). There is even more of an encampment if war rises up against me; in my heart I hope, which does not fear, being strengthened by divine fear; 'fear of the Lord surpassed all' (Psalm 34:9), and 'there is no loss to those fearing him' (Psalm 34:18). 'In this I hope.' I am confident that this heart becomes everything to me. The virtues are the weapons of piety. 'Let us put on the weapons of light, let us cast off the works of the flesh' (Romans 13:12). The weapons of light are the virtues, the pious thoughts, the mysteries and doctrines of the truth. In these secure fortunes, no one is shaken, but has unashamed hope. 'In this,' therefore, 'I hope,' not simply in my thought, but in that which is thus secured.

One thing I asked of the Lord, this I will seek (Psalm 81:10). God the Giver is of many good things; for He 'will give good things to those asking Him' (Psalm 81:11), and He fills the desire with His own good things; for He is 'the one filling your desire with good things' (Psalm 81:15). One can therefore say more probably that these good things are, in essence, virtues, and in essence, the mysteries of the truth. When someone—so that I may say it this way—possesses the genus of the virtues, he possesses all. Therefore, he asks for one request, all virtue. When someone does not already possess well-established virtues, he does not send up one request; for if he is in the process of advancing and becoming greater in other things, he pours out requests again and does not ask for one request. But he who sends up a prayer for the whole of virtue and for the piety of the doctrines sends up one. It is also possible to say this: the...

There are many progresses. These are signified by the name of the tabernacle, as it has been shown many times. If anyone becomes in some progress and asks to have God as a helper, to have Him as a succor, he does not remain in this request; for he passes from progress to progress, becoming better than himself. Many tabernacles are spoken of, but there is one house.

Therefore, the one having come to perfection asks one request. 'One' then, 'I asked from the Lord' (Psalm 27:4). And this is also possible: their help—so that, having been prepared for the wars and the encampments that arise, they are able—does not ask one request. They seek much help: a military encirclement, the strength of walls, constructions. But he who has God himself as a helper and asks for this [one thing], asks one request. 'All in all' happens, as each of those having been perfected has Him as all things: as bread, as light, as teacher, as shepherd. 'One' then, 'I asked, this I seek out'. He who says 'I seek out' and 'I asked' shows that the one seeking does not yet have [it], and longs to find. For no one has perfection unless even if he reaches the very goal and the end of virtue and of union with God.

4 [of] dwelling with me in the house of the Lord all the days of my life (Psalm 27:4). I did not begin to ask now, but because of the beginning of the end I began; for the one beginning an art begins because of the end of the art. Those having reached this dwell. 'Blessed are all those dwelling in your house' (Psalm 68:1). He who has the blessed life is in the days; it does not happen in nights. Even if ever it becomes in night, but he takes up the beginning of longing for life, he comes out of the night.

4 [of] beholding my part in the delight of the Lord and sheltering in his temple. Just as I dwell all the days in the house of God, so in all the days I behold the delight of the Lord and I shelter in his temple. But the delight of the Lord is the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Body as a Tent and the Mystery of the Incarnation
english: His participation. And his state is his temple, in which God is found, in which God dwells. Perfect virtue is a house of God. 'And Christ as a son upon his house, of which we are the house,' and; 'Do you not know that you are the temple of God?'; except that we have called both virtue and perfect holiness a house, and secondly, faithful men. For this reason they become a house, because they possess virtue and holiness. It is not that the virtue makes the participants a house of God, but because of the virtue do those sharing in it become a house. And that which is over all is written as an end most especially. But because this does not happen all at once, we call the things before the end 'ends'; for there are also ends before the end: 'I have seen the end of all things' (Psalm 37:30). 'When a man has completed, then he begins.' So when he has completed, he sees the end of a certain progress; then, beginning, he seeks to see another end, and over all things he encounters the end that is over all things.

Take for me an example from the construction of a city: he who desires to build a city magnificently and—what more can I say?—royal, begins the construction. He begins to quarry stones. Often the quarrying completes much. When he has prepared those which are needed and as many as are needed, then he begins to seek a place where he will raise up the city. It becomes 'God all in all' (1 Cor 15:28), not all in each one, but 'in all'. In one he is a mourner, when someone hastens to be such; in another a good judge, in another righteous, in another a dispenser of grace, in another as a teacher to a disciple. And in all, indeed, he becomes all things to those who have drawn near to him, but not all things in each one, but either one, or two, or three gifts. And so that we may make this clear regarding the gifts: 'Receive of the Spirit'; one has the word of wisdom, another the word of knowledge, another the gift of healings. But when someone becomes perfect, no longer having the 'earnest of the Spirit' (Eph 1:14), but the Spirit itself, he becomes all things in each one. I become a perfect bearer and a bishop of the temple of God, not having anything else before my eyes except this, the temple of God, seeing it; for he has hidden me in his tent in the day of my evil. For this reason, 'One thing I have asked and this I will seek: that in the day of my evil he has hidden me in his tent' (Psalm 27:8). And progress was being spoken of. Amidst many evils lying ahead and those willing to harm me, he has hidden me. And it is sometimes said...

And the body is a tent; for it is said, 'the earth is a tent for the prudent' (Ps 103:29), and, 'we groan being in the tent' (2 Cor 5:4). Often, while we are still dwelling in the tent, the body hides us so that we are not harmed by it when someone, as I said previously, surrounds the death of Jesus in the body and strikes the body and enslaves it.

'He covered me in the secrecy of his tent.' For the secrecy of his tent is not harmful, but a covering. But the accessible part of the tent, which is already [laid] bare, harms rather. In this way, I am a body dwelling as if not being in a body, being swallowed up of the mortal 'by life.'

To swallow and to swallow up in the Scripture signifies victory; 'in whom they raised [us], therefore we would be swallowing living ones,' instead of 'he conquered us.' And, 'Israel was laid waste, now it has become among the nations like a useless vessel' (Ps 79:6). 'All,' he says, 'who eat him will transgress.' But the eater is being swallowed up. In the tent, therefore, 'in the secrecy of his tent he hid me.'

One who has become in the body is also able, if he perceives the cause and the mystery through which it has happened in him, to be hidden in the secrecy of it; for having immediately known the mystery and the cause, he will harm himself and will not be swallowed up. And this can be said about the Savior or toward the Savior. If regarding him it is said: 'in the secrecy of his tent he hid me,' he had a tent, he became man. The descent of the Savior has a hidden mystery.

He who is able, after the one who became flesh has tabernacled in him, to say: 'we beheld his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth' (John 1:14), was covered 'in the secrecy of his tent.' His covering has become the perceiving of the mystery of the Savior's coming. The Jews, indeed, did not perceive, and as many as are such, and they were not covered 'in the secrecy of his tent.'

And it is possible also, according to the previous argument, for the secrecy of the tent to be the end; for because of this they advance, even if it eludes those who advance; for unless someone reaches it, he is not able to see it as it is, seeing God then 'as he is' (1 John 3:2), when he comes to the end of blessedness. But, have we beheld already? — we certainly do not know. In part...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Commonality of the Righteous and the Rock
english: We know. But is it the human race that says these things? It is not the Lord's man who says these things, but the race of the righteous, the collection of the saints; for even the Son of God does not say according to man, 'The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?' (Ps 27:1). Many times I have said that the things said about the righteous men and about the Lord's man are said in common; but they are common not according to equality, for without comparison he surpasses all even in these things. I say these things are common according to participation, just as I say the medical art is common to the one who has been perfected and holds it without lack, and to those still progressing. I do not say common according to quantity, but according to quality.

The adulterer is not hidden, but goes outside the tent; for he does not abstain from 'the fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul' (Gal 5:17). But he who clearly lives all things according to the flesh—being uncontrolled, living in luxury, and altogether preferring pleasures over the watchful ones, even if they be unendurable—he has his tent manifest, he has the body manifest; it is evident that a body surrounds him. For he who says, 'But you are not in the flesh', teaches being outside the passions of the flesh. But he who is outside the passions of the flesh is hidden in the tent. According to another sense, the tent is a hiding place, not known to all.

'You have raised me in a rock' (Ps 92:14). It is not a great thing to be raised in a sensible rock so as to send up grateful praises. All things happening by God, on which it is fitting to give thanks, which must be praised, are not at hand, nor are they able to be present to everyone. The rock, therefore, is the unshakeable Word of God himself, who, becoming the one around, is not cast down. For it has been said also in others: 'The judges laid hold of a moving rock' or 'their strong [ones]'; and indeed, rulers being outside the rock seem to be strong and to prevail over the uncertain. But when they become near the rock, they are immediately defeated.

And I said also yesterday, that the swallowing up signifies the victory; 'in rising up against us living, they would have swallowed us up', and; 'those swallowing up Israel with their whole mouth' (Ps 83:5). The one being defeated is swallowed up, the one surrounding swallows up. You have, therefore, some enigma having happened in the Exodus, Aaron having thrown his staff according to the guidance of God; and it has become...
the scepter of truth
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Psalms and Chronology
english: A shout of victory is offered at his tent. The shout signifies victory, for it is a loud cry made against fallen enemies. For instance, when they encircled Jericho and blew the horns and shouted, the walls of Jericho fell at their shout. Jericho, allegorically, is a place on earth, interpreted as the moon; the place on earth is not according to its increase, but according to its decrease, like the fool: for 'fool' means 'as the moon changes.' Therefore, when he encircles his tent according to all interpretations—the progress was called a tent—the one progressing and succeeding truly becomes a circle of it. And again, the body was called a tent. When the inner man resolutely sets himself against the body, he becomes a circle around it and conquers. When anyone encircles the tent, the body of Jesus, through faith, he is proved a conqueror.

6 I will sing and I will play to the Lord (Ps 94:1). It was said to us in the earlier psalms that to sing means to have contemplation, to send up praises and songs without an instrument. It was said that to play means to practically pour out the song of triumph. Both, then, he says, are sufficient for me: I will play and I will sing. I sing by contemplating the truth. He who takes in the dogmas of piety and having contemplation of their scientific and wise nature, sings. But he who, taking the body as an instrument, both a lyre and a psaltery, striking its strings which are all the impulses and the senses, being able to bring forth a psalm harmoniously, that one plays. This, then, is the holy man who is promised to do the two: to sing and to play. He who subdues his body and disciplines it and performs the moral virtues, such as one doing almsgiving, one establishing gentleness, one advancing in courage, he plays. But he who contemplates each mystery of the truth and is able to penetrate with knowledge every dogma of piety, he sings.

Regarding: 'In the fiftieth, as if we receive some confession upon sin?'—obviously it lies there: 'When Nathan came' and rebuked him concerning Uriah (2 Sam 12). It was a time of confession, and the psalm there sends up a confession. After he had reigned and entered to Uriah, that psalm occurred. Here, however, 'before being anointed' is sung, so that also...

This one differs from that one in time and in practice. But how then is one singing? For virtue is unchangeable. Judas neither saw nor sang to the Lord. Those handed over to the Satan, in order that they might be disciplined not to blaspheme, had not possessed a certain dwelling place and progress in faith and virtue.

However, observe that the various psalms are not altogether spoken concerning one and the same person; for this we have said, that they depend on what kind of person is established according to virtue or wickedness. It is not the same thing to say that a man is without sin and to say that a righteous man is without sin. The one possessing righteousness is not able to be made subject to sin; for how could it be, if the opposites do not coexist? The one possessing evil is not able to have good, unless he first turns away from the evil. Look to what kind of person, not to this one or that one; for when I say that the faithful man is able to do all things, I do not say this one or that one, but all things for the one possessing faith. And even if ever, being faithful, someone possesses the power to do all things and succeeds, but the things of faith fall away from him, I do not say that the faithful man does not succeed, but that this specific man does not succeed.

But is the psalm after this one not earlier in time? The psalms do not require such an order as you seek. That psalm is the one rebuking the Syrian, David. King Saul was at his peak and very much in strength when David was slandered and fled. But much later happened the things concerning Uriah, and much later happened his reigning over all after the final anointing—and this was the third. And much later happened the things concerning Uriah. He was not yet reigning when David threw him out as having taken loaves and the sword of Goliath. Not thus, therefore, is the order of the psalms sought according to the order of times, but according to the successes, but according to the events.

The number fifty has something exceptional; and because of its virtues, the psalm of confession was placed upon it. Observe, then: according to the number fifty, repentance is accomplished. Immediately, too, when the Savior was murmuring at the grumbling of the Pharisees concerning the woman cleansed by him and who came to wash his feet with her own tears and to wipe them with her own hair three times, he proposed: 'Two debtors were to a lender; one owed ten drachmas...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Significance of Seven and Seventy
english: Fifty, and the other five hundred. And he observes that regarding both of those who repent, he has arranged the number in five; for the five hundred has a relationship to the fifty, since the fifty, having been multiplied tenfold, becomes five hundred.

Therefore, such a mystery is concerning the number, and the psalm of confession is arranged in this; for the number is indicative of mercy. Indeed, those who have conquered a war also receive a fiftieth. And on behalf of those who did not fight, but kept the vessels, the fighters, having survived, give a fiftieth. And the priest, beginning to officiate from twenty-five years until fifty years, remains. After fifty years he no longer officiates, but guards the tent.

And the word shows that it is necessary first to establish and to perform all things priestly and to become a perfect priest so as to reach the number fifty, and then to guard the things in the tent. And the word teaches that in the labors of works and growth there is need, but when one is perfected, he ought to guard what he established. Just as one taking up health is in the healing, in the bringing of aids to him. But when he has firmly obtained health and a stable tent, he subsequently brings to himself things for the guarding of health, not doing those things that create health, but guarding things.

For this reason also God placed Adam in Paradise 'to work and to guard it' (Gen 2:15). To work, so that he might bear fruit, so that he might bring forth perfect fruits; and to guard, in addition, the plants that bore fruit. Just as to work and to guard signifies the two—to work being the exercising of virtue and of the knowledge of truth, and to guard being the keeping of things perfected—so also the priest, as much as remains of the number fifty, is in officiating. But when he fulfills this and is shown to be perfect, then he, such as that is, guards the things in the...

In the tabernacle, he no longer works himself, but receives the firstfruits of others working and takes the tithes. This number is the beginning of a square number. A square is measured equally, twice two, thrice three. Thus this is seven times seven; and moreover, the addition of the unit is cast down as the beginning of another seventy times seven. For this reason, when the Savior is asked by Peter concerning repentance, 'How often does one sin?' he says, 'Until seven times'; he says, 'I do not say to you until seven only, but even seventy times seven' (Matt 18:22). Seven times seven is a square. This has holy sides; for the seven has been shown to us many times to be blessed everywhere: 'God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it' (Gen 2:3), and, 'The eyes of the Lord, looking upon all the earth, are seven' (Prov 4:4). I do not say seven as three and four, but it is a most full oversight and supervision.

Thus also in the feast of the weeks, the Pentecost is celebrated according to the old and the new covenant; for you have in the Acts of the Apostles that when the Pentecost was fulfilled (Acts 2:1), the gift of the Holy Spirit was given, and the various gifts of the Spirit were measured; for it was necessary to exceed the seven times seven number and to take the beginning of another such number and thus be perfected. The fifty, therefore, is received over many great things. The seven, indeed, is again perfect. The tabernacling is done in the seventh month according to the Hebrews. Again, for six years the earth was sown, but in the seventh year it was unsown. That year remained, being kept for the poor. And there also, if a festival is led through seven years, that year is again weekly. Seven times seven is also led according to what is called the Jubilee by the Hebrews. The Jubilee is a Pentecostal year. Through fifty years it completed some festive things.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Seventy Years and the Nature of Prayer
english: oikonomia (household/management)

He asks: 'Tell me, when do you think that which is in Isaiah will be fulfilled?' 'And it shall be,' he says, 'after seventy years Tyre shall be restored to its ancient state' (Isaiah 39:7). From when of the seventy years are they counted? Not so that I may take them according to history, but seventy cycles of the sun of righteousness, seventy years. For the sun goes around, illuminating souls and making the doctrines of truth manifest and sending forth its rays. Therefore, when anyone is perfected and has reached the end of his progress, then the seventy years are established for him. As for the stated text, the deviation is not appropriate, but as a question, it is necessary.

Listen, O Lord, to my voice, which I have cried out (Psalm 142:1). I cried a voice to You, requesting what it would be good for me to have. And that which is paradoxical: it sends back a prayer of prayer; for he who entreats someone whose prayer has failed, offers a prayer in place of a prayer. Praying, I cried out to You again, beseeching, so that You might listen to this voice, which I cried out to You. For not everyone who cries according to the inner man cries to God, but he who says the things of God, bringing a petition to Him. The Sodomites also cry, but not to God: 'The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has filled [the heavens] and their sins are very great' (Genesis 18:20). And concerning the Ninevites it is said: 'The cry of their wickedness ascended' (Jonah 3:4), the multitude of wickedness. And in Isaiah: 'I waited to do justice, but he made a cry instead' (Isaiah 5:7). Thus, the cry of the Sodomites is an injunction of wickedness.

But he who prays cries to God when he has an uplifted voice, when he prays concerning great things, not concerning trivial and contemptible things, the one requesting that good things might be given to him. And the other Evangelist, the Holy Spirit, interpreted the good things; for writing in the same place, Matthew says: 'He will give good things to those asking Him' (Matthew 7:11), while Luke says: 'He will give the Holy Spirit' (Luke 11:13). The Spirit, being one, is a multitude of good things according to His various gifts; for he who has the Holy Spirit has the gifts of the Spirit, which are many good things. And in essence He is one, but in His thoughts He is many good things, just as God is one in essence. It is said also that He is many according to various thoughts: good, unshakeable, unchangeable, fountain, light; and likewise the Savior is one.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Satiety and the Divine Light
english: That which is called life and truth according to its underlying reality. 'Ask,' he says, 'the great things, and the small things will be added to you.' Thus, the one asking for small things says to God, but not with a shouting voice. 'Ask,' he says, 'the heavenly things, and the earthly things will be added to you.' Therefore, the one sending up a prayer concerning sensible things previously does not cry out to God; he speaks to Him calmly. But the one asking for those truly great and heavenly things and those making one god-like cries out to God. For thought is the cry.

7–8 'Have mercy on me and hear me,' my heart has said to you (Psalm 51:1). My mind has said to you: 'from you I ask mercy.' My heart expects mercy from you and says to you, 'hear me.' These things turn back toward themselves: the one being shown mercy by God is heard, and the one being heard is shown mercy. It is not possible, then, to say one before the other. But to hear precedes to show mercy. Yet not in time before. And just as it is not possible to say appearance before color, nor color before appearance. If there is color, there is appearance. If there is appearance, it has been colored. Appearance is pre-conceived. It is necessary for there to be an appearance, so that there may be such color. And the 'it is necessary' I do not take according to time, but according to thought.

'My heart has said to you.' It signifies persons. According to every word, the three persons are signified: the one speaking, and that toward which he speaks, and that concerning which he speaks. Therefore, the person of the one praying is the one now announcing. And he announces the petition to no one other than God. 8 'I sought your face' (Psalm 27:8). My heart saying, 'have mercy and hear me.' I did not seek your face before now. Your face, I did not entreat only now: 'let your face shine upon me and we shall be saved' (Psalm 27:9). And 'I sought' signifies a seeking that was not raised. 8 'Your face, Lord, I will seek.' My heart, Lord, will seek your face. Even if 'I sought' and I had it grasping me, I do not cease until this. Again I seek it. 9 'Do not turn your face away from me' (Psalm 27:9). The eye which is healthy and preserves the virtue of sight, when light is present, has a desire for it, and it is never satisfied; for light is insatiable for the eyes: 'sweet to the eyes,' as the Preacher says (Psalm 19:8). But no one takes satisfaction from the sweet. There is sweet...

Things that satisfy the child, like the sweetness from honey. But that which comes from the light has no satiety, especially when the vision possesses its own inherent virtue. Therefore, moving from the sensible to the intelligible: the eye of the inner man, or the eyes, are never filled and never receive satiety from the face of God; for it is always appearing, illuminating and increasing the desire. 'The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord' (Ps 4:6); it remains. But that of the sun, or generally of the sensible light, does not remain. For if anyone withdraws from seeing the light or closes the eyes, he does not have it marked. But the intelligible light appears to remain to the one having been illuminated; it is not cast away.

Do not turn away in anger from your servant (Ps 103:13). It is possible for one to seem as if God is turning away, but not in anger. Some thought that He turned away from Job when his possessions, his children, and his body were delivered to the one asking; but this did not happen in anger. May it not happen so concerning me, from our own sluggishness, so that you should turn your face away from me in anger. Both are therefore possible; may such a thing not be done to me, so that having been angered, you turn away from me. Or thus: may you not be angered in such a way that I am deprived of your presence. 'Become my helper, do not cast me off' (Ps 142:5). Some manuscripts have: 'do not forsake me.' To cast off, to reject, to send away, is the same as to cast off. For in Isaiah it is carried: 'and he casts him off' (Isa 17:4). And observe the precision of the word; it does not always mean the occurrence of a becoming, but rather signifies that which the addition intends. And 'become my helper' is applied here. For one who is becoming a helper to someone does not simply 'become.' I have also said at other times that verbs which imply a becoming, if they are spoken unrestrictedly, signify a creative act: 'all things came into being through him,' instead of 'all things came into being through him.' 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth' (Gen 1:1). It is not 'what He made,' but this very thing: 'heaven and earth.' And when it says: 'become my helper, do not forsake me,' it says: 'become a helper to me.' The relationship signifies the helper in relation to the one being helped. So we also say: 'become my teacher,' and it does not mean they are a teacher, but 'become a teacher to me.' Such things are also...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The distinction between hating parents and hating God
english: Things said about the Savior: 'Understand the apostle and high priest of our confession, faithful in him who made him' (Hebrews 3:6). He made him an apostle; he did not merely make him, but an apostle. And behold, the essence of the Son is eternal. But to become an apostle happens then, when some depart from him; for he is sent to those far off. And observe that the becoming an apostle co-exists with him being far from certain ones, those having been distanced from him.

Again, he becomes high priest when he is set over those for whom he is consecrated. But it is not then that the hypostasis of the Savior has become, as those think, but the beginning, the high priesthood. Thus also in the deeds of the apostles he says: 'Let all the house of Israel know securely this, that God made him both Lord and Christ' (Acts 20:25). He becomes Lord of those fleeing to serve him. If therefore anyone begins to serve him even today, he has become Lord to him today. And if anyone subjects him to his own kingdom and to his own priesthood, he has become Christ to him today; for the Christ declares nothing other than king and high priest.

Indeed, Aaron was said to be the Lord's Christ, and the kings were said to be the Lord's Christs, and concerning Saul: 'The Lord is a witness, and his Christ' (1 Samuel 24:6). And this: 'Do not touch my Christs.' 'My helper' therefore means 'become, do not lead me astray'; do not send me away from you. Concerning some it is said: 'God will cast them away, because they did not listen to him, and they shall be wanderers among the nations' (Psalm 80:12). When they depart, they were led astray here and there, no longer having a firm purpose. And he assigns the cause to us: 'because they did not listen.' It is not God's will to cast anyone away from him. But it is his will to send away those who did not listen, so that he might not seem to hate virtue. And since they did not listen, 'according to the abundance of their lawlessness, cast them out, because they have turned aside from you, Lord' (Psalm 64:6). This is what it means to be led astray.

And they say also that the word is etymologized such that the iron filings are called the 'koras'. Easily the filings are scattered like dust. May I not become such a thing as to be led astray. I wish to be a vessel of gold or a vessel of bronze, but certainly not the dross.

And [it] is sent away and cast out. 9 And do not leave me, Lord God my Savior. For you are also my Lord—for I serve you—and my God—for I am a child of Abraham, and God is 'of Abraham and of Isaac' (Gen 21:10) and clearly of them—I am as a slave toward a lord, as one worshipping sincerely toward God, being healed, as one being saved toward a Savior. Since therefore all these things have become mine, you do not leave me.

10 For my father and my mother have left me. I wish to clarify this with an explicit evangelical sense, so that it may be understood from that. And the Old Scripture and the Gospel and the very exhortations of the Savior teach to love father and mother. Listen: if anyone hates a father, he does not hate him as a father, but as an impious man; and he hates him not in his capacity as father, but in his capacity as impious. And he who loves a father, does so because of this, that he truly pursues [him] when he is thus trained by fear and instruction, when he is thus trained as a righteous man. 'Well' indeed 'a father trains a righteous man'. I have said therefore that almost all the Scriptures speak against and punish those who fall away from the honor of parents: 'he who slanders a father or mother shall be executed by death'. Therefore listen: 'he who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me'. Even though [it says] 'honor your parents and love father and mother' (Ex 20:12), but when [one does so] above God, he is slandered; for when he is about to confess the truth while being restrained by persecution, and when he says, 'because of the old age of the father and the mother I do not wish to die', and betrays [them], loving the parents above God, he has preferred the disposition toward the parents over the piety toward God. And this is what is slandered.

In the Gospel, indeed, the Savior says: 'Having turned', he says, 'Jesus said to the crowds: If anyone wants to come after me, if he does not hate his father and his mother and his wife and his brothers and his children, he cannot be my disciple' (Luke 14:26). If you have legislated honor concerning parents and promised me great labors saying: 'Honor your father and your mother, so that it may go well with you and you may be long-lived on the earth' (Matt 19:17), how do you now say: 'If someone does not hate father and mother, he cannot follow me'? The hatred here is called differently, the [hatred] not...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Virtue as the Foundation of the House
english: To prefer something over God. Since God is to be loved most in a time of struggle, in a time of persecution, the love of God must be preferred above all. If one pulls away from parents or the old age of a parent, 'honor God, since you are not able to follow me' (Exodus 20:12). Therefore, to hate the father and the mother does not mean that kind of hatred by which we are provoked and loathe, but rather according to not preferring them to God. In this same way, [one treats] the wife and the children, and in this same way, the brothers. 'And he will hate even his own soul' (Matthew 10:22), he says. He hates his own soul while enduring death for the sake of a witness, but on account of the Savior; for see what he says: he who hates a father 'because of me' (Matthew 10:37), not utterly. The Savior is to be preferred above all. Just as if someone hates a mother because of the Savior. This hatred does not bring slander. He who thus has hated the parents for the sake of the Savior is abandoned by them. Therefore he says: 'for my father and my mother have abandoned me' (Psalm 27:10). The abandonment is unto the end. Psalm of a song of the dedication of a house; to David.

A resurrection occurs both according to the soul and according to the body; 'Awake, sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you' (Isaiah 26:19). Here, the one sinning is dead; for 'the soul, the one sinning, this one shall die' (Ezekiel 18:4); and: 'sin, having been completed, brings death' (Romans 6:23) to the one sinning. Therefore, awaken this one into the life that was before the fall; for this was the life with virtue. Thus also in Jeremiah it is said: 'Does not he who has fallen rise again?' (Jeremiah 31:12); and a resurrection also happens to the body; for its formation was not its fall, but the corruption after the formation. Therefore also it itself rises. And in general we say this: the beautiful leads the bad. For indeed even bad craftsmanship is after the art, and the error after the correct, and the transgression after the law; for transgression is nothing other than a [deviation].

The command is given. And again, the 'para-' prefix is always used to signify deviation: 'to think wrongly', 'to overlook', 'to step aside'. Therefore, virtue is the first thing; for observe where the word flows: the rational has come to be so that it might possess virtue; for it did not come to be so that it might possess wickedness, since virtue was the very thing that was the opposite of wickedness. Since almost all begin from sin when they reach into material life, if it were granted that the soul never lived before material life, then things began from wickedness, and sin is not actually sin, but rather virtue; for no one is said to sin by doing what is natural or what is characteristic of their nature. Those who practice arts and act according to them, when they do what is characteristic of the art, are not said to think wrongly or to step aside.
