Thus, it is the building up of the fallen house and the return from captivity. According to a former principle, we say that the inhabitant and the house are the same thing. But it can also be taken more universally: the sum of the faithful, the church, is the house; 'that you may know how one must conduct oneself in the house of God' (1 Timothy 3:15); and 'I have loved the beauty of your house' (Psalm 26:8). And those who inhabit it are these faithful ones, those living according to virtue. But if the soul is the house, the earnest thoughts which are connatural with it are the inhabitants. Then both the building up and the dedication happen at once. And renovation occurs when those who were previously outside of it take up habitation within it again.

'A psalm of song'. We said when we began the twentieth psalm, that they are psalms, they are songs, they are psalms of song and songs of psalms. And we were saying that the psalm signifies the practice. And the one singing strikes an instrument called a psaltery. But it is possible to sing even without a psaltery; for he who uses only contemplation—to understand God, to know the truth and to partake of it, so that he may take it for himself, since it certainly has the practice sung to it, when someone, come now,
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Humanity and Divine Capacity
english: He contemplates and scientifically applies what knowledge is, and what the 'mystery of the kingdom' is, which this one sings. Again, as many as practice—and this alone is what they stand at until they practice—they sing; as we said also concerning the rams, that they have a life that is well-proportioned, but if they are not led, they have neither a life nor the necessary works of life. He sings.

But he who both sings and practices, and sings and contemplates: if he begins from practicing, it is a psalm of song; but if from contemplating, it is a song of a psalm. We see these things happening: often some, wishing to contemplate, stand at the virtues and their works, and taking from the standing itself the possibility to succeed, they come to the practicing. It has become a song of a psalm. The song led, the contemplation.

'Having desired wisdom, he kept the commandments' (Ps 119:2); the one desiring saw; he kept the commandments, he sang; and again he has songs being provided to him. It happens therefore sometimes to begin from the song and receive the psalm, and again he, the psalm having made a way for the soul, again brings a song. If therefore the beginning and the thought of the beginning arise from work as a craft, it is a psalm of song; but when someone, having begun from contemplation, receives the desire to live according to virtue, it is a song of a psalm.

It was necessary therefore for the one being brought in to inaugurate the house to dance thus for the inauguration of the house. This is called a sequence. And sequence is when the one follows the other and does not turn back. But if the following turns back, as it happens that the former becomes the follower and the latter becomes the leader, it is a sequence. The 'to David' indeed refers to this one who succeeded, to whom the victory and the hymn are referred, or to the singer himself. Even if the singer says it, it seems he speaks from the Holy Spirit.

It is not the same to say that 'a man says' and 'a learned man says'; for when we say a man is the one announcing, the things announced are human, but when [we say] a learned man, they are knowledgeable. The knowledge is subordinate to him, and he becomes as a servant of the knowledge. The 'worthy' one therefore 'with hand' sings this psalm or this song, the psalm of the song or again. And every practical man is 'worthy' 'by hand'. But the Savior most especially has this; and g...

But others receive capacity from him. John, indeed, looking at his greatness, said: 'I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandals.' Again, if capacity is given from him: 'Our capacity is from God, who made us worthy to be ministers of a new covenant.' Those who are driven to this and seized by love of the matter become imitators of Christ, seeing him acting 'competently' and they themselves act 'competently' according to what is possible for them.

He began saying in the Psalms that what is said about the man whom the Savior took up, might be said about every imitator of him, not only what is said about him as the only-begotten Son and the Word of God; it might be said—I do not speak about humans, nor even about rulers, but about no created thing at all. What is now being said fits the man of the Savior; therefore also others are able to do these things. 'I will exalt you, Lord, because you have lifted me up' (Psalm 30:1). What I have said many times, and now I say: what is said about God, is understood as being about God; but what is said about humans, is understood as being about humans.

Sometimes, what is said about humans, if not as mortals and as men, but as rational beings, is said, and about angels and generally about every spiritual substance; for according to the spiritual, man is of the same kind, according to the capacity for becoming perfect, 'just as the Father in the heavens is perfect' (Matt 5:48). For what more can an angel bear fruit according to what is possible? Then the Savior says to men that I and my Father will come, 'and we will make a single dwelling with him.' What more has a diligent angel to acquire? And furthermore: 'Give, that just as I and you are one, these may be one in us' (John 17:21). What more has the higher being to acquire? We take the difference according to more bodily things: the angel does not have flesh. But it is not the meaning of being rational for man to have flesh, since all things having flesh are rational.

See then: if, therefore, it says among us about being exalted from a lowly place to a higher one and being moved upward above, it is necessary first to change the place. It is impossible for one not changing place to be exalted or to be humbled, I speak locally. When therefore the saint says: 'I will exalt you', this he says: I will give thanks to you. If anyone thinks of Christ according to...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Healing Ointment and Immediate Response
english: Not according to the flesh, but when one no longer perceives according to the flesh, but beholds 'his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten from the Father' (cf. John 1:14), and knows that he who has seen the Son sees the Father, and this is to exalt him.

Therefore, because he says this graciously, the following is brought forward: 'because you have taken me up' (John 14:19); having taken me up, you exalted me. When I was exalted, then I knew your height.

And this can also be seen from things held in the hands; one approaches by skill; not yet the magnitude, not yet the beauty, not yet the height of it he sees. But if he begins to grasp it and is improved by taking in each part with what has already been made known, then seeing the magnitude and the height of the skill and the art, he exalts it, that is, he confesses its height.

For indeed, when he stands over the height and magnitude, he sees much remaining to himself. 'Your knowledge was marveled at from me; it was strengthened, I am not able toward it' (Eccl. 6:18). As much as I stand over it and marvel at it, it becomes strong, and I am no longer able toward it, as long as I am in a body.

This also Solomon says concerning wisdom: 'I said, I will be wise, and it was lengthened far beyond what it was, and a deep depth, who will find it?' (Eccl. 6:18). It was far from me, and when I desired to receive it, it became far from me beyond what it was before. And therefore he gives the reason: 'a deep depth, who will find it?' The 'who will find' may mean 'no one.' And the 'who' is the smallness and not a joy to my enemies upon me. Many enemies lie in wait for me, intending to harm me.

And they were saying that these things are also commonly said concerning the man the Savior and of those imitating him. And the saints had enemies and the Savior had enemies. And no one at all is able to approach him according to the divinity, in order that he might be tested to harm him. And to hate is to approach not for the sake of another but to harm.

And therefore, in the person of Jesus, it is said according to the man and of every imitator and of his member becoming [so]: 'because you have taken me up' (John 14:19); for if you had not taken me up, my enemies would have rejoiced having taken me in hand, and would not have exalted you. It is also possible from the person of the Savior, no longer dividing us and saying according to God the Word or according to man, as we were fully saying concerning the skilled man: 'I will exalt...'

You, Lord, have taken me; you took those two for me, for whom I cried out (Ps 132:13). 'Behold, I and the children, which God has given to me' and 'I will give you the nations for your inheritance' (Ps 2:8). The Savior regards this as his own contest and his own benefit; therefore 'I have not rejoiced my enemies' (Ps 69:20). For the captives were snatched away because of me, and on my account, and on account of those holding them, I will exalt you, but they do not rejoice.

Lord my God, I cried to you, and heal me (Ps 130:1-2). The voice has been heard; for if he cried concerning healing, he already received what he desired. 'I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you' (Ps 130:1-2). He had not yet been healed, for he who says this is confessing and repenting. The face of the Savior says this: 'I cried to you, and heal me'; I received an ointment, therapeutic and medicinal 'for every disease and weakness.' Why then did I have the ointment? So that he himself might become a medicine for those who were wounded. Then my healing occurs when the ointment heals others being my body. 'Lord' therefore 'my God, I cried to you, and heal me.' If each of the righteous says this, he will be heard by him to whom he cries. 'While you are still speaking, I will say, Behold, I am here.' The 'I will say, Behold, I am here' shows the work for which you are worthy, I find myself present to you; for your prayer does not delay my gift, but it happens at once; you have prayed, you have the thing. Let us take examples from the Scriptures; a leper came to the Savior saying, 'If you wish, you are able to cleanse me' (Lk 5:17). He says, 'I will, be cleansed'; and the cleansing happened as if there were no delay. By thought alone previously the worthiness occurred before the cleansing, not by time before. Again: 'Do you wish to be well?' Immediately: 'Rise, take up your bed and walk' (Lk 5:17). And the work of Jesus's command did not happen a second later. You know that the reflection imitates the thing seen, and it is not possible to say which is first, but by thought.

Lord, you brought up my soul from Hades (Ps 138:3). Having healed me, you brought up my soul from Hades. This could be said concerning Jesus; since I had an ointment and was wounded because of certain sins—perhaps those having sins in Hades—they descended there, so that the ointment, having approached...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Confession and the Life in His Will
english: May he heal them. For the healing is the bringing up of my soul from there. I became there not to remain myself, but neither to simply depart and return, but to lead up those there. 'Having been put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit, in which he also preached the message to the spirits in prison' (1 Peter 3:19), he led them up. And because of these things he went down there, and because of these things he says he is ascending; for he went down to lead up. If he were not ascending them, he would not have gone up there; for he did not descend or ascend for his own sake.

And this can also be said: the soul is truly our rational being. As it is said of a certain man of God, so it might be said of a soul. 'You have brought up my soul from Hades' (Psalm 42:5). You saved me from those descending into the pit (Psalm 49:15). Those descending into the pit are called the days, because those above are fallen; for the pits are not springs; they do not have water being supplied from anywhere. And Hades because of this is continually called a pit in the Scriptures, because the souls that fall there are falling.

'You saved me from those descending into the pit' (Psalm 49:15). For even if I descended into Hades, I was not seized in the pit like the falling waters, but I was saved, so that what happens to those falling into Hades does not exceed my harm. 'Praise the Lord, you saints of his' (Psalm 149:5). Therefore, while praising and extolling because he was received, he intends to fall upon the hymn even those whom he led up from Hades, the saints having been shown; for those around Abraham and the other saints were there.

And other souls were there too, but some were shown to be the souls of saints, and others were not; for we do not say that the Savior sanctified all, but those souls which were awaiting him there. They were saying, therefore, toward: 'Are you the one coming, or do we await another?' That man knew he was about to die; for being in the prison, he sent this voice, asking: 'Are you coming there yourself, or are you sending another?' Not that he was doubting, but he wished to serve there beside him, having learned from him, being commanded by him. He writes to the saints: the achievement is for us or is common to us and you. Just as therefore I sing a psalm, you also praise; you join in with instruments to our song, which I send up on behalf of you, saying.

“I will exalt you, O Lord.” 5 And you confess the memory of His holiness. Confession here is not called the disclosure of sins; for this too is called confession, as if one says, “Confess your sins to one another” (Ps 50:4). But most often in Scripture, confession is signified by the word thanksgiving: “We will confess to You, O God, we will confess to You” (Ps 106:1). The memory is moved here by dogmas, he says, “of His holiness.” Discipleship-remembrances are not now but before. If anyone is sanctified, having shared in the holy, he has obtained holiness. And so it has happened, so that one might be holy not by essence, but by choice, having received the holy and the good in advance. Therefore, do not neglect, while confessing and singing, that holiness is your own; because you have become [it], take hold of it; you have become [it] so that you might be holy, not profane; yet you have become in filth and profanity. Reclaim your holiness, and thus desire to become [it].

6 For wrath is in His mind and life is in His will (Ps 30:5). Because of this, I urge you to sing as those having become holy and to confess the memory of His holiness, “for wrath is in His mind” (Ps 30:5), so that you do not fall into wrath and anger; for if you remain in the same [state] as before my arrival, having me having accomplished so much, and in the same [state] regarding the things for which I have come, He will receive wrath, because after so many helps and so many benefits and exhortations you remain in the same [state]. And just as it becomes like wrath in the mind, so also “life is in His will” (Ps 30:5). He who follows His will and works it, asking to know it from Him—indeed, someone sends a prayer saying, “Teach me to do Your will” (Ps 119:35). Through saying with a reason, “For You are my God” (Ps 73:28), it is shown that the will of God is alone life. And our own will must also cooperate, so that He does not say, “How often I willed, and you did not will.” Therefore, “life” is “in Your will.” The Word God can also be said to be will here. In Him all things came to be; all things through Him came into being. In the will, therefore, of Him who brought you into existence, life lies. 6 Weeping shall turn to joy in the evening and in the morning (Ps 30:5).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Integrity of Character and the Beauty of the Soul
english: Rejoicing. The evening is the end of the day and the beginning of the night, just as in the morning the end is of the night and the beginning is of the day. But many times it has been said that the 81 are co-existing as opposites, the good and the evil. It is possible to receive in the evening the end of the shadow, the end of the letter.

But when someone wishes to be among them having received the end of the letter and of the shadow, he weeps rather, no longer seeing the pleasantness of the letter, no longer beholding the flower of the Scripture. But when the life-giving Spirit has risen and the New Covenant has been revealed, it is a beginning of the day bringing rejoicing.

Likewise also the more common things: when the assembly from circumcision received the evening of the powerful Sun of Righteousness—for 'she emptied herself,' 'bearing seven, the sun had not yet departed while the day was still in the midst'—she bore seven; then the Sabbath was reached, so that according to it he might spiritually complete all things and become a mother of good thoughts and works; but she emptied herself: she did not receive the fullness, from which having received, John, who signifies the letter and the old Scripture, says: 'of his fullness we have all received' (John 1:16). Because of this, her soul was discouraged, desiring the sun 'while the day was still in the midst,' while this age is still standing; for he himself is also often called day. 'And into the morning' therefore, 'rejoicing.'

7 'And I said in my prosperity, I shall never be shaken for ever' (Ps 92:12). The expression is ambiguous. It can be read thus: 'And I said in my prosperity, I shall never be shaken for ever.' When I am prospering, I said this: I shall never be shaken for ever. But it can also be thus: 'I said, In my prosperity I shall never be shaken for ever.' Both markings have meaning. When he prospers, sowing into righteousness and having harvested generations of righteousness, it was determined thus, that I shall no longer be shaken for ever; for if 'he who does the will of God remains for ever' (1 John 2:17) and 'his righteousness' is 'immortal,' having brought the generations...

Regarding righteousness and uprightness, I said: for I said so with my disposition, as if toward the [statement] 'no one says Lord Jesus,' both in disposition and in life. I confessed this, bringing forth generations of uprightness and virtue, that I remain unshaken for ever according to: 'he who believes, and everyone living and believing, shall by no means die for ever' (cf. 1 John 2:17); and: 'the righteousness of the Lord remains for the age of ages' (Ps 37:29). And it is also possible thus: to verse differently, 'I said in my uprightness'; when [they] were being upright and seemed to be resting, [he said] 'I shall by no means be shaken for ever.' If indeed help had not come quickly, he would have been cut down, because he had encouraged himself, having great confidence in the fruitfulness. If, therefore, the saying is the face of the Savior, let the former thought be held; but if it is of the others, let this also be accepted.

8 Lord, in your will, grant power to my beauty. That is, he says, either gracefully or thankfully. Let us see what kind of beauty he speaks of. He does not speak of bodily beauty, but of spiritual beauty and of the inner man. This beauty, which is perceptible, which is manifested in the face and in the form, has its constitution from the proportion of the members, if the members of the man were proportional to themselves, and not to be such that some exceed and others fail; for the beauty is distorted. It is necessary to have a fitting eye for the nose and this for the mouth; for if the members were disproportionate, even if it might seem beautiful in itself, it does not make beauty for the face. This indeed he says: those [virtues] which follow your will, the individual ones, so that my thoughts, having been proportioned, are the actions. And in the song of songs, he who praises the bride: 'All beautiful is my beloved, and there is no flaw in you' (Song 4:7). Because of this, 'all beautiful are you,' because there is no flaw and nothing in you is outside of proportion or shame.
9 To you, Lord, I have cried out, and to my God I will help. It is possible, so that we may explain more popularly: To you, O Lord, as...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Lord's Mercy and the Transformation of Mourning
english: I have cried out to the High Priest as a physician, and I will help toward my God, without dividing the Father from the Son. He who cries out to God cries out toward the Trinity; for the Trinity is one God, not the same as the numerical identity, if it is necessary to speak of numbers.

What profit is there in my blood, in my descending into corruption? I descended into corruption; what profit has occurred? Behold, they remain in their own evils. But he does not say this at all. Rather it is said: 'you were bought' with the blood of Christ, and that: 'not with corruptible things, silver and gold, were you redeemed from your vain manner of life, but in precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish and spotless, Christ' (1 Pet 1:18-19). And this is possible: the whole sum of the saved is called the Body of Christ.

Since, therefore, the Savior arrived and received all that we previously mentioned—the darkness and the cross and the descent into Hades—not all returned, not all took up virtue and faith, but some and others; according to this he says: 'he turned my face away' (Ps 49:15) from certain things being members of me, being my body, 'and I became troubled.' If, therefore, he saved and redeemed and set free by his own blood, how does he say: 'what profit is there in my blood, in my descending into corruption?' Much profit has occurred—but toward those who remain in evils. As for how much has reached you, no profit has exceeded in my blood, my descending into corruption. He says, moreover, that he stirs them up toward repentance.

For this reason he has said: 'shall dust confess to you or announce your truth?' (Ps 65:2) Behold, there are some being dust. But I have come to suffer, so that I might transform them and make them heavenly from being swine. Since, therefore, they remain still wearing the image of the swine, they do not confess to you, nor do they even announce your truth. But I have come so that I might also make the truth manifest, exposing the wandering and the falsehood, and so that I might grant confession, so that someone might cast off the image of the swine and take up that of the heavenly. He says therefore: 'shall dust confess to you?' If dust does not confess to you, as much as has reached him, no profit from my blood has exceeded my descending into corruption. Then—since I have said...

He says this because of those being pressed by former evils; and we have confessed that he also redeemed many by his own blood—thus demonstrating them. 11 The Lord heard and had mercy on me (Ps 117:2). By showing the mercy of the Lord, he speaks of their salvation, that they might receive mercy. 11 The Lord became a helper to me. The verb 'became' signifies that they were not previously so: 'A helper and a protector became to me for salvation.' 11 The Lord heard and had mercy on me (Ps 117:2). I was lamenting, because having descended into corruption, no benefit from my blood has occurred to anyone; but building up the pitied ones, and demonstrating those who are at their peak to be such, that they shall one day be saved; the medicine will one day work in them.

12 You turned my mourning into joy for me (Ps 30:11). He was cutting away the dead out of philanthropy, so that he might raise them up; for immediately a certain understanding took hold: if he mourns and laments because of my sinning, I owe much more to do this. Therefore, 'You turned my mourning into joy for me': their benefit is joy to me, and when we were sinning, my lamentation and mourning were theirs. 12 Having torn my sackcloth, you girded me with gladness. I was carrying a sackcloth of mourning, a severe life, rough, but he changed it into gladness. Thus we have also spoken regarding: 'If in Tyre and Sidon the powers became, long ago they would have repented sitting in sackcloth and ashes' (Matt 15:28; Jonah 2:5). We say that the name of the sackcloth signifies the severe, bitter, and cleansing life of the one lamenting. After this sackcloth, someone takes ashes and sits, no longer acting against it, but sits, ceasing the anger of evil. He groaned over this, which bore chaff, thorns, and thistles; for he was not able to sit among the thorns and thistles, but having burned them and shown them powerless, and that quality by which they were vile, having risen up, he sat upon them.

13 So that my glory may sing to you and I may not be dejected (Ps 82:1). Some say a hint: 'I shall not be dejected'; while my glory sings to you, I am not dejected. But this reading does not satisfy me. Many in the church read it this way. The term 'dejection' (katanyxis) often signifies a repentance. For when Ahaz repented:
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Hope and Divine Justice
english: "Did you see how Ahaz was consoled?" and "you gave them a spirit of consolation," a spirit of repentance. This is therefore what he says: my glory sings to you, I act according to your will, and I do not repent, I am not brought low by sorrow. He is not brought low as if by evil, so as to no longer be active. Therefore he connects [the thought] and says: "Lord, my God, I will give thanks to you forever" (Ps 116:17). "Lord, my God, I will give thanks to you forever." Since, therefore, I will give thanks to you forever, singing to your glory, I am not brought low, nor do I repent.

To the end: A psalm of David; of ecstasy. The name of ecstasy is homonymous; for it signifies many things, one of which is deviation or folly; the one who wanders is in ecstasy (stands outside himself). But the name of ecstasy also signifies wonder; for he who wonders is said to be in ecstasy (standing outside himself): "I perceived your works and was amazed" (Ps 138:14) having seen their greatness, the art by which they came to be. And there are many expressions declaring that wonder is made manifest by the name of ecstasy. Thus also Isaac "was in great ecstasy" when he received the blessing from Isaac. And again, ecstasy signifies becoming something outside of one's former state, as if he says: "But I said in my ecstasy, 'Every man is a liar'" (Ps 123:4). When he stood outside himself and was no longer a man, but had become God by making room for the Word of God coming to him, then he said: "Every man is a liar"; for if we take this simply, he lies. If every man is a liar and he himself is one of men, he lies. But in him saying "every man is a liar," they are not altogether liars. The things of men are uncertain, unstable. Such is also what the apostle says: "What eye has not seen, and what ear has not heard, and what has not ascended into the heart of man" (1 Cor 2:9). He is not, therefore, [merely] the same man, but he brings forth: "But God has revealed them to us through the Spirit" (1 Cor 2:10), to us who are no longer [merely] men, those who are able to say with boldness: "We have stood in ecstasy with God, we are of the same mind with you." He, therefore, who says these things in the psalm was also in ecstasy; he has become another, he has become God by participating in the Word of God; he has ceased to be a man. For certainly, observe that he does not speak human things, but things that it is fitting for a man having been made divine to proclaim.

And to sing. Upon you, Lord, I have hoped, that I might not be put to shame for ever (Psalm 25:3). For I am not put to shame when the things of the petition exist; for then the one praying suffers shame when he does not happen to get what he expected. And if we take 'the age' more simply, this says: in the time of my life, let me not be put to shame, always attaining those things which I entreat to receive from you; for it has been said many times that the time extending the life of man is called 'an age', just as: 'I will not eat meat for ever'. And it is possible also to say thus: since you are eternal and your existence and your kingdom extend through all the ages, and I too am immortal according to the soul, 'let me not be put to shame for ever'; for I am always with you. Now I know in part and I prophesy, but the one who is perfect will receive that which is in part, so that my hope becomes greater, having a greater remainder of expectation. Therefore, the one who hopes in the Lord is without shame.

Save me in your righteousness and bring me out (Psalm 70:1). The beginning of this seventieth [psalm] has a certain kinship and likeness. And in the seventieth lies the 'bring me out' itself, concerning which it is said: 'righteousness bowed down', when having bent the heaven, it came down. It has come to loose injustice; for the world having come about on earth was full of injustice; for 'the earth was filled' with iniquities (Genesis 6:13), just as before the flood, when 'all turned aside, at the same time they sinned, there is no one doing goodness' (Genesis 6:11). Just as the light rises and becomes there where the darkness is, and the darkness is made manifest by the presence of light, and when virtue shines forth, evil is driven away—so, when righteousness is revealed and those entreating it are saved, all injustice is dissolved.

Incline your ear toward me, hasten to bring me out (Psalm 70:5). Even if I cry out to you, I am small-voiced as toward your majesty. If you do not incline your ear toward me, my cry is not able to ascend to you. If you do not descend with me, you will not receive my voice. And in another way: since he does not observe all the lawlessness of those being judged and examined by him, it is necessary for him to incline the ear, so that he may hear; for whatever kind of knowledge and whatever kind of power...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Spirit and the Soul in God's Hands
english: The prayer remains, and does not ascend to him if it does not incline toward him; but it inclines by descending together. When you incline your ear to me, receive me and quickly take me out from those holding me, from those attacking me. Even if enemies are, 'quickly let me be delivered' (Ps 145:14). Did he say these things in amazement? He did not say that foolishness is shown here, but rather the wonder of becoming outside of himself. You are ignorant of this, that there is not one single perfection. For the one having been perfected says: 'I have seen the end of every arrangement' (Ps 71:20); for he does not say these things having an end that is beyond all.

Become for me, O God, a protector and a house of refuge to save me (Ps 18:2). Become for me an invincible fortress, an unpierceable wall; become for me also a protector, your shield, your weapon. When you become my protector, none of my enemies can harm me. A beast cannot overcome me, the very one snatching, about whom we were sending a prayer: 'never snatch my soul like a lion' (Ps 18:48). 'And into a house of refuge' (Ps 18:49). Become for me that which is called a stronghold, where one fleeing enters within walls; for a building is a guard by means of salvation.

For you are my strength and my refuge (Ps 18:2). You are everything to me, both strength and refuge. I flee to no one, not to a ruler, nor to wealth. And my strength: from you I have the power to hold fast, participating in you, just as a king holds fast. For the sake of your name, you will guide me and nourish me (Ps 143:8). He says this because since your name is called upon me, because of this name of yours which I wear, grant both to me; and guide me, so that I may finish the race without fault and be able to say: 'I have run without lawlessness and I have directed my course' (2 Tim 4:7), and: 'I have run the path of your commandments' (Ps 119:30). And let me be nourished by you. Your way and bread is your Son. 'Way' is he saying, 'I am the way' (John 14:6). He himself is both way and bread. Therefore, 'for the sake of your name,' which you granted to me, so that I may have salvation; for I grew and said: 'O God, in your name save me.'

Bring me out of this snare which you hid for me (Ps 124:7), because you are my protector. Enemies are many, some deceivers, they have prepared a snare for me, so that they may hunt me. I do not only entreat that you may not let me depart there, but also...

Unless they enter, so that you might lead me out from it. One must examine and thus [see] 5–6: 'for you are my protector, into your hands I will commit my spirit' (Psalm 31:5). I do not commit my spirit to another, but into your hands.

And if a holy man is the one saying these things, his spirit is that which is joined to the soul, concerning which it is said: 'your whole spirit and soul and body.' Some say the spirit is something other than the soul, others [say it is] its mind, and others [say] its will. But in all these interpretations, God preserves the spirit. If it is the soul, it is committed into the hands of God so that, being covered, it might remain unharmed, not being struck by enemies, not being destroyed.

Because it is sometimes said that the soul is spirit, Stephen teaches; for as he was about to die, and he exhorted [them] not to let the sin of those murdering him stand, he says: 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' (Acts 7:59), instead of 'my soul.' And James writes: 'just as the body without spirit is dead' (James 2:26), calling the soul spirit. And it is said, as I have said, that something rational is also joined to it, like an inseparable thing, so that it might be a teacher of the soul, [namely] spirit.

And since this belongs to the soul when it possesses God, he says this: 'may such a thing not happen to me, so that my spirit might be outside your hands, but may all virtue be made straight for me, so that my spirit might be in your hands.' It is also possible to call one's will 'spirit,' so that he also wants it to be guarded in the hands of God.

Therefore, also the interpretative [points]: the two covenants can be the hands of God. Into these, then, I commit my spirit, wanting to understand both the old, that is, those things protected there, and the new. May both your hands contain my spirit. And it is possible also to say not only two hands of God; for it was not spoken in the dual, but in the plural; and there is no difference between the plural and the dual. However, if the two covenants exist, the hands are spoken of in the dual. But if all the power of God is named his hand—for we say 'the hand of a king' regarding military power—into your military power, finding it to be a guarding hand, I commit my spirit. Toward the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Divine Wills and the Walls of Ideas
english: before me you are always

If they are of God, they are wills of God. And take by way of example that which is being observed: he who intends to construct a city outlines the whole city and its parts with his own intellect, and according to those thoughts, he constructs the perceptible things. For certainly, if he does not take the meaning correctly—for instance, of the marketplace or the precinct or the others—he does not construct the perceptible things well.

Therefore, the ideas are able to be the walls, written in the hands of God, which are wills. Thus, these walls have their being in the will of God. And I say: 'In Christ,' he says, 'all things were created, those in the heavens and those upon the earth, the visible and the invisible, whether principalities or powers; all things exist through him; and he is before all things, and all things in him consist' (Colossians 1:16-17). In him the visible and the invisible were created; just as if the parts of a city were built in the mind of the architect, that is, in relation to those [ideas], being held together by them; for they are words of a sustaining kind. In Christ, therefore, all things consist.

If by reflection you wish to take away the word from the existing things, these things do not stand. They come together by the lifting up of the word. So also the walls; all security is written in the hands of God. And if you also call the virtues walls, the virtues too have ideas, which you will have as archetypes. For example, I have justice, but not all of it, but I have fashioned it according to itself. And the thing being thought of is not without the partaker, just like an idea; not 'idea' in the way you are accustomed to saying. If, therefore, you take away knowledge, the qualities of the knowers are taken away; they come together with it, and being placed there, they partake of it, and they are qualities according to a part. But there is another [idea] besides these, which is more original and more certain. For certainly, this one does not accept the more and the less, whereas that which is in the partakers accepts this. Therefore, the walls signify security. Lord God of truth, redeem me.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Deliverance from Necessity and the Broad Place
english: He is ransomed by God, being made outside of all disturbance. Thus the God of truth ransoms from deception; since God is the God of truth, He ransoms from deception and false glory. When someone has mistaken and false opinions, he cries out to God, so that by His truth He might make him outside of all deception. Again, the God of righteousness rescues from unrighteousnesses; for it is said: 'Hear me, O God of my righteousness' (Ps 25:1), so that you might make me outside of all unrighteousness, so that you might bring low those who work unrighteousness against me. And so it is for each one: Joseph called upon the God of self-control, so that he would not fall into the snares of the rebellious toward incontinence; and Susanna, so that she would not fall to the elders toward adultery. The God of self-control hears, not that He is another and another.

You hated those who guard vanities for nothing. Since you are the God of truth, and you hated those who guard vanities for nothing. But vanities are not true. And he said 'for nothing' because in a certain way they do not exist. Every falsehood is unsubstantial. Concerning the one who conceived the temple of Jesus, when I say 'she has brought forth' (τέτοκεν), I speak truly; but if I say, 'she has brought forth from a man,' I lie; it is not that she has brought forth, but the lie occurs regarding the manner. Every evil happens for nothing, it has no end. Therefore he says: You, O God, hated those who guard vanities for nothing. If anyone among those guarding such things receives understanding, who is the one hating such things, will he cease or will he hate himself?

But I have hoped in the Lord (Ps 118:49). You, O Master, did not 'hate those who guard vanities for nothing,' but I have hoped in you as my Lord; for it was possible to say, 'But I have hoped in you.' Instead he says, 'I have hoped in the Lord.' He speaks these things as a slave. From the disposition of a slave and the work of a slave he speaks these things.

I will rejoice and be glad in your mercy (Ps 118:54). Upon your mercy; for even if I confess you as Lord and I have hoped in you, it is not by my own power that the end is achieved, but by your mercy. For you have seen my lowliness (Ps 118:6). You have seen my lowliness which is about to receive [mercy]. Forgiving, you will not let me fall into it. You saved my soul from necessities. More simply in the Scripture, necessities are called tribulations; 'he...

For it is said, 'he will be brought out from necessity,' and, 'they cried to the Lord, and he heard them, and from their necessities he saved them.' He has brought [me] out from all tribulation, making it evident by his answering the plea; for a prayer was sent up, so that I might be rescued from enemies, from the impending wars.

It is possible, in a more logical way, to speak of the necessities of evil. Out of necessity, the evil man does not receive righteousness. I do not say that the man is not receptive to righteousness, but the unrighteous [man]. It is not that the outward state of the afflicted becomes [different], but that they are not defeated; for thus we also heard: 'save us from the evil one' (Matt 6:13), and 'do not bring us into temptation' (Matt 6:13). And if the apostles of Christ and the other righteous ones were pleading this, that they might not be tempted, they were never heard, if they are telling the truth saying: 'in everything we are afflicted, but not crushed' (2 Cor 4:8).

'And you did not shut me up in the hands of an enemy.' I am shut up in the hands of those attacking, when I am defeated by necessities and tribulations. But when I am saved from them, I am not shut up in their hands, nor do I do what they want to bring upon me. 'You have set my feet in a broad place.' This too must be understood in two ways. The movement according to the surrounding place, and that which is called broad and spacious according to evil.

It is a great thing having happened in this broad place and spaciousness: not to be dragged under, but to stand. And standing comes from God. Therefore he says gratefully: 'You have set my feet in a broad place.' My feet do not feel the tribulation surrounding [me]. For those saying: 'who shall separate us from the love of God? tribulation, distress' (Rom 8:35), they will say: 'You have set our feet in a broad place.' Even if the place in which we have come to be, and the road in which we find ourselves, is narrow, we see it as broad, you widening the tribulation. You provide a wider road of tribulation by helping.

'Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am afflicted.' But you say—and indeed you said: 'You have set my feet in a broad place'—so that the saint may pray unceasingly; for there is not one tribulation, for there is not one crisis in life, for there is not one temptation. If anyone, having pleaded, is rescued from one thing or from some people, he again sees others attacking, and again prays concerning those; for they afflict him...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Unity of the Soul's Attributes
english: Things are expected. Or, does the prophet foresee them in advance? Such things even a prophet is not able to foresee. I am in a place where many are evil. They hate the righteous one who is there. Even if they once attack and bring a net or a snare and someone comes out of it, knowing their subsequent evil, he remains wide awake expecting such a thing again; 'for not indeed,' he says, 'will they sleep, unless they do evil; their sleep is taken away and they do not sleep' (Ps 31:3). And having been rescued many times, he also prays concerning the following.

My eye was greatly troubled in anger (Ps 32:3). My mind was troubled not in my own anger, but in the anger of the enemies or in your anger; for thinking against those committing sin, having sinned, I fell to the anger and my mind was troubled. My soul and my stomach (Ps 32:4). Not alone, he says, my eye—that is, the mind—was troubled by anger. And this is also possible: 'in anger my eye was troubled.' When I rage, my mind is disturbed; for the passions are disturbances of the mind. And my soul was troubled, of which the eye is the one troubled by the anger.

And 'my stomach'; he does not mean here the stomach of the body, but that which was receiving from the bridegroom and bringing forth: 'from your fear we have taken in in the stomach and labored' (Ps 31:7), so as to no longer save what was received, but to cast it away as small things. And this is also possible: because making the stomach calm, I did not receive the bread of heaven, but I received some other food, harmful, a poison, and my stomach has been disturbed. Therefore, he does not cast away salvation.

Or, the soul being disturbed? Some wish to say that the soul is threefold; rather, they say it is thick and divided. And they call the rational part of it the mind; for this is receptive of knowledge, and this is able to have knowledge. The desiring part does not receive knowledge, but sometimes is persuaded by the rational; being persuaded, it does not itself have knowledge. And just as when the winds of the air blow well, it becomes possible for the pilot—the ship not having such motion, but not opposing the skill of the winds not being contrary—and the desiring part again is persuaded by the rational, not having a calculation itself. Therefore, no one would be saying the mind while sinning. But all things together...

The soul is a single thing. Let us take an example. One takes a flower. The flower has such a color, but the color is not the flower itself. It also has such a fragrance, but the fragrance is not the flower. It also has such a shape. Therefore, all these things taken together are the flower. So when we say, 'The flower is fragrant' (Ps 143:6), we signify only one part of it, namely that it emits a sweet breath. And again, if we say it is bitter, we signify not only its juice alone. But the juice is not the flower; rather, all these things together are the flower.

Thus, when speaking about his own intellect or his own mind, saying that it is troubled by passion, the soul also says this. You know that when the helmsman is badly dragged, the whole vessel is damaged, and when the pilot is overturned, the ship is overturned. Therefore, the one called 'eye' is a certain intellectual power that steers the whole soul. If this is troubled, the soul is also disturbed.

And what about the generative womb? —which I have said many times, and now I will say: regarding sensible things, each thing is a specific kind and cannot be something else. A plant cannot be gold, and gold cannot be a man. But regarding intelligible things, it is possible through various relations and thoughts. For instance, I was saying yesterday that when the soul seeks, and seeks indeed to know itself, it possesses the word of both the seeker and the thing sought. And if it cultivates itself like a plant, the plant is not something else and the farmer is not someone else; difference is found in thought alone.

Therefore, if he says 'eye' and 'womb', it is possible to speak of both regarding the same power; because the mind is called an eye because it sees, and the womb is called a womb because it can generate and bring thoughts into the midst. 'For my life has wasted away in pain, and my years in lamentation' (Ps 102:9). Since my life has wasted away in pain—for I always had it painful—I sometimes lament and sometimes not; I always lament, desiring virtue; I always toil, I always sweat for the sake of the acquisition of the good. Since I suffer this through life, in a way my life has wasted away in pain and my years in lamentation; therefore I beseech you, so that I may no longer endure so much toil; for if I toil again guarding it, it is not the same toil as that of acquiring something and guarding what already exists. And what about how they are kinds in general? —if one requires the word of a man, not...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Scorn of Enemies and Neighbors
english: He gives the Socrates example: do not say, 'Bring it, Dion.' The definition is, 'a mortal being is a rational animal.' And if I say, for instance, that the righteous man is outside of injustice, I am not speaking of this specific righteous man, but of the righteous man in general. For indeed the beginning of the psalm has become thus: 'In you, Lord, I have hoped, let me not be put to shame for ever' (Ps 25:2), regarding everyone who has hoped and is seeking an unashamed end of expectation; all the words take hold of this. For he who speaks in praise does not speak of this one or that one.

11 And my strength has grown weak in poverty, and my bones have been shaken. Here, poverty does not mean the deprivation of material goods. Strength here is spoken of in distinction of weakness. The strength which consists according to the soul is from wealth, but the sensory and bodily [strength] is not necessarily so; there are strong ones possessing nothing, and weak ones being masters of many goods. Just as if someone were to speak also concerning virtue or knowledge: 'Since I have fallen into poverty from virtue and knowledge, my strength, which I ought to have had from the presence of these qualities, has become weak.' 'My bones have been shaken.' Bones are parts of the body that hold the other parts together. While bones exist, nerves, veins, and the others can also be. Therefore, when the strong powers of the soul, called bones, become weak, the whole [soul] becomes in weakness.

And that he speaks of bones, not those of the body: 'All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like you?' (Ps 35:9); for the bones of the body do not have any concept of God, so that they might be able to say, whether there is anyone like Him or not. For it is necessary first to know God, and then thus to say. If therefore he says, 'All my bones shall say,' he means the powers of the soul which are well-proportioned and hold the other powers of it together, the sensory, the phantasic, the mnemonic. And again: 'My bones have been scattered by the netherworld,' those who confess and repent say. But regarding this netherworld, which is accustomed to be spoken of, the bones of the body cannot be scattered. And even if they were, as some say, under the moon, the bones of the dead do not undergo that. But when the powers of the soul, which through well-proportionedness are called bones, become [weak] by sin,

They were scattered like scorpions by the song, no longer preserving their own harmony. 'I have become a reproach to all my enemies and greatly to my neighbors' (Psalm 69:8). This psalm was said both before and in the presence of the Savior according to the man: 'I have become a reproach to all my enemies.' It alludes to the cross; for he says in another psalm, which Paul took to be from the presence of the Savior: 'The reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me' (Psalm 41:9). I have received them. Some reproach you, O Father or O God, and these reproaches have fallen upon me. And it is nothing wonderful; often even a learned man, when he sees [others] mocking the learning, draws the reproaches upon himself. Those sinning are his enemies. This is said: 'For being enemies, we were estranged' (Psalm 51:11). The one sinning is an enemy of God, not God is an enemy of him; for God is an enemy to no one.

'And greatly to my neighbors' (Psalm 69:8). His neighbors are those promising to know his Scripture and calling themselves his partakers. Therefore, 'greatly': for example, let the Gentiles be enemies; for they sin and act impiously. I have become a reproach among all those, as having endured the cross, as having descended into death. 'And greatly to my neighbors.' But when those owing to me and promising to have their own buildings near me do the same things to enemies, the reproach among these has become great.

And a fear to those known to me. Those knowing me, having seen me suffering these things, had either a similar reverence, or had a fear of not suffering the same things. Those seeing me fled away from me. Those seeing me, having seen these things happening concerning me before, were seeing from outside me, not having departed from me, but they fled outside. Everyone fleeing Jesus becomes outside of him, outside of salvation. I was cast out as if dead from the heart. The enemies reproaching me, and the neighbors having done this greatly, cast me out from their hearts. And of the dead, a quick forgetting happens. For those undergoing afflictions say thus: 'From where the dead was placed, it is blotted out,' it says, 'the sorrow is blotted out from the soul.' They hasten...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The nature of reproach and shame
english: Men do this thing quickly. 'I was forgotten' therefore 'from the heart.' They cast me out from their own heart; for he did not have me purely as the apostle says, 'but Christ lives in me' (Galatians 2:20). I no longer lived in them. When anyone having the word in himself no longer works according to it, he rejects the amount [of the word] in him, and it becomes in his forgetfulness. But hear about forgetfulness thus: not as not knowing that he once had it; for many such things are said both in common usage and in the Scripture. For many times indeed we say to friends, 'You have already forgotten me,' not saying this, that 'you have no memory at all.' But the Scripture says: 'The evil of a time causes forgetfulness of pleasure.' Now the one, having been harmed by pleasure, forgets the time. And again: 'and they shall forget,' he says, 'their former tribulation, and it shall not ascend again upon their heart.' Thus you think, that the one having come out of tribulation forgets it.

Furthermore: 'I have become a reproach to all my enemies' (Psalm 69:8); he did not say 'to all men,' but 'to my enemies.' And enemies are not just bad men who justify, but enemies by disposition; for he himself is an enemy to no one, but many are enemies to him. 'Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word; say, brothers, to those who hate you' (Isaiah 43:26; Luke 6:28). They hate and are enemies. And you, he says, call them 'brothers' not by voice, nor by utterance, but by disposition, or you demonstrate toward brothers by a disposition of brotherly love. And this is enmity: to have an opposing disposition. If even the Savior says this—let us say that it can be said from the person of the Savior as a man—he says the Jews have become his enemies. But not all have become his enemies; for the apostles also were Jews, they were Israelites. He did not therefore say 'to all the Hebrews, to all the Israelites,' but 'I have become a reproach to my enemies.' They reproach the righteous...

Not according to the first reading. Even the Savior is reproached by the wicked. Not every reproach brings a boast to the one reproached. There are times when those reproaching are themselves refuted, and again, those reproached because of sin.

Indeed, in the writing of Proverbs, it is said to the wise man: 'Do not acquire the reproach of wicked men' (Proverbs 22:8). By adding 'of wicked men,' it showed that even serious men are a reproach. For instance, the disciples rejoice when they are reproached. These are not the reproaches for which the apostles are refuted, namely, the reproaches of wicked men.

Furthermore, since it is up to us to do things worthy of reproach, it commands: 'Do not acquire the reproach of wicked men, nor envy their ways' (Proverbs 22:8); for he who envies their practices and their thoughts has become a bad man, having acquired a reproach of evils. Concerning this reproach, it is said that some rise up 'unto reproach and eternal shame.' But not all rise up 'unto reproach and eternal shame,' but those who seem to be good in that place. When those considered serious and holy men rise up and the shames of their soul are revealed, these rise up unto reproach; for those who are openly evil do not rise up unto reproach, but unto punishment.

And if the Savior says this, he calls the cross a reproach; for this is what the apostle taught: 'The reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me' (2 Corinthians 12:5). Again: 'Who, despising the shame, endured the cross instead of the joy set before him' (Hebrews 12:2). Reproach and shame are the same thing. And see how much it reached him, that joy was set before him, a man not having sin. Therefore he despised the shame, he trampled it.

Reproach does not happen from friends and those having the same virtue, but from enemies. Consider, therefore, the reproaches which they bring against the Lordly Man: 'Do we not speak well, saying, You are a Samaritan and have a demon?' (John 8:48). Not serious men offered this to him...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Many vs All and the Fear of God
english: A sound, not the apostles and the others. Again, if they say, 'By Beelzebul, the ruler of demons, he casts out demons' (Matt 12:24), they are not friends, they are not virtuous men. 'And my neighbors very much.' The Jews were his neighbors, if the Savior is the one speaking; and the hypocrites of virtue are significant.

They are my neighbors, and they have their own buildings near my house; for the house of the righteous is the upright conduct. For the 146th [Psalm] having heard the words of Jesus and having converted them into works, builds a house upon the rock, whereas the one building upon the sand [is foolish]. Since both have become hearers of the words of Jesus, they seem to be neighbors, they seem to be similar.

'The houses of the lawless shall undergo cleansing, but the houses of the righteous are received.' The law-breakers are not lawless, but they have the same law, yet they transgress it. But when it is said, 'Blessed are those to whom the lawless deeds have been forgiven,' those have no experience of law. 'Law-breaking brings a man to reproach'; for in a way the lawless do not even stand up for judgment so that they might be reproached. To be reproached is a lesser punishment. Therefore, those having received the law and having transgressed, these stand up 'for reproach and eternal shame.'

And that this is so, we will understand from the prophecy of Daniel; for in it this lies: 'And from the sleeping ones of the earth's dust'—he did not say 'all'—'these stand up for life, and those for reproach and for shame' (Dan 12:2). The resurrection is also found in the 91st Psalm; the ungodly stand up not to be judged. The law-breakers, those having received the law and having transgressed, the sinners, stand up for judgment. The righteous are raised up not to be judged, but to receive the promises.

Now therefore he says: 'And many of those sleeping'; for he does not count thus the ungodly who are not raised for judgment, but those standing up 'for reproach and eternal shame.' These are the sinners. The righteous [stand up] 'for eternal life.' Concerning these two ranks, the Savior also says in the Gospel: 'Those who have done the good shall come forth for a resurrection of life, but those who have done the evil for a resurrection of judgment' (John 5:29). He does not even mention the ungodly here. Since, therefore, the rank of the ungodly is set apart...

He did not say that 'all' rise up, but 'many of those sleeping'. If anyone considers this interpretation to be violent and says that the ungodly and the impious are also arranged among the 'many', we hear 'many' thus instead of 'all'; for all are many, and it is not a contradiction. However, let the 'many' be said here instead of 'all'.

And the apostle writes this: 'just as through the obedience of one man many will be made righteous, so also through the disobedience of one man many will be made sinners' (Rom 5:19). And here 'all' are signified by the 'many': all those who disobey, all those who obey. It is not a contradiction. If some are 'all', it is not necessarily that the 'many' are 'all', for example: 'many will say to my soul' or 'and fear to my known ones'. I have become a fear to my known ones, bearing this state which many reproach. Indeed, even the apostles, having been afraid, were scandalized at a certain time.

But here he speaks of a fear which is passive, which is followed by cowardice if it is not itself cowardice. It is possible also to receive a divine fear. Those observing me, knowing the mystery of my visitation and for whose sake I was crucified, had a fear equal to reverence, concerning which it is said: 'the fear of the Lord surpassed all things'; see, for what does it say: 'my known ones'.

The diligent are known by God; for the Lord knew those who were His, and they know Him. For the apostle says also to the Galatians: 'but once they did not know God, but now they know God, and even more so they are known by God' (Gal 4:9). When we know God, He knows us; for 'if anyone' 'is ignorant, he is unknown', clearly meaning that if anyone knows, he is known. Therefore, 'fear' 'to my known ones'.

Those worthy of being known, and knowing me, had a fear equal to reverence, concerning which it is said: 'then you will understand the fear of the Lord', after many mistakes. 'Those observing me fled from me'.

The Savior and Lord of us is both God and man at once. But He is seen and observed according to being man; for He is invisible being the 'image' 'of the invisible God'. And it is necessary for the image of the invisible to be invisible. But if it is said: 'he who has seen me', let 'having seen' be taken homonymously instead of 'he who observes me intelligently, he who sees me divinely, he who sees as...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Encirclement of Jesus
english: Imposing [the mystery] upon the invisible, he who also understands the mystery of the presence and the passion. Therefore, those outside are looking at me as outside, those who know Christ only according to the flesh, and such people are those about whom Paul writes: 'For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified' (1 Cor 2:2). They are of the outside and run outside, such as those are who hear in parables; for it is not the parable spoken unclearly that has made them outside, but their own external intellect has led them outside to this.

He became as if dead from the heart. The one understanding Jesus as being life—for he says: 'I am the life' (John 14:6)—and living, is the son of a living Father; for he says 'I live' because of the Father—they never forget him; for being present in their intellect, he always enlightens them, so that each one says: 'But Christ lives in me' (Gal 2:20). Such a person is in Christ and has Christ in himself, living and working. But when someone perceives him not as living nor working, he forgets him as if dead; for Christ does not live in all, but in those working according to him. And those who consider themselves to be Christians, but do not work according to Christ, do not have him living in them.

See: the foolish man lives according to wickedness, being 'more a lover of pleasure than a lover of God' (2 Tim 2:22), doing all things hedonistically. He considers the righteous man to be dead, because he is stripped of his own foolish life and does not receive it in his intellect. 'I became as a lost vessel' (2 Tim 2:21). I have not become a lost vessel, but like the lost vessel. And take for me the example: the other men being crucified beside the Savior seem to have become useless vessels, vessels of destruction. This one saying these things as if he has become the lost vessel, but not lost. Just as sin became not the same thing to others as being sin, but so that they might become the righteousness of God in him, he was made like sin (2 Cor 5:21), he was made like the lost vessel. For that men are called vessels is not unknown, and these indeed are for honor, but those for dishonor. This vessel according to Jesus is not of destruction; for he did not know sin. But it has become like the lost vessel. It has become a curse, so that it might bring blessing. But no curse brings blessing, but rather it diminishes the blessing; not—
For he was a blessed man, though cursed. This one, having become a curse, has become a cause of blessing, and not for one man, but for all who believe.

I heard the slandering of many dwelling around. I heard many slandering me, not having set themselves apart at all. The Israelites were dwelling around Jesus. They slandered him: 'He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the ruler of the demons' (Matt 12:24). 'He is a sinner because he does not keep the Sabbath' (Matt 12:2). They were around. If those saying these things were Gentiles, they would not have been his circle. These have become a circle. For he says: 'And they encircled me like bees, Lord' (Ps 118:148). They encircled me aggressively.

In the gathering of them all at once against me. He mentioned enemies, neighbors greatly reviling him; he mentioned those attacking him from the heart; he says those dwelling around and slandering. These were gathered together at once 'to take his soul,' especially when 'nations and peoples raged and labored in vain' (Ps 2:2); for here also nations having raged were not yet entirely set apart from him or separated. 'Why did they rage?' They attacked the Hebrews more arrogantly. And the Hebrews in vain and emptily labored over the prophecies concerning me. All the things said: the hosts 'were gathered together at once, they deliberated to take my soul.' The magnitude of the attack is shown, that 'at once all were gathered together to take his soul.' Not one, nor two, nor ten, nor a thousand, but all at once. The unshakeable and the irresistible, or the not being overturned, of the soul of Jesus is signified. They hardly gathered at once to take my soul or deliberated, and they did not seize it. 'No one takes my soul from me; I lay it down from myself, so that I may take it again' (John 10:18).

They deliberated to take my soul. They have gone as far as deliberating to kill him. If he himself does not give himself, they were not able to do this. For they came greedily to seize him, he says: 'Whom are you seeking?' (John 18:3) and he says: 'Jesus the Nazarene' (John 18:5). 'I am,' as he said, 'they went backward and fell to the ground' (John 18:6). And again a second time: 'Whom are you seeking?' and he said the same to them, and they fell to the ground again. He says a third time: 'I am,' therefore me...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Unit 22 rem close
english: lot/inheritance
from mere images
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Deceitful lips and the hidden goodness of God
english: I have called upon you. Then I am not ashamed, if the things of the calling exist. For is there not a word of the Savior? Sharp changes of persons occur. So also it is done in the prophets.

And something else concerning the bare man: just as each of us, frequently narrating about a man, sometimes indicates him from the soul, and sometimes from the body. If I say that he is a beautiful man, 'pyrakis'—so that I may speak from the Scripture, 'with beauty of eyes'—[it is] immense; then I say that he is a learned man, a slave of God, he is subject to the Lord; for the change of persons is not outside of all things. When it is spoken concerning a composite, the changes of persons are carried from part to part.

Since, therefore, also the one saying these things is not a man alone, nor is he God alone, but God having become man, the certain things are said as from the man, and the others as from the God Word or concerning the God Word. 'And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father' (John 1:14). You take it upon the same [subject]; for he does not say: 'Let your face shine upon your slave,' the other to me; me, your slave.

The ungodly were shamed and were brought down into Hades. The 'were brought down into Hades' again has a certain power. He did not say 'they descended into Hades.' But for those descending voluntarily, there is the descending. These, however, are not being brought down into Hades voluntarily. Also, concerning Capernaum, it is said: 'And you, Capernaum, which shall be exalted to heaven, shall be brought down to Hades' (Matt 18:17). It is being brought down by others. Then they are ashamed when they know that they are ungodly and do not have the impulse of readiness to descend into Hades. Because of this, they are brought down so that, having received the understanding of where they are about to descend, they might be shamed. Furthermore, they will do even more evil to themselves because they have become ungodly.
Let the lips be without sound.

The deceitful ones speak lawlessness against the righteous. He does not cast them down; rather, he blesses them; for he did not say, 'Let their lips become silent.' The 'deceitful ones' become silent when they are deprived of devilish words. Their lips are not entirely [silenced], but rather 'the deceitful [ones]'. Having cast away the [deceitful] word, they otherwise speak with boldness and truth. Thus it is said: 'The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the loud-sounding tongue' (Psalm 12:3). When the loud-sounding tongue—that is, the word—is destroyed, that from which it is destroyed, the person then speaks the remaining word of God.

19 In pride and contempt. Since 'of the righteous' lies absolutely, it can mean both of a righteous man and of a righteous matter, concerning which it is said: 'Rightly the just' (Psalm 115:3). But he who speaks against the righteous and against him who possesses it and is convinced by it, speaks in pride and contempt; for then their lips become silent when they know what kind of lowliness they are, when they know that the one whom they will despise is not worthy of contempt.

20 How great is the multitude of your goodness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you. Since it seemed to someone to speak in a strange way, but looking into the intention of the speaker, we say that they are not curses, but rather blessings. And you wish for them to be found good. Since it happened that those not ignoring the goodness and the end of the saved were being rubbed, you hid it from those who fear you. But he says 'fearing' here to mean those having the punishing fear, not the righteous, nor those having that fear which has no deficiency, nor those surpassing all. He says: since your goodness is inborn with your goodness, and you do all for the salvation of all, and you make the dark things and the falling of someone dark to be dark, but because those being rubbed through carelessness were going to be harmed, you hid it from those who fear you, not...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Manifestation and Hiddenness of God
english: To those who love: for here we receive the fear that is being set aside for the sake of love—'perfect love casts out fear' (1 John 4:18). And love is perfect when we do not love for the sake of another. Therefore, 'perfect love casts out fear because fear has punishment'—not that which is said concerning it: 'it is no loss to those who fear him.'

I have worked for those who hope in you against the sons of men. I have worked this concealment. Some are sons of men who are not reproached. But men and sons are often reproached when it is said: 'Sons of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted?' (Ps 39:13) But when it is said: 'The Lord looked down from heaven, he saw all the sons of men' (Ps 145:5), these sons of men are praised.

And I say a paradox: when they are lifted up toward God, they are righteous men and sons of men; but when they are toward the righteous, the sinners are sons of men, being vile, concerning whom Paul writes: 'For where there is strife and jealousy among you, are you not human?' (Gal 5:20) and concerning whom: 'But you, indeed, as men, are dying' (1 Cor 3:3), having fallen from being the sons of the Most High. Toward the holy men called or named gods, the vile are called sons of men; but toward the sons who are the cause for God, those whom he looks upon, they are diligent.

And again: 'You will save men and cattle, Lord. As you have multiplied your mercy, O God; and the sons of men hope in the shadow of your wings' (Ps 36:7). 'A great man and a precious man is the merciful one.' Here the man who is 'according to the image and likeness' (Gen 1:26) of God is praised in greatness. But when someone, having fallen from being the son of the Most High, becomes a son of man, this man is vile.

'I have worked for those who hope in you against the sons of men'—the diligent ones—and let those know the work: the concealment of the wealth of your goodness. You will hide them in the secrecy of your face, the sons of men for whom I have worked your mercy. And someone is hidden in the secrecy of God thus: God has a face appearing through his own creatures; for it is said: 'Analogously, the Creator is seen from the greatness and beauty of the creatures.' He is seen from the analogy of creation; for just as if someone sees a ship, the imagination of the shipbuilder...

Where is it received even if not present? And he who sees a ship sailing straight from afar immediately comes to the understanding that there is one steering it. And a chariot being carried in order from afar, even if the one seeing does not see the driver, he remembers him. In this way, as the cosmos is being carried in order and having a beautiful nature, a vision of the beauty and greatness of God is known; for if the things created are great, much greater is the Maker.

Therefore, when someone takes a vision of God from the cosmos, the order, the concept, and the judgments of providence, he has not been hidden into the secrecy of His person. Such also are those who have philosophized among the Greeks; for from the greatness of the created things and the beauty, they took a vision of God. But he who, receiving a vision of God without the creation, has seen the Son and through the Son the Father—for 'he who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9)—this one is hidden in the secrecy of the person of God. And the creative Word is a secret.

Again, so that I may speak more popularly: Jesus had two persons, of man and of God. Those who know Him according to the flesh, receive Him in the manifestation of the person. But those who, turning away from knowing Him according to the flesh, have come to knowing Him as the Divine Word, these have been hidden in the secrecy of the person of God. And furthermore, since we were saying that the outward vision of the cosmos is a person, the Word through whom the things created came to be, and through whom they are provided for and governed, is the secret of the person of God; and the creative Word is a secret.

God often hides His own goodness from the small ones who fear Him. We examined yesterday those who fear, abstaining from evil through the fear of punishment, if it must be called this abstention from evil. 'Perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment' (1 John 4:18). The disposition of knowledge of good and evil, and desiring the good and, having bowed to it, abstaining from evil lust, stays away from evil not by the fear of punishment, but turns away from evil. If, however, some word persuades him that there is no punishment, he practices what he chooses as evil. God, therefore, often does not bring punishment immediately, but [brings] goodness.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Son of Man as the Archetypal Human
english: And goodness. He hides the abundance of the wealth of his kindness because of those who fear, because of the small [ones], because of those who refrain from evil through the fear of punishment. 'How much indeed is the abundance of your kindness, Lord' (Ps 52:10). He hid it; for the knowledge of it was making them stumble into evils. If anyone should bring forth words of indignation even unto the point of causing amazement, and hide the kindness as if he were about to punish, if the son had known that the threat is only in form, he would have despised his kindness and would have been lost and become responsible for wrath. In truth, much kindness is his, a great abundance.

For the apostle also says to some: 'Or do you despise the wealth of his kindness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?' (Rom 2:4). And the one not knowing this thinks that he is not being unyielding to evils, and therefore does not come forward. And Peter, the foremost of the apostles, writes the epistle and has said such words: 'The Lord is not slow concerning the promise, which some count as slowness, but is patient, not wishing anyone to perish but all to come to repentance' (2 Pet 3:9). Behold the kindness. It was not necessary for it to be made known to the many; for they would have despised it even more. You have therefore hidden from those who fear you the abundance of your kindness. 'I have worked for those who hope in you, against the sons of men' (Ps 146:9). Those who hope are those who are watching for the divine rewards and the promises which God promised to those living well. 'I have worked' therefore this, 'for those who hope in you.' I have worked this, to hide the abundance of your kindness, so that even those who hope in you might not see this, that for a certain reason you do not bring forth wrath. He says therefore, 'against men.' The abundance of your kindness is not hidden forever, but only as long as those men are, concerning whom it is said: 'But you, indeed, as men, are dying.' And: 'For where there is strife and jealousy among you, are you not acting as men?' (1 Cor 3:3). Therefore, against these sons of men, I have worked this hiding according to the abundance of your kindness; for to them also he opens this. The God of all things is called many times [human]...

It is not that he has become a man or is a man, but because he descends with men, he governs their affairs in such a way, and as their judge, he becomes like a man who sympathizes. 'He shall nurture him as a man nurtures his son' (Deut 32:6). He observed your ways by nourishing and governing you. This is confirmed by this: 'If he observes iniquity, Lord, Lord, who will stand?' (Ps 139:24), and: 'His eyes examine the sons of men' (Ps 17:24). With eyes alone he sees what is being done.

Just as the one who sent the Son, having approved of his coming, governs men as a man provides benefits, so also this one is a 'son of man'; he is the son of a man who is thus led. And another thing: the particulars are in a certain way the offspring of the general. And the general human has become 'in image and likeness' (Gen 1:26) of God; for this was not said only concerning Adam, but the human nature, the general species, became 'in image and likeness' of God. He who preserves the prototype, the almost-general, is therefore the son of man.

Since, therefore, the soul of Jesus preserved the image—for he neither knew sin nor did it—because of this, he is called the son of that man who became 'in image and likeness' of God. It is also said otherwise: although Jesus did not have a father according to the man, he had a mother. And the woman is a human. To refute the opinion, he is called son of man. Even if he does not have [the status] from a father, he is from a mother. Thus indeed it is said, 'born of a woman' (Gen 3:15).
