If therefore we approach the light, by which we ceased sinning, our faces are not being shamed, and we have much boldness; for he says: 'if our heart does not condemn us, we have boldness toward God' (1 John 3:20). If someone sees himself as uncondemned by heart and conscience, he has much boldness toward God, as to say: 'the Lord lives, to whom I stood before him'. Having spoken with boldness: 'in the morning I will stand before you and I will watch; I will see many things, but even more I will observe; I will observe things to be seen'. 'And your faces will by no means be shamed' (Psalm 5:12).

We say that when sin exists, the face of the soul is covered by shame so that its beauty and the proportion of its melodies can no longer be seen. But when illumination comes, the remaining 'with an unveiled face, the glory of the Lord is reflected' (2 Cor 3:18). No one having a covered face reflects the glory of God, but rather if someone has cast off the coverings that came upon him. Those, indeed, having received perception, that evils have become by themselves, say: 'dishonor has covered our face'. Dishonor has become a covering for us, the shame, of our face.

7 This poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him (Psalm 34:6). 117 They show someone to be poor by being in sin, poor in all evil. If someone, having become without evil, having cast off the wealth of ignorance, cries to God from this evil, he has Him listening. Perhaps, as they implied locally regarding the time, that which belongs to the lesser and the greater, encouraging those already illuminated and blessing 'the Lord at all times' (Psalm 34:8) to be rich, he says: and if the poor man approaches and cries, he is heard.

And it is possible also to say this concerning the people from among the Gentiles, that: the people 'not having hope and being godless in the world' (1 Thess 4:17) approached and cried and had Him listening to them. For he says with other things in the same psalm: 'the rich have become poor and hungered' (Psalm 39:7), saying those from the circumcision have become poor by having cast away the law and the prophets. Because of this, he also says pointedly: 'this poor man'; worthy.
a poverty that produces wealth
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nourishment of the Inner Man
english: Is it against [the law]? Observe: one angel, at the will of God, struck down one hundred eighty-five thousand in a single blow (Ps 78:49), and perhaps he was not a pure angel, since he was not acting to punish. Therefore, the perfect man who guards holiness, being God's own eyewitness and servant, is able to save many who fear Him.

If the explanation seems violent to anyone, not so: just as it is said, 'God made man' (Gen 1:26), to be the ruler of irrational animals, and we are not speaking of the individual kind, nor of this specific one, but the whole species. 'I made earth and man upon it' (Gen 1:1); thus he named the whole species. Even so, the angel here may signify the general, that those fearing the Lord have angels intervening and surrounding them, saving them from every tribulation.

You have this in the Gospel: 'See that you do not cause one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble; for their angels always see the face of our Father in heaven' (Matt 18:10). They stand before God, we see His face, they see the invisible one invisibly. Behold, therefore, of the many little ones, many angels are spoken of, but of those fearing the Lord, one angel is said. It is said singularly, for not even one [is excluded].

And this can also be said: the little ones do not fear God, but have a passive fear; for 'perfect love casts out fear' (1 John 4:18). And: 'fear has punishment'. 'Do not fear those who kill the body but are not able to kill the soul' (Matt 10:28); but those who fear God have an excessive fear, about which it is said in Sirach: 'the fear of the Lord surpassed all things' (Sir 1:14), which comes to him who seeks Him with much progress.

Therefore, these who fear the Lord can have one angel intervening and saving them, the Savior himself, about whom it is said: 'His name is called Angel of Great Counsel' (Isa 9:6); for in many writings an angel is mentioned not applying to any single person. Jacob also says of him: 'the angel who saves me from all evils' (Gen 48:16). But no one is able to save from all evils except the Savior who has the authority to forgive all sin. And of the sin...

Once the punishment is assigned, the following afflictions follow, joining together with that evil. It is like a perimeter and a wall surrounding them, keeping them safe from harm. And in Zechariah, namely the eleventh of the twelve prophets, it says: 'Jerusalem shall be inhabited desolately' (Zech 8:10), and it says: 'And I will be around them like a pillar of fire and a wall encircling them' (Zech 2:5). But it is fire for the purpose of harming those approaching more; for immediately in that same region of the prophet it says: 'because he who touches you touches the apple of his eye' (Zech 2:8). To touch there means to harm, like: 'Touch not my anointed ones' (Ps 105:15). Taste and see that the Lord is good (Ps 34:8).

Many times it has been said to us that the sensible and bodily things are like this: each thing is only what it is; for example, a stream is nothing other than a stream, or bread. But the thing that nourishes the inner man is called food according to various thoughts. It is indeed called light, it is called a spring, it is called bread and flesh, true nourishment. It says, therefore, 'taste' by the incorporeal taste of the inner man, 'and see that the Lord is good' (Ps 34:8), because He is good. Just taste, know that He is nourishment, see the spring of goodness, the spring of kindness.

Blessed is the man who hopes in Him (Ps 1:1). The one hoping in the good Lord—for he tastes Him—and he will experience His sweetness, and from this food he will have all things, and being nourished athletically he will be strong, so that in the struggle he no longer has it 'not toward blood and flesh, but toward principalities and powers' (Eph 6:12). 'Taste and see that He is good' (Ps 34:8). If anyone is weary and sick according to the soul, let him taste Him as nourishment, as one preparing health, as one removing harm. And this food not only satisfies, but also removes, casting out the harmful things.

Therefore, 'blessed' is not simply the man, but the 'man' who has done away with 'the things of a child' (1 Cor 13:11), who has not walked 'in the counsel of the ungodly' (Ps 1:1), nor sat 'in the seat of scoffers' (Ps 1:1), nor 'in the way of sinners' (Ps 1:1), nor 'on the seat of scoffers' (Ps 1:1), but having 'his will in the law of the Lord' (Ps 1:2). This one has his will in the law of the Lord; for many observe the law so that they may not be punished or so that they may be honored with praise. But the holy one, the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Poverty of the Rich and the Fullness of Seekers
english: A perfect man has his own will within the law of the Lord, in such a way that his will is not something different from the legal will. And this legal will is this: to forbid evil and to protect virtue. Therefore, when someone becomes a law to himself—for 'these are to themselves a law, not having a law' (Rom 2:29)—it is as if he has his own law intertwined with the law of the Lord. 'Fear the Lord, all his saints' (Ps 112:7), for there is no lack for those fearing him. I urge all the saints to fear him, the Lord. It has been said in Isaiah: 'He himself shall be your fear' (Isa 33:15). Let him himself become your fear. And just as food becomes nourishment to some, and wisdom makes others wise, and righteousness makes others righteous, so they also partake of sanctification; for he himself is also the sanctification, 'who became to us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption' (1 Cor 1:30). Therefore, 'fear the Lord, all his saints.' His saints; for they are not merely called holy in a simple sense, but not [necessarily] his. As many as are being shaped into holiness seem to be saints, but not of God. And he gives the reason why 'all'; for 'there is no lack for those fearing him.' The fear of God makes [them] unshakable and unabandoned. 'Fear the Lord, all his saints.' Since 'there is no lack for those fearing him,' in order that you might become unabandoned, fear him, the God. And the fear of God is not passive, as I have said, but equal to reverence, equal to piety. When we take up a conception of God, fear immediately increases and piety arises; for we do not fear him as if we were terrified of him, not as if he were some bogeyman, but as something supremely venerable. And since the holy church stands glorious at the right hand of the Savior, all those completing it are saints. Therefore, concerning the calling of the Gentiles, it can be said: 'Fear the Lord, all his saints,' for there is no lack for those fearing him. 'The rich have fallen away and are hungry, but those seeking the Lord shall not lack any good thing' (Ps 34:10). The former, those completing the assembly before the arrival, [were] rich...

Being rich, they fell into poverty. The rich became impoverished and hungered, but those seeking the Lord shall not be diminished from every good thing. When the kingdom of God was taken from them, when the understanding of the divine writings departed from them, when they turned away from the old writing and from themselves, they became poor from being rich; for indeed this wealth fully benefits the possessor—for it becomes for him both food, and a covering, and a garment—so he says that these rich ones, having become poor, hungered. They cast away the spiritual food, they turned away from the 'bread of life'. They became poor; yet even if they themselves became poor, those seeking the Lord are not diminished from the good things, but they become full of them, they shall partake of them perfectly; for just as the kingdom of the heavens was taken from them—this also the mother of Jesus says: 'He has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty' (Luke 1:53).

Those formerly rich were sent away empty; for even if they possess the books of Moses and the prophets, they are empty of their divine fullness. Fullness, therefore, of the divine writing is not the shadow, but the truth and the Spirit. 'Those seeking' therefore 'the Lord'—the seeking implies a longing—are filled with all good things. Concerning this also the singer says, conversing with his own soul: 'Bless the Lord, O my soul, who fills your desire with good things' (Psalm 103:2). And: 'Trust in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart' (Psalm 37:4).

Upon it, those passing from the shadow of the law and from partial knowledge and prophecy, find all things good. But primarily the spiritual things of the law are good, unceasing and most full; for these lead one toward the truth face to face, that which brings the perfection, in which no one shall be imperfect. 12 Come, children, listen to me. I will teach you the fear of the Lord calmly, concerning the necessity of taking up fear toward God, and how some, having fallen away from him, have become poor and needy from being rich, and that those seeking the Lord whom they fear, are filled with all good things; therefore, toward all those becoming his children, he composes the teaching, saying: 'Come, children, listen'.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Unity in Virtue vs. Division in Vice
english: Not according to any flesh. Those rushing toward wisdom are children of the wise; those desiring to be sanctified are children of the holy; those establishing righteousness are children of the first righteous one. For it has been said to us at the beginning of the psalm (Ps 1:1) that even from the face of the Savior, according to the human, it is possible to be proclaimed. But those attending to virtue, those rushing to take up the knowledge of the truth, are children of the Savior.

Therefore he calls them 'forward-moving,' not so that, having moved transitively from place to place, they might come, but from disposition to disposition, from a lesser state to the greater and more perfect. 'I will teach you the fear of the Lord' (Ps 34:11). And these children, toward whom the word is addressed, 'infants in Christ,' are able to have a fear—not the perfect fear, nor the one making one unshakeable, but the one producing an avoidance of practical evil, the fear of punishment; for such people are children found imperfect. For he who fears the Lord is one who has not left Him, and these have not left Him, not possessing the perfect love which casts out the aforementioned fear, but some other thing of the divine participation. 'God' indeed 'is love' (1 John 4:8). And just as the one participating in righteousness is righteous, so the one having approached by this love and having become one with it is a child of wisdom, a son of love.

'Who is the man who desires life?' (Ps 34:12). When they were in the lesser fear, being those who bring on punishment and fearing the punishment so that no one might sin, they were a multitude. But when they henceforth rush to approach the one calling so that they might be taught the fear of God, the things being proclaimed are announced as if to a single one; for having been equipped 'with the same mind and the same judgment' (Phil 2:2) and each having been joined to the Lord and having become one spirit with Him, they cast off the multitude; for the multitude, especially that according to the soul and the inner man, or from opposition...

It happens either from a difference in being more or less. If all the called possess virtue, but do not possess it in the same way, there is a multitude. And this multitude is not one of opposition. But when they also possess opposing perceptions, many become [divided] because of the present evil; for evil is not unifying, but rather dividing. Therefore, we speak of a following of virtues, not of vices. It is impossible for vices to follow themselves; for they are excesses and deficiencies. And excesses and deficiencies are oppositions. Therefore, all those receiving virtue perfectly are one, and they become one toward God.

Immediately, therefore, all those believing according to the right faith have one heart and one soul, unlike those not having this. Thus, some are called double-souled. Therefore, the discourse is made toward man alone. For man is one according to essence; even if they become diverse and many men, they have a multitude from the qualities that occur. But according to the first underlying subject, the recipient of the qualities, they are one; for all are of the same substance. It is the task of man to set life, the task of the one saving according to the image, to be a man. A female horse does not set life.

Furthermore: 'What is a man?'—not the small thing, nor the impossible; but the one's own kind which we call individual, so that it may be: if anyone is a man of this kind, let him come and let him learn the fear of God. Do you love to see good days? (Psalm 34:12) Stop your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit. Immediately there follows the desire of life and the learning of the godly fear, to become in good days; for we are not as sincere as some think, to consider the well-being of the body and the surrounding wealth to be good days; for you have many such things in the Scripture: 'Honor your father and your mother, so that it may go well with you and you may be...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Synergy of Wills and the Crucifixion of the Self
english: "Long-lasting on the good earth, which the Lord God gives to you." If you were to take [this] regarding this earth and these immediate parents, it is a lie. Regarding the present [text], it is not said "which he gives to you."

"Stop your tongue from evil." He calls you to learn the fear of the Lord, so that having learned, you may become holy, undefiled, lacking no virtue. Therefore come, so that you may stop your tongue from evil. Let the tongue of the inner man no longer have evil. Then indeed it becomes all outward, when it has and brings forth the good. And it follows the stopping of the tongue from evil and the lips no longer speaking deceit, and it also calms the hypocrisy; for one who acts deceitfully is to do evil.

"Their tongue is a piercing arrow, deceitful are the words of their mouth." These are those from the heresies, those who stand before ungodliness. One can therefore say regarding the explicit [text]: since at that time especially when we say this, all were running toward evil, as for the remainder to sing laments over them, he was saying toward such people: for he did not say "each of my brothers" or "each of our brothers", that is, of the saints, but of those desiring to have one father, those born of the devil through wanting to do his desires; for "you are of the father the devil and you want to do the desires of the devil."

Regarding such brothers, born for the father and the evil one, he says: "every brother stumbles"; for indeed their father is such: by deceit he led all under himself and leads those following him by wickedness. "And every friend" is such [that he] "will fall". He is not speaking about those who are truly friends. Jesus says to the disciples: "You are friends"; and he gave the reason: "because all things of the father I have made known to you." None of these friends will fall. Because of this they are free. Therefore the word is toward those who are such: "they will by no means speak truth." Regarding those not speaking truth, the word is: "he did not stand in the truth." He who is not standing in the truth has once been in it. But we never say about anyone that he does not stand in a craft, unless he has been tested in a craft or in many crafts and...

He might pass from one [state] to another. If he had not become one in the truth, not standing in it would not have brought him reproach. And behold the doctrine: how 'God wants all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth' (1 Tim 2:4)? If no one opposes His will, how is it that some are lagging behind, despite His wanting all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth—so that I may not say, the majority? If He wants [it], and if we also want [it], and a convergence of the two wills occurs, salvation happens; for no one is good against his will, no one who does not want is saved, and no one hurrying toward approaching God and having kept His law is able to know the truth.

For this reason also the Savior says in the Gospel: 'If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself and let him take up his cross and follow me' (Matt 16:24). 'If anyone wants': as far as it concerns the Savior, He wills him to do this, but He does not compel; He moves the choice, He awakens the desire. 'If anyone' therefore 'wants to come after me', 'if anyone wants to follow me'—for this is what 'to come after me' means—, 'let him take up his own cross': let him be crucified to the world, let him put to death 'his members which are upon the earth', let him become inactive toward the world. He who is crucified has his feet hindered from walking as he wants, and his hands from doing what he wants. Therefore, when someone is crucified toward the world, he neither walks according to it anymore, nor does he do its things; and by this, the world is also crucified to the one crucified, so that the world may also be inactive toward him, neither walking according to him, nor doing those things that harm him.

'If anyone' therefore 'wants to come after me': perhaps not, perhaps yes; for virtue, when spoken of continuously, is virtue and perfection, not as in other actions. Just so also the apostle writes: 'Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, giving thanks in all circumstances' (1 Thess 5:16-18). He who rejoices always possesses the virtue always; for he rejoices not upon anything else except upon being well-pleasing in the pleasing God. 'Loving to see good days' (Ps 90:16). The 'to see' here means to be tested, and 'to be tested of good days' means to enjoy. 'Keep your tongue from evil'. Let your word be restrained, let it be tested; let it desire to have an unsearchable word; as it writes...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Pursuit of Righteousness and the Nature of God
english: The apostle calls the 'healthy word' 'unfailing' (ἀκατάγνωστον). He who possesses an unfailing word fulfills many commandments of Jesus. It is impossible for one not possessing an unfailing word to keep that: 'Let your yes be yes and your no, no' (Matt 5:37); for one who is not believing is sometimes required to swear an oath. But if one always possesses a word that is not scrutinized, no one ever doubts him, whether he previously tells the truth or not, or whether he says and does as he says, when an oath is required and his yes is yes and his no is no, such a word is indeed unfailing. Again, he who goes through the doctrines of the truth and demonstrates them scientifically possesses a word and is unfailing concerning them. No one is able to accuse him of lying, of thinking poorly, or of being outside the truth.

Turn away from evil and do good (Rom 12:21). This says: if you happen to be in evil, if you are settled in it and acting according to it, since I call you to the doing of the good, turn away from the evil. It is impossible to be outside both. Let the infants be circumcised now (cf. Acts 7:50). He who is not in good is in evil; he who happens to be outside of evil participates in the good. Therefore, 'turn away from evil.' And the turning is a matter of choice, for it protects and advises. But no one protects or advises one who does not have choice. I call you to do the good. You cannot do it otherwise and act according to it, unless you turn away from the evil. Thus also it is said in Isaiah: 'Stop from your evils, learn to do good' (Isa 1:16); for as long as anyone is in his evils, that is, his wickedness, he is acting [in them], and this one is unable to learn to do good. Again the law-giving apostle writes: 'Test all things, hold fast to the good, abstain from every form of evil' (1 Thess 5:21-22). Therefore also, 'turn away from evil and do good.' It is not sufficient to turn away from evil unless one also does the good; for it is possible to turn away from evil being prevented by fear of punishment from going toward this, but this one does not do the good by choice; for if you bypass the good by will, it is no longer at all good.
Seek peace and pursue it (Ps 34:14). Evil is a crowding thing and works turmoil in the soul; for the race of wickedness has much difference...

Evil things occur either in a small way or in excess, such as cowardice and rashness, or superstition and impiety. One must pursue peace; for to pursue it in this way does not mean that one has driven it away. You have this also in the Proverbs: 'those pursuing,' it is said, 'love righteousness' (Proverbs 15:27), meaning that God clearly loves them, that is, those who pursue. The righteousness that is pursued is all virtue. For Wisdom says: 'Evil men will seek me and will not find me' (Proverbs 1:28). The evil men seek wisdom only to hide it and make it vanish, as much as it reaches them. But those eager to become wise do not seek wisdom in this way, but they pursue it.

And I say, since you love these interpretive things: Herod sought Jesus in order to kill him. Often the Jews sought him in order to kill him. But the disciples sought him in order to be benefited, in order to partake of him. For someone said to him: 'The crowds seek to see you,' because they wanted to believe and see paradoxical works and hear words and chance upon healings. Therefore, 'pursuing' is a homonym.

16 For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous (Psalm 34:15). Much exhortation again, much instruction. This is what it says: the eyes of God are ready to see and save, and his ears are ready to obey. 'Turn away' therefore 'from evil and do good, and seek peace and pursue it' (Psalm 34:14); for immediately you will have God as a supporter. Only desire to be righteous, to pursue righteousness, and you have the eyes of God lying upon you and his ears ready to receive the requests which you make to him. 16 And his ears toward their prayers.

Often it has been said that what is spoken of humans regarding God must not be taken literally, as they think it is anthropomorphic; for they want there to be a human face concerning God, and they say that the man made according to the image and likeness of God has become so according to the construction of the body. But such a thing has been overturned by wise men; for they say: 'If by this the man is according to the image of God, because he imitates God physically and his body has a likeness to God, how then is God said to have wings: "In the shelter of your wings you will protect me" (Psalm 17:8)?' Therefore, a wingless being is the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of the Wicked Death
english: Man is such that he is not, according to the body, 'in image and likeness' of God. But if you reflect upon what the wings of God are, you will see that man also possesses such wings, intellectual ones, suspending him. Again, the eyes: since they take in all things according to history, the man having two eyes is not 'in image and likeness' of the One having seven, so that those things being lifted up from the sensible, the things concerning man being lifted up from the sensible, they preserve the likeness toward God.

And the face of the Lord is upon those doing evil (Ps 70:1). This he says because those doing evil are not righteous. And not being righteous, they are not feared by God, nor are they heard. However, they do not remain invisible to him. But when they fall into certain calamities and come to a realization that because of the evil things being done and thought they have come to these, they receive a vision of him. For Moses also pursued Pharaoh and his whole army with great speed, and he said he heard of God saying: 'I shall be glorified in Pharaoh and in all his army, and the Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord'; for how did they know? Having become submerged, no longer being able to escape, they received a vision of God. And it is set forth in the Psalms: 'Let them be ashamed and be confounded and perish, and let them know that your name, O Lord' (Ps 76:10). After the perishing, after the being ashamed, they knew God, and this is to be the appearing of him to be and to have a face upon those doing evil.

But how else does he say: 'And you turned your face, and I became troubled' (Ps 31:7)? Elsewhere it is said: the voice belongs to the Savior. Listen then: to turn the face he does not say is from those doing evil, but from those having it appearing to them. And having been slightly troubled, they thought it was happening outside the face; therefore also they were troubled. I perceived by sense that something unpleasant was above them. And the turning of the face happened thus, toward stirring up those who previously saw him and did not have him turned away, so that they might encounter him. But for those doing evil, neither is this the cause, but so that they may perceive that by the providence of God they were judged, that by the providence of God they are in calamities. And this also happens to...

The end is useful; 17 to destroy their memory from the earth. It is not merely 'their memory', but 'from the earth', so that they are no longer counted as belonging to the earth, no longer thinking of earthly things. Just as we say that he drove this man out of the country where many prostitutions are; for it is no curse that one should remove him from there, having placed him among the opposites. 18 The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them. And rightly so, since he has ears toward them; having cried out, they happened to find him listening. Pay attention, for two things are said, one praiseworthy and one punishing; 124 it is praiseworthy that the eyes of the Lord and the ears are toward the righteous, but the face of the Lord is punishing 'to destroy the memory from the earth'; for even if the end is not a decrease, but happens through evil, it is like through cauteries and surgeries and very sharp draughts.

Regarding the other thing, the preceding says: since the ears of God are toward the prayer of the righteous and his eyes watch over them, having cried out they did not fail; for he 'heard' 'them'. And toward the other: 'the face of the Lord toward those doing evil', in the following he says: 'but the death of sinners is evil'. Not every death is evil, but the death of the sinners. And the word is not now about the common man; for that is of a living being, not of one doing, not of a sinner, not of a righteous man. Even if you call him common, when he dies as a sinner, he has an evil death—for he will receive punishment—and if the other, that which is truly appropriate to the sinner, 'sin', he says, 'having been completed, brings forth death'. But sin is completed not from outside those doing it, but in the men doing it. Therefore the death following them is evil.

And regarding the former meaning, we say the death is evil as a maker of evil, as a corruptor. But here we say evil according to the second attribution, that it is outside of goodness. The grammarians therefore read evil as 'evil as a corruptor'. 'And all the evil diseases of Egypt I will not let touch you', the grievous plagues which the Egyptians suffered according to history. And when he says: 'abstain from every form of evil', we do not say...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The crushing of the heart and the path to glory
english: They are divine matters

"...that the man's heart shall be lifted up." The proud man hears words against pride, and at times he experiences the trial of afflictions, seeing that he is blinded. If you fall by this crushing, which leads you more effectively through the pains concerning humility, the heart is not lifted up. Before the rebuke—so that I may speak thus—and before the lashes, he has a lifted-up heart. For when he falls through afflictions, he recognizes that because of his own pride he has fallen down to the thoughtless.

Thus it must be heard also regarding: "Capernaum, which until heaven you were lifted up, shall be brought down to Hades" (Luke 9:79). And to be brought down to Hades is a crushing. Before this crushing, he had been proud. "Before glory, one is humbled" (Proverbs 18:12). It is necessary first to be humbled voluntarily, so that one may attain glory; for second, glory comes after the un-blinding. For this reason also the Savior said: "The one humbling himself will be lifted up" (Luke 14:11). And behold, "everyone lifting himself up will be humbled" (Matthew 23:12); he will be crushed here. Before this crushing, he has a lifted-up, vainglorious, proud heart.

Again, glory is brought to the one humbling himself, so that he may be un-blinded. Before this glory, it is necessary to be humbled; it is necessary to work, so that he may receive a reward. Therefore, he receives glory of the un-blinding from God. In this way also Peter exhorts, saying: "Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, so that you may be lifted up in due time" (1 Peter 5:6). And Job indeed says: God is the one "making the humble into height" (Job 22:9).

And "crushed" here he says "the heart," not those whose hearts are harmed. And sometimes the name of the crushing signifies such a thing as not having healthy thoughts, not having straight understandings. This crushing of the heart needs a physician, and a physician who heals what is hidden; for it has been said: "The Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersals of Israel, he who heals the crushed in heart" (Psalm 147:2). These were crushed like wounds. In this way also the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Humility and the Preservation of the Soul's Powers
english: Having descended from Jerusalem, that is, to Jericho, that is, to the place around the earth and its city called Jericho because of the interpretation of the name—for Jericho is interpreted as moon. And it is said, 'the fool is like the moon, changing,' like a moon which does not have increasing light, but diminishing. And the bride who is being hymned in the Song of Songs, 'emerging beautiful like the dawn' (Song of Songs 6:10), becomes 'like a chosen moon.' This change happens toward the better, toward the perfection; for in one way the moon changes: passing from the moon-like, it comes to the full moon. And there are four transitions of the progress of growth: moon-like, half-moon, quarter-moon, and full moon. And again, from the full moon it comes to the quarter-moon, and from the quarter-moon to the half-moon, and from the half-moon to the moon-like. In this way, the bride of the Word, the perfect soul, the church having been betrothed to him, emerges like the dawn. And she changes so as to become beautiful, chosen like a full moon. And after this he says: 'as a sun, a haze.' And from the lunar light it comes to the solar, being fulfilled of that prophecy which says: 'the moon shall be as the sun' (Malachi 3:1).

Someone, therefore, is being crushed when he is fulfilled of crushed thoughts, of mindsets alien to the healthy thinking of truth. Of these crushings the Savior becomes the physician; for 'he who is being healed' [is] 'those having crushed hearts and binding their fragments,' binding their wounds (Psalm 51:17). And I take by way of an example: someone is crushed many times in a struggle, contending against the adversary, and he attains a crown. Let not these crushings bring him mockery. But when he is crushed by beasts or robbers, we question him—not according to history I say, for he undergoes this through ignorance—but: 'Why has this happened where the beasts are, or why did you approach the spiritual robbers of wickedness?' 'And he will save the lowly in spirit.' Spirit here means the judgment. This is equivalent to that said in the beatitudes of the Gospel: 'Blessed are the poor in spirit' (Matthew 5:3), those poor in judgment. These are those who through the Word rightly achieve blindness, those having heard from the Savior saying: 'Learn from me, for I am...'

"I am also humble in heart." But opinion and heart are the same. Just as the Savior is humble in heart, so also those learning from him become humble in opinion. And these are the poor in spirit (Matt 5:3), those who do not wish to be rich in arrogance.

Many are the afflictions of the righteous, and from all their afflictions he will rescue them. It has already been said to us many times that from all of them he rescues (Ps 34:19). 'Many' are 'the afflictions of the righteous'; he said that through life and until a later breath.

The Lord guards all their bones. If they are rescued from all the afflictions so as not to fall and be crushed, all their sustaining powers, called bones, are guarded by God. And it was said before this that the powers of the soul are called its bones; for they are the sustaining powers of the whole soul, while the bones are the sensible powers of the whole body. It was impossible for the flesh or the others to stand; the things sustaining the members of the body are bones.

And the sustaining powers of the soul, such as the mnemonic or the contemplative or the aesthetic of the beautiful, when they are unbending and perfect, are held by God in this, not by their own power. Therefore, they come by preconception toward this willing, but they are perfected according to this, God having cooperated.

Not one of them shall be broken (Ps 34:20). If they are righteous and have cried out to God and were rescued from all the afflictions, 'one' of their bones 'shall not be broken', instead of 'one power'. And that I may begin from the more aesthetic of the powers: there is a certain visual power. When one does not see, so that he may desire the beauty of women and not be conquered by the desire of beauty, this bone was not crushed by the Lord, but is guarded by him harmlessly.

When, having looked into the heaven, one sees the sun and the moon and does not prostrate himself and worship, but from the seen creation understands Him who showed all things, and by analogously contemplating the greatness of His creatures and their beauty, this bone of the sight is strengthened. Thus I take it as more aesthetic, when someone does not accept a vain hearing, but judges by what kind of words he will be persuaded and by what kind not, and by what kind he will agree and by what kind he will be renewed—'compare your ear to the words of the wise', and 'he will not accept a vain hearing'—this one has...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Passive vs Active Injustice
english: And the bone, the hearing, the sensation of the hearing, remains uncrushed and healthy. 22 The death of sinners is evil, and those hating the righteous shall suffer lack. For the bones of the righteous are kept by the Lord, and not one of them shall be crushed, but the death of the sinners is evil. It has already been said to us that 'evil' is spoken in two ways. If death, which follows sin, tears one away from the blessed life—according to: 'sin, when completed, brings forth death'—then this death is evil. Again, since they are handed over to punishment having escaped from life, they have died again in order that they might be punished. For it is said: 'Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints'; for how could this be evil, or death be evil, being planted together with the death of Christ? 'For if we are of the same kind,' he says, 'we have become indeed by the likeness of his death, but also of his resurrection.' And: 'If we died with him, we shall also live with him.' 'And those hating the righteous shall suffer lack.' The sinner, if he receives remission of sin, hates the righteous. But hating the righteous, he hates virtue. For the sinners hate the righteous not as a man—for they do not hate the sinners—but as being righteous. But he who hates a physician as a physician, hates the medical art. Because of this they shall suffer lack, they shall be punished.

23 The Lord shall redeem the souls of his servants. Therefore he says: even if an evil death touches the sinners and for those hating the righteous there shall be lack, yet he redeems the good souls of his servants. He redeems the souls from those who previously held them in a painful grip. Again you take it both ways: he is redeemed from punishment and he is redeemed from sin; for if he is redeemed from sin, it follows that he is to be redeemed from punishment. 23 And all those hoping in him shall not suffer lack. All those hoping in God shall not suffer lack like those who suffer lack, namely those hating the righteous; for if for those hating the righteous the lack signifies punishment and penalty, then for those hoping in the Lord, the not suffering lack signifies not being punished, not being penalized, and not falling to those who cause pain.
1 To David. Judge, O Lord, those doing me wrong, fight against those fighting me. No one

He demands a judge, having thoughts as if he were being wronged. It is not the voice of one committing injustice, but rather of one being wronged, rather than one committing injustice. And no one at all prefers being wronged; rather, when both committing injustice and being wronged are set forth, if it is not possible for both to exist—for it is not possible—one chooses rather to be wronged than to commit injustice; for the one committing injustice undergoes punishment, and unrighteous ones are not able to inherit the kingdom of God. But the one being wronged is not tested by these things; for he is being wronged voluntarily. Let us add that even if he is not able to defend himself, he does not exhaust himself in struggle because he cannot take vengeance, but observing what has happened, he sees that the one being wronged is more sympathetic and has many who pity him.

And the unrighteous man, even if no one punishes him, is worthy of punishment. This whole matter of examining injustice and desiring to defend oneself as if one were not committing injustice—his conscience condemns him. There is much boldness for the one saying the psalm: 'Judge, O Lord, those who wrong me, fight against those who fight against me' (Ps 35:23). I do not fight them. And I am 'peaceable among those who hate peace' (Ps 34:14). I am persuaded by the Holy Spirit saying: 'Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word: say "our brothers" to those who hate you, so that the name of the Lord may be glorified, but they shall be ashamed' (Isa 54:17).

'Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word: say to those who hate you "our brothers"', so that I may speak truly and not merely with a voice; for those saying 'Lord, Lord' with voice alone, He says: 'Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?' (Luke 6:46). But the one saying 'in the Holy Spirit' [calls] Lord Jesus, through the participation of the Holy Spirit, by means of those things which he does and thinks; he cries out 'Lord Jesus' according to the Spirit. Therefore, 'say "brothers" to those who hate you'. Let them hate, but you call them brothers truly, not by speech alone, but you act out the obligations due to brothers toward them; for in this way the name of the Lord is glorified; for it is known that someone performs these things through God; for as far as it reaches the hating, he has not spoken of those who hate brothers. 'And they themselves shall be ashamed' (Isa 54:17).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Transformation through Christ's Passion
english: For those who are shamed do not rub [the wound]. Therefore, the saint fights no one. But the one being fought strives not to oppose, but to suffer nothing; and so I shall express it—since it is a violent thing and because of the vividness of the image—that he uses only a weapon, not a sword-shield, nor a defender capable of resisting and opposing.

'Fight those who fight me' (Ps 18:34). There was still in the act of doing wrong to him and in the act of fighting. So that they might no longer do wrong or fight, he asks God for an ally, not so that he might wrong them or fight, but so that he might remain unharmed while being wronged and fought. And the nature of the rational being, if it does not suffer perversion, possesses this as its own characteristic.

'Fight,' therefore, [meaning] prevent them from surrounding me with destruction. Take the weapon and the shield and stand up for my help (Eph 6:16). The shield of God extinguishes the flaming arrows of the enemy, of the evil one. Take therefore this shield, place it around me. I do not say this: 'You shall shield yourself with the shield.' Rather, take it in order to grant it to me, in order to make me secure. The weapon and the shield can be parallel. Perhaps also the kinds of weapons signify [something].

One may pray that the incarnation might happen; for when he takes hold of a man who is able to secure us and fight on our behalf, he took hold of a weapon and a shield and rose for our help. He rose from the bosom of the Father, so that, bending the heavens, he might descend, so that he might be seen fighting on our behalf; for he has come not to fight himself, but to fight on our behalf, and he has come not to suffer simply, but to suffer on our behalf. And behold: 'By the grace of God he has overcome death' (2 Tim 1:10).

We were all under death; our whole race was mortal. And the mortal is subject to death. To say of the one suffering through so much that 'he overcame death.' And that he did not suck up the whole mire of death—for it seems appropriate—thus it was made clear to me also in Isaiah: 'By his wound we were all healed' (Isa 53:5). And his wound, they say, is the cross. Regarding the nature of the cross and the greatness of the injury, it is not a wound. But it is a wound in the sense that, as a wound to him, it is not harming the one possessing it, but benefiting those for whom he bore the wound. So also 'by grace'...

He becomes the righteousness of God through death. For having become in death, he loosed death. And the suffering of the Savior is the loosing of the sufferings; for having become in the sufferings, he loosed them, not being mastered by them.

And just as one becoming a curse looses the curse so as to provide a blessing in its place—for we say he became under a curse not so that he might suffer, but so that he might loose the curse and extend a blessing in its place—so too, he did not make sin for us who did not know sin, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him (cf. 2 Cor 5:21). Sin becomes the means by which those having righteousness are made righteousness. It is not called sin simply, but sin for the purpose of making those previously mastered by sin righteousness, not simply, but the righteousness of God.

This signifies a participation in the quality; that those who participate are called by the same name as the quality they possess. They possess the quality of the righteousness of God. He conquered so much and mastered so much that not only the unrighteous, but that they might be called righteousness itself. And in many places of the Scripture you will find such things. It says, 'God is love' (1 John 4:8). See the greatness of love: 'God is love' (1 John 4:8). The same essence is signified by both names, God and Love.

Then he says that the one approaching God and loving him with all heart, and with all soul, and with all power, becomes love; for are the things said about love elsewhere—'love does not swell, does not wander, is not unseemly, does not count the evil, covers all, believes all, endures all' (1 Cor 13:4-7)—not things said about virtue? For I do not say that virtue endures or covers or believes. He named the one having love 'love' by the same name. Thus also those holding to righteousness become the righteousness of God from the sin made on our behalf, no longer merely righteous of God but the righteousness of God.

And this signifies perfection, progress. For many of the optative forms in Scripture are presented in the imperative character—perhaps also with others—and so that we may not depart far: 'Hallowed be thy name' (Matt 6:10), which is 'May thy name be hallowed.' 'Thy kingdom come; thy will be done' (Matt 6:10), which is 'May thy will be done.' 'Let the deceitful lips be removed'—instead of...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Pouring Out of the Word and Spirit
english: "that it might be born"—"those speaking against the law of the righteous". Does one pray to Him? To Him, yes. I say: if I wish to receive something from another, but I say it is from God, I would not be praying to that person, but to God, so that He might give us such a helper, so that He might lead such a person as a general into our midst. But when it is to Him, God: if someone prays to Him wishing to receive something, he brings both the request and the expectation of receiving to Him.

It is as if I say to God: "Drink from my merit," I am sending a prayer about prayer. "Hear my voice, O Lord, for to You I have cried" (Ps 130:1); and I am sending a prayer about a prayer; for since God needs cooperation and for the prayer to be heard, I call Him again a partner through the prayer, so that He might fulfill my prayer by hearing it. This is also what I mean by "arise to my help, not unarmed, but taking up a weapon." Receive my body and my soul; for through these you will be able to help me.

Often a physician, having great capacity, is unable to heal small things or small people. Sometimes, therefore, he prepares one of his disciples, one of the lesser ones and much more advanced than him, so that he might be able to approach this one and heal him. To take up a weapon and a shield means to take up a man, to assume the form of a servant. And such things often happen.

Therefore he says: if he proposes to help me as God, the help is superior. Having become a man, help me. And he says to Him: "Gird your sword upon your thigh, O Mighty One, with your beauty and your splendor" (Ps 45:3). You have beauty and splendor; for you did not commit sin, nor did you know it. "Gird" therefore "the sword upon your thigh." Often the name of the thigh signifies the things of generation, as if saying: "every thigh shall be moistened," meaning euphemistically and decorously through the thigh the functional organs of generation. Because of this also...

Abraham, sending his son for the marriage of Rebekah, says: 'Put your hand under my thigh, and I swear you' (Genesis 24:2); for since he was about to receive a virgin and lead her from a far place to a far place, he necessarily secured his prudence. And it is also possible in this way: since the one coming for the salvation of all is to come from my thighs, there 'put your hand, and I swear you'. And the Scripture very solemnly names many such things.

Concerning the dragon, that is to say, the devil, it says: 'Behold, his strength is upon the loins, and his power is upon the navel of the belly' (Revelation 12:5). Concerning the man, it named the loins, but concerning the woman, it solemnly said that organ 'the navel of the belly'. From the nearby parts, it revealed the use of what it spoke.

'Pour out your sword and shut against those pursuing me; multiply the sword, give us a sword against the enemies' (Psalm 149:6). And the living Word of God is the sword. And again the word of the Spirit: 'and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God' (Ephesians 6:17).

To pour out signifies always, as if it says: 'I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh' (Joel 2:28); it signifies a bountiful gift and a rich provision through the word. 'The love of God is poured out in our hearts' (Romans 5:5). And again: 'Your name poured out as oil'. The poured out oil goes out from the containing vessel and sends out its fragrance to the utmost.

When indeed the Savior was in Israel alone—for 'in Israel great is his name' (Psalm 72:17)—it was as if his name were in a vessel. But when 'how wonderful is his name' has become 'in all the land', and that has been filled: 'As your name, O God, so is your praise to the ends of the earth' (Psalm 72:17), it has become poured out oil. This word therefore signifies a bountiful provision. This then says: make each of us a sword-bearer, pour out the sword; for then you shut against those of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Depth of Judgment and the Nature of Shame
english: They persecute us; for indeed we become soldiers, approaching them with swords, not in order to strike down, but so that we might suffer nothing.

Regarding: what is the 'confinement'? The 'confinement' signifies many things, but most especially it has become a confinement that is like a gathering of the conclusion, which prevents the impulse of one desiring to philosophize. For even those who engage in dialogue have been accustomed to say, 'I have shut him in.' It also signifies something else, as it lies within the philosophy of Paul: 'God gave them all over to disobedience, so that He might have mercy on all' (Romans 11:32). And observe the sequence of the words: the Gentiles, having believed in the Savior, were descending [into the fold] from the Jews. And previously, again, the Jews prevented the nations from being called unto salvation; for they were saying, 'You are receiving into salvation those from the descendants of your cursed fathers, from idolaters, from many gods.' Therefore, He has made a confinement; He has reproved both.

And such an image is to be used: let someone have a son remaining with him and another cast out because of a malice that preceded. If, the cast-out having repented, the father wishes to receive him in, the son who remains opposes him, saying, 'Does this man become a co-heir with me? He has done such and such.' He reproves even that one upon other sins, saying, 'It is not for this reason that this one is cut off from the lot; and you cast him out, because you have done such and such.' And eventually he no longer argues; for this one too was shut in, that is, he was shut in by the reproofs, just as that one was.

'So that He might have mercy on all'—this is what He has done; for not so that He might prove them to be such, having pursued the reproofs, but so that He might prevent each one from the rest. For neither does the Greek still ascend above the Jews through the cross presented to the Savior by them, nor do they [ascend] above these; for all were found under sin. This is therefore what he says: 'Just as once you disbelieved in God,' you Greeks—even if now you have embraced the gospel and set before yourselves to be God-fearing, but once you also were impious—'but now you have been set free by their disobedience'—if Israel had not been disobedient, you would not have had salvation, for they were arguing and preventing—'so,' he says, 'these also,' the Jews, 'disbelieved in your mercy, so that they also might be set free.' Therefore, as a conclusion, it followed...

For God gave them up to all unrighteousness, that He might have mercy on all (Rom 1:24). The depth of the judgment: 'O depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God; how unsearchable are His judgments and untraceable His ways; for who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has become His counselor?' (Rom 11:33)—the one who shut up all into unrighteousness. Regarding wars, 'shutting up' is taken thus: when every way is removed from them to tread upon and to harm severely; for one is shut up in this way.

Just as the Jew reasoned to himself: 'Do not reproach the sin of the Gentiles; for you also have done the same things' (Rom 2:24). Again, the Greeks who were trampling upon the Jews and saying, 'The murderers and such like.' He says: 'When were you unrighteous? You were idolaters.' Having said to my soul, 'I am your salvation.' Say, O God, truly to the soul: 'I am your salvation.' But when do you say, 'I am the salvation'? Either when you save, or when you bring everything to my soul, leading it toward that same salvation?

Those seeking my soul were put to shame and were ensnared. These are the ones doing wrong, these are the ones warring, concerning whom he said: 'Judge those doing wrong to me, war against those warring against me.' 'They were put to shame,' he says, 'and were ensnared.' It is not possible for anger to be in them, but shame because of the things they they do; for in this way they will cease. Indeed, those having known this, that they have come into shame, say: 'We have slept in our shame, and our dishonor has uncovered us.' It is 'having known,' that they have come into shame and that they were exposed by dishonor.

And this shame and dishonor came from sin. Something like this also in Ezekiel, toward someone being insolent and acting impudently, he says: 'Be ashamed and take your dishonor.' As if someone, suppose, were condemned to serve in public works, such as in a mine or in metal, and thinks greatly upon this, we say to him: 'Be ashamed, know that you are in dishonor.' But—was it the shame of Adam? For not every shame is of the same kind. The scripture itself says: 'There is a shame that follows sin, and there is shame of glory and joy.' And behold: many regarding those things in which it is necessary to sink and to hide and...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Wicked as Chaff and the Angel as Tormentor or Corrector
english: They are glorified for appearing shameful. For the apostle says: 'of whom God is the womb and the glory in their shame, those who think on earthly things' (Rom 8:4). In those things in which it is necessary to be ashamed, they are bold; and we see such things by nature even among men. But he who awaits the Savior, the God Word, knowing that they are being transformed toward the more glorious and toward becoming conformed to the body which He Himself possessed, no longer thinks greatly upon shameful works.

'Let those who consider me evil turn back and be ashamed.' The word 'backwards' is used differently in various places of the Scripture. The phrase 'to turn back to the rear' carries a reproach. For instance, the wife of Lot, leaving from that place of destruction, heard: 'do not look to the rear' (Gen 19:26), meaning, do not set your heart upon that which you are leaving behind. Again, in other places it is said: 'my enemies turned back to the rear.' They turned back to their own rear, so that they might no longer pursue the same path as enemies. 'No one, having laid his hand to the plow, and having turned to the rear' (Luke 9:62). It was not said 'of someone,' but simply 'to the rear'; for when the plowman turns, he breaks the furrow. And the breaking of the furrow hinders the work. It is said that someone turns himself to the rear; this is praised, but this is a reproach. If one hastens to flee a path and turns, this turning to the rear is a reproach. But if someone is pressed toward evil and is checked and turns back by words of repentance, this turning which comes from repentance is praised.

For he says: 'since they pursue toward evil and it is their eagerness to harm me, they turned back from this intention.' Thus, they consider me evil in two ways: when they wish to surround me with sin, they consider me evil; when, wishing to attack, they want to bring something evil upon me, again they consider me evil. The two elders who remained, according to Sosannas, both did this: they considered it evil toward her, wishing to lead her into adultery. Having failed in this, they considered another kind of evil, to overthrow her, to stone her. Consider the same regarding Joseph and Egypt: there too, the matter of fornication was considered evil, e—
To which he was determined to destroy him. However, failing in this, he attempted another way of evils, leaving a slander against him, through which his supposed master was driven as a tormentor.

Let them become like chaff before the face of the wind. Let them become worthless. This is also said in the first Psalm: 'Not so the ungodly, not so, but like the chaff which the wind drives from the face of the earth' (Psalm 1:4). Their worthlessness shows not so much of substance as of intention; for 'those who think on earthly things' (Colossians 3:2), having become entirely of the flesh and of the members, are chaff not having a sheaf, nor a stable seat. Thus a wind briefly moves them. And this wind is able to be either tribulation or a deceptive word. For thus some are carried away by 'every wind of doctrine' (Ephesians 4:14) deceptively 'in the gambling' of those professing that cunning teaching of those practicing it.

And an angel of the Lord driving them out. They have an angel of the Lord driving them out. In the preceding Psalm, 'the angel of the Lord encamping around those who fear him rescued them' (Psalm 34:7). Here, however, the angel of the Lord drives them out, being a certain tormentor sent to punish them. But it is possible and praiseworthy to take the angel as 'encamping around those who fear him'; for the one who uses reproof drives out the sinner, persuading him to depart from what he thinks is pleasant.

Let their way be darkness and a slipping place. Their way—not that of God, not that of virtue, not that of the commandments of God, as it is said: 'I have run the way of your commandments' (Psalm 119:30)—but their way, in which they swell themselves, in which they think they run brightly. Let them know what their way is, let them slip; for this fall is shameful. Just as one who departs from running the straight way falls into a great evil, so the one hastening to run toward evil, when having slipped he falls, takes the beginning of repentance.
And an angel of the Lord pursuing them. As I have said, both reproving and striking or punishing them.

Because you have hidden from me for nothing the corruption of their snare. Evil is often called corruption; for it destroys the truth, makes the inner man evil from good, the just man wicked from the righteous, and the God-fearing ungodly from the God-fearing. And because evil is called corruption:
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Corruption, Punishment, and Vain Malice
english: He says, "they corrupt good habits, bad associations." This corruption—for it is not a physical corruption of the members—corrupts the habits. And the corruption of morals is a moral wickedness. "Bad associations" are deceptive associations.

And so that I may use an image of the prostitute introduced in Proverbs, namely false doctrine or licentiousness: the prostitute woman corrupted the good habits of that young man; for she had approached him with some sophistry. "A sacrifice to me is peace, today I pay my vows"—wherever you wish, the word "today"—"because of this, I went to meet you." But she lies. He did not go out in order to pay his vows, but "desiring." "Because you have hidden from me the corruption of their snare for nothing."

Many errors and false thoughts arise for those unable to distinguish homonyms. The name of corruption and of spoiling signifies many things according to the Scripture. "If anyone," he says, "destroys the temple of God, God destroys him." In this very same expression, two meanings of corruption lie: "if anyone destroys the temple of God" through sin, the body, for "your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, which you have from God." Therefore, all wickedness is corruption.

And the kind of wickedness is called corruption, the dissolution of virginity. Thus indeed we say to corrupt the virgin, and to corrupt the child having just tasted of the pleasures of Aphrodite. However, even if the genus of wickedness is called corruption, and even if the species, they are subject to a single signified thing: for such a corruption both destroys and ravages both the soul and the body.

It is said in the prophet: "Because of uncleanness you were destroyed by corruption." And uncleanness of soul is wickedness. It has been said indeed in Proverbs concerning some evil that: "it is crushed because of the uncleanness of the soul." And in the Lamentations of Jeremiah it is said: "her uncleanness is toward her feet," instead of: her way is unclean; for she treads upon the forbidden way of death, the evil way. "Because" therefore "of uncleanness you were destroyed by corruption." And uncleanness of soul is wickedness, as has been said, according to the twofold manner of the said corruption, and according to the genus and the species of wickedness, that is, both according to licentiousness and according to other kinds of wickedness. "Because of uncleanness you were destroyed by corrupt...

And it is also possible to take the other meaning of corruption from this: 'if anyone destroys the temple of God, God destroys him' (1 Cor 3:17). God destroys by testing. And just as the name of loss is taken in two ways regarding the soul, we say both that the sinner suffers loss and that the one being punished suffers loss: 'fear him' (Matt 10:28) who 'is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.' Here, loss is a punishment, which is also called corruption. Thus it is possible that 'because of impurity you were destroyed by corruption'; that is, you have fallen under punishment because you loved to be impure, because you hurried to have the impurity of the soul.

This impurity is the opposite of purity, which, coming upon the heart, brings presence and vision; for 'blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God' (Matt 5:8). Concerning this it is said: 'cleanse your hands, you sinners' (Ps 26:6)—and they become clean when they pursue 'the righteous thing righteously'—but also 'purify your hearts,' and right understanding through the contemplations of the truth. Therefore, 'they hid it from me in vain' (Ps 58:10), wanting to corrupt me to bring me down to wickedness, or even to attack and lead me into harm.

But each of these is doing in vain—for 'in vain' here means 'vainly'—that is, that because I did not provide a cause. The one previously set to act unjustly and to suffer evil rather than to do the opposite will say: 'those surrounding me do this in vain, as God becomes my helper' (Ps 58:10), or: 'they do it in vain because I did not provide a cause.' For example, if Susanna had been condemned by the elders through slander, she would have said: 'they decided against me in vain, since I provided no cause.' Joseph would have said this too, as would the disciples of Christ being persecuted, being denied, and being reviled for the sake of the name of Christ; for if any of the Christians is attacked not for any other reason but because he is a Christian, those attacking him attack him in vain; for sometimes some act against Christians, wanting to harm them, and they find a cause from within them. In vain they reviled my soul. For I did not do anything to cause reviling. And it was also said...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Joy in Providence and the Nature of Trials
english: By another meaning, it is signified that I suffered for nothing, because no cause was provided for me to suffer for the sake of the name of Christ and for no other thing. And again: 'He shall not take the reproach of evil men' (Psalm 34:18). 'He shall not take,' since it is up to us to acquire. But if, even though we have not acquired [it], some surround us with reproaches, 'vainly they reproach our soul.' Do you not say that Jezebel and those who breathed with her vainly reproached Naboth, to hide from him for nothing the corruption of their trap? Furthermore: the 'trap of them'; he says 'traps' not in which they are being trapped, but in which they wish to trap. The drama prepared against Susanna by the elders was a trap of theirs, not in the way that they themselves are being trapped, but in the way they intended to trap her and subject her to punishment and shame.

Let a trap come upon them, which they do not know. This he says: those who are powerful against some, devising machines and attacking them, vainly are never placed before their eyes, that they are able to ensnare those whom they themselves prepared; for example, 'he who digs a pit' (Psalm 7:15) for his neighbor, 'he shall fall into it.' They do not quite consider that they themselves fall into the pit, since they did not dig it. Therefore he did not know that the trap was coming upon them, which they were preparing for another in order to surround him and catch him. 'Which they do not know,' therefore, which they did not have before their eyes, since they were not even preparing it.

And the hunt, which they hid, let him catch them, in order that they might hide from others and without warning hunt those. 'Let him catch them.' 'They dug a pit before my face and fell into it' (Psalm 35:8). And in the trap they shall fall in it. In this one which they prepared for others, they shall fall. Upon the fall of others they themselves have fallen in such devices as some make, and they come against themselves. It happens in some entanglement of providence. The discourse concerning providence has a great entanglement, even if it is ignored by many, lest I say by all. And my soul loves...
She will rejoice in the Lord. Moses says, 'Do to him the way he has done evil to his neighbor' (Exodus 22:25). Having these things happen, she will rejoice, knowing that she has suffered nothing.

Is she rejoicing over them? No, but marveling at the providence and rejoicing that she was not overtaken. For example, the soul of Susanna rejoiced, not because the elders were judged, but because she was released from the indictment. And it happened according to what was destined.

And indeed, when the saints are in tribulation, they pray, praying only this: 'Let us not be taken by the tribulation' (Matthew 6:13), not rather against those surrounding them with tribulation; for they receive it as a contest, not as a punishment. And he who receives it as a contest is not so against the opponents, as to wish them no longer to exist. 'Bring us not into temptation'; for he has not said, 'Strike those who tempt us.'

I once asked, how did the marriage of the saints come to be without pleasure—not that 'the marriage is honorable and the bed undefiled' (Hebrews 13:4)—and I was told that the saints only understand the marital duties when there is also the occasion of coition. After coition, they do not touch. Therefore, it was said that their intention was not pleasure, which they intended to preserve, but to serve procreation. And pleasure is also necessarily joined, but they do not come together for its sake.

And the same happens regarding food: one is being fed not for the sake of anything else than to satisfy the appetite, in order to be satiated. But if it happens that the things being eaten are pleasant, he does not choose them for that reason because they are pleasant. And especially regarding medical aids, this happens: often the aid is pleasant, but it was not brought for the sake of pleasure. Indeed, even if it is tasteless, it approaches, because it does so for the sake of health and what is beneficial. And if, then, those who inflict [trials] cause the righteous to suffer the same things, he rejoices that it has not seized him. Therefore, let the 'if' and 'what they have suffered' fall away. But I marvel whether it is perfect according to the holy.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Relational Identity and the Bones of the Soul
english: This is understood by those making progress: that they have labored to possess something, but not perfectly. For what is the difference between 'upon the Lord' and 'in the Lord'? One who takes the prepositions unskillfully will say there is no difference. But it can be so: for instance, someone is rejoiced upon his child if he is healthy, but rejoiced in a drink of wine. He has a different cause for each.

Let us take the proof from another word: 'everyone' (as he says), 'who confesses in me in the presence of men' (Romans 10:10)—he did not say 'upon me'—'and I will confess him.' If the preposition had been placed simply, 'in' would have been placed even in the denial: 'and everyone denying in me, I will deny in him' (Matthew 10:33). But it was impossible 'to be denying in Christ' the one denying him, or for Christ to deny the one existing in him. Therefore, the one denying has been severed. The one who denies God has been severed, and his God has turned away. But the one confessing him is in him, so that you may not receive the confession by voice alone; for those honoring with lips confess, but they are not in him.

Since, therefore, our connection to God is also different, at times we say we rejoice upon him as upon a savior, as upon a benefactor, as upon a general who has secured the victory for us, but at other times 'in him' as in wisdom, as in sanctification, as in righteousness. The one confessing, therefore, is in Christ. And take from another example: one confessing knowledge cannot confess it otherwise than if he knew it.

But if so, is it as in essence or in quality? Let these things be left for later; for now the inquiry is about the difference of the prepositions. Whether one participates in essence or in quality, let it be at another time. And the same: for God is not a different Father becoming of the righteous, a different Creator of them, or a different King of them, in thought. From which we take the thoughts, since there is not in it a distribution of thought from thought. God is light, and is also sanctification and righteousness and wisdom, and it is not possible to separate existence from existence. But we separate relation from relation. Let a man be father and master and teacher and ruler; for he does not differ from himself. If, however...

You may hear that a ruler is [a ruler] in relation to those being ruled, and a king in relation to those being kinged, and a father in relation to the one born, and a master in relation to the slave, and a physician in relation to the one being treated, and a teacher in relation to the one learning; it is not the person himself in relation to himself that makes the difference, but the relation which is directed toward one other and another that makes the distinction. Just as it happens to the same person to be both father and teacher and the others, it also happens for the same disciple to be to the ruler and to the learner. Again, since one is not always said in relation to one—for it happens to find a son of another and the same one to be a disciple of another and a friend of another—9 he will be delighted in his salvation. Regarding 'salvation' here he means 'salvation'; for often 'salvation' signifies 'salvation'. And there is a case where even the agent of salvation is called thus, as if he were saying: 'The ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God' (Ps 18:45), instead of 'the Savior.' Therefore the soul 'is delighted' in 'the salvation.' It does not seek salvation from elsewhere than from this God, from Him, eternal salvation from the one saving; for 'Israel' 'is saved by the Lord with eternal salvation' (Ps 106:1).

10 'All my bones shall say, Lord, Lord, who is like you?' (Ps 62:11). First, it is theology to know what the holiness of God is and who is able or unable to be made like Him. Therefore apply this theology and the knowledge of God to your own bones, from which it appears that he is not speaking about his own bones, those which hold together the other members of the body and the flesh and the nerves, but about the agile powers, of which we have often said that they are the bones of the inner man. Therefore 'all' 'my bones shall say'; the agile doctrines, my agile movements, according to which I recognize and understand, confess God, that no one of the created things happens to be like Him. Furthermore: the 'who' [refers to] how? —in the context of the impossible, as in: 'God, who shall be like you?'; regarding the Son we do not take this [to mean likeness in the future]; for he does not have the likeness in what is to come, but being the 'character of the substance' he is eternally like. Therefore two things can be taken: if concerning likeness of essence, no one is made like Him. But if concerning [likeness] according to virtue and holiness, he who is made like Him is rare.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Purpose of Goodness and the Sackcloth of Repentance
english: Him. Rescuing the poor from the hands of those stronger than he. If the similarity is taken regarding this action, the verse signifies: God rescues the poor and the needy from the hands of those stronger than him. And this is over men, such as rulers, powerful in strength, and also the devil himself. Therefore, only God rescues from these. If, however, as I have said, he is rescued from practical matters, the verse is also able to do this; for it is not a great thing to rescue from lesser things. Those remaining according to Sosannas seemed to be stronger than her; for they were rulers and judges, but that woman was a chambermaid and a private person. And God rescued from the stronger. And this is to be understood: everyone who is of some lesser strength is poor according to this, the one unable to benefit himself, the one not able to help himself and to make himself out of the surrounding circumstance. And poor and needy from those seizing him. And it happens especially according to the underlying subject to be both poor and needy. If he is outside of wealth, he is poor; but if he is satisfied by his toil, he is a needy man; for 'the rich have become poor' (Job 22:28). If, therefore, you lift these things up, you take the man from the Jews who believed to be the poor, and the needy as one not having hope, but also being godless.

Unjust witnesses arose, things which they did not know, they questioned me. The unjust witnesses question him about things which the one whom they wish to testify against does not know. Here, 'things which they did not know', [is] 'things which they were not tested'. The name of not knowing sometimes signifies ignorance; 'but at that time not knowing God', it declares ignorance. It also signifies not having been tested, as if I say: 'the one not knowing sin', the one not having been tested by sin. Therefore, he knows her according to something; he understands her nature. But he does not know her without having used her. Thus also regarding wives and women in general, it is said that: 'he did not know her', 'he knew her'. He signifies the experience here. 'And Adam knew Eve his wife' (Gen 4:1). This was said when they had come together; for he approached: 'and having come together, she bore' (Gen 4:1). Therefore, the unjust ones are witnesses who say against someone things which are not present to him. Such also is this: 'as the evil was turning away from me, he did not know'. Repay me evil for good, and barrenness to my soul (Ps 31:11). It was necessary for him...

They did not realize that I was not being kind to them, nor did they know what I am asking; for I was about to be punished, and because of this, not only will they not be punished for me, but as much as it concerns me. Thus we also interpreted the Gospel: 'Be well-disposed toward your adversary until you are with him in the way' (Matt 5:44).

And since the word of well-disposition is this: 'Well-disposition is a will of good things for the sake of the neighbor,' for many times I desire to provide good things to him in order to gain something from him. Therefore, they wanted to punish me, who had done them no wrong, but had also provided them an opportunity for salvation. Such also is what is said by Jacob to Laban: 'Know, if there is anything of yours with me, take it' (Gen 31:32). I do not want any of yours; I am well-disposed toward you, I give back to you the things. Instead of the good things which I did for them, I have done good things to them so that they would not be established for the sake of being punished because of me, since I did not show them.

Even Susanna would not have said concerning the elders: 'They intended to tear me away to adultery; I was not well-disposed toward them; I did a good thing to them; as far as it concerns me, they have not committed in sin to make me barren' (Sus 3:7)? The 'they repaid me' is common; just as they repaid me evil instead of good, so also they repaid my soul with barrenness. And what about the offspring of the soul? Right thoughts, excellent deeds. 'From the fear of you we conceived in the womb and labored and brought forth' (Ps 22:3).

And I, while they were bothering me, was putting on sackcloth.
