Behold, their evils and the reason for wanting to make her barren—they bothered her by name, as the one who said, 'sophistical disturbances bother me more than they harm me.' However, I was putting on sackcloth so that, not being abandoned, I would not be captured by them, and on their behalf so that they would cease their insolence toward me; I was putting on a certain strict life, bearing in some way a sign of repentance, so that I might not be harmed by the bothering, and on the other hand, so that they might not be emboldened. And it is much more for the good, if they should cease. And they humbled my soul in fasting (Ps 35:6). I was not putting on sackcloth alone, that is, strictness of life, but also 'they humbled my soul in fasting,' both according to the literal sense and according to the original sense, no longer being nourished by those painful things.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Humiliation of the Apostle
english: And the use of history often happens for assistance; for we have seen many things accomplished through fasting, such as the city of Nineveh not falling to destruction, and the nation of the Jews being saved from Haman. 'And my prayer shall turn into my bosom' (Ps 17:5). By the name of the bosom, in many writings, the governing principle and the mind are signified, as if it says: 'everything shall turn into the bosom of the unrighteous.' It is equal to: 'I have given their ways into their own heads' (Ps 106:15); for again the heads signify the governing principle: 'his labor shall return upon his own head.' The holy man prays that good things might come to be. And there is no other prayer than a 'petition for good things from God.' When someone obtains the good things for which he prayed, his prayer was turned into his own bosom. It was not cast away and remained outside, whose voice was sent up and was scattered into the air, but it brought what he had asked. And this means that his prayer is not sent up in vain, but is received into the heart of the one praying, into what he asked: 'the one filling your desire with good things.' The one desiring them is filled with them. 'This deception is in the land of Egypt, in their bosom' (Gen 41:54). And: 'the woman who is in your bosom,' whom you love, who is of one mind with you, who is in agreement with you. 'And my prayer shall turn into my bosom.' The one asking good things from God prays. When he obtains what he asks, his prayer turned into his bosom, into his governing principle. And I have diverted from many sayings, that the governing principle is often signified by the name of the bosom: 'this is their deception in the land of Egypt in their bosom.' And again: 'everything comes into the bosom of the unrighteous.'

But the bosom signifies intimacy. So also in the bosoms [of the patriarchs] Abraham found rest, having the same courage and endurance, and: 'the woman who is in your bosom,' your own, living together with you. As a neighbor, as our brother, thus they were pleasing. This says that: no one has an excuse to be angry with me, no one takes from me a cause to be an enemy to me; for toward each one I was thus as a neighbor, as a brother, and thus they were pleasing through brotherly love, friendship, and sibling-love. As one mourning and dejected.

Living, thus I was humbled. 'Thus I was humbled' because of them. Those whom it seemed to be neighbors and brothers were gathered against me; they waged war against me, as in the beginning of this psalm: 'Judge, O Lord, those doing wrong to me, fight those fighting against me' (Ps 54:5). Again he says: 'To me they spoke peace, but they were plotting deceit in anger' (Ps 55:21). Because of this, as one mourning them and as one being gloomy toward them, thus I was humbled; for if I were providing them with things that gladden, I would be exalted, rejoice, and be glad from cheerfulness.

But what about 'thus I was humbled'?—if someone has a son whom he loves and desires, and sees him burning, he is humbled, because not as he wished him to live, thus he sees him suffering evil. Since therefore I was providing opportunities for virtue as toward neighbors and brothers, but they themselves were proving to be enemies and foes, I was humbled toward them, though it was necessary for me to rejoice toward them. What do you think of Paul concerning Hymenaeus and Alexander, was he not humbled seeing them shipwrecked concerning the faith? Was it not previously thus toward them, that he did not love, did not give opportunities toward blessedness? And if these things are said regarding the face of the Savior, he is able to say these things regarding Judas and regarding the whole people of the Hebrews. And they rejoiced against me and were gathered together.

But do you wish to know that the descent upon one sinning is humiliation? Paul writes to the Corinthians, stirring them up toward repentance, he says: 'Lest coming I should find you and my God should humble me' (1 Cor 4:14). The holy man is exalted when he sees those being helped by him becoming better. And a father, having rejoiced over children and being glad, is exalted. If I had been preserving the love which I was preserving toward them, toward me, I would not have been humbled, but I would have been exalted, having such as equals, having sharers. 'And they rejoiced against me and were gathered together.' But I was thus toward them from most private compassion; but they, from the opposite, having been gathered against me, rejoiced or, having rejoiced against me, were gathered together, in order that they might bring more evil and misery to me. Scourges were gathered against me, and I did not know. The eagerness is to do evil. I said in the previous readings from one of the psalms, that the same evils are to some as scourges, and to others as contests, when...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Unawareness of the Virtuous in Suffering
english: The subject at hand is: 'Many are the lashes of the sinner.' Here, lashes and evil powers may be said to be meant. 'They seized him, and he did not know' is similar to what was said: 'While the evil one was turning away from me, I did not perceive him.' The evil one was approaching; he provided no place for himself, having been persuaded by the apostolic opinion which says: 'Do not give place to the devil' (Eph 4:27).

I have not exhausted his examples. One of the ancient philosophers is said to have scourged himself so that he might fall from his own city, so that he might be accused by his fellow citizens. Fearing lest he should even utter a single word in pain, he bit his own tongue and cut it and threw it to the one who was assaulting him. That man was not able to say 'I did not know'; for indeed he knew a little, unless he had secured safety from some other source. But the holy man did not. Isaiah was sawn with a wooden saw.

And behold the wickedness of Manasseh the apostate, who practiced idolatry. And when the idol that he himself had set up fell, after Isaiah looked upon it and other things, they set forward accusers and two charges were brought against him: one, that, saying Moses said, 'No one has seen my face and shall live,' this man says, 'He saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne' (Isa 6:1). But if he stood precisely in the truth, I perceived his slandering. He did not say at all that he did not see his face. He saw it concealed, so that we might show them to be slanderers according to the word.

This, therefore, was the charge brought against him, and a second, that, regarding the ruler of the discerning race, of the holy priesthood, of the royal people, he said, 'Ruler of Sodom,' and regarding the people whom God loved and whom God honored, he said, 'People of Gomorrah.' Because of these two charges they slandered him, even though they previously knew that he did not say such things about him, but when the idol fell, they acted so that they might not appear as if they were avenging a god who was not manifest, but instead they attached a charge to him.

Isaiah might also say, 'whips were drawn against me, and I did not know.' Consider the malice of Manasseh; so that he might remain suffering for a long time, he was sawed with a wooden saw, so that the flesh being removed by those mills might prepare more pain and more duration.

Regarding the question: do they present punishments as if for a wrongdoer, and because of this they are whips? But I did not know them as whips, for I struggled and was crowned through them. Then I tested them, to see if I was such a person as those seemed to punish. Hypothetically: perhaps they also whipped Susanna, those who worked the slander against her; for there was such terror in her falling, as to say, 'distress is all around me.' If they offered these atrocities as if for an adulteress, they were whips. But she did not know them; for she was not lawless.

Let virtue, therefore, be like fish-glue to the saints. Let fire be offered, such as the burnings of shameful passion. She did not know that the present thing is a burning, that is, she was not tested; but the fish-glue, being bodily, is consumed by the fire, and then the fire of Him who was anointed is poured out, and he was not previously harmed. But for him whose virtue is a bonfire, the fish-glue-like substance remains always, and the fire never prevails against the one possessing virtue.

Regarding: 'He set the Most High as his refuge, and no whip shall strike his tent' (Ps 91:7): we find many having been whipped and having died in the whipping. If, therefore, we say that the one being whipped with sensible things does not feel their pains, it is not a struggle. This is not a great thing, and anyone could endure this. But they did not know, and this happens while being forced by the whips into being tested and being made to do something against their will. Behold, the examples of Susanna have become manifest; let the example of Joseph also be taken: how whips were presented as if for a lawless person, and neither of the two knew anything.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The division of tongues and the meaning of regret
english: Nebuchadnezzar plotted and was scourged as one blessing God, just as the devil said instead of blaspheming, and he did not realize; for he did not cast off godliness. Furthermore, it is not said improperly: 'I will hide you from the lashes of the tongue' (Psalm 52:2). What is this 'lash of the tongue'? Do not take it in a sensory way. It is a false word, a slander. In this way also the evil powers, since they are overcome more by the lashes of the ruling faculty being unguarded against them, are called 'lashes.' And that these lashes are such, they 'were gathered together.' To be gathered together is according to some logic. They were split apart and were not unified. Agreement upon evils is a great evil, it is harmful.

Thus, those coming from the east and coming into the plain of Sennacherib, where also Nebuchadnezzar raised his image, once agreed in one mind. And see that this is evil. It is interpreted as 'a scattering of teeth.' Often teeth are taken instead of words; for instance, 'he crushed the teeth of the sinners,' and we do not mean these sensory millstones; for this was never recorded. And: 'The Lord crushed the millstones of the lions.' He does not speak of the sensory, four-footed, and wild beasts, but of such humans. Therefore, agreement upon evils is most trivial. But the scattering and the division of these is something good.

If those realize that because of private malice they were scattered from those being in agreement, and by the sparing of God—just as the Sadducees and Pharisees once agreed according to Paul, when they also brought him into the council, and the high priest gave him to them so that he might be bound to know something about him—they had taken haste to overthrow him. But they deemed themselves worthy to have him led away and to stand upon the steps. 'Knowing that the one part belongs to the Sadducees and the other to the Pharisees,' something said that dissolved and split their agreement; for he said: 'Concerning the resurrection of the dead I am judged today' (Acts 23:9), and they were split, some saying: 'He says nothing absurd' (Acts 23:9), and the other part, the lying. If they had realized from this split, they would no longer have plotted against Paul. They were not unified, therefore; they did not know the cause of the division. And David, indeed, prays and says: 'And cut off the tongues...'

Their tongues are divided; for then their tongues are divided when they begin to fight in speech. This indeed happened to the elders according to Sosannas; their tongues were divided, the first saying one thing and the second another. If they had realized [their error], they would have ceased the accusation and would not have endured what they underwent.

Thus 'they were split' and 'they did not realize'. The one who split them did so so that they might realize and repent; but they did not know the cause of their splitting and their division. Regarding 'they did not realize'—they did not change their mind. To realize is to set aside one's former thought and original disposition. Indeed, when Ahaziah realized what had passed, God says to Elijah, 'Have you seen how Ahaziah realized?' (2 Kings 9:27), for he returned weeping. And regarding this change of his, He called it his realization. And the Saint, if he says, 'so that my glory may sing to you and I may never realize,' he means 'may I never change my mind.'

Regarding other matters, realization happens concerning things not going rightly. 'They tested me, they mocked me with a sneer.' It was necessary for them, having realized, to cast away their anger against me, but instead they laid upon me, they attacked, they tested me, they mocked me with a sneer. However, even though they tested me, they did not find me as they wished; they did not enter into temptation, I was not seized by the snares of their temptation; for this is also what is interpreted: 'lead us not into temptation' (Matt 6:13). 'They mocked me' means they treated me with contempt. And again, bravely standing against their sneer, I showed nothing.

'They gnashed their teeth at me.' One gnashes his teeth sometimes against another, and sometimes against himself when he changes his mind, having fallen into the cruelties of what he has done; 'there will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth' (Matt 13:42), because knowing that they are punished because of their own impiety and sin, they weep and gnash their teeth in repentance. Another gnashes; therefore 'he gnashed his teeth at me' is said concerning the devil, and concerning the wicked here: 'they gnashed their teeth at me.' Failing in what they were striving for, they gnashed as if having done evil in vain or having fallen into a trial of what they intended to do, suffering what they intended to do to another. Regarding the words, then, must we take the teeth?—if [there is] repentance.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Restoration from Malice
english: It also signifies the anger of those who did not endure what he intended to do; we take this from 'they gnashed their teeth', so that the gnashing of the teeth signifies their destruction, or a pain coming upon them because of what they encountered. But if you wish to take the teeth otherwise, it is not from this specific word; for often it is true to take a theological insight, though not necessarily from this word. And because it is true, those who are unable to harmonize the meanings with the words accept it.

The teeth are often called the masticatory powers of the soul. And with these masticatory powers which mince the foods, if one were to use them properly, he eats the 'bread of life', the fruit of the 'tree of life', the flesh of Jesus. But if he were to use them badly, he eats the flesh of the dragon. And the flesh of the dragon are impious doctrines, they are great sins; for just as the body of Jesus is filled up from the doctrines, as it says: 'vainly puffing oneself up' in haste 'with a mind of flesh and not holding the head, from which the whole body being joined together increases the growth of God'.

This says: he who has a fleshly mind, that is, he who approaches carnally and sensually, has a mind vainly puffing itself up being flesh, and does not hold the head of the doctrines, he does not hold the Savior, who is the head of the doctrines. And the great [things] of those being theologized are the head of such a body, 'from which the body being joined together through every ligament and sinew increases the growth of God'. In this same way also we, when more words and many headings have their reference to one thing, we say the word has been embodied.

If we take that the masticatory powers of the soul [are the teeth], we say something true, but not regarding the immediate context. But if you also take this, that some use these masticatory powers treacherously against that: 'if you bite and devour one another' (Gal 5:15), and: 'those devouring Israel with the whole mouth' (Rev 9:5), and these refer to punishments, it is also possible to think thus: 'they gnashed their teeth against me'; they gnashed these teeth, and because of this they will undergo destruction; for 'you crushed the teeth of the sinners' (Ps 58:7). Lord, how long will you look on?

When you visit so as to forbid them, and to make me outside of the harms? For regarding 'to turn away' and 'to look away', we have often said that to pass by signifies long-suffering. 'Lord, when will you have pity?' For if you have pity, you will also do good to me, looking upon me and having mercy on me, and you will set even them outside of their haste toward evil, so that they do not harm me, nor do they remain any longer in that beastly malice which they are still practicing.

Restore my soul from their malice. He says this because lying enemies are present, many and having much planned maliciously against him. And from the beginning of the psalm this is presented: 'Judge, Lord, those doing wrong to me, fight against those fighting against me' (Psalm 35:23), and the following: 'And until I saw, Lord' (Psalm 34:19); 'they gnashed their teeth against me' (Psalm 35:16); 'whips were gathered against me, and I did not know' (Psalm 38:11).

He says therefore: make my soul outside of them; for indeed it was outside of them; for this is what the name of 'restoration' remembers. No one enters into a place where it never was, it is said to be restored, but one having come from one fatherland to another fatherland, or from one place to another place. He says therefore: they wished to ensnare my soul, being holy, to subject it to corruption. Then it is restored from the malice of the wicked, when it suffers nothing from them, when it does not act against them.

Susanna was overturned regarding her self-control, and she was very much self-controlled having been educated according to the Law of Moses, despite how far she had fallen into adultery by the elders attacking her. She pleaded, saying: 'Restore my soul' (Psalm 31:6), to lead her back into that same self-control from the malice of these men. All who are plotting against one say these things. And the soul of the martyrs is restored, having been tested in nothing.

For as to what this 'to restore' signifies, in one of the psalms he says: 'You are the one restoring my inheritance to me' (Psalm 71:19). According to this meaning we say the man is restored into Paradise, because entrance there has become possible for him, when the penitent heard: 'Today you will be with me in Paradise' (Luke 23:43). 'Restore' therefore 'my soul'. They have acted with such malice toward me as to have become wild beasts. 17 [Restore me] from lions, my only one.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The distinction between unique and only
english: "Restore my only-begotten from the lions" (Ps 51:7). He says that he has his soul as only-begotten. He had it as only-begotten; he had it as alone. It is not possible for more than one soul to be tested, since therefore it is only-begotten to me.

And in another way: "God made man upright" (Gen 1:26), "in his own image" and "likeness" he created him. When it remains in this state according to which it was created, it does not become outside himself; it does not become outside himself. Since therefore it is the person of the Savior saying this—which Jesus had as a soul—it does not belong to anyone else.

And our souls become those of the rulers; for whoever is defeated by someone, to him he is also surrendered. And it is indeed possible to fall away from the true Lord to other masters and from one to others, when discordant sins occur; for the one having repented is restored from the malice of those surrounding it into goodness. Since therefore the soul of Jesus "has been tested in every way according to likeness without sin" (cf. Heb 4:15), it never belonged to anyone else except to the one who took it. Because of this he calls it his only-begotten.

And it must be said also thus: "my only-begotten"; for all souls become of the Savior: "receiving the end of faith the salvation of souls" (Heb 2:4). Concerning salvation, therefore, is the seeking and searching of a prophet. They are, therefore, "receiving the salvation, the end of faith" of the Savior. They are indeed members of him, all of them becoming his body. But this one is to him differently from those; for this one he chose to have as an instrument and a temple, so that through it he might dispense the energies, through it the salvation.

So also, having been born in Hades, he did not remain there; for he was only-begotten of him. And "only-begotten" often signifies "alone." Aetius the Arian, the father of Eunomius, who overwhelmed him, used to say: "as great" (meaning), he says, "are they being granted to Christ because he is the only-begotten of God." He says: "and others are only-begotten; the world is only-begotten, the sun, the earth." I say to him: it is not the same to be called only-begotten and an only-begotten offspring and an only-begotten child. Only Jesus is said to be "only-begotten Son" (John 1:14); for it is said: "we beheld his glory, a glory as of the only-begotten from the Father" (John 1:14). And the "only-begotten from the Father" child...

It is not 'only-begotten'. And it is always so: 'For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son' (John 3:16). He never said 'only-begotten' simply, but 'only-begotten Son'. And again: 'because they did not believe in the name of the only begotten Son of God' (John 1:18). If something were a unique creation, as you say, 'monogenes', but not a unique work—for there are also other works of God—it would not be a unique creation.

Therefore, when the saint says: 'Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am alone and poor', he means 'I am alone'. And Elijah, saying: 'I alone am left, and they seek my life to take it from me' (1 Kings 19:10), it would have been said 'alone', not 'son' or 'child'. And here he says: 'my only one from the lions', the cruel ones, those having risen up against me. Save and redeem my soul, which is mine alone; for this one alone did not know sin, this one alone 'has been tested in all things without sin' (1 Cor 10:13).

Furthermore: how was he restored? He did not fall into sins, but rather, how much he was reverent toward the cruelty of those lying in wait, that he might not suffer this. Now we speak from the perspective of the holy man. And the examples of Susanna and Joseph are clear. And the devil himself has devices, sophistic thoughts, which only he and every diligent person can know. For Paul says: 'we are not ignorant of his devices' (2 Cor 2:11). His thoughts are his methods, his very wiles, the sophistic thoughts through which he wants to campaign against us.

Therefore, 'restore' us; for the state of being frightened was entirely a pre-passion. And he wants to bring us out from that pre-passion; for he did not say 'from my wickedness'. Furthermore: to what state of indifference? He did not say, while being frightened, 'restore me to indifference', but to a state where he no longer even has pre-passion. I have a feeling that I am disturbed. 'Restore' therefore 'my soul'. 'Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why are you troubled within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him' (Psalm 42:5); for he did not say to another; he spoke to his own mind: 'Why are you sorrowful and why are you troubled within me?'. You have Him who stops the disturbance. As if someone were saying while burning and being agitated: 'Why do you burn so? There is a physician able to...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Critique of Protagoras and the nature of perception
english: To be freed from the fever. 'Hope in God, for I will confess to him' (Ps 34:8). Once she persuaded herself to hope in God, she was restored from dread and turmoil, which dread and which turmoil arose from the malice of evil powers and from the devil himself. 'From lions, my only-begotten one' (Ps 22:1). He named these malicious ones and lions those who wish to fight, those who attack and come like whips against him.

Since 'he has been tested in all things, yet without sin, according to the likeness' (Heb 4:15), we grant her a pre-passion. But pre-passion is not sin; for if you do not grant this, you introduce another essence into the soul, and it would have neither glory nor worthiness of praise and crowns if it were not shaken. For you have in the Gospel that: 'she began to be terrified and to be in distress' (Mk 5:38); for is not the 'beginning' something other than the pre-passion? This beginning is only the beginning itself; it has nothing with it. This alone, before the choosing of evils, chose the good. This has often been said.

The essence of the rational [soul] is receptive of those things it is naturally disposed to receive. It is receptive of passion, desire, grief, turmoil, and fear. When something presents itself that moves fear, the rational essence is certainly troubled. Sometimes, however, it establishes the turmoil immediately as if nothing were with it. This they call pre-passion.

You say: is it the same to say 'a man' and 'a doing man'? If I say a man has died, I do not speak of the 'doing' man, such as the righteous man. The death of the righteous is not necessarily the dissolution of the soul from the body, but the ceasing of being righteous. This is the corruption of the righteous. Often, being ignorant of the false opinions of the ungodly, we fall into them. And falling into those, we lose the right opinion. You ask: how do you say that I have not understood? I do not call him righteous. But if another understands as has been said and calls him righteous, he is the same [man] both righteous and unrighteous. Listen then, because...

What have I said regarding the opinion of the Protagoreans—for Protagoras was a Sophist—they say that being for those that exist is in appearing. They say: 'I appear to you now sitting; but when away, I do not appear sitting; it is unclear whether I sit or do not sit.' And they say that all existing things are in appearing; for example, I see the moon, but another does not see it; it is unclear whether it is or is not. To me, the healthy one, there comes a perception of honey that it is sweet, but to another that it is bitter, if he is feverish; it is therefore unclear whether it is bitter or sweet. And thus they wish to dogmatize incomprehensibility.

If then we also say: 'Since it does not appear to me, by what reasoning has he spoken, I consider him unjust and impious.' If it appears to another, by what reasoning has he spoken, he appears just and pious to that one. And another again does not even stand by the things said by him; neither is he pious nor impious, and we fall into the Protagorean opinion. Let us see then: it is necessary first to understand things and thus to judge or not to judge. He who does not speak of him correctly nor healthily spoken, what kind of intellect of the words does he speak of?

But how then does Job speak? (Job 3:3) If I say: 'Let the day perish in which I was born,' let the genesis perish; for I have come from better things to worse; for it is profitable for me that the evil should perish. As if Jeremiah speaks concerning the people of the Hebrews—and each of the captured Hebrews will say—'Let the day of captivity perish,' he does not say this: 'let there be no more captivity.' 'Let there be no more,' he says, 'that day, it has passed away'; for has it still stood? It had one hundred and forty-eight years when he said these things. How did that day, in which he was born, remain? For it passes away and it is not possible to turn it back. And he says: 'Let it not be a fruitful day' (Jeremiah 31:14); for does someone pray for that day, having occurred in so many years, to turn back again? He therefore curses the genesis of the flesh, the genesis...
The Greek text ends abruptly mid-sentence.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Comparative Good and Evil
english: of the life that is imminent. Furthermore, does he not sin then? — does not he who insults Satan sin? Does the impious one, 'in being cursed,' curse the impious one, 'Satan, he curses his own soul'? He curses Satan not because he is a creation of God, but because he is evil and impious. And he himself is also impious. Therefore he curses himself, and this curse is not empty. If someone curses him because he is impious, he hates the cause, which is that perceived satanic thing. And impiety is the cause. And perhaps he has ceased, or if not ceasing, he will be punished. If the captives are now cursing the day of their captivity, they do not say this so that they might no longer be subject to the captivity—'do they perhaps have the captivity as a cause'—and be exalted by it.

Furthermore, does he then curse 'that day'? And why did he also add 'that'? For one day does not differ from another. Then he says: 'May he who is about to grasp the great whale curse it' (Psalm 70:1). Why did he not say: 'He who made the sun, he who constructed the cosmos,' but 'he who is about to grasp the great whale'? For the Savior has come and, 'having grasped the great whale,' described the genesis of humans, so as to give them another genesis, the 'from water and spirit' (John 3:5), which is principally called regeneration. And regeneration is genesis upon genesis, just as 'repetition' is song upon song. And he called the resurrection of the dead regeneration; for he says to the disciples: 'You also will sit in the regeneration on twelve thrones' (Matthew 19:28), instead of 'in the resurrection, in the age to come' (1 Corinthians 15:52).

If I say: 'May I not see this day,' being in affliction or disease, do I say 'may I not see' regarding the time, since it has passed? For time does not turn back. Furthermore, has he said that that cause of his genesis is sin? — I do not say this again, but that he who curses a day or blesses a day does not bless or curse with respect to time, but with respect to the things that have happened in time. I say: does he not say 'it is better to dissolve and be with Christ' (Philippians 1:23)? He does not say that being released from this life is better. Furthermore, will he say that being joined to it is better or worse? — neither worse nor better. Furthermore, is it indifferent? — if this is indifferent, then the opposite [is also...]

It is indifferent. Or, is it not [considered] as evil, but as toward the better? Opposites do not coexist. If one of these is good, the other is evil, and if the other is evil, the other good must be accepted, as it is regarding virtue and vice, injustice and justice, piety and impiety. If the other is bad, the remainder is good. But when neither of the opposites is bad, neither is the remainder. White and black are opposites; and since white is indifferent, being neither good nor evil, so too is the black of the white.

Or, do you say that the outside of the body becomes good according to the one saying 'to dissolve'? Look from the end: the one having dissolved becomes in Christ. Or, is this comparative? Pay attention to what you say. The things said to be comparative are said as being of the same kind, not as being opposed; just as when I say, 'Sodom was justified because of you' (Gen 19:28), it is not that Sodom has been justified. 'Because of your own sins, O Jerusalem' (Jer 15:9), because a prophet was killed and has become a traitor to the Savior. That Sodom incited one man, Lot. 'That [Sodom] was justified because of you.' Not simply was it justified—for it has not been justified—but 'because of you.' And if it says again: 'He loved wickedness rather than goodness, and deceitful lips rather than to speak righteousness' (Ps 52:3), these things are said comparatively, not oppositely; for this is said because, once one is decided, the other is immediately placed.

The 'dissolving' then [is] 'and to be in Christ'—if you say it is indifferent to 'remaining in the flesh,' and this is indifferent; for it has been shown to us that the things being compared and added have this state: if the other is bad, the remainder is not important. If it is important to be 'with Christ, the one having dissolved,' the turning away from the world, being outside the flesh, or being in the flesh, even if it is, according to you, inferior, [it is] good. The inferior is intended to perish, so that he may become a master of the greater. And I say the loss thus: the hindrance, his ceasing. Just now John wished to remain such as he was on the day of his departure. Or, does he not say so? Therefore, he who desires the better knows this, that it is not the better nor even good. He does not wish for such a state to pass away from him. And the passing away of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Weighty Riches and the Just Praise
english: To perish is to no longer endure. One is agitated by the name of destruction and of disturbance. But one ought not to be agitated. Paul, therefore, was not agitated by such things: 'in part,' he says, 'we know and in part we prophesy; if the perfect comes, the partial will be done away with' (1 Cor 13:10). And they think that being done away with is a worse thing than perishing. Thus we have often said that the partial is done away with not utterly, but that the partial exists, and we received such an image regarding the earnest money.

Furthermore: how do we give, as righteous or as a sinner? It is not this alone you wish to learn; for many things are understood by him. If you had remembered what you heard, you would not always have been agitated about these things. I said: let a king be the ruler of the inhabited world, about whom all are filled with the conviction that he is righteous and whatever he does, he does as a righteous man. 'Bless, O my soul, the Lord' (Ps 103:1). If I keep it thus active toward what was set by the Creator, it is only-begotten. But if at other times it acts otherwise and serves someone, it is no longer the only-begotten of the possessor, but at times it is his, and at times it becomes outside of him.

And in order that I might receive according to the Gospel: he who departed from his father's house became a stranger outside of himself; his soul was no longer his own. But indeed, when he repented, he says: 'having entered into himself' (Luke 15:17). Consequently, he became his own; his soul consequently became his own. This is similar to 'know thyself.' He who knows himself is within himself.

'I will confess to you in a great church, in a heavy people I will praise you' (Ps 18:24). Then a great and many church is called, when it is filled from each side by many; for it is not called a great and many church if it is from small and lowly men. 'He speaks wisdom among the perfect,' says the apostle. These, becoming the same and 'being completed by the same mind and the same judgment,' are a many and great church. And just as I say a wise church when those filling it from each side are wise, and I say a stable and knowledgeable city when the citizens filling it from each side are stable and knowledgeable, so I say a many and great church of those filling it having greatness—but greatness of soul and of mind, not of the body. Again, he says 'a heavy people' regarding the...

For they have become accustomed to call things that are honorable and most precious 'heavy'. This too the Scripture witnesses; for how much the Queen of Sheba came to Solomon, it says, 'in great power' (1 Kings 10:1). And it says the 'heavy power' is her possession, which she had brought. She brought many precious stones, many delicacies, gold, silver, and other accompaniments of wealth. And that power of wealth was called 'heavy' instead of 'precious' or 'valuable'.

Therefore he says that when each of those who complete the people—as I have said concerning the church—is most precious and honorable, for 'glory and honor and peace to everyone who works the good' (cf. Rom 12:10/1 Pet 5:10), if the one working the good possesses glory and honor, the people are an honor. Moreover, it is said about it that it was a 'royal priesthood, a holy nation' (Exod 19:6). The 'holy nation' is completed from all those who are holy, and the 'royal priesthood' is composed of many healers of God. Therefore, 'in a people, I will praise you greatly' (Ps 5:11).

He also prepares him, so that he may also be able to send up a hymn. But he is able to do this when he becomes straight according to the soul and the mind; for 'praise is fitting for the upright' (Ps 5:11). May those who hate me unjustly not rejoice over me (Ps 35:25). Great boldness is in saying these things. They hate me unjustly. They do this, though I provide no pretext or cause for them to lie hostile toward me. Since, therefore, the enemies rejoice when I fall into evils, let me not fall into evils so that they might rejoice over me or assail me; for he who wishes to lead someone into lawlessness rejoices over him, being evil, when he falls into what he strove to surround him with. Let this, therefore, not be to me, so as to make those who hate me unjustly rejoice.

Those who hate me without cause and roll their eyes (Ps 35:19). The 'unjustly' and 'without cause' are the same, 'without reason', and 'rolling eyes' against me; they do not only speak against me with words, but they also roll their eyes. And since often, when the heterodox, regarding those who do us harm, agree with those toward whom they roll their eyes with their own minds, they are of one mind in impiety, because to me they are peaceful...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Deception and Divine Patience
english: They were speaking and calculating deceits in anger. This is a kind of impiety; while speaking peaceably, they were not acting peaceably. This is an injustice. One speaks peaceably to friends and companions as a lover of peace, but calculates deceits in anger. Anyone who approaches a neighbor with any deceit and is angry with him does this. And I say: anger is a desire for punishment. For anyone approaching with deceit wants to harm that person, so that the deceitful one is also an angry one. And many times, appearing not to be, he seems to be speaking peaceably.

This indeed is also said in Jeremiah concerning someone: 'He speaks peaceably to his neighbor, but holds enmity within himself' (Jeremiah 9:4). 'To me,' he says, 'they spoke peaceably.' They did not simply speak 'peaceably,' but 'to me'; wanting to deceive me, they spoke peaceably; for the truly peaceful man does not speak peaceably to someone while holding another intention against him. Immediately also the Savior says to others that 'the peacemakers are blessed,' 'because they are sons of God' (Matthew 5:9). To be peaceful is to be sons of God. And he said 'peacemakers' to mean those making peace. When they lead those who have been divided by intention into harmony and friendship, they are peacemakers. And they are peacemakers toward themselves also.

First, having made peace within themselves, so that they do not have fighting thoughts or works within themselves, then they made peace in themselves. And they carry this peace also to others; for they want those being taught to be as they themselves are. They teach to make peace between the soul and the body and the body and the soul; for when the soul 'subdues the body and brings it into subjection,' and the soul rules and the body is ruled, it is a peace of body and soul. Just as they constructed peace within themselves, so they do this toward others who are beloved and loving, or even toward those fighting. Because of this, it is also said in the Didache, the book of instruction: 'You shall make peace with those who fight.' He who brings others who are fighting into peace and social dealings has first made peace himself; he has no strife within himself, he has no fighting thoughts.
21 And they opened their mouths against me. They opened their word against me, speaking peaceably. But their mind was groaning under the deceit.

Being led to the same end, not in a praiseworthy way, but so as to lose one's own virtues. This is also possible: 'they spread [the lie] against me' (Ps 50:21), as they spoke peaceably, but while calculating deceits in anger, they thought I was being deceived. Then they began to flatter and to spread their word against me.

You have such symbols in history: Delilah, who was brought in the book of Judges (Judg 16), a prostitute, was plotting with deceits to have Samson brought, so that she might give him to the other nations who wished to kill him. And she was saying: 'In what weakness will your strength be, or in what way will you become as weak as one of the hundred and forty men?' She was not telling him the truth. Then, having thought that he believed, she bound him and did other things, and as she was cutting his hair, she was saying: 'Other nations against you, Samson.' See, she spread the mouth [the lie] against him. Formerly she spoke peaceably, she was flattering. But when it seemed that she had caught him within her snare, as one cutting hair, she was saying: 'Other nations against you, Samson.' And behold, she who formerly spoke peaceably and calculated deceits in anger, when it seemed he had become self-controlled, spread the mouth [the lie] while now acting grandiosely.

'Well done, well done, our eyes have seen' (Ps 50:21). Those who think they have obtained the hand they wanted, thus they speak: 'Well done, well done, what we wanted, our eyes have not seen; we no longer see you as you were supposed to be, but as we desired. We have found you easy to capture.'

'You have seen, Lord, do not remain silent' (Ps 50:22). The 'do not remain silent' is the 'do not long-suffer any longer' (Ps 50:23); for from many words we showed this: 'I was silent from eternity, shall I also be silent forever?' (Ps 50:24). I was long-suffering, I did not go out against the evils being done. This shall not be forever. Goodness is again known by the one threatening the one already being punished, so that through the threat he may be stirred up and be brought to repentance. And in another psalm he says: 'To the sinner God said: Why do you declare my judgments and take up my words through your lips? But you hated instruction' (Ps 51:16). Then at the end: 'Having done these things, and I was silent'—not going out—'you assumed lawlessness, that I would be like you' (Ps 51:20). But long-suffering does not remain always; for 'I will convict' 'you and present against your face' your sins. And therefore the threats of God happen out of much goodness.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The distinction of God as Lord and Creator
english: The title 'Judge' is introduced alongside 'the righteous'. 22 Lord, do not turn away from me. May such a thing not be done to me, that I should turn away from you, you who are the helper, the protector. For God distances himself from the wicked, just as he draws near to those approaching. For the great apostle James writes, 'Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you' (James 4:8). It is as if you were saying even to the wicked, 'Draw near to virtue, and it draws near to you.' We do not receive the presence of God in a place, but in relationship and disposition.

23 Arise, O Lord, and attend to my judgment. The voice is one of boldness. No one being accused concerning adultery or murder or anything else says to God, 'Arise, and attend to my judgment'; for you know that the attention of the judgment will condemn him. Therefore, the voice 'attend to my judgment' is one of speaking with boldness regarding cleanliness and regarding being blameless. 'Attend to my judgment,' [he says], 'examine that which is against me and that which is against them, and that which they say against me in vain, that they are hating me without cause.' Often 'Arise' signifies a stirring up. For we often say, 'Arise this man so that he may pay attention to himself,' and it does not signify a physical bodily form. If, however, you wish it as from sleep, it is said, 'Arise; why do you sleep, Lord?' God sleeps not, wishing to pass by unobserved. Therefore, this does not speak maliciously, but wishes to learn the cause, since your wisdom does nothing by chance. Even if you are patient, even if you withhold the punishment, even if you do not cast down those laying hands on me unjustly, tell me the cause; for thus, having known the cause, a wise person will be even more patient and will endure even more. 23 My God and my Lord, unto my judgment. You, and my God and my Lord, arise for me unto the judgment, judge me. He does not pray for his enemies to suffer evil; for the prayer of one holy who loves his enemies is that those enemies should no longer be enemies, that they should no longer be such people. It seems, however, to signify the punishment. For punishment is...

For the lover of pleasure, to become outside of pleasures; for the uncontrolled, to become far from self-control. He wishes them to perish because they are such. And this, however, is not for everyone to say: 'God' therefore 'and my Lord'; for he who does what he says to Him truly calls the Savior 'Lord'; for he says: 'Why do you call me, Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?' (Luke 6:46). And again: 'They acknowledge God, but deny Him by their works' (Titus 1:16).

The saints call God 'God' not by mere voice, but having been made intimate with Him and serving Him like priests, becoming healers. But they also serve Him by doing His will; for 'not everyone' 'who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven' (Matthew 7:21). He is called 'God' in the sense that He is Creator: 'In the beginning' 'God made the heaven and the earth' (Genesis 1:1). Thus it is also said, 'God of spirits and of all flesh,' according to the creation. But otherwise He is called 'God' of the saints, according to worship. In this way, God of the patriarchs has been said. And according to creation, as was being signified, He was God of all, of all things which He has made. And again, He is Lord of all, being to them the very being and governing them under His providence. But in another way, He is Lord of those doing His will, of those practicing what was commanded, and as a master to slaves. 'Judge me, Lord, according to Your righteousness' (Psalm 7:9). 'According to Your righteousness judge me.'

It seems again that what is said exceeds and contradicts with other words. But the difference is not made by the meaning, but by the voice. 'He shall not be justified,' he says, 'before You every living thing,' instead of 'no living thing.' And he says 'living' meaning living according to soul, most rightly; not 'before You.' As if they are nothing toward You. Just as you would say also concerning lamps, that they do not shine before the sun. But this does not indicate that they do not shine.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Desire for Righteousness and the Praise of God
english: But facing the sun. Thus it is also said in Job: 'the stars are not pure before him'. Therefore, this 'according to your righteousness' does not at all mean: not according to your unapproachable righteousness, but according to your righteousness, in which you judge human things. Do not judge me according to their enmity, but according to your righteousness; for your righteousness hates the unrighteous.

25 Let them not say in their hearts, 'Well done, well done to our soul.' Even if they do not say it with words, let them not even say to our soul in their hearts, 'Well done, well done.' 25 Let them not say, 'We have overcome him.' Let them not say that we have surrounded him and conquered him; for often this too has been made clear, that according to the Scripture, downfall signifies victory.

26 May those rejoicing in my evils be shamed and put to shame. It brings salvation to those being shamed and being put to shame because of what they are doing badly; for since they want to surround me with evils and rejoice having seen what they strive to complete, let them be shamed; for having been shamed, they will no longer lie in wait for me, having been put to shame, they will no longer do these things bearing mockery and accusation. Moreover: he says 'evil things', not 'wickednesses'? For he who says, 'Judge me, Lord, according to your righteousness,' truly had no wickednesses; he who says, 'those rejoicing in me unjustly.'

26 Let those boasting against me be clothed in shame and confusion. The great ones speaking against me arrogantly and rejoicing, may they be shamed and put to shame, and may they know themselves. But this happens as a call to them, and I no longer have them lying in wait like that. Previously he prays for them, but secondly also for himself. Moreover: the 'to clothe oneself'? As we say to clothe oneself in a virtue, or to clothe oneself in a wickedness, or to clothe oneself in a 'garment of salvation': 'Let my soul rejoice in the Lord; for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a robe of gladness' (Psalm 31:11). The quality becomes like a garment of the thing.

27 May those desiring my righteousness rejoice and be glad. 230 When 'those boasting' are said to 'clothe themselves in confusion and shame', 'those desiring my righteousness and my peace' rejoice and are glad. When the enemies are shamed and put to shame, the friends rejoice and are glad.

They are those who desire my salvation, my virtue, and my righteousness. And let them say continually, 'Magnified be the Lord.' Then they magnify the Lord continually, when I remain continually in righteousness, in not falling to the evil ones.

They are those who desire the peace of his servant—me, his servant. 'Let them say continually, Magnified be the Lord,' seeing me making peace, seeing me not having fallen to trouble or confusion or uprising or war. We have said many times that sometimes the whole is shown through the individual parts, and we used to employ this witness by saying: 'Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, and who shall stand in his holy place? He who is innocent of hands' (Ps 24:3). Then he says: 'This one shall receive a blessing from the Lord.' He does not say something explicit, but if anyone is such a person, if anyone has ascended the mountain and stood upon the mountain of the Lord and is innocent of hands, everyone, if anyone is such a person, 'shall receive a blessing from the Lord.' Similarly in Psalm 119, it is said: 'The law of the Lord is perfect, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful' (Ps 119:29, 138). And he says many things: 'For indeed your servant keeps them' (Ps 119:138). He does not say only himself, but if anyone is such a servant of God.

Being therefore inferior, when he speaks of achievements, he says 'to the servants of God,' but when of failings, 'to himself.' Some say that those approaching God are sons of God, but those who have reached them are these servants; for from servants they become friends and sons. The greater, then, are 'those who desire,' those who are like sons, those 'perfect as their father' who is the 'perfect one in heaven'; they desire to be the peace of also those who are lower. Or thus, that all desire the peace of each individual servant.

And my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness, all the day your praise. It shall meditate thankfully. When that which I requested exists, my tongue meditates on your righteousness. This I always recount, in hymns I bring it forth, in narrative words I name it. 'Day' here he says, the whole time of human life, just as in others he says: 'Because of you we are being killed all the day' (Rom 8:36), that is, because of strife. And the praise of God he does not say 'lordly'; rather, it is called a hymn and a song upon God, but upon men...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nobility of God's Servitude
english: Praise. It would be rightly called the praise of God and his praise. And 'praise of God' is possible, which he himself gives; for he himself praises those worthy of it. He says: 'and then praise shall be given to each from God' (Ps 18:9).

1–2 To the end; to the servant of the Lord, David. He says that the lawless one sins in himself. Much has been said about the end, that it is that end for the sake of which all other things happen, but it is not for the sake of anything else, which is called the last desirable thing. We desire certain things for the sake of something else. None of those is the end, but they are makers of the end. But the end is that which does not happen for the sake of something else, but for its own sake all other things happen.

Someone wants to learn grammar; he learns, he meditates, he listens to a teacher, and none of these is the end. But the very attainment of perfect knowledge is the end. Therefore, perfect virtue is the last desirable thing, with which there is no other thing to seek as a completion. We use laws for the sake of virtue; the giving of the laws is not the end. We are persuaded by exhortations, by teachings approaching moral training; but all these things happen for the sake of something else. But perfect virtue, the unsurpassed, established after all progress, is the end. Every servant of God pursues this end. Because of this: 'to the servant of the Lord, David'.

If it says 'to the servant', it is not only the end of this David, the son of Jesse, but of every one who has served God. If, indeed, we praise someone in grammar and say that he is able to write as is necessary, and to read as is fitting, and to explain as it is, the harmonies, we do not speak only about him, but about every grammarian. However, let us look at his service, so that we may thus see the others, the fellow-servants.

'I have found', he says, 'David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do all my will' (Acts 13:22). The virtues according to species are the wills of God. But the general one is called one will; for he says: 'Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter, but he who does the will of my Father' (Matt 7:21). Here he named the general virtue as a singular will. And he performs the virtues according to species by doing all the wills of God, if anyone is a doer of the wills of God, if he...

If one turns his commandments into works, and if he does not cast away the things that are to be thought, then the truth of God has been shown. This one is a servant of God. And behold, he was a king saying these things, and he preferred the servitude of God to kingship; for to be a servant of God is a great nobility.

Indeed, it has been said many times that the saints position themselves in their prefaces thus: 'James, a servant of the Lord God Jesus Christ' (James 1:1), and 'Paul, a servant of Christ', and Jonah being asked, 'From what country and what people?', then he says, 'I am a servant of God' (Jonah 1:9). And just as those who are being promoted by virtue of their ranks claim their rank and dignity, these saints, as if professing a greatest nobility and surpassing fame and great rank, profess the servitude of God. The servant of God, knowing the will of God, knows also the things that are contrary to the will of God. For impiety, lawlessness, and every kind of evil oppose the will of God.

Therefore, the servant of the Lord, having known the end, which is virtue over all things, also knew lawlessness; for of the contrary things, there is the same knowledge. He who possesses medical skill knows not only the healthful things among the remedies, but also the harmful ones, so that he may use the former and reject the latter. Thus the servant of the Lord, being lifted up toward the end, says in the song: 'The lawless one says that he sins in himself' (Psalm 19:13).

The wording is ambiguous. It signifies one thing thus: 'The lawless one says in himself that he sins'. 'He says in himself that he sins'. First, he joins himself to lawlessness and sin, and thus comes to practicing it. It is impossible not to sin if one has not been pre-disposed toward sin. Thus 'he says' 'the lawless one that he sins in himself'. 'He says in himself'. For it is to be read thus: 'The lawless one says in himself that he sins'. But it is also possible to take the other part of the ambiguity thus: 'The lawless one says in himself that he sins'; for he knows that he has no boldness regarding sinning. Everyone who sins while following it hides the evil; for no one indeed makes himself manifest as he is. Even if he were a fornicator and wished to lie with someone, he does not want the one describing him to say he is a fornicator. Therefore, they are even more condemned, because they wish to hide what they are doing. No one...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Distinction between Lawlessness and Transgression
english: But one who does good wants to be unknown—and sometimes does this because of blindness—but he strives to have such works as being illuminated in addition to men, so that the Father who is in the heavens might be glorified; for 'let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in the heavens' (Matt 5:16).

2 There is no fear of God in the face of his eyes. No one having the divine fear before his eyes sins; for the divine fear is a refuter of sin. When [men] despise [it], sinning occurs, having become outside of the divine fear. In the same way also the divine writing of the proverbs introduces wisdom, saying: 'The fear of the Lord hates injustice, and insolence and pride and the ways of the wicked' (Prov 8:13). If the fear of God hates these things, no one having it acts unjustly; for 'the fear of the Lord hates injustice.' He is not an insolent man, he is not a slanderer, he is not self-willed. And the name of insolence (hybris) at times signifies slander, and at other times exaltation and arrogance. 'And the ways of the wicked the fear of God hates.' And the 'ways of the wicked' are the ungodly opinions and the lawless actions. Since, therefore, he does not have the fear of God before his eyes, because of this he says in himself that he sins. 'But from the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil' (Prov 16:6).

3 Because he acted deceitfully in his own presence to find his own lawlessness and to hate it. In his own presence he acted deceitfully. He hides the evil through deceit, knowing that, if he does not hide the lawlessness through deceit, once found, hatred is activated in the one who has found and known it. So that he might not be hated because of the lawlessness, he hides it through deceit; for the one finding it hates it.

232 You know that many times probabilities overshadow evil works, so that they may go unnoticed. For example, the false prophets, being 'snaring wolves' according to the opinion, bring a sheep's fleece, so that they may be thought sheep. And from which they want to be known as sheep, it is evident that they hate the wolf-like way; but they hide it; for if it is found, hatred is activated. And no one is so dishonest as to say: 'I love lawlessness and I hate piety'—for possessing it and finding pleasure in practicing it, he does not want to hate it—for if it were made manifest, he would be shown...

For it also brings punishment. The words of his mouth are lawlessness and deceit. The words which he brings forth are lawlessness and deceits. If he sins morally by being uncontrolled, angry, or unjust, his words possess lawlessness. If he deceives with false opinion, those words possess deceit; for he acts deceitfully so that the impiety of his words may not appear, lest they be trampled upon and some turn away from them.

Furthermore: did he not say 'transgression'? Transgression is lawlessness, but lawlessness is not always transgression. If one acts outside of the law, he is acting outside of it, and that is lawlessness. But if, having received the law, he violates it, he acts contrary to the law, and that is transgression. Therefore, transgression is lawlessness, but lawlessness is not always transgression. The one acting contrary to the law and acting in opposition to the law is judged by the extent to which it reaches into actual deeds. If, however, we see the disposition of the one acting, even one who has received the law but does not act according to it, he transgresses. But if he has no law, I say—as it is written—he only commits lawlessness. 'As many as sinned in the law' (Psalm 78:52), he says; those sinning in the law are transgressors. 'They sin lawlessly' are those not possessing the law. However, the thing being done is one and the same. I take the difference from the volition and the disposition of the one acting, so that at times he is called lawless, and at times he is called a transgressor.

He did not will to understand the good. Lest anyone think that it is nature which separates the servant of God from transgression, and the diligent from the wicked, [but rather] that he has assigned both to volition, and says that according to his own will he is either evil or diligent; 'he did not will.' But another wills to understand the good. The diligent man wills this very thing, to do good things. Again, he who is not in these things will have become outside of them by his own will. Thus the word constructs self-determination and that which is autonomous and free through volition, because no one is a transgressor by nature, and no one is good by essence; for we all humans are of the same substance. But according to our own choice, or flight, we are either wicked or diligent.
He reckoned lawlessness upon his own bed. He says this to mean that not only when he is awake and acting does he work lawlessness, but also upon the bed.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Straight Paths of Virtue
english: He is considered to be practicing lawlessness, yet it is necessary to imitate that man who is blessed, the one meditating on the law of the Lord day and night: 'But his delight is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night' (Psalm 1:2). The one meditating on the law of the Lord day and night is not considered to have lawlessness upon his bed, but the law.

It was said by the hierophant Moses from the face of God: 'And all these words, as many as I command you this day, shall be in your heart and in your soul' (Deut 6:6). Then: 'Going on a road, looking, wandering.' If he speaks the words of God and is looking, he is not considered to have lawlessness upon his bed. It is possible even to call the body a bed of the soul.

Even if the soul is in a body, it already meditates on becoming outside of it, subduing the body and leading it as a slave. Thus indeed it is said concerning those having such a mindset: 'You are not in the flesh' (Rom 8:8). Even though they had flesh, they were not in the mindset of the flesh. And again: 'The mindset of the flesh is enmity against God' (Jas 4:4). And again: 'Those who, being in the flesh, seek to please God, are unable' (Rom 8:7).

If he speaks concerning this flesh, all the saints, being in it, pleased God. But the mindset of thinking according to the flesh, being entirely lifted up by the flesh, and consequently becoming fleshly—who is this fleshly person, or he who sells himself to sin? 'But I am fleshly, having been mastered by sin' (Rom 7:24). 'He considered lawlessness upon his bed.' According to the ascent: just as he considered lawlessness in the bed of the body. But it was necessary, while remaining upon this bed, to strip himself and to be pitied, because in the considering there is lawlessness, so as to say: 'With my tears I will wet my bed' (Ps 6:6). The voice of one repenting: but he who repents is not considered to be practicing lawlessness. And concerning others it is said in the prophet Micah: 'He was considered to be thinking of evils upon his bed, and at once with the day he completed them' (Mic 7:3).

They are often covered in the night by lawless things and at the same time complete them with the day. It is necessary, therefore, if an injustice has ever occurred upon the bed, to be convicted of it; for this is what the word protects: 'Be angry and do not sin; what you say in your hearts, be convicted upon your bed' (Ps 4:4). For if you are convicted, the devil finds no place.

He stood in every way not good, but he did not approach wickedness. He turned away every good way. And the virtues are ways. Therefore, do not pay attention to Elymas the sorcerer; the apostle says: 'Will you not cease perverting the straight ways of the Lord?' (Acts 13:10). They are straight and good. And the virtues are called straight because of being a mean; for in a straight way there is no deviation. 'God knows the ways on the right, but the ways on the left are perverted' (Ps 16:6). And it is also good to say 'not good'; for he did not say 'evil.' Not every thing that is not good is evil. It is impossible for something to stand in every bad way by being contrary to it and concerning wickedness. The cowardly cannot be bold, nor the impious pious. Therefore these things are not good. In decision they are the same, but in condemnation they are not the same. 'He did not approach wickedness' (Ps 36:6).

Lord, in heaven is your mercy, and your truth unto the clouds (Ps 36:6). Concerning those dwelling on the earth according to the mindset, we say, 'those thinking of things on earth,' whom the God-Word, blaming, says in the prophet Jeremiah: 'You have sunk down into the earth in sitting' (Jer 48:10), if it is possible, and you want to be lower than the earth, thinking of nothing rising, not having 'your citizenship in the heavens' (Phil 3:20), not having your heart there toward those saying: 'Let us lift up our heart to the high one in heaven.' And it is said again concerning some this: 'But they sought my soul in vain, they shall enter into the lowest parts of the earth' (Ps 118:17). And Moses, in a triumphal song against Pharaoh and those with him, was saying: 'You stretched out your right hand, and you swallowed' (Ex 15:1).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Height of Righteousness and Divine Mercy
english: They [are] earth. Yet it is not earth that sinks them according to the history, but water. For it has been said: 'Immediately they sank down like lead in fierce water' (Ps 69:2). And if God stretches out his right hand against the wicked, they are swallowed up from the earth, they become entirely earthly, they are handed over to 'sufferings of dishonor', they are handed over to 'the desires of their hearts unto impurity', they worship 'the creature rather than the Creator' (Rom 1:25). His 'mercy' is therefore 'in heaven'; for he 'makes mercy unto thousands for those loving him' (Ps 103:17). Just as one ascends a ladder of mercy into heaven; for the nature of the mercy of God is not of the things below, but is above. And if ever it happens in the earth, that is to say, in men—for it has been said: 'the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord' (Ps 33:5)—those being pitied by this mercy are lifted up into heaven.

'And even unto the clouds', he says, 'is your truth' (Ps 36:5). One must not pay attention to those who remove providence from the earth and say it is limited even to the mountains of the moon because of the saying: 'your truth is even unto the clouds'. The prophets are clouds ministering to us a spiritual rain, from which the paradise of God is watered, the seed that fell into good earth, which Jesus cast so that it might become a hundredfold, and a hundred and sixty and thirty (Matt 13:8). Therefore, until these clouds which minister the spiritual rain, concerning which it has been said: 'let the clouds rain down righteousness' (Job 36:28), the truth of God is. If anyone is a cloud able to pour out spiritual rain and righteousness, he has God's truth.

'Your righteousness is like the mountains of God' (Ps 36:6). The mountains of God are interpreted in many ways according to the Scripture. When it says: 'you shine wondrously from eternal mountains' (Ps 104:1-2), 'eternal mountains' refers to the saints who no longer look at the things seen as being temporary, but at the things unseen which are eternal. 'Draw near to eternal mountains'. These mountains, the sensible ones, are not eternal. If the earth and the heaven produce, fragments and parts of the earth, the mountains, they depart with it, they produce with it, so that those are not eternal. But you look toward the eternal, the unseen, the superior, the higher; those are mountains [of the] citizens...

Having a height of pious mindset. Therefore, 'approach eternal mountains' means approach through disposition; take up that same high mindset for them. 'The righteousness' which is 'as the mountains' is 'of God'. The righteousness in humans, when it grows those who possess it, makes them like the mountains of God.

It is possible to call the mountains of God, according to another sense, all the superior things toward which the ninety-nine sheep remained when Jesus came to save the one that went astray from the mountains, having fallen there into error, pursuit, and death. Therefore, 'approach eternal mountains' means approach through disposition; take up that same high mindset for them. 'The righteousness' which is 'as the mountains' is 'of God'. The righteousness in humans, when it grows those who possess it, makes them like the mountains of God.

It is possible to call the righteousness of the descended Savior, according to another sense, those whom he saved. For 'he who did not know sin made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him' (2 Cor 5:21). Those having become the righteousness of God in him who became sin for us are like the mountains of God, like the angels, like the archangels; for they were perfected in the upper creation. 'Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth to the clouds' (Ps 36:5).

God is merciful in one way and humans in another. The mercy that happens among men and the benefit toward the neighbor is human; for they know how to help and nourish and do other things in a human way, and this mercy is that which draws near to the earth, that is, to human things. But the God who shows mercy lifts up those who are being lifted up so as to carry them into heaven. 'In heaven' indeed 'is your mercy'.

And this too is possible because: when showing mercy, you do not show mercy humanly; for even if you 'give food to all flesh' (Ps 145:16), and even if you provide health to the sick, this righteousness is not touching the heaven. And so that I may express it more clearly: the things touched by the gifts of God are not only of the righteous, but also of the wicked, and of the rational and the irrational; they are not heavenly. But those alone are of heaven and lead into heaven, which are truly good and heavenly. And in another psalm you have: 'the earth is full of your mercy' (Ps 33:5). He sends down that one to show mercy to the earth.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Truth and Knowledge
english: The mercy, which fits those upon the earth. But the mercy which 'makes into thousands those who love' is heavenly and carries up into heaven. It is possible to speak of heaven here as the rational essence, the spiritual existence; for some have taken it thus: 'In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth' (Gen 1:1), the earth signifying the more bodily existence and essence, and the heaven the rational. For it is said also in other places: 'The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord' (Ps 103:19). And it is possible for heaven to be, not this one which is visible, not only that which is in our sight, but all.

But the 'heaven of heavens' which is divided into seven is the divine state; for it is said that God is in heaven, not that He is in a place. For it is said in the Gospel: 'No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man' (John 3:13). And Jesus alone descended from the truly heavenly, that is, from the state which fits God, the likeness of God. For certainly the devil was found in heaven; for there he fell along with those who blasphemed and were puffed up. For it is said toward him: 'You said: I will ascend into heaven' (Isa 14:14). Being in heaven, how does he ascend into heaven? He was in heaven, in which also other divine and blessed essences are. But he took a fantasy and a desire to be God. Thinking he would become 'like the Most High' (Gen 3:5), he named the likeness to the Most High 'heaven' while being in heaven.

Therefore God alone is in that called heaven, not that it is a place or a body or a creature, but a state, like a state of God, a likeness of God. Therefore, having taken the desire to be God, it seemed to him in vain, since he is able 'to ascend above the clouds and throw his throne above the stars and become like the Most High' (Ps 108:4). Because he said in short: 'I shall be like the Most High', he had to receive the understanding that the likeness to the Most High is not in the future. But it carries the same existence as the infinite; from the infinite and unto the infinite He is the same, without beginning and without end. But he who says 'I shall be' showed that he is not at all. And he who is not in this way, would never even become God. So the matter stood for him only as a desire, and he fell even from what was present; for he was otherwise in heaven, and [said]...

He says: 'I will ascend into the heaven' (Ps 48:9), which implies he fell from the heaven he possessed; for how 'did the morning star, rising early, fall from heaven?' (Isa 14:12) by saying 'how did he fall?' He showed that he was in heaven, but by saying 'I will ascend into the heaven and I will be,' he showed that he desired to become in another heaven. It is appropriate to take the clouds as belonging to the heaven.

We said yesterday that divine natures often signify the name of the clouds; for when God speaks concerning Israel as being a vineyard, and that instead of grapes He brought forth thorns—instead of the appropriate fruit He brought forth shameful desire—and these thorns the Savior spoke of—He says: 'I will command the clouds not to rain a shower upon him' (Hos 2:3). This shower is not perceptible, whence even the clouds flowing into it are not [perceptible]. For it has been said: 'The clouds shall rain down righteousness' (Ps 85:12). And righteousness flows and descends, not from perceptible clouds.

And I will say something paradoxical: there is a truth which was not previously dwelling with God. Paul says: 'The truth of Jesus is in me' (cf. Phlm 1:11), as if it were another truth which is not primarily called the truth of Jesus; for all things are His, He is the creator of all. And His creatures, being intelligent, have knowledge inherent in them and truth, which someone is able to receive from the intelligent ones.

There is, then, truth, I tell you, in grammar and in geometry and in the other sciences. He is not speaking of that truth belonging to Jesus entirely, nor that it is not also His; for the intelligent things, in which are knowledge and truth, are His creatures. And I say: let some mechanic construct a clock. There is certainly in the thing constructed knowledge by which it came to be; for he constructed it according to mechanical knowledge. And there is truth in the construction when it has such proportions as make it a faultless clock. If anyone therefore receives that knowledge from the apparent clock, he has received the knowledge from the one who constructed it. And the clock is a middle ground between these two states: that of the one who has made it and that of the one who has come to know it from it. Let us give an example: the intelligent people, in being such, do not [possess knowledge] in the way they know, but in the way...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Unfathomable Judgment of God
english: Such people hasten to be, and they recognize the same things when they ascend to the very boundary and end of knowledge. Therefore, let that knowledge and truth of the knower which is progress toward all things be spoken of, not because it is not of God and introductory; for because of it, this is received. The prototype and every idea of truth is the Savior. And it is possible to participate in this truth. The one participating has received a state called truth, concerning which the saint said: 'There is truth in me' (John 14:6), and: 'I have not hidden your truth in my heart' (Ps 118:11). This truth has come to be through the truth, by becoming a seal in wax or some other thing through the prototype seal.

So, indeed, do not neglect also the question of another quality of it, so that I may say this: some more human difference is still found. This quality itself does not accept the more and the less. But that which is in the 'quality' [the substance] accepts it. Yet the receiving and the not receiving are not the same. It is one way and not another way. But if it has come to be in a state and disposition, it accepts the more and the less. But the [quality] itself can be perceived; for even he who strictly wishes to see quality does not take it from the 'quality' [the substance], but from it he knows the quality having been thus established. Your judgments, O Lord, are a great abyss (Ps 35:6).

In men, much difference is found, both of those falling from without and of those from their own disposition. It is possible to find difference from the outside. Some are rich, others poor; others are rulers, others submissive; some are healthy, others sickly.
