Likewise also concerning these capacities: some are naturally sharp and slow in soul, and others having permission toward virtue and others toward wickedness. And of these there is much difference; for no man is in perfect virtue, even if someone hastens toward it, even if he makes progress according to it. There, where there is the more and the less, there is much infinity. Likewise also with wickedness. And to speak well, virtue, accepting the more and the less, will at some time be released into the end, when there is no longer one who is more eager than the eager, or a wise man more wise than the wise. But wickedness is always in infinity. It has no end at all; for how could it be possible for the end of its wickedness to be, while it is discordant and differing?

In excess and deficiency there is infinity, but in a mean there is a determined end. Since we humans cannot say—even if they seem to possess knowledge—why one is poor and another is rich; for if you say, 'he has a certain incomprehensibility.' Often we say that God, seeing that one, having obtained such wealth or status, exceeds and tramples all others, does not give to them, and we find such people trampling and standing up against all, having wealth.

Likewise, regarding health and the movements of the soul, we say that the difference of these things happens by the judgment of God. And that it happens by the judgment of God, let us take the word from the Gospel and clarify it, if it is possible, having been led into this history; in the Gospel the Savior says: 'Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida; for if in Tyre and Sidon the powers that occurred in you had occurred, long ago they would have sat in sackcloth and ashes and repented' (Matt 11:21). If the tremendous powers had occurred to the Sidonians and Tyrians, they were called to repentance. But these spoken cities, Bethsaida and Chorazin, having been tested—why did the tremendous powers occur there, where they did not repent? It is a word resembling an abyss.

'Unsearchable' said the apostle, the judgments of God (Rom 11:33). No one searches them, no one is able to grasp their depth. But barely perceiving the things being done and as if being judged, we take a mental image that God is the one judging and ordaining each thing. But the 'why' we are not able to say, why this one, for instance, is strong and another is weak. We do not have the 'whys' to say.

And as I have said once, that there is a cyclical treatment, and if anyone receives each help for himself, he seems to grasp it, stumbling sometimes and blaming the physician. But then he understands it well, if he knew, why these things happened before him and these things will be after him, and until when it is so that health may exist. But the sick man is not able to understand this. We therefore take a mental image concerning them so that we might at last know that these judgments happen by the judgment of God. 'Your judgments' therefore are not simply 'an abyss,' but 'deep.' And the simply 'abyss' is very deep.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Good Shepherd and the Transformation of Sheep into Men
english: He has an unbounded abyss, and the 'much' is much more. His covering signifies through the 'much', just as the 'unsearchable' of the judgments. In other psalms this was said: the hymnodist spoke of theologians, 'the abyss is like a garment, his surrounding' (Ps 18:11). And in another: 'he set darkness as his hidden covering' (Ps 18:11). He speaks of obscurity and incomprehensibility. This darkness, being hidden, is that of obscurity, that of incomprehensibility, and it is a garment resembling an abyss.

You will save men and cattle, Lord (Ps 36:9). He saves men and cattle. And if we take cattle according to what is at hand, we also take men in sense perception. But he governs all, both the rational and the irrational animals; the rational according to themselves, and the irrational as things having come to be through the rational; for the irrational fulfill the needs of the rational. Some bear burdens for them, some pull the plow, and others provide service in another way. Since even these he is able to let fall into harm and death, he saves even these. He saves also the man. 'Men and cattle you will save, Lord' (Ps 36:9).

The same unsearchable quality of the judgments is found in these also, that he saves all men, though differently: some with much suffering, others with some rest and pleasure. But if he speaks of true salvation, of saving men, and prays concerning that which has been said, that 'the Savior became the cause of eternal salvation to all those who obey', the saint, referring to what is signified, said: 'Our God, the God of saving' (Ps 98:6); here the cattle are to be allegorized; for those who have come to godliness and to the teaching of the Gospel itself, some are called disciples, and others sheep: 'my sheep hear my voice' (John 10:27). They hear a single voice. But the voice is the immediate rendering of the Scriptures which disturbs and strikes the soul and its hearing, not indeed the mind. Of the voice, therefore, of Jesus, the sheep...

They hear of him as a good and true shepherd. When he says to some, 'You call me Lord and Teacher, and you speak well; for I am truly a teacher. And I am your Lord, for you serve me by keeping my laws' (cf. Luke 6:46)—these are not sheep, but disciples, disciples of wisdom, disciples of the truth. But the sheep, being shepherds, are sheep.

There is another condescending intention of the Savior, that he be a shepherd. Since he wishes to save and improve all, then salvation and improvement ascend when, toward the capacity of being benefited in what is possible, he calls some listeners up to his voice, and others to his word, to his teaching. Thus he saves men and cattle so called. And he saves the sheep so that they may no longer be sheep, but that from sheep men may become.

This indeed is hinted at by the twenty-second psalm: 'The Lord,' he says, 'shepherds me, and nothing shall I lack. Into a place of pasture he has led me; upon waters of rest he has nourished me' (Ps 22:1-2). He speaks as a sheep; he reports what exists with the shepherd gratefully. Then he says: 'He has restored my soul. He has led me' (Ps 22:3). And shortly after he brings forth: 'You have prepared a table before me' (Ps 22:5).

It is no longer a place of pasture, no longer a meadow, no longer grazing land, but a table, upon which lies 'the bread of life,' 'the bread which came down from heaven' (John 6:35, 51), the flesh of Jesus, the true nourishment. And after the progress of the table, he partakes also of the cup, of which wisdom 'who has mixed wine for herself' (Prov 31:6) offers. It is your cup, if you pour it for me; and my cup, if you have measured it for me, which I am able to drink. O God, how you have multiplied your mercy. By the mercy of God, men are saved. Then the mercy of God is multiplied and his abundance is shown, when he also saves cattle. Even if regarding a teacher...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Teacher's Goodness and the Wings of the Soul
english: Regarding perfection, you say that his goodness is known when he instructs wise and perfect listeners; then his goodness is multiplied when he also descends to the simple, attempting to lead them into a greater state. Indeed, the teacher of Christianity is a debtor to the wise and the simple, to the Greeks and the barbarians. He is not only a debtor to the wise, but also to the simple.

To the wise he 'speaks wisdom among the perfect' (1 Cor 2:6), but to the simple he does not speak wisdom, but rather proposes those lessons that remove them from thoughtlessness, so that they, no longer being simple, may later receive wisdom. Again, to the Greeks, he speaks as Greeks, those having a refined intellect capable of following; but as for the barbarians, regarding the soul, he says those things that remove the character of a barbarian nation, of such a wild disposition.

But the sons of men hope in the shelter of your wings (Ps 17:8). The sons of these men. If, according to the previous explanation, 'men' are said to be mortal rational animals and 'cattle' are those serving them, then the sons of these men have hope in the shelter of God's wings. These wings are intellectual, lifting the mind upward. Thus the saint says: 'Who will give me wings like a dove?' (Ps 55:6). We do not say that he prays to be given wings of a sensible animal; for this is impossible. And that which is impossible is neither love nor prayer.

'As an eagle upon its young ones has hovered' (Exod 19:4). Then they were winged, they were able to be taken up 'upon the transforming ones' of God. And what is it for us to be thus winged? Listen to what the prophet Isaiah says: 'Those who wait upon God shall renew strength, they shall fly up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary' (Isa 40:31). And another prays saying: 'Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's' (Ps 103:5).

When the saint says of being winged, his wings are to be understood as virtue, understanding, and wisdom; for these things, as a catapult, lift man upward. 'They shall be covered from the heaviness of your house, they are covered under the wings of God.' Their shelter becomes the wings of God. Then they are covered so that they may become winged, so that they may be made healthy, as they might become under the wings of God. Their shelter becomes the wings of God.
unformed souls
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Soul as Multi-faceted Reality
english: It is the church of the living God. The richness of this house is perfect teaching, the wisdom spoken among the perfect, the 'solid food' of which the 'sensory' parts of the inner man partake, 'having been trained for the discernment of good and evil.' And these drink the wine harvested from 'the true vine.' Thus, these partake from the richness of this house of God. The richness of this house of God is perfect teaching, the unceasing knowledge of the truth.

And if he also calls the man the house of the Savior, since he says: 'destroy this temple' (John 2:19). 'This, he was speaking concerning the temple of the body,' not only that the body had a temple, but that this part of the temple could be destroyed by men. For he certainly took the destruction of the temple upon the body alone. But when he says: 'I lay down my soul, so that I may take it again' (John 10:18), he does not say: 'destroy my soul.' Thus they were saying something paradoxical: if he lays down his soul so that he may take it again, 'and no one takes it from him, but he himself has the authority to lay it down and take it' (John 10:18). Observe why: life was not taken from him by a common death. For certainly those crucified with him had their legs cut off so that they might die. Thus, without the Savior undergoing this, he was found dead. For 'bowing [his head], he surrendered the spirit' (Luke 23:46).

And if no one took the soul, but he himself laid it down from himself so that he might take it again, in this way, as it is said in one of the psalms: 'I became like a man helpless among the free dead' (Psalm 116:15), it has happened. And according to the immediate sense, we say that those being delivered from sins while 'being constricted by the chains of their own sins' are not free dead. Since, therefore, Jesus did not commit sin nor even knew it, he was free among the dead. Only this soul was seen to be free there. For certainly the gatekeepers of Hades flew it away.

According to a second sense, 'free among the dead' has happened thus: all those coming out of life and leaving the body, if they are diligent, are led by light-giving angels, while others are led by tormentors of some kind. For it has been said: 'the poor man died and was carried by the angels to the bosom of Abraham' (Luke 16:22). He did not become there by himself, but angels [carried] him.

Not led away. And to another animal-loving commentator it is said: 'O fool, in this night they demand your soul from you.' If a soul is demanded and is itself carried away to Hades by certain tormentors, only the soul of Jesus went out free; neither were angels requested to guide it, nor was it dragged away, not having the causes to be dragged. This indeed is to lay down and to take the soul, and 'no one took it' from me, he says, 'I have authority to lay it down, so that I may take it again' (John 10:18). The divine education by the Savior having become human is the sweetness of the house.

And the paradox: things said to be spiritual and intelligible are not paradoxical. Things that exist sensuously are not something else than sensible. But the being that is intelligible can also be sensibly perceived. It is therefore impossible to take the same high priest and lamb through sensation. But Jesus is both lamb and high priest. It is impossible to take the same door and house upon the sensible. But Jesus is both, and the door entering into the house, and that very house into which the door leads. And in a general sense, all intelligible things are such.

And concerning the soul of man, we say, that he cultivates himself, and the plant is the teaching, and that it is a ground receiving seeds and bearing fruit, and that it becomes a bride of the God Word and bears children of salvation. And it becomes also a sheep. And we take it according to various thoughts, names, and benefits. When the soul is called ground, the things capable are the seeds of certain teachings; but if it is called a bride, the women falling into it, and the cosmic things concerning it, are the practical and ethical virtues and the intellectual and perfect virtues. Again, when it is called a sheep, the teachings are called pasture, the educations are called grass. Therefore, all things are able at once to be other things and others.

And this must be understood: the so-called house is also a vine bearing wine; and again it is flesh nourishing; and it is a farmer tending plants so that they may bear fruit. And behold, that he himself is both farmer and vine and shepherd and sheep. According to various thoughts, being taken this way, they show that there is an intelligible essence concerning which these things are said. For instance, when a Greek demands: 'How can you show from your Scripture that, come, the soul is intelligible...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Vision of Light and Mercy to the Knowing
english: Is it so? For all things reported about it signify their own bodily properties, I was saying this: each of the bodies has that form according to which it is; but when it is spoken of in terms of participation, nothing is spoken of sensorially. God is called, Spirit is called, Light is called, as a man shaped and having limbs; for Spirit does not have limbs; God does not have a seat and a resurrection and feet and the rest; from which it is evident that the essences, about which these things are said, are certain things intelligible.

9 And you make them drink from the torrent of your delight. The flowing liquid is able toward quenching thirst and leading into a sober drunkenness. He names it a 'torrent of delight,' just as it is said, 'a river of delight issues forth from Eden and waters the paradise' (Gen 2:10). And the provision of teaching, the participation of instruction, is called 'torrents' of 'delight.' 'You make them drink upon it.' And it is well also to say, 'you make them drink upon it,' since after this torrent they come to be and are in that very spring. As infants they are being made to drink, and so that I may speak from apostolic wording: to those being led in, Paul writes, 'I gave you milk' (1 Cor 3:2). And those unable to drink for themselves are being made to drink; those being instructed are being made to drink. When they are made to drink from this river of delight, they consequently come to that life from which this river flows, 'for with you is the spring of life' (Ps 36:9). Since with you is the spring of life. He did not say, 'for with you the spring of life has become' or 'a spring of life shall exist,' but 'with you is the spring of life.' This spring of life is always. But when those being made to drink approach, a stream also flows and becomes from the spring, called the 'torrent of delight.'

10 For with you is the spring of life, in your light we shall see light. Behold the spring again here; he has spoken differently; and the light is spoken of as a spring. But these things are not possible regarding history or bodily imagination. If, therefore, the good things flow from it and it does not receive them from elsewhere like a pit or a head, it is a spring of life. And what am I saying? He himself was saying, 'I am the life' (John 14:6). It is the same to say 'life' and 'spring of life.' Life, indeed, because it vivifies and leads into immortality; but a spring, because it does not receive the vivifying thing from elsewhere, but has it itself within itself. 'In your light we shall see light.'

If this voice speaks to the Father, it says: since he who saw the Son, being true light, sees you as existing in light, in your own light we shall see you as existing in light; for 'he who saw the Son saw the Father' (John 1:18). And 'he is the image of the invisible God' (Col 1:15) indicating the one of whom he is the image, and 'he is the character of the divine hypostasis' (Heb 1:3) revealing the hypostasis of God. Therefore, 'in your light we shall see light'. And if this is also spoken to the Son, in your luminous instruction and teaching we shall see you existing as light.

Where he says: 'extend, O God, your mercy to those who know you' (Ps 103:8), he speaks of that knowledge concerning which it is said: 'this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God' (1 John 5:20). These ones, having this knowledge, are loved by God. And God 'makes mercy into thousands for those loving' him. We take 'into thousands' in this way: this number has a kinship with the unit. Therefore, those approaching the one God following and becoming one spirit with him, following, become thousands and myriads. But this is said in this sense: 'the chariot of God is myriad-fold, thousands of the straight'; for we do not take thousand in this way, as ten times a hundred, but because of the intimacy with the unit. And mercy becomes for them.

If, then, the mercy of God is extended into a thousand, as it is said: 'for his mercy is unto the age', he rightly says here: 'extend your mercy to those who know you'. Otherwise, he shows mercy to those coming in a manner of repentance, those asking for the forgiveness of sins. He shows mercy to those knowing him so that they may be established and ascend to that which is above all things unto the end. And your righteousness to the upright in heart. And upright in heart and pure in heart are the same. It is therefore good for the pure in heart to see God; for 'blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God' (Matt 5:8).

Let no one of pride come upon me, and let the hand of sinners not shake me. Let 'the pride of the foolish' not strike my intellect, that is, let no path of pride arise in me; for it is often said of the members of even the best and the most skillful. In proverbs, indeed, it is said: 'the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Inheritance of Those Waiting on the Lord
english: The feet of folly lead those who use it after death into Hades. Those who walk according to folly, using the feet of folly, are brought down into Hades. Just as there are feet of folly, so there are feet of pride.

Therefore, 'let not come to me the feet of pride' (Ps 26:4), meaning let there not be a walking of pride in my soul and in my mind. 'Nor let the hand of sinners shake me' (Ps 145:18). For hand is often said to mean practice, as if saying: 'Thorns grow in the hand of the drunkard,' meaning the shameful desires, the unrestrained pleasures.

13 There the workers of iniquity fell (Ps 1:4). Where the foot of pride and the hand of the sinner [are], 'they fell, those working iniquity.' It was not nature that led them into the fall, but the energy and work of iniquity. 13 They were driven out and are not able to stand. For since they themselves brought themselves down to the foot of pride, and are handed over to the hand of the sinner, which they chose to have, and this handing over is called their expulsion. And God, being a benefactor, drives them out so that they may not be able to stand in the evil. It is not, therefore, a nature or some external force casting him out, but his own work being iniquity and wickedness. He drives him out so that he may not remain, so that he may not hold a fixed stand in it.

And it is necessary to clarify the Scriptures more greatly. The truly God-wise man does this. However, if they were not clarified in this way, but more inferiorly, neither their magnitude nor that of the [God] who gave is shown. The Jews, indeed, taking them according to what is at hand and according to the human, are said 'not to perceive even what they say, nor concerning those things of which they are certain' (John 5:39). 9 That those committing adultery will be destroyed (Rom 1:28)—to be destroyed, but they are being destroyed in the way that they are evil, so that they may no longer be such. And it also signifies the punishment. And the punishment is again an impediment to wickedness. 9 But those who endure

They shall inherit the Lord a land. Those waiting on the Lord inherit the land already interpreted as being in highness, lying in the heaven. And this David said: 'I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living' (Psalm 27:13). He was a king. And to be a king is to have the good things of one's own land and to rule over it. But no one believes to receive what he already has, but believes to have received.

And this one says: 'I believe to see,' not 'I have seen' those good things, which God gives 'to those asking him,' when they pray sincerely concerning them. 'Those waiting' therefore 'on the Lord shall inherit the land' (Psalm 37:34). Endurance is a greatest contest of virtue: 'the tribulation works out endurance' (Romans 5:3). You see that after tribulation comes endurance. He therefore waits on the Lord as is necessary, having no endurance other than Him. And just as wisdom, righteousness, and sanctification become to some, so also endurance.

This David himself in another psalm says: 'And now what is my endurance? Is it not the Lord?' (Psalm 40:1). This endurance they always strive to have, those contending for virtue and piety. The hymnodist himself again says: 'Waiting, I waited on the Lord' (Psalm 40:1). Not simply 'I waited,' but 'waiting,' as in: 'to pursue the just thing justly.'

The servants of God have an inheritance. And listen to the paradox: to inherit is that of a child, not of servants. Therefore, the excess of the goodness of the thing inherited, as far as it reaches into their own state and nature, leads servants into an inheritance. And they used to say a parable for: 'By grace you are saved through faith, not of works' (Ephesians 2:8). And they used to say that it is impossible entirely to have faith without works: 'it is dead' indeed 'without works' (James 2:17). He says therefore: 'through faith, not of works.' And they used to say such an image: when a philanthropist is, instead of those whom some are working for and whom he is healing, he gives a reward...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Place of the Meek
english: Exalting the value of the reward. And they received such an image: let someone be an owner and let him trust a laborer, and let him say to him: 'If you take care of it as is necessary and work it as is fitting, a gift I give it to you; have it as an inheritance.' We say that he received the inheritance not from works, but from the grace of the one willing. 'There is an inheritance to those serving the Lord' (2 Tim 2:19).

And yet, in a little while, the sinner will no longer exist. This is said: 'Do not be envious of those committing adultery, nor be envious of those practicing lawlessness' (1 John 3:10). God fashioned a lover of good as a creature. To be a lover of good is not to desire the temporary and present things; for the temporary and present things belong even to sinners. Therefore, do not be envious of them, whether they prosper or whether they are healthy; for they do not remain always. And if [gap]... I do not speak of the essence, but the quality.

Regarding the 'temporary'; if you wish to take it readily, he who seems to no longer sin is not a sinner. And then he does not enact the things of sin. But 'the enjoyment of sin is temporary' (1 John 2:17), as Paul writes. The enjoyment of sin no longer exists. Therefore, we say to the many that he who seems to no longer sin is no longer a sinner; but according to the true word: sin neither was from the beginning nor shall be unto the age (1 John 2:17); for concerning the most supreme kind of it, this idolatry, it has been said: 'neither from the beginning nor unto the age.'

And if the most surpassing of evils had no beginning, such as to be unceasing, nor would it ever receive a manifest end, 'yet in a little while the sinner will not exist.' You also have in the ninth Psalm: 'Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked' (Ps 9:9). He did not say 'a sinner,' but 'the.' And if 'the arm of the sinner' is broken, it is much more than the inferior. 'And you will seek his place and will not find' (Ps 9:10).

Again, readily: for it is necessary to speak even the more popular explanations. The place of the sinner seems to be the place concerning the earth; for here lawlessness happens, here sins are completed. Therefore the earth will pass away along with the heaven. 'And you will seek his place and will not find' (Ps 9:10). Place is mainly called the position of each. And indeed, concerning Judas it is said that he passed by the place of service: 'from which Judas passed by' (Acts 12:4).

A position is a place of service, such as the position according to service; for when Paul says, 'first apostles, second prophets, third,' they are shallow because they are revealed only by their position. Likewise, in military ranks they say one has the place of a benefit-receiver or an assistant, and similarly in the churches.

The place of the sinner will not be found if he is no longer a sinner; his place was sin. 'But the meek shall inherit the earth' (Ps 37:11). Shortly, the sinner will neither be seen nor his place found, even if searched for; the place of the meek remains for ever; for it is eternal, it is immortal. And concerning the righteous it is said, 'his righteousness remains unto the age of ages.'

Therefore the meek, that is, those having gentleness, those perfecting themselves in lack of anger, shall inherit the earth; for the one without anger is gentle; for one should not say of others that he is gentle if he becomes angry at those whom it is necessary to be angry with. This kind of gentleness is more political and rhetorical. What does that mean? For the excellent man is without anger; and it is said in the falling verses, 'cease from anger and leave wrath' (Ps 37:8).

And they shall delight in abundance of peace. When does this abundance of peace occur? When the prayer of those saying, 'grace to you and peace be multiplied' is heard. He who is able to say, 'among those hating peace I was peaceful,' has an abundance of peace, and delights in this abundance of peace. It is possible to say that, having been relocated from this land, where wars and disturbances occur, they become in the land of the meek, where peace is lived out.

I have also said elsewhere regarding this, in matters of practical application, 'what virtue is needed?' and he says that when all are righteous, there is no need for courage. But he calls courage the more political kind, that which stands together in wars. When all are righteous, there is no need for courage; but when courage is present, there is a need for righteousness. And there, therefore, they delight in abundance of peace, when they are gentle. And the gentle man, as it was said to us, has a tranquil disposition toward anger. And from the one teaching and preparing for the imitation of himself, the greatness of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Protection of the Wing and the Character of the Just
english: Observe virtue: 'Learn from me,' he says, 'for I am gentle and low in heart.' He did not say 'lowly' simply, but 'low in heart.' According to the disposition, I am gentle; according to the heart. He who possesses blindness is 'low in heart.' Since the evangelical word has been uttered, those saying that Jesus lacked mind, but had an irrational soul, must be rebuked. In all the writings, both new and old, the heart is said instead of the mind; for when it says, 'Listen to me, you who have lost your heart,' it means those who have lost the capacity for thought. And 'stony heart' is a stony intellect. If therefore he has a heart and this also has virtue—for he is gentle in heart and low—he has taken up a perfect man.

The sinner will watch the righteous man and gnash his teeth at him (Ps 35:16). This says that the sinner always wants to be an enemy of the righteous, and not only an enemy, but wants to be a murderer against him. And see how 'will watch' lies; primarily this watching means to observe how one might harm someone. What kind of person is armed? He who wants to shoot him with an arrow watches which part of him is naked, and where he sends the arrow. Since therefore the righteous is protected, he is not naked, but has put on 'the armor of God' (Eph 6:11) and 'has taken up the breastplate of faith' (Eph 6:14) and is entirely secured.

If, however, 'will watch' is instead of 'will keep'—for often verbs said after an intention mean the same, such as 'going' and 'descending'; the one descending goes down—if it is 'will keep,' then two things are meant, either that to watch has been said or to guard. If indeed the Savior says in the Gospel, 'Holy Father, keep them' (John 17:11), he says, 'protect them.' 'When I was with them, I kept them' (John 17:12), if it is of 'was guarding.' And those saying, 'You will preserve us from this generation' (Luke 21:36), say, 'you will protect.' It means, as I have said, to 'keep' is to 'watch/observe.' It is said, therefore, 'He will keep your head, and you his wing.' The saint watches the head of the serpent, so that having risen up the head of his evil, he might leave the whole thing dead. But the serpent is not able to keep the head of the man, but the wing, the extremities...

He preserves his powers that approach the earth. No serious wound or harm occurs upon the wing. For it has been said also in other places: 'The iniquity of my wing will surround me; then I was afraid in the evil day' (Ps 90:7). If the iniquity had kept my head, it would have clung to my head like that one, concerning whom it is written: 'His pain will turn back upon his head' (Prov 22:8). And again: 'I gave their ways into their heads' (Prov 19:3), instead of: 'into their mind.' And it is good also to say 'the righteous,' not simply 'righteous,' but the perfect righteous, the irreproachable; for it is said many times also concerning those progressing in name who are accused according to the perfect, such as: 'The wise do not depart from the mouth of the Lord' (Ps 119:105). No one of the wise becomes outside the word of the Lord, always working with the word. And it is said: 'Rebuke a wise man and he will love you' (Prov 9:8). Behold, a wise man.

The sinner borrows and does not repay, but the righteous shows mercy and gives. He not only returns what he borrowed, but also becomes a benefactor to others. By showing mercy, he gains. 'He who shows mercy to the poor lends to God' (Prov 19:17). The one borrowing from God is righteous, having gathered a multitude of works and of reasonable silver, and he benefits another; for the evil ones harm those who are with them, but the righteous ones benefit. And that the evil one is harmful is manifest. For it has been said in proverbs that the wise man benefits and improves: 'Rebuke a wise man and he will love you' (Prov 9:8). Being rebuked, he receives the rebukes well as to love the one rebuking him. But having loved the one rebuking him, he no longer works the things upon which the rebuke occurred. Just as 'he is a brother to the one who loathes himself' (Prov 27:11), the one doing evil. Therefore, the evil one harms himself above all.

The righteous, therefore, shows mercy and gives, and he is full of grace and simply participates in good things toward his neighbor. Those saying that, 'if a brother or sister are naked and lacking of the daily food' (Matt 25:35), that is: 'Go in peace, be satisfied,' but do not give to them the necessities, did not benefit them, since they do not 'show mercy and give.' And it is possible also to take it thus: the sinner, borrowing from God the common concepts given to him and the commandments, 'does not repay.'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Blessing and Cursing in Relation to Justice
english: Neither what he has nor what he received, nor the profit nor the interest. 'But the righteous' [Ps 112:5] God even more 'shows mercy and gives.' He who receives does not give back, but he himself even more 'shows mercy and gives.' And I say: then the mercy and the benevolence appear, if the receiver is ungrateful. 'He is kind even to the ungrateful and the evil,' [Matt 25:34] he gives. Those receiving are ungrateful—for by not giving back what is necessary to give back, they are found ungrateful and evil—but God is still kind even to these. Therefore the righteous even more shows mercy and provides.

The imitator, therefore, of God, 'who shows mercy to the poor and lends to God' [Ps 112:4], even if the one being lent to does not provide what he owes to provide, he is still merciful, he still provides. And take for me the parable of the Gospel concerning the talents: 'to each according to his own ability' [Matt 25:15] he gave the rational things belonging to him, not to each according to his nature, but according to the ability which he himself had prepared by choice. 'And to the one he gave five, to the other two, to the other one' [Matt 25:15]. 'The one having received five talents worked with them' [Matt 25:16] and doubled them. Having borrowed, he paid back. The one with two likewise. The one having received the one and having buried it in the earth, neither worked with it nor gave interest, he hid it in the earth [Matt 25:18].

When you see a man having the ability to do good or to be a philanthropist and not doing it, he has buried what he received into the earth, he has buried it into his own material choice. And being asked for it, when the time remained to 'gather' [Matt 25:19] to those who had received the rational silver, he says: 'See, you have the sponge' [Matt 25:24]. And he accused God, wanting to write his own slowness upon another: 'I knew,' [Matt 25:24] he says, 'I knew that you are a hard man, removing what you did not set, reaping where you did not sow; and having been afraid, you hid your silver in the earth' [Matt 25:22-23] and to no one did you give it. From which things he said, he had the rebuke and the condemnation: 'Man, wicked slave, you knew that I remove what I did not set' [Matt 25:26], if I remove not what is mine, I overstepped my own, not what was received; if 'I reap where I did not sow' [Matt 25:23]? In any case, they were taking mine, if you had given it on a table so that it might be multiplied. Therefore, even this was deprived. And the sinner, therefore, many times...

If one is rising up but does not pay back what he owes to pay back, his benefits will one day be taken away. He will no longer receive from the righteous, much more from one pitying and providing. 22 For those blessing him shall inherit the land. Those blessing the righteous. One must receive both kinds of returns: namely, the righteous man or God. He who does those things which God requires of him blesses God, so as to say: 'I will bless the Lord at all times' (Ps 112:1). And the righteous man is blessed: 'for the blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the righteous' (Ps 112:3), and: 'this one shall receive blessing from the Lord' (Ps 37:3). 'The land,' that land, concerning which it was said: 'and he will lift you up to inherit the land' (Ps 37:11).

22 But those cursing him shall be destroyed. Therefore the impious one curses the righteous by speaking about him, or toward those whom he speaks to: 'Woe to them, because they have departed from me; they are wretched, because they have done evils against me; I redeemed them, but they spoke lies against me.' 'I,' he says, 'redeemed them,' meaning he led them into the bath of regeneration, having freely granted the complete forgiveness of sins, having wiped out their lawlessness. But they speak lies against me, not doing those things for which they were called. And they had the forgiveness of sins; for not for this purpose did I redeem them, so that they might sin, but so that they might become outside of sin. If, therefore, after the ransoms and the means, someone does something absurd, he speaks lies by saying in a certain way: 'He did not benefit me,' he says lies against him.

23 The steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he will desire his way (Ps 37:23). The man walks volitionally from the inferior to the superior, from the temporal to the eternal. And to him belongs the willing of the good, since it is 'not of him who runs nor of him who wills, but of the God who shows mercy' (Rom 9:16) to successfully complete the way. 'The steps of a man are directed by the Lord.' The steps are not given; for it is ours to will to walk from the bad to the good. Immediately, indeed, in the epistle of John, he writes: 'We know that we have passed from death to life' (1 Jn 5:13). 'We have passed,' not 'we were led.' God, directing the steps, did not force us into this by violence.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Unstumbling Way
english: By making these things happen, they are set on right steps. And you have many such things in the Scripture: 'I ran the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart' (Psalm 119:32). Because God enlarges the heart and has given breadth to the understanding, someone runs the way of the commandments. Not that he ran and his heart was enlarged, but that God was enlarging it, casting out all narrowness from faulty thoughts and afflictions; because of this, we ran the way of God.

Again, if it is said in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 10:23), do not think it as an opposition: 'I know that the way of man is not his own, nor does a man direct his steps.' The prophet's meaning is twofold. Nebuchadnezzar threatens the destruction of Jerusalem and the deportation of the whole Hebrew race. The prophet said that, even if the threat existed and we ourselves provided the causes for this to be suffered, 'I know that the way of man is not his own' (Jeremiah 10:23). You are able to prevent his way against us; for even if a man is thought to be great, his course is not made straight if you prevent it.

It is also possible to take it according to the meaning already assigned to: 'not by the willer or the runner, but by the God who shows mercy' (Romans 9:16). Set your intention to run the saving way. It is not within our power to run the way, but to will to arrive at the end of the way, so as to say: 'I have finished the race' (1 Corinthians 9:24). From Him is the directing, from Him is the guiding. 'Lead me in your truth' (Psalm 25:5). The one being led by God does not make himself straight. But he intends to be made straight and has given himself to the One who is able to lead him into perfection.

Such things as are according to God, I say, and seeing toward Him, are richly fulfilled, and it is not possible for each to be divided from each other. If someone has set before him the good, he strives to be an imitator of God, to set and to take up virtue; having set it before him, he does not stand still until the setting, but acts, meditates, strives, and disciplines himself.

To aim at good things. 'Has it not been announced to you, O man, what the Lord requires from you: except to love mercy, to do judgment, and to be ready to go with the Lord your God?' (Micah 6:8). He who prepares himself to always go with the Lord your God is entirely unstumbling. Only let him prepare himself for this, saying: 'My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready.' And no one among those who are stumbled by shameful thoughts or some impulse can say: 'My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready'; for he has bonds, 'he is constricted by the chains of his own sins.' God desires the path of the one being directed in his steps. And he who has spoken, 'I am the way' (John 14:6), walks willingly, running the way of life. He treads and runs upon it. 'And he shall desire his way' (Psalm 37:24). It is also possible to say this: he whose steps are directed by God desires the way of God, into which He leads him, upon which He guides and escorts him. And even if it should ever happen that he falls, he is not destroyed.

24 When he falls, he shall not be shattered (Psalm 37:24). Take for me such an example: let a runner be excellent, having by nature swift feet and having the art of running most prepared. This one, having sharpness regarding the running and having trained the feet of the inner man, if ever he should stumble while running, receives in some way a brief sensation of the stumbling; for he is neither turned over nor, as if struck by a blow, does he stop from the race. And even if it should ever happen to be some slipping, he is not destroyed. Judas slipped from the way of truth and fell; for it has been said: 'Becoming headstrong, he fell in the midst' (Proverbs 29:1). But he would not have become headstrong if he had not been shattered. And good is also this: 'When he falls, he shall not be shattered' (Psalm 37:24). And even if some stumbling should occur, it does not provide 'a place for the devil' (Luke 10:18), so as to turn him and shatter him entirely. Someone saw a woman toward desire until...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Judgments of the Righteous
english: Regarding pre-passion: it seemed as if he were falling, but he was not shattered; for when desire has chosen to follow the thought and conquers it through beauty, he is shattered and has fallen. Such are the elders who remain, according to Sosannas. 24 For the Lord upholds his hand. 'Hand' is often said to mean the practice, the active power. Upholding his active power, He does not allow him to fall down completely. He finds where to rest the hand. And the Lord becomes for him a support, according to what was said before: 'And the Lord became my support.' He holds his power so as to say: 'You have grasped the hand of my right, and by your counsel you have guided me.' Behold the grasping 28 and the seed of the ungodly shall be destroyed.

Ungodliness is [this]. It is being done toward God. The 'seed' stands for 'the offspring of the ungodly.' But the 'seed' can also mean the disposition of the ungodly. And it is destroyed appropriately. In order that it may not bring forth anything remaining, the seed is destroyed. 29 The righteous shall inherit the land and shall dwell upon it for an age of ages. Upon the land spoken of. 30–31 The mouth of the righteous shall meditate on wisdom, and his tongue speaks judgment; his law is in his heart, and his steps shall not be slipped. The mouth of the righteous speaks wisdom. When the wise man is enlightened, he brings forth luminous words; for it has been said: 'The wisdom of a man lights up his face.' He who speaks this wisdom has the face of the mind enlightened; for 'discourse' is 'wisdom through all things of the pious one.' And again, he who obeys the one saying to him: 'Open your mouth with the word of God,' saying: 'I opened my mouth and drew in spirit,' speaks wisdom. Therefore, 'the mouth' [of the one] 'the righteous shall meditate on wisdom.' He always meditates on wise things, not only the theories of piety, but also the wise things of practice. 'His tongue speaks judgment.' Having been judged, he utters all things; an 'idle word' is not brought forth; for he knows that 'from his own words a person is justified, and from his words he is condemned.' Because of this, having been judged, he speaks. And just as the thoughts of the righteous are judgments—for 'thoughts' are 'judgments'...

Regarding 'judgments': they do not simply have casual thoughts, but judged, examined, and established ones. From such judgments, even a word is brought forth as judged. For this reason, 'the tongue of the righteous speaks judgment.' If it speaks what is judged, it speaks judged and examined thoughts, and its word is of this kind. Furthermore, he gives the reason: 'his law' is not in the ears only, but 'in his heart.' For 'God gives his laws into the heart and writes them upon the mind' (Ps 119:11). Since his heart is filled with the law of God, for this reason he meditates on wisdom and speaks judgment.

This being present and made straight, 'he does not slip in his steps.' He walks straight, he does not stumble—so that I might say it this way—he has upward-pointing feet. He who has upward-pointing feet does not slip, nor does he fall. For the wise has put on 'the preparation of the gospel of peace' (Isa 52:7). 'The preparation of the gospel' becomes the footwear of the righteous; for these shoes are upward-pointing, lifting upwards. For God also says to the soul: 'I have clothed you with hyacinth' (Song 2:3). He did not permit any other to put on this footwear, but He Himself clothed it. And the hyacinth loves to imitate the color of the ether. Therefore, I have clothed you with ethereal footwear.

The sinner perceives the righteous and seeks to kill him. He perceives [him] not in order to imitate him. Paul writes to the men in Christ: 'perceiving them unto the provocation of love and good works' (2 Cor 9:2) and other things. They perceive in order to imitate them: 'obey' 'those who lead you,' 'who spoke to you the word of God, whose outcome of conduct observing, imitate the faith' (Heb 13:7). Here, perceiving is praiseworthy. But the sinner perceives the righteous, not to imitate, not to accept, but to kill. In both ways the sinner kills the righteous: if he turns him away from righteousness, he kills him, or he kills him by treacherously bringing death against him, as the elders intended to do according to Sosannēs. And he will by no means abandon him into his hands, nor will he condemn him, when...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Vanishing of the Ungodly
english: He is judged. Even if he is laid upon, he will not abandon him into their hands. We speak of a difference in the meaning of the word 'abandon'. Even if Naboth (1 Kings 21:166) was taken by those who attacked him, he was not abandoned into their hands; for then, it was called abandonment if they achieved what they intended. The martyrs were taken by some, but they were not abandoned into their hands. For then, they were being abandoned if they were being sacrificed.

When a sinner is judged by a righteous man, the righteous man is not condemned. The elders were judging with Sosannas, and she was not condemned in the judging of them; for they were shown to be false informers. 'Wait for the Lord and keep his way, and he will lift you up to inherit the land' (Psalm 37:34). Therefore he exhorts: even if there are many things troubling, even if many are the enemies wanting to harm and take away, but 'wait for the Lord and keep his way', so as to say: 'I have finished the race'; for then he will lift you up and you will inherit the land. The contest of endurance showed that: he will make you high, he will take you up, he will lead you into heaven.

You shall see the sinners being destroyed (Psalm 37:34). This says: you shall see the sinners being destroyed and you will know yourself that you have inherited the land, because you waited for the Lord and kept his way, you did not fall with them. 'I saw the ungodly being lifted up and exalting himself like the cedars of Lebanon; and they passed by, and behold, he was not, and I sought him, and the place of him was not found' (Psalm 37:35-36). Often the ungodly think themselves great and elevate themselves like the cedar in Lebanon.

And it is possible, since it is said after a clause, even the devil himself to take [this way]: I saw him exalting himself among all the others, saying: 'I will seize the whole inhabited world with my hand, as if I were taking up abandoned things', as if he were taking a plague; you know that he who encounters beautiful things easily takes them. Even if they were just newly born, it has happened again to them to have a strong and elevating wind. From much arrogance and insolence, he thought he had such an inhabited world, that is, all the people, towards...

Not even according to the soulless breaths, according to the sicknesses having been made, was he able to be exalted, but he remains still in the pit. Thus 'I saw' the ungodly, this one saying: 'With my strength I will do, and with the understanding of wisdom, I will remove the borders of the nations and with their strength I will provide care' (Ps 71:3), I saw him being highly exalted.

I passed through in thought into the life after these things, into the account of providence, and I no longer saw him, nor was his place found even when sought. Ungodliness has ceased; there is no longer ungodliness. He is not among the immortals, just as concerning righteousness he says: 'Righteousness is immortal.'

For, 'like the cedars of Lebanon' (Ps 92:12)? Often he signifies the haughty ones by this wood: 'And the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon.' There are also praiseworthy cedars. But concerning the great ones in this life, he signifies by this name: 'Open, O Lebanon, your gates; fire consumes your cedars' (Ps 104:33). Then he interprets: 'Because the giants have greatly afflicted me.' He said the giants [are] the cedars. So there are also praiseworthy cedars, but the word is not concerning these now.

'And they passed by, and behold, he was not.' They passed by in thought, and I saw him not existing. I saw him acting insolently because of wealth, because of human rule. They passed by in thought, and I saw that the ungodly is not among those existing. He is still highly exalted according to Lebanon and its cedars; for I searched among the existing things for his place and I did not find it.

God has made all things 'very good' (Gen 1:31). 'From the mouth of the Lord neither the good nor the evil shall come forth' (Isa 27:2). He does not say that neither the good nor the evil, but rather that the good shall come forth from the mouth of the Lord, and the evil not. Thus, the good [are] in the plural. For this reason, there is no place for the evil among the existing things; for God has made all things 'very good.'

And 'He does not delight in the destruction of living things' (Ps 115:6). 'The generations of the world are salvific; there is no medicine of destruction nor a kingdom of Hades upon the earth' (Ps 145:9). Guard innocence and see uprightness, for it is a remnant for a peaceful man. Therefore he says these things: 'Turn away from evil and do good, and dwell for an age of ages' (Prov 3:7). He says: 'Guard innocence, see uprightness,' having become outside of all evil. But he is innocent according to the present.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Remembrance and the Sabbath
english: This is what is meant. The one possessing virtue sees and perceives the uprightness. 'For there is a remnant for man, peaceful' (Ps 94:7). This says that it is impossible for the peaceful man to be utterly destroyed. Even if he is left behind, he possesses a remnant.

38 But the lawless shall be destroyed in the same way. At the same time the lawless are being destroyed; for this is to fall upon the same destruction. 38 The remnants of the ungodly shall be destroyed. But there is a remnant for the peaceful. The remnants of the ungodly shall fall into destruction.

39 But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord. This says that even if the righteous should ever think they have not received salvation from men—such as Abel and how many others were targeted, righteous ones—their salvation is from the Lord, the eternal salvation, not the temporary. 39 And He is a defender of them in a time of tribulation. If a time of tribulation overtakes, He is a defender of them. He puts forth His own shield over them, so that they might remain unhurt, not at all in the body, but in the soul.

40 And the Lord will help them and will rescue them. By helping them, He rescues them. If not in this manner, then they shall be rescued at some time; for if they are targeted through piety and think they will die, but not [by] punishment. This is truly to be helped by God, to be rescued by God. And [it] has both: helping and rescuing. He rescues them from the surrounding pains. 40 And He will bring them out from sinners and will save them, because they hoped in Him. Since they hoped... for salvation or Him, He will bring them out from the sinners and will place them outside of all... And here the one harming the righteous, as he thinks, harms himself. This indeed God... 'he who touches you as he touches the apple of his eye' (Zech 2:8); for he who targets... does not harm himself. But He took the example to show that he himself is harmful to himself, not that he sets aside that one, but himself. As for the 'bow' how it takes...
A Psalm of David, a memorial for the Sabbath (Ps 51:6: Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger).

Remembrance differs from recollection; for one is reminded when another recalls the first things to him. Thus some have said that those desiring to be saved come 'into the knowledge of truth' (1 Tim 2:4). This is the same as 'into remembrance'. For one is reminded of what he knows. No one is said to be reminded of what he already says. For previously, they recognized Joseph, and he himself recognized them; for they knew him. To take a memorial for the Sabbath is to have the beginning of some good.

The Sabbath means rest. To keep the Sabbath is not to keep it in the six days, but when one goes beyond these. This, in which we spend our time, the visible and the immediate, was brought about in six days. But when one goes beyond these and lives super-cosmically and super-heavenly in the heaven, he keeps the Sabbath in such a way. This is the true Sabbath of the Lord.

And for the one walking on earth but having his citizenship in the heavens, he has his mind keeping the Sabbath in the world while in heaven. And there they will one day have their heart and are already keeping the Sabbath, 'the sweet, holy Sabbath to God', to him who says: 'Come to me, all you who are weary and low in heart, and you will find rest for your souls' (Matt 11:28). We keep the Sabbath in a figurative way, but truly they are not the originals, it is evident; for 'no one', he says, 'is about to...'.
If the festivals and the new moons...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Divine Correction
english: And the Sabbaths—these Sabbaths are shadowy. [Gapped] ... to have rest becoming the people of God. 'In remembrance concerning the Sabbath. Lord, do not reprove me in your anger' (Psalm 6:1). Thus the Sabbath was remembered, in which nothing is worshipped [Gapped] ... is led there, he remembers the most beautiful thing there [Gapped] ... they sing the psalm. He who sincerely repents [Gapped] ... for so shall sincere repentance be shown; [Gapped] ... it seems he does this hypocritically. It is necessary, therefore, to suppose such a repentance, so that its magnitude and its beauty may be seen.

2 Lord, do not reprove me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath (Psalm 6:1). [Gapped] ... then he offers [something] on account of sin. This is therefore what he says: 'I will be anxious concerning my sin' (Psalm 40:17). Because I am a sinner, discipline me. Having taken remembrance concerning his own sin, he says these things. [Gapped] ... he knows sin in one way, but in another way he does not understand it; for in the one way he has experience of it, he knows it, but he does not understand it. If he had understood that it is harmful and both destructive and brings the greatest loss, he would not have understood it [meaning: he would not have been subject to it]. Therefore, he is able to know it and yet not understand it, he who is taking experience of it while being outside of it. The man according to Jesus was said not to have known sin nor to have done it (Hebrews 4:15). According to the other meaning of 'to know,' no one more than he knew it; for how had he come to have known it? 'Lord, do not reprove me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath' (Psalm 6:1). [Gapped] ... to have the [Gapped].

An outcome: often an anger and a plague that comes upon someone shows that person's sin. He endured much impiety, and was delivered to the Assyrians, and to the Babylonians into their hand; for it did not happen that the handing over of Israel occurred by chance, but because of sins previously committed; 'Jerusalem has sinned a sin' (Ps 51:5), and it became a reproach. He sinned much sin, and not simply he sinned, but also 'a sin': 'Jerusalem has sinned a sin'.

Therefore, when someone falls into grievous reproaches because of sins previously committed. He did not say, therefore, 'do not rebuke me at once' nor 'do not discipline me at once', but 'all things being reproved are made manifest by the light'. The reproof through light through teaching happens. The holy person does not waive such a reproof.

Again, someone is being disciplined in anger, not knowing he has acted and thought badly. He wants to be reproved thus as it has been said. But this reproof is not of passion, but of perception, as it has been said. When the sin is made manifest and [the person is punished]. And that of passion is less, just as the reproof of painful discipline is less.

In the presence of those who have strayed through wickedness, he says: 'Lord, discipline us before the judgment comes upon us; reveal to us the continuing punishment, remove from us—do not bring the threats upon us in their actual operation—and [let us be] in judgment, reveal to us even clearly what is to be done. The priests profane the Sabbath in the temple and are without cause [guilty]'. In such a way it is profaned, they are said to [do so] because of working...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Stages of Development and the Priority of Virtue
english: Those performing priestly services seem to profane the Sabbath. Or perhaps, according to the assumption of those saying, 'your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath' (Matt 12:2), he shows by this word that the priestly things are not transgressions, for they are not considered so, but are without fault; for he who does these things does not break the Sabbath.

One finds rest from the world, its activity, and its desire, for 'Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest' (Matt 11:28). There is a higher lifting up, which the divine ones call the Sabbath-rest to be spoken of. Just as someone walking on earth has his citizenship in heaven, so someone being in the world yet doing his work from above, he sabbathizes. The Sabbath did not simply renounce work, but service. And the priestly exaltation, being supra-cosmic, makes [one] free.

These are not works of God as works of service, nor are they things God works, but things He commands to be worked by those who obey Him. And he shall receive not something else instead of the corruptible, but the corruptible itself changing into incorruption, and the very psychic becoming spiritual. See then what he says: the other of the body is incorporeal. If anyone says that what we shall receive is a different body, he does not know what is said; for he has arranged 'body' regarding both: 'a corruptible body is sown, an incorruptible body is raised; a weak and dishonorable body is sown, a strong and glorious body is raised; a psychic body is sown, a spiritual body is raised' (1 Cor 15:42-44). In a certain way, then, it is both something different and the very thing being raised is [different from] the fallen one. If he says that if there is a psychic body, there is also a spiritual body, he says in his thought that...

There is no difference, and he says: 'not first the spiritual but the psychic, then the spiritual'. The first and the second seem to be two, but I say two as if I say the man is first an infant, then a child, and not first a child but an infant, and I do not say two hypostases of a human, I do not say two men but one; but two ages. Just as the ages do not make the one growing up to maturity a different substance, but by way of manner and mind and change or transition occurs, so also from the child a man is made and the man is not a different man from the child, but the same man.

Someone truly and bodily becomes in heaven and sabbathizes, no longer walking upon the earth and having his citizenship in the heavens, but already having settled in those heavenly regions, already abiding there under the 'great high priest who has passed through the heavens' (Heb 4:14). And that he did not begin the things concerning men from wickedness, but from virtue, 'for remembrance' he says 'concerning the Sabbath'. When someone becomes in virtue, he is reminded that he once was in it.

Therefore I wish to hint at a deep word. If the beginning of men and of the soul is from this living, then wickedness is before virtue, but virtue is to be taken up. We have life with the body, we have life even without it. And that having cast off the body we become in incorporeal life, is evident everywhere. Let it be sought, whether this too was before the body. It is not manifest, but let it be sought and examined.

If, therefore, the life of the rational is from the entering-in life, then wickedness is before virtue; for we see that being filled from wickedness, the Word begins. But if, as it is the truth, virtue is before wickedness—for 'God has made man upright, but they sought out evil counsels' (Wis 1:13)—and see that the seeking of evil counsels is after the uprightness. And virtue prepares the uprightness. 'A man being in honor did not understand, he was cast down with the irrational animals' (Ps 49:20). It did not come from a beastly manner to the man, but from the human to the beastly it came. And in every way the beautiful things are always before the false things. It is necessary for skill to be before bad skill; to know something erroneously is after knowing it correctly; for how can we...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Instruction vs Wrathful Punishment
english: To say entirely that this is erring, unless we knew the straight path? For this reason, therefore, [it is] 'for the remembrance in the Sabbath' (Ps 94:11). And since keeping the Sabbath is to spend time in virtue and to live pleasingly to God and to serve by doing what God wills, human life began from virtue; but this does not appear in the more bodily life; for virtue is something to be taken up by those with bodies, it is something to be taught. Therefore, the one becoming in the good is remembered.

But what is the thirty-seven? It is not something one can impose on everyone. Now, someone might say this: that the thirty-seven is composed of two holy numbers; for the three is indeed praised in the Scripture. But, neglecting the tithes, it brings only one of the fruits of the holy earth; for 'one hundred, and sixty, and thirty.' And so that we may not always say the same things, it is sufficient to say everything in all things: that the number three is holy, whether it is taken in units, or in tens, or in hundreds. And the seven is also holy; for often regarding this it has been said that it is incorruptible, it is a virgin, it is without seed, it is without womb. 'Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath' (Ps 119:125). One does not avoid being rebuked or disciplined at all, but in anger and wrath. Yet it is possible for someone to be disciplined logically and systematically, according to what is signified by the holy one praying—or rather praising and blessing—saying: 'Blessed is the man whom you will discipline, Lord, and from your law you will teach him' (Ps 119:99). He showed that this discipline happens through instruction.

And often there is also rebuke and discipline through anger and wrath, through harsh things, through bitter things. And often there is rebuke when the one in whom the error is, is shown by word to the responsible party; for this says: 'Rebuke the wise, and he will love you' (Prov 9:8). The wise man rebukes the lesser wise man, the one being led in. And again: 'But all things being rebuked are made manifest by the visible light' (Eph 5:13). And many say such things about rebuke, that rebuke is like a syllogism of contradiction. Let us say, for instance, someone is in wickedness. The one dividing the wickedness from virtue, bringing a syllogistic argument and recognizing the good, takes the bad into mind. And this rebuke is not one happening in anger.

But it is in instruction; for the knowledge of opposites is one, if we know the good, we shall have knowledge of the evil. And from the Scriptures one can take examples: the Ninevites had become in much wickedness, as if 'their cry of wickedness had ascended' (Jonah 4:11) to God calling for punishment and retribution. But God sent a proclamation of repentance. They approached the proclamation. They were instructed and reproved, not in wrath or anger. For example, the Sodomites were reproved and instructed in wrath and anger. Therefore, He does not want to be reproved in this way, not even to be reproved properly while setting aside [the alternative].

'For your arrows have struck me' (Psalm 69:4). Because of this, I avoid the reproof that is in wrath and the instruction that is in anger, since 'your arrows have struck into me' (Psalm 69:4). They gained knowledge of the punishments being brought against the uninstructed, against the unreprovable. Often, the arrows of divine instruction signify the punishments; as if Job, having become in many afflictions, says: 'The arrows of the Lord are in my body' (Job 6:4). That terrible pull, he said 'arrows of the Lord' finding itself in his body. And the paradoxical thing: providence is introduced through this word. These heavy things, such as arrows, signify to me: that unless by the judgment of God, these heavy things would have risen above me; 'for the arrows are of the Lord, whose wrath pours out my blood; when I begin to speak, they pierce me' (Psalm 7:13). And see, that the heavy thing and that evil pull, he said 'arrows of the Lord.' And again in the great Psalm 171 of Deuteronomy, God says: 'I will drink my arrows from blood, and my sword shall devour the blood of the wounded' (Deuteronomy 32:42). Often again the sword signifies punishment: 'for if,' he says, 'you will not wish nor listen, a sword shall fall upon you' (Deuteronomy 32:41). Such also is that which is said in Isaiah: 'My sword has become drunk in heaven' (Isaiah 34:6), instead of: the punishment has touched heavenly things. And if God subjected 'the angels who did not keep their own dominion' (Jude 1:6) to 'eternal chains,' the sword of God—that is, the punishing power—has become drunk, and in heaven. And perceive the same thing even here: if anyone thinks he has a citizenship in heaven, such that heaven is 'to recount the glory of God,' when he falls by an unexpected punishment, then in the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Piercing Arrows and the Hand of God
english: The sword is intoxicated in heaven, regarding the promised possession of a heavenly citizenship. Such is the saying: 'Sons of the kingdom, you shall be cast into the outer darkness' (Matt 13:41-42); for they are not [the ones] who exist. But it is also taken as praiseworthy: 'Your arrows, having been shot, O Mighty One, shall cause peoples under you to fall' (Ps 126:4). Your words, having been shot, are directed toward passion and love; for you are powerful and you powerfully send out your words, and you direct those who are being cast [by them] toward love. Likewise, the soul undergoing this—that is, the Church—says: 'Pierced by love am I' (Song 8:6). Thus, the arrows are both praiseworthy and piercing. Since these were named with wrath and fury, they are not directed toward passion and love, but are producing a sensation, of which there is some evil.

And you have placed your hand upon me. Often again, the punishing power is signified by the name of the hand of God; as if saying to Pharaoh: 'Now, having sent the hand, I will strike you' (Ex 7:17). And: 'Behold, the hand of the Lord shall fall upon your livestock in the fields' (Ex 9:3); for those livestock were struck down with destruction. And again it is said: 'Your hand has destroyed the nations' (Ps 18:47). When the active, creative, and covering hand of God is named, it is called 'the right hand.' For this indeed leads toward salvation. He who has experienced being guided by it says: 'You have grasped the hand of my right hand' (Ps 63:8), the practical power of the good.

And there is no healing for my flesh from the presence of your wrath. The name 'flesh' signifies different things according to the Scripture, being homonymous. It is sometimes said that 'flesh' signifies our sensory choice; for when it is said: 'I will break their stony heart from them and put a fleshy one in' (Ezek 36:26), 'stony heart' means the flinty intellect having been deprived of all sensation. In its place, a fleshy one is placed, sensory and yielding to the laws of God. Thus, the yielding and the sensory are often called flesh. And 'flesh' is also said to be being cut off from the spirit. 'Spirit' means the intention, while 'flesh' means that which is being cut off from the intention. Therefore, when someone thinks of the things of the flesh and acts and lives according to them, he is far from the spirit. But when he follows the sp...
rational departure
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The distinction of flesh and the meaning of bones
english: Having taken the distinction from the soul, it is troubled by the opposite of death. 'All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is as the flower of grass' (Ps 103:15). Again he says, 'All flesh shall come unto thee' (Ps 22:27), that is, every man. 'All flesh shall see the salvation of our God' (Ps 22:29). All things that are homonymous are divided from those having the same name by the addition of certain [elements]. If it is said in the Scripture, 'He who gives food to all flesh,' we hear of every living creature by nature. But if I say, 'I will pour out from my spirit upon all flesh,' I speak of receiving the bestowed gift of spirit.

4 There is no peace to my bones from the face of my sins (Ps 32:3), because I see my sins present. But not everyone takes understanding of the face of them, but he who repents and wishes to flee them. The one sinning and being ignorant of this very thing that he sins, does not see the face of his sins, nor does he see their shame. But the one perceiving those things which he does, and seeing that he performs them according to the transgression of divine commands, has the face of the sins appearing to him.

He does not say 'bones' of the body in every way, except according to the lowestly understanding, just as it was also said concerning flesh. And it has been said in those preceding: 'All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like unto thee?' (Ps 73:26). If the bones say, 'Lord, who is like unto thee?', they have received the understanding of the Lord and of His form, so as to know that no one is like Him. For the likeness toward God and the unlikeness [which brings] knowledge of God and theology makes [it] manifest; so that he does not speak concerning the bones of the body, but concerning the strong and firm dogmas of the soul and its powers; for then the sensible bodies are held together by the bones; for it was not possible to have nerves and veins and the rest, if he did not have bones. Where [is it said]: 'There is no peace to my bones?'—when the powers of the soul follow one another, they are at peace. When the soul does not divide...
the calculating faculty, the desiring faculty
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Body of Death and the Nature of the Soul
english: He finds pleasure in the burden of wickedness rather, and distances himself from Jesus. For this reason it is also said in Isaiah: 'Egypt has grown weary, the commerce of Ethiopia, and the Sabeans, lofty men, shall pass over you and shall be your servants and shall worship you, for God strengthens and there is no god besides you' (Isa 18:7). 'Egypt has grown weary' at the time when those who are of the wicked have received sensation, practicing idolatry and possessing idle chatter regarding curious things, regarding augury, regarding necromancy, and the demons lying near them. But when they do not have sensation of these, they do not grow weary. 'The commerce' therefore 'of the Ethiopians' or 'the trades of the Ethiopians' grows weary then. And 'Ethiopians' refers to those darkened according to the inner man.

Thus also the devil in the Epistle of Barnabas and in the Shepherd is called 'the black one,' not according to the body, but having been darkened according to the mind, having become outside the brightness of the saints. These therefore the Ethiopians have a journey or a way, where their commerce is. And they grow weary then when they receive sensation, for howsoever one finds pleasure in sinning, he does not grow weary.

'They swelled and my sores decayed from the face of my folly' (Ps 38:3). I had sores from the arrows of punishment or from the burning arrows of the evil one; for it has also been said to have burning arrows. When someone receives impressions, that is, thoughts and memories of evils and impieties, he is in a sore. But when these have increased and having become unburdened they swell, then they also undergo putrefaction. 'They swelled' therefore 'and my sores decayed.' But from where did I have the sores, from where has their putrefaction happened? — 'from the face of my folly.' It is necessary to expose my folly and to turn away from it. Someone undergoes folly when he does not possess prudence.

The stings of thoughts and of desires, these make sores. It is necessary to heal these quickly. Someone saw a woman toward desire; he had a sore. Let him heal, and until the passion, let him set the anger in order; for in this way neither desire shall swell nor bring putrefaction. But when the mind remains, these bring both putrefaction and stench and uncleanness. When he does not have this prudence so as to know what ought to be done and what not, having the things said in a mixed way as indifferent, in...

It is in folly. And folly, regarding those things that boast of being small sins so as to compare them to madness, nourishes and strengthens, and becomes a stench and corruption. Likewise, regarding the essence of which the word is spoken, it takes the resemblance and the corruption; for nothing bodily appears; for many foolish people are healthy and have strong bodies.

I was wretched and was bowed down to the end. The unseemly and burdensome things often bring wretchedness. And the body itself indeed makes the one burdened wretched. This concept is submitted by the apostolic word which has it thus: 'Wretched am I, man; who will rescue me from the body of this death?' (Romans 7:24). Since indeed I am in the body of death, I am wretched, and not by chance will the Savior make me out of such wretchedness; for he immediately brought forward: 'I give thanks through Jesus Christ' (Romans 7:25), who freed me from the body. We say, therefore, that wretchedness comes to the soul from the body of death.

We do not at once take the body of death to be any body, but a body of this kind. When someone uses this body as if to do sins toward death, a body of death remains surrounding him. But it is possible to make it not a body of death; for when I separate from it those things making it a body of death, it is no longer a body of death. And just as this perceptible body has underlying matter and the form of a body, it is possible to separate this body from the thick body. When it takes only the three dimensions without matter, this body is not essence.

In these readily available things, when it is said, for example, 'color in body,' does it not also mean 'in a certain body,' because by saying 'color in body' it showed that this body means the seen thing, which we touch? But when it says a single form is the quantity of the body, it does not say this; for how can an essence be a genus of essence? So the body is homonymous: for that which is taken according to the three dimensions without matter, this is the quantitative body; for that with matter, we take not only the dimensions but also the underlying essence with them. This body is something else. The body, therefore, is then a body of death, when those things working in it and its movements happen sinfully. It is possible, therefore, to separate this from...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Lessons of Sin and the Desires of the Soul
english: Regarding the body: when I take an eye that does not see, seeing in a harmful or adulterous way, I have removed the eye of death from the essence. And upon every member and upon every sense, if this happens, the body of death is cast off. It is not the body we cast off, but the body of death. And if we see a worthless man having changed into a significant one, we say that the worthless man was destroyed, not the man.

'And we were bowed down.' Lowly wickedness is, it bows down the one possessing it; for always the great sorrows lie upon one, crushing and bowing down the one carrying them. Immediately, indeed, regarding her who had that 'spirit of infirmity' for eighteen years, it says: 'she was bent over and could not raise herself to the full.' She never raised herself up. The one sinning, therefore, bends down and looks below.
