It says, therefore: 'they set their eyes to bend down toward the earth' (Ps 118:25); and again in Jeremiah it is said: 'having turned away upon the earth they have written' (Jer 17:13). Those having turned away from the divine spring are written of, being enrolled in the earth, as having the citizenship below and bearing 'the image of the jar' (cf. 2 Tim 2:20). But of the disciples, 'the names are written in the heavens' (Luke 10:20). He does not speak of these designations by combining letters, but of the very qualities which signify them, for the definition of a name is given thus: a name is a principal designation representing the quality of the one named. This is the descriptive name: man, heaven. 'Is written,' therefore, that is, has been arranged.

7 I was walking, mourning all the day. Even if 'I was bowed down to the end' because of the approaching misery, I did not become insensitive to this. Mourning, therefore, I walk, 'working the godliness according to God, the sorrow leading to repentance unto salvation without regret' (2 Cor 7:10). And so mourning I walk all the day. And the 'I walk' is good. It does not remain cast down, but it walks. It did not 'sink down to earth in sitting,' it did not set its transferred habits upon the earth, but it walks. 'Mourning,' therefore, 'I was walking.' Those things were working which were transferring me out of the misery. Then, however, I am transferred out of the misery, if I cast off the causes of the misery. 8 For my soul was filled with instructions. My soul was filled with sins. And instructions are...

Regarding sins: the deceiver plays with the deceived, and thus the soul is filled with lessons. In some copies, it says 'my loins.' It is said concerning these that the seeds consist. When someone is thus drawn into lawlessness and hastens more toward lust or toward being a lover of God, he has the loins filled with lessons.

“And there is no healing in my flesh” (Ps 32:18). As long as I am filled with these lessons, not only is my flesh not healthy, but having become diseased and thus disposed, it does not receive healing. Just as it is impossible for a sensory person, while still in the state of being sick, to recover health, so the one filled with lessons is not able to make the flesh peaceful, that is, sober, or not divided against itself.

“I was afflicted and humbled exceedingly” (Ps 32:3). It is possible to say 'I was afflicted and humbled' voluntarily. Since I have become in sensation of the swelling of evil and harm and blindness, I led myself volitionally toward humiliation so that I might be exalted; for “everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Mt 23:12). One must take the affliction and the humiliation from a parallel source. But then it happens voluntarily when, as I have said, the one who was exalted humbles himself, so that he might be exalted by God. It is also possible in this way: from the surrounding oppressors and heavy burdens, “I was humbled, I was afflicted exceedingly.” I had the affliction stretched out.

“I cried out from the sighing of my heart” (Ps 34:1). Not mockingly wailing about the evils surrounding me, but “from the sighing of my heart”; understanding in what kind of sighing one must sigh, a sigh.

“And all my desire is against you” (Ps 38:9). The righteous man always has love and longing for the virtues and for things done praiseworthily. It is indeed said concerning the righteous: “All the desire of the righteous is good” (Ps 37:4). And the good things have the boldness to be additional to God. “Against you,” therefore, that is, before you, is “all my desire.” Praise is therefore to be taken here for “my desire,” which is also what this same one says: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, who fills your desire with good things” (Ps 103:5). All such desires, being the righteous, are bold to be additional to God. But it is also possible to take the word toward the other meaning. Because...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Light of Knowledge and the Strength of the Heart
english: This person was humbled and was utterly crushed; because of this, I am consumed, and my groaning comes from soul and heart, since I have come to know that every bad desire I possessed is manifest to you, and no desire is outside of your presence. The term 'moreover' is more appropriate. 10 And my groaning was not hidden from you. Having a good desire and longing to be in goodness and virtue, I groan as much as I see myself failing. This groaning, however, comes from a desire for beauty, from the expectation of something better. Even if I often hide my groaning from many, so that I might not seem to be self-indulgent and appear to be repenting only outwardly, my groaning is 'moreover' to you; it was not hidden from you. The Egyptians indeed oppressed the Hebrews. When the 'sons of Israel' (Exodus 2:23) rejoiced in the works of the Egyptians, their groaning was hidden from the face of God. But when they began to groan over the works, when they perceived that the Pharaonic works were destroying both the land and, even more, were doing [evil] outside of God, then they groaned, and the groaning was not hidden from God; for He immediately set them free. When they were rejoicing, they were held there, and they did not attain freedom. This groaning corresponds to 'the sorrow that works repentance unto salvation' (2 Corinthians 7:10). This sorrow is another from that of the world, which works death. If, indeed, you see a man groaning because he does not attain what he desires, even if they are bad things, this groaning is destructive.

11 My heart was troubled, and my strength left me. When the heart is troubled, that is, the mind, then strength becomes distant. Strength is that which is appropriate to the peace and stability of the heart. He who learned from Jesus 'that He is gentle and humble in heart' (Matthew 11:29) does not have a troubled heart; for he imitates Jesus. And he who imitates Jesus is outside of all trouble. Until he does not have this trouble, strength remains with him, so as to say: 'I can do all things in Him who strengthens me' (Philippians 4:13), and: 'I will love you, Lord, my strength' (Psalm 18:1). 11 And the light of my eyes is not with me. The light of my eyes has become distant from me. But the light of the true eyes...

For those seeing sharply, the knowledge of truth is present; for it has been said: 'light up for yourselves a light of knowledge' (Ps 119:130). For the word is not about these eyes nor about sensible light; listen to the one saying: 'the commandment of the Lord is far-reaching, enlightening eyes' (Ps 119:105). Indeed, the keeping of the far-reaching commandment enlightens the eyes of the inner man; for many are those seeing sharply, yet they are transgressors of the commandment of the Lord, and they guard it in a different way, and being encompassed by it, they are dull according to the appearance.

It is not, therefore, at all about the eyes that it is said: 'and the light of my eyes is not with me' (Ps 38:11). He has left me, because I turned away from it, because I myself did not guard it to remain with me. 'My heart was troubled, my strength left me' (Ps 38:10). When the intellect is troubled, if it endures, strength becomes far-reaching; for when the intellect is strengthened and the mind is made precise, strength is present to one thus disposed, as to say: 'I am strong in all things in the one empowering me' (Phil 4:13). 'I will love you, Lord, my strength.' But one is left behind by this strength if, when troubled, he endures in the heart, if he has troubling thoughts. Therefore, it must be guarded not to give 'a place to the devil' to the one casting disturbances, so that our strength may remain and we may be able to say: 'The Lord is my strength and my song, and he became for me salvation' (Ps 28:7).

'And the light of my eyes is not with me' (Ps 38:11). When the heart is troubled, the strength appropriate to the heart leaves it, and that very light is not with the one having suffered these things; for it is necessary to 'sow into righteousness and reap into a fruit of life' (Gal 6:7), so that, 'having lightened for themselves a light of knowledge' (Ps 119:130). Therefore, when the heart is troubled, the strength that empowers the inner man becomes distant, and that very light of the eyes which enlightens the inner man leaves him, having delivered himself to darkness and ignorance.

'My friends and my neighbors drew near and stood opposite me' (Ps 41:9). Such things happen in circumstantial times. And Job, having been born in distress, said such things: 'My friends have become merciless, they have known [others] as three times more than I' (Job 19:14). And in the Wisdoms it has been written that friends only then [fail] and the [goodness] of friends...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Devil Standing at the Right Hand
english: They demonstrate and demand [something] when someone is in prosperity, whom they perhaps love. But when there occurs in someone a certain perversion of things pertaining to him, and they care for the external things, then those [people] become distant. For there are three kinds of friendship. There is friendship according to the self, when it does not pursue anything other than beauty or virtue. But if it is because of something, namely wealth, this friendship of theirs will cease when they are gone, and so will the friendship. And this friendship is said to be a second kind, being for the sake of the useful. And a third kind of friendship is the pleasant. Many wish to be friends with monks, not so that they may be monks, but so that they may say, 'Those who live alone love me.' And others [wish to be friends with] the rich, expecting nothing from them, but sometimes even bestowing [things] upon them.

One is able to call the neighbor a friend by analogy, or the friend a neighbor. And so, those near by through proximity, and according to kinship, 'my brothers.' And yet, should this be taken regarding bodily [matters]?—But if you say it spiritually—if they are also friends and kinsmen according to the spirit—observe: when someone diminishes himself and is no longer such, those whom he previously had as friends become strangers to him, because he has diminished himself, so that I may not say that he has become worthless; for the following is no longer reported as concerning the worthless or by the worthless. Having wholly troubled the heart, he is not cast out; for another is the one who destroys this. It has been said, indeed, in Isaiah: 'those who have lost their heart' (Isaiah 35:10). And the heart is lost when the intellect becomes outside of the harmonious state. And it is troubled if it has some confusion. And to be troubled comes from receiving thoughts and impulses that are not fitting. 'From the opposite they approached and stood.' Not as companions, not as friends, not for the purpose of being united to me, but 'from the opposite,' in order that, being present, they might oppose. Such an observation I also had in Zechariah and in the 118th Psalm. It is said concerning Judah that: 'let the devil stand at his right hand.' And concerning 'Joshua the high priest, the great...'

Regarding Josedech: 'the devil stood at his right hand to oppose him' (Psalm 109:1). And see that for both Judah and Jesus the priest, the great, the purest and holy, the devil stood at the right hand. But concerning Jesus it is said: 'to oppose him.' He stood in order that, being positioned against his right side, he might wage war against him, because he performs practical matters on the right and has such a disposition. But regarding Judah, it is not so. The right side of Judah was already seized. He gave a standing to the devil in these things. And here 'they stood opposite.' For this reason they drew near, in order that they might harm and trouble.

12 And those near to me stood from a distance. There are two kinds of friends; there are two dispositions of those near. When former enemies become pretended friends and flatterers, in order that they might oppose, they do this. And so that I may take from the Pastoral teaching the catechetical meaning, I say: two angels are with the man, and the one suggests evil things, and the other good things, and one is of righteousness, and the other of unrighteousness. If, therefore, the one of unrighteousness becomes near, the one suggesting evil, the good angel is distanced, as soon as he draws near to him, this evil one opposes; for the opposites, the good and the bad, do not coexist; for the evil acts when the good is at hand. If, moreover, this is said in the person of the Savior, he is able to say: my former friends, my sons, whom I begot and raised up, have become distant by having rejected me. But those from the Gentiles having believed and become friends, are besides near and 'opposite to me,' instead of 'against my person'; for we no longer take 'opposite' as 'positioned against,' but as being alongside, in addition.
13 And those seeking the soul were forcing their way, and seeking evils, they spoke vanities to me. No one of those loving my soul forces it, but draws near or becomes one with it. But the others...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Meaning of Muteness and the Timing of Rebuke
english: They are driven and, seeking evils against the one who is being driven, they speak vanity; it is nothing profitable, nothing contributing to the knowledge of the truth, but only about vanities. For all the evil things, the trivial things, and the transient things are vain, and they are things seen and easily dismissed and easily described and perishing. It is necessary to seek the soul profitably. But to those who approach 'the evils' against 'those seeking my soul and being driven,' it is evident that they are trivial. He who approaches the sinning soul toward repentance and leads the one having fallen away from the truth toward this, seeks the soul praiseworthily and profitably. For the Savior indeed 'has come to seek and to save the lost' (Luke 19:10). He, seeking the soul, seeks in order that he might lead it into salvation, so that he might restore it according to its former state. Just as therefore the Savior does this through instruction and through contributing to the good, so also the disciples and angels and men of the Savior do this. And none of these, seeking the soul, speaks vanity, and none seeks evils against it, but good and profitable things.

And they practiced craftiness all the day. They practiced crookedness all their life; for how should they not have practiced? They had 'crooked thoughts which separate from God' (Psalm 94:8), and their heart had become crooked and stumbling, which the holy man avoids having, saying: 'a stumbling heart has not clung to me.' He who has crooked thoughts practices crookedness all the day, with works and thoughts in accordance with his crooked thoughts. These indeed are the crooked thoughts cast into the soul by the devil; for it has been said: 'a serpent, a dragon, is crooked.' He is made crooked. It has also been said carelessly in others: 'all the crooked things shall be for straightness.' The crookedness receives straightness when it casts away the crookedness. But he who practices this all the day has also crooked works, a crooked choice, and a diverted disposition.

And I, as if deaf, was not hearing, and as if mute, was not opening his mouth. He lets out praise of himself. The one repenting, if the devil casts into him evil or crooked thoughts, let him be as if a deaf man were not hearing, let him not understand them, let him not provide to them the hearing of the inner man, but let him be thus as if mute, as if deaf, not opening...

The mouth is closed. Here, 'mute' does not mean one who has lost his hearing, but one who does not speak; for often, especially according to the Scripture, this meaning lies regarding speech: 'after the demon had gone out,' he says, 'the mute man spoke.' He did not say, 'the mute man heard.' Yet I do not say that this word does not also mean one deprived of his hearing. It signifies both.

Again, God to Moses saying, 'I am slow of speech and heavy of tongue,' said: 'Who gave speech to man, and who has made the hard-of-speech or the mute, the seeing and the blind?' (Exodus 4:11). Here, 'mute' can lie regarding speech or regarding the loss of hearing. And the phrase, 'after the demon went out, the mute man spoke,' means a mute one who does not have vocal organs, one who does not have an active tongue.

'I became like a man not hearing and not having a rebuke in his mouth.' This says: I have not become a man who does not hear, but 'like a man not hearing.' I did not accept the words and the announcements of the deceitful, even though I was able to rebuke them. Knowing that rebukes are not brought against such a person at the right time, as if one were not able to rebuke him, the word shows that both rebukes and contradictions ought to happen at the right time. And we take the 'right time' from the object and the one being argued with. Just as food given at the right time benefits and nourishes, but offered at the wrong time harms more.

'Do not rebuke evildoers, so that they may not hate you' (Proverbs 9:8). The word teaches not to avoid being hated by the wicked, but says this: rebuke, so that you may be useful. Approaching to rebuke not at the right time—for 'there is a rebuke that is not beautiful'—does not benefit the one being rebuked, but rather makes him even more wicked, as to hate the one rebuking. 'Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you' (Job 5:17). If the wise man being rebuked loves the one bringing the rebuke, it is clear that the one who hates the rebuke is wicked.

It has also been said elsewhere: 'He will not love the uninstructed the ones rebuking him, but with the wise he will not converse.' The uninstructed does not love at all those rebuking him, but the wise man intends this. Nothing of what the wise man says is added to the evil man who hates those rebuking.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Duty of Rebuking and the Silence of the Soul
english: Regarding 'rebuke'—it is said in a double sense; often one is unable to rebuke. One lacks such boldness or such power of speech as to rebuke, and so pretends not to hear. For example, a heretic is present, speaking atheistic doctrines and heretical opinions. If we are unable to rebuke the things said by him, we are called 'men who do not hear,' for rather than benefiting, hearing such conversations causes agitation.

For it has been said: 'Bad conversations corrupt good morals.' If anyone possessing a good character knows this—that he cannot stand against bad conversations—he is not obliged to provide his hearing, but rather to become as if deaf. Another, possessing the ability to rebuke the most shameful conversations, does not do this when he knows that it is not at all effective to rebuke him in that way; for it was said that just as foods are administered medically at the right time, so also are the aids to the soul.

Such things are aids to the soul, for instance: 'rebuke, reprove, encourage.' When you have made manifest through rebuking the one sinning, reprove. When you have reproved again, having performed the reproof sufficiently, encourage. Let the aids to the soul follow one another. It is not for anyone by chance to know these, but for the one who understands the medicine of the soul. 'For in you, Lord, I have hoped; You will hear me, Lord my God' (Ps 31:2). Since I hoped in You, You will hear me.

I am confident that all things that are possible for him to be present with me, shall be present. Therefore, being confident in You, the Greater One, and the One who knows how to rebuke and whom it is necessary to rebuke, I kept silent, as if I had become deaf, not having rebukes in my mouth. And thus it must be said: 'Since I hoped in You, You will hear me'; for having become deaf and mute toward him and not having rebukes in my mouth, I cried out toward You in my mind.

So it seems to have happened also in the Exodus of Moses, when Pharaoh violently pursued them with all his power and his army, and the Hebrews were in a certain way hemmed in so as to be even less able to cross over. The army of Pharaoh and the tyrant himself pursued; the Hebrews, 'the sons of Israel,' were being pursued. Some were armed, bringing all manner of equipment and military, cavalry, and infantry power, while the others were naked in their hands.
They were hemmed in
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Resilience in Discipline and Repentance
english: They are being greatly shaken. And he is able to say these things because: 'My heart was troubled within me, and my strength has failed me, and the light of my eyes is no longer with me' (Ps 38:10), my feet were slipped, but they did not fall. For such things happen to those who are most penitent, and it is to be learned from another psalm: 'How good is God to Israel, to those of an upright heart. But my feet were shaken but a little, my steps were spilled out a little, because I zealously pursued the lawless ones' (Ps 73:27-28). It is the countenance of one repenting.

It is not being announced by the one repenting as a countenance from the disposition of one pretending to repent; rather, he knew that 'as good is the God of Israel to those of an upright heart' (Ps 73:27) He does what He does. And I, the uncertain limit—who otherwise introduces the penitent—must be slipped but a little and fall. And I say an apostolic accompaniment to this: 'We know that the law is spiritual' (Rom 7:14)—we, the perfect, the disciples of the Spirit, those having received the divine and spiritual law. 'But I am flesh, sold under sin' (Rom 7:14). It is not the one knowing that the law is spiritual who is flesh, sold under sin; for he was separating himself from those [things]. 'We know that the law is spiritual,' he says generally concerning the saints. 'But I am flesh, sold under sin.'

And many doctrines this very brief expression subverts: 'I am flesh'; not by nature, nor am I such by construction, but 'having been sold under sin.' For he who is sold under a certain master in order to become [so] is not fleshly by nature; for his state has become such through an action. And here: 'How good is God to Israel, to those of an upright heart. But my feet were shaken but a little' (Ps 73:27), makes the soul manifest. And this 'but a little' shows that he is not entirely slipped. For he who says: 'I was slaughtered but a little,' shows that he was not slaughtered. 'My steps were spilled out a little' (Ps 73:28). I was running well, I was walking as was necessary, I was taking steps straightly. But these were spilled out only a little. And it is spilled out when the runner is startled and turns toward the rear. And from this very word, observe: 'Take me up to a high, sandy place.' I have seen the branch of my feet...

They magnified me as if I were a fallen corpse, speaking words of pride. One might say in another way: 'Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall stand up.' But he who speaks now says I did not fall at all, but only my feet were shaken; for if one who falls stands up and leaves the enemy's triumph, he is much more than one who never fell. It is easier to stand and steady the feet when one is shaken than to rise up having fallen. Therefore, if the difficult thing happens, the easy thing is much more quickly established.

For I am ready for lashes. Even if I am in motion and my strength has left me and the light of my eyes is not with me and my feet were shaken, I am ready for lashes; for I do not refuse to be lashed by you, as one whom you discipline as a beloved son. 'Do not slight the Lord's discipline; for whom the Lord loves He disciplines, and He lashes every son whom He receives' (Heb 12:5-6). Since therefore I am a son, even if I have shared in the cause of lashes myself, I refuse to be magnified by them, that is, their treating me as one being overturned. But I am ready to be lashed by you.

And my pain is before me always. I suffer because I have become entirely among those who bring rebukes, those who bring lashes. He who grieves the 'godly sorrow that brings repentance unto salvation' (2 Cor 7:10) has this pain added to himself always. Just as one who has a dead person and wails over him, weeping as much as he sees him, so the one who has come into the bringing of lashes wails and weeps as much as he sees them, and has this pain added to himself always. Let us say, for example, if someone has become ill with an incurable disease; from the pain of this disease, he has pain added to it. If a physician or the help of God describes the cause of the pain as the disease, he immediately casts away the pain and says, 'You have turned my mourning into joy for me' (Ps 30:5). And he says, 'The Lord has heard and has had mercy on me' (Ps 30:2). And so that I may speak more clearly: Lazarus, the brother of those around Mary and Martha, died, and in as long as he was in death, those there grieved and wailed as much as those who had come to entreat me to weep with them (John 11). But when he said, 'Lazarus, come out!' and the mourning was cast away, no longer...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The struggle against sin and unjust hatred
english: They were suffering. Indeed, they were performing thanksgivings and drinking together when he said, and 'Lazarus was one of those reclining' (Luke 16:20). As far as I have the causes of the pain, I have it added to me throughout. If, therefore, you, having heard, bring a helpful secondary remedy like the lashes in a useful way, having been healed, I will no longer suffer.

19 For I will proclaim my lawlessness. He says this: by proclaiming my lawlessness, I do not hide the pain; for always remembering and going through it, having the pain, that I have become in it. And I do not proclaim it only so much as to want to find the one healing it. 'I will care' indeed 'about my sin.' Not everyone sinning cares about his sin. Cain sinned and he heard: 'Have you sinned? Be silent.' If he had been silent, I would have cared about his sin, how he might cast it away and no longer let it act, no longer being persuaded to be according to it. 19 And I will care about my sin. Here, lawlessness and sin can be said in parallel. Concerning this, John writes in the epistle attributed to him, saying: 'Everyone who practices sin also practices lawlessness, and sin is lawlessness' (1 John 3:4). Therefore, 'I will care' 'about my lawlessness' being sin. For I proclaim it, I do not hide it, I do not wait for what is from without to convict me, I do not wait for another to say to me: 'You are in sin and lawlessness.' It was said to us that: 'his righteous one,' he says, 'is an accuser in the first instance; as when the adversary brings a charge, he is convicted.' And we took that; he says: 'say you the sins first, so that you may be justified.' Do not wait for the accuser. One must be an accuser in his own first instance; for if this happens, then he is ashamed, since you cared about your sin, how you might no longer act it.

20 And my enemies live and are prevailing against me. For this reason I call upon you as a helper; for this reason I have made myself compliant toward being scourged by you. Since, therefore, from the

To sin and to have lawlessness—'they live and are held fast against me' (Ps 38:10)—for they nourish my wickedness; therefore, do what I ask of me: 'I am anxious' (Ps 38:11) 'concerning my sin.' Therefore, strike me, bring near strenuous helps, so that I may be healed; for then the rest become weaker than me, they are crushed under my feet; for Jesus alone is able to crush Satan under the feet of the saints. And again: 'And the God of peace will crush Satan under your feet quickly' (Rom 16:20). As long as neither he nor those after him is being crushed, they live.

20 And those hating me unjustly were multiplied (Ps 35:19). However, great is the praise that he hated not justly. For instance, if someone were to hate someone as if he were proud when he is not proud, but also entirely blind, he hates him unjustly. The elders who rose up against Susanna hated her because they did not find her fault. This hatred is unjust. Egypt hated Joseph. This hatred is unjust.

21 They beset me, because they persecuted righteousness. I did not harm them; for no one is 'justly pursuing the righteous' (Ps 34:12) and persecuting righteousness—the 'persecuted' here does not mean to pursue in a hating way, but to pursue after, as it signifies. Just as if one says: 'Seek peace and pursue it' (Ps 34:14).

21 And the beloved cast me off as if a dead thing to be loathed. I worked good things for them, and it was necessary for them to receive good from me instead of good. But 'evils' 'instead of good' they provide to me, being unfeeling, as they are of the evil ones; and in what disposition I am toward them, I am such as not rejoicing in their evils, but loving them and desiring to make them outside of the evils. The beloved of me, whom it was necessary to love, they rejected as a dead thing to be loathed, as if they were fleeing from me, a stinking corpse. And it is also good to say 'the beloved,' not 'the one being loved'; for he hated. 22 Do not abandon me, Lord; my God, do not turn away from me. Even if they themselves have abandoned [me]...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Tongue as the Beginning of Sin and Virtue
english: Not because 'righteousness has persecuted me' [Ps 22:19], but do not forsake me, do not become distant from me. God forsakes someone when they are worthy to suffer grievous things. I do not say this to mean that He tests them with grievous things; He is not not-forsaking, but when one, having grievous things, is defeated and cast down, then You do not forsake me, if You do not depart from me. I have clung to You; I have become one spirit toward You. When one clings to the Lord, and the Lord to him. 'My soul has clung to You behind You' [Ps 63:8].

Cry out for my help, O Lord of my salvation [Ps 27:7]. You stand away from me if I sin, not if I am hated unjustly, nor even if some magnify themselves against me. And You are Lord and God of my salvation. But salvation does not touch the flesh, nor is it found regarding external things, but regarding the soul itself. This is the said eternal salvation; for it 'became'—the Christ, clearly—'eternal salvation to all those obeying Him.' The flesh's 'eternal salvation', which doctors bring to it, or that which a pilot saves for those sailing, is not eternal; for these will soon die again. But the salvation of God is eternal; He is their salvation.

1–2 To the end, to Ithium. I said: I will guard my ways so as not to sin in my tongue. This is one of the Psalms. In Ezra and in the [Book of the] Remaining, there is a memory of each name of those being submitted. And this, then, is one of them, or perhaps he himself composed the psalm for David, or having received it from David, he proclaimed it. And it is the work of the Psalms to say their psalms, both those they themselves composed and those others arranged.

This, then, is a victory song. Often the sinner is troubled by these things, but after conquering and trampling him and taking him under hand, [the psalmist] sends back the song; for no one sings a victory song while still warring and being warred against, but in the having conquered. Likewise, Moses and all the Jewish multitude did not say a victory song when they were against Pharaoh, but when they saw him become a drowning man: 'Let us sing to the Lord, for gloriously He has been glorified; He has cast horse and rider into the sea' [Ex 15:1]. When the horse and its rider were cast into the sea, and Pharaoh's chariots and the power of the...

God cast the Red Sea into the sea, and then a victorious song was appropriately sent up. And David says in the seventy-first psalm: 'In the day when he rescued him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, then he said: I will love you, O Lord my strength' (Ps 71:5), and all the rest which the song contains. It is a prayer before the war and in the war, but a victorious hymn and song after the destruction of the war, after capturing the enemies.

I said: 'I will guard my ways so as not to sin in my tongue' (Ps 34:13). For almost every practical sin has its beginning in the word. Regarding the young man whom the prostitute—who is personified in the proverbs, that is, being a woman or a false glory or a deception starting from words—is able to ensnare: for it is said, 'She led him astray with much intercourse' or enticement, and 'with the nooses through the lips she hollowed him out' (Prov 2:3/7). And behold, the word has become the beginning of sin. And the elders, indeed, those remaining according to Sophronius, started a word toward her.

If, therefore, someone does not sin in the tongue, he guards the ways well; for he said that the beginning of these ways is the word. And from the opposite of all good works, the word is the beginning. But he does not speak only about those ways; he added, 'so as not to sin in my tongue' (Ps 34:13). Yet sinning in the tongue is not the same as saying, 'My tongue will meditate on your righteousness' (Ps 119:9). 'The beginning of your words is truth' (Ps 119:160). The cause of saying your words is your truth; I will make this manifest if I know it. Therefore, upon the virtues and the well-flowing ways, truth is the beginning, the cause. But upon the forbidden ways, from which it is necessary to guard oneself and from which it is proper to turn away, the word is the beginning, as has already been said.

I set a guard upon my mouth (Ps 34:13). Remember how he said 'not to sin in the tongue': 'I set a guard upon my mouth.' Since 'from the words someone is justified and from his words he is condemned' (Matt 12:37), it is necessary for the mouth to place a guard, so that I may say the [good] things and not the [bad], that we may speak the profitable things and be silent about the harmful ones; for no one is able at once to bring forth words that both justify and condemn. Something like this is said with an enigma in the proverbs: 'Death and life are in the hand of the tongue' (Prov 18:21). And the 'hand' of the 'tongue' is the word.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Wisdom in Silence and the Renewal of Sorrow
english: The activity of the tongue. He who speaks what is beneficial and leads into the kingdom of life has life in the tongue. But he who speaks the opposite and the forbidden things has death in his own word called a 'tongue'. And in another scripture it says: 'With your words make a balance and a weight' (Prov 16:11). It is necessary to speak having weighed; it is necessary to have a balance and to cast the words upon each scale. And if the upright words are found to be balanced, it is proper to choose those and to proclaim them, but to turn away from the bad ones.

Again it is said: 'The lips of the wise are taught by perception' (Ps 51:13). When someone speaks having perceived, the lips are taught, not opening them to every word, but to what is beneficial. 'I will open my lips and my mouth shall proclaim your praise' (Ps 51:14). He who has the taught lips, having perceived that what he intends to speak is beneficial, opened them. But when they harm what is being uttered, he closes and binds the lips with perception; he binds the word.

'In the standing of the sinner against me, I was made deaf and humbled, and I kept silence for the sake of good things' (Ps 31:5). Often appearing, the sinner provokes and is called out to the things pleasing to him. If, therefore, he ever stands [against us], it is our part to make him stand; for if we do not give him a place, he is not able to stand. But to stand in this way is to stand in battle. It is necessary to be silent; for he often provokes; because the serpent, having stood against Eve, provoked her word and harmed her. It was necessary to be silent, having received perception of her own weakness or of the sin that had come before, not to speak anything to her, but to keep silence for the sake of good things.

And the 'keeping silence for the sake of good things' does not say 'not to speak the good things', but to have a silence made wise from the good things. For example, having taken up virtue, a prudent man knew that he must not respond out of the good, that is, out of prudence. I kept silence toward the standing revealed and provoking toward sin. If, therefore, that young man had been responding to nothing from right understanding toward the harlot, he would not have 'been led astray by much association' (1 Tim 5:15) nor 'been enticed by the morsels of his lips' (Prov 5:3). I kept silence, therefore, when the good things had come upon me, persuading me not to respond to him. He does not say: 'I kept silence so as not to speak the good things', but 'so as not to speak the provoking things'. And this silence has become to me from...

The wisdom of the good things which hinders such a conversation. "He is found wise while being silent." He who thus remains silent is found wise. And it is indeed wisdom to know to whom one must speak and to whom one must not, and when to bring forward words and when not. "He is therefore found wise while being silent, and he is silent, for he has no answer." And this man possesses a certain quietness of mind; for having known that he has no answer, he keeps peace. "And he is wise, being silent, knowing the right time." This man is perfect.

And "my sorrow was renewed" (Psalm 39:10). Then the sorrow is renewed when the sinner stands in reflection upon what he has done, upon which it is necessary to grieve. And just as the sorrow received a renewal, renewal is to dwell in a house at first. A renewal, therefore, is to lead that which has already withered and is silent into flowering. "My sorrow" therefore "was renewed." Having said, "I kept my ways not to sin with my tongue" (Psalm 119:11), I knew that I had sinned. Therefore "my sorrow was renewed." And it is blessed for one who has sinned to experience a renewal of sorrow and not of pleasure; for he who rejoices over what he has done and brings those things back into the midst again, renews [the sin]. But he who grieves, having perceived that it is necessary to guard the ways and not to sin with the tongue, renews the sorrow, weeping and grieving, "working the sorrow according to God, which is repentance." In this, he grieves entirely in the recognizing that it has entirely happened in such matters.

"My heart was warmed within me" (Psalm 39:3). One may say: my heart has received heat just as warmth, and from the renewal of sorrow. And one may also say this: because I seized myself intensely and I am being consumed and I weep aloud the sorrow, "my heart was warmed," it has become fiery. "In" indeed "my practice, a fire burned up" (Psalm 39:2), consuming and making me ash; for they were hay and wood and other things. I have this consuming fire not only in the being perfected, but also in my practicing the sorrow. And the "within me" is also good. The heart becomes hot so that the heat spreads even to the outside. Those, indeed, who are burning with passion do not have a heart warmed within, but, having spread to the outside, they have the state of one being pressed. It is as if it were said: "I was troubled and I did not speak."
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Number of Days and Enlightenments
english: Having experienced a disturbance in thought or in reasoning, and having done nothing according to that disturbance of thoughts, nor even having spoken, he possesses the state of having been disturbed and not having spoken. Such a person has within him a heart having been warmed. 'And in my meditation fire shall be kindled' (Ps 39:16). My inner self. And thus for each of us, two men have stood, the one outside, the other inside. Therefore, when a disturbance arises in the soul and does not transfer the disturbance to the outer man, but keeps it within so as to recognize it and weep over it, he has within him a heart having been warmed, not in order to act, but in order not to act. 'In my meditation the fire burns.' In others, by voice and by action and by thought, a fire burns, consuming them, burning them. 'Their heart was warmed like a fiery furnace.' Here the meditation is like a fire that has burned, having a combustible material lying beneath. And the meditation and the heat of the Holy [Spirit] is the all-consuming, which comes to pass by the blowing Spirit. Therefore the fire burns in order that it may act, not in order that it may harm and consume. 'Was not our heart burning within us while he opened to us the Scriptures?' (Lk 24:32). This burning is to be praised. And observe also regarding manufactured things: some are heated in order that they may be reshaped and become a vessel, gold or silver. But if wood or something else is set on fire, the heat is harmful.

'I spoke in a tongue.' Even if I did not let it become outward, but it remained within me, through a burning from meditation it made itself for me, and so I spoke in a tongue: 'Make known to me, Lord, my end' (Ps 62:5). From my own tongue I said this; for the tongue according to the nature of the possessor is this: for example, the temperate man, speaking the things of temperance, speaks in his own tongue, the tongue of the temperate man, not in the tongue of a human [deceiver]. And the one desiring to learn his own end and to offer his life to God, in my tongue, not in the tongue of a deceitful man, but I, desiring to know my end, spoke in a tongue. This my word is not a counterfeit. When a hypocrite speaks concerning temperance while not being temperate, he does not speak in his own tongue. But the temperate man, when he delivers discourses concerning temperance, speaks in the tongue of the temperate man. No hypocrite, therefore, speaks in the natural tongue, but in the counterfeit tongue. The wolf, when he [is...]

Begging like a sheep to enter Christ's flock, he speaks not in his own tongue, but imitates the voice of the sheep, so that, meeting like with like, he might harm. 'Make known to me, Lord, my end and the number of my days, what it is' (Psalm 39:10). Observe how the one saying this is a repentant person. 'Help me to guard my ways, to set a guard over my mouth' (Psalm 39:11-12). When the sinner stood against me and was provoking, I received good in my mind from the experience of not speaking to him.

This is therefore what I say; since I saw myself lacking much—for I had only just begun to progress—'Make known to me, Lord, my end,' so that I might know how much time of life remains to me, if it is sufficient for completion and fulfillment. Thus also another was saying: 'Declare to me the brevity of my days; do not bring me back in the midst of my days' (Psalm 39:13). In a certain way, I am in the midst of the days that come from the Holy Light. Do not then bring me back in such a way. Therefore, fulfill my days.

But God fulfills the days of some not by providing an increase of them; for when it is said, 'I will fill him with length of days' concerning the righteous, we do not say that he makes him many-years. There are also impious people who have lived many years. 'And the number of my days' (Psalm 39:10). It is also possible to say 'the number of my days' meaning: you have enlightened me much, I have become [composed of] days; for each enlightenment is a day. Therefore, reveal to me the number of my enlightenments, so that I might know what I lack.

As if someone, having taken up a desire for art or science, lest he should have a perfect knowledge of his education, says: 'Reveal to me what are the luminous things of science, so that I might know what I have and what I lack.' It is blessed to have things, works, and thoughts that are countable, those worthy of being numbered. Regarding the prostitute, it is indeed said: 'They are countless, whom you have slain' (Hosea 13:9). This does not necessarily mean that they are infinite, but that they are not worthy of being numbered. They do not exist in any word or number. So that I might know what I lack. If I learn the number of my days and my end, until when it is reached, I recognize in what things I lack, which are the things I have not yet learned. Therefore, those making a desire for science...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Meanings of Hypostasis and Substance
english: More completely, they say the insights grasped by them are to be taught at the same time as the beginning, so that they may also know what they lack, and take up a desire to succeed and recover.

"Behold, I have made my days into wrestling matches." The former reading, this more common one, is: "I have made my days into old wrestling matches." I am not young or a newborn, not having begun to live just now, but "I have made my days into old wrestling matches." And this must be said: that which approaches always makes old that which has passed. Thus also laws grow old. Therefore he says: the old days which I had, when I lived as a man of old, have grown old and have departed; I have clothed myself in the new. But the one at hand will say: "Behold, I have become an old man. Make known to me the end, when I shall die." "Behold, I have made my days into wrestling matches." Since the name "wrestler" is homonymous—meaning also the one contending in the arena, and also indicating a certain measure—it is possible to take it both ways. He says: "I have made my days into wrestling in the arena"; for we always have those who fight against us. At times human temptation comes and fights and wears out human passions, and at other times evil powers; for "our wrestling is not against blood and flesh"—for us, but for others, yes—"but against the principalities, against the powers" (Ephesians 6:12). In order that this may be, "I have made my days into wrestling matches." And it can also be said by measure: as toward the age of the ages, the days which I live hold the character of a wrestler. And just as he says that all the nations are many things, "a drop from a bucket"—as toward the bucket of rational drops all the nations are—and "a weight on a scale"—until the weight tips and oscillates, not so as to pull the scale plate down—as toward the magnitude of the aging and the length of the days, which the one capable of living well endures: "the one loving" (Exodus 20:12) "his father and his mother shall be long-lived." And this is not yet found according to the literal word.
And my substance is as if nothing is against...

The name of hypostasis signifies many things. Regarding the present, there is a need for two meanings. Sometimes essence is called hypostasis; for instance, when the Son is called the 'character of the divine hypostasis' (cf. Heb 1:3), meaning the divine essence and existence. Hypostasis is also called perfect endurance, by which someone stands firm against hardships.

Thus he speaks in both senses: 'the essence of my soul is nothing before you' (Ps 51:6), as if toward you a certain great essence. And [saying] that it ought to be perfect according to you, the Father, I diminished it. And that this is so, he says concerning some: 'Children of Zion, the honored, adorned with gold and silver, how they became earthen vessels?' (2 Tim 2:20). Behold, their essence was diminished. It is clearly necessary to take this: they have become earthen vessels. The gold, being reviled, is diminished and falls far short of its own value. He who does not realize the honor coming to him from God 'is compared to the mindless cattle' (Ps 49:20), and his hypostasis, through poverty, was considered nothing.

And since it also signifies endurance, he says: even if I endured desiring to see my end and I entreat you that you make this known to me, yet my endurance is not something brief in this way toward you. Moreover, all things are vanity, every living man (Eccl 1:2). This must be known in two ways: all things are vanity through man, as the Preacher has clearly interpreted. Regarding the things that have ascended above and are perfect and truly eternal, the hypostasis is vain, except 'every living man.'

Thus it is possible to say: even if all other things apart from man are vanity, such as mortal animals, the transient things, even if they are soulless, man alone is living, living according to that life which they live according to Abraham; for 'God is not of the dead, but of the living' (Mk 12:27). And the man who lives according to the human [standard] is himself vain. Therefore, it must be distinguished thus: all these things are vanity; for even if they were mortal, having died.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Treasuring in Heaven vs. Earth
english: They are no longer. But the man is living. Even if he should die, he still lives. Or in this way: a man living who does not become outside of human life is himself vanity; so that it is thus: 'except all things are vanity and every living man' (Eccl 1:2). Or in this way: 'except all things are vanity, but the man is living'. Beyond this: the essence? Even if the man lives differently than a mortal would live, in view of the excellence and the greatness of the divine life and of God himself, the fountain of life, he is nothing.

The small things and the things no smaller than small are said in relation to something. And the small does not have a limited amount; for it is said in reference to the greater. We say, for instance, that the wrestler is greater than the boxer. Indeed, you have in categories a small mountain and a large gulf. 'But indeed, a man wanders in an image' (Eccl 1:14). I said that he speaks about the others besides the man, saying that 'all is vanity'. Only the man is living. And he has more than the others. He has an immortal soul.

However, even if he is living, he does not always have this motion; 'but indeed', for he says, 'a man wanders in an image' (Eccl 1:14). He did not say whether he wanders in praise or in mockery; but however anyone wanders, however he acts, he is in some image. Taking it more generally, it is to be said that it is either of the heavenly or of the earthly. And it is shown from such a word that the man is self-determining; for if he were good by construction, he would always wander in the heavenly, if he were evil by essence, in the earthly.

And it is possible to divide these general images into kinds. And I say that one is in the image of a fox, another in the image of a lion, and a certain mare becoming a horse carrying another image, and another in the image of a dove, except 'in an image every man wanders'. 'But indeed, a man wanders in an image' (Eccl 1:14), except vainly they are troubled. But the worthless are vainly troubled. 'Except vainly they are troubled'. And he therefore speaks of the vain trouble, because this striving concerning human things is such. For instance, he 'stores up' 'and does not know to whom he gathers them' (Eccl 2:18). He stores up and does not know to whom he gathers them. In Ecclesiastes it was clearly said that: 'he does not know whether he will be wise' (Eccl 2:19), the successor of those who are.

His [words] 'or fools'. And often what one has treasured, he leaves behind. Sometimes, as a year passes, he falls away into other things. Therefore, it is not necessary to be anxious about treasuring in this way; for 'lawless treasures will not profit, but righteousness rescues from death' (Prov 11:4). Therefore, the righteousness that rescues from death and from every other evil is to be treasured. This wealth is treasured in heaven.

'Do not treasure for yourselves treasures on earth, but treasure treasures in heaven' (Matt 6:19-21); because where the treasure is, there also the mind is, which is called the 'heart'. It is to be treasured in heaven so that we may have the mind there, and one should refrain from treasuring on earth, so that we may not have the intellect there. It is said concerning some: 'those treasuring injustice and misery in their lands'.

The man, therefore, wandering in an image, treasuring, did not know to whom he was bringing them; for it is unclear to him what he will bequeath. Therefore, the diligent one hears to treasure in the heavens. He has wealth set aside in good works. This is also what Paul writes to Timothy: 'command the rich of this age not to be high-minded concerning wealth, but in God, who provides all things' (1 Tim 6:17).

It must also be said concerning false wealth, such as the heretical opinion of the dogmas of the atheists. And he who treasures these things did not know to whom he was bringing them. But he leaves them to another; for until the present life, he holds the promise of 'the pseudonymous knowledge' (1 Tim 6:20); for when the truth shines forth, it is dissolved and vanishes.

And what about 'only in an image'?—even if every man is living, he is not living without transgression in the praiseworthy living. For if he had remained in the true image, the first, according to which he was created, he would not have been troubled, nor would he have treasured in vain. But indeed, even if he has become living, he wanders in an image; and not altogether in the first, but rather wandering in an image; for never can the rational animal be able to act outside of acting according to reason. And acting, he acts either praiseworthily or falsely, thinking and doing certain things and certain others.

And what about 'but in vain they are troubled'?—it has often already been said to us that these changes occur in such a way. When they do not guard this image according to which they have become, they are a multitude of the vain.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Discipline of Correction and the Escape from Punishment
english: They are being disturbed. When he signifies the life of man, he says, 'every man lives' (Ps 39:1), and 'yet a man wanders in an image'—not in the same one, but because the images are diverse, and especially because many are false and deceptive, many are being disturbed. And now, what is my stability? Is it not the Lord? Regarding others, the things spoken have been said. But as for myself, I say: 'What is my stability? Is it not the Lord?' (Ps 39:17) I do not wait for another. And just as 'wisdom, righteousness, and sanctification become' those who participate, so also stability becomes to the one waiting, the Lord himself. And my subsistence is with you. Concerning the Lord, he says that his stability is. But toward the Lord, who is, he says his subsistence is: 'and my subsistence is with you' (Ps 39:18). It is possible to call subsistence here the strength by which one is able to stand, because, with you cooperating and being my stability, I stand against all things. And the 'subsistence from you' is a praise to me. And it is possible to call subsistence instead of essence. And my subsistence of the rational soul, of the rational animal, is with you; for you have given me a soul; from you I have the soul, not beginning from seeds, not being composed according to an opinion like the Stoic school, but 'my subsistence is from you' (Ps 39:18).

Save me from all my lawlessness (Ps 39:19). Not from some, but 'from all,' so that I may become outside of every false image. A reproach of foolishness you have given me (Ps 39:20). From the beginning we said that the whole psalm bears the face of one repenting and progressing. It is a trivial thing to be reproached by a righteous man, but to be praised by a fool. For the fool indeed reproaches regarding good works and with zeal. For this reason, even in proverbs, as if there were no difference, reproaches are mentioned: 'Do not acquire the reproach of evil men' (Prov 22:8); for he did not say at all, 'Do not acquire reproach,' but 'of evil men.' Do not reproach regarding triviality; for there are those being reproached regarding good things. To the well-known, Jesus says: 'Rejoice and be glad when they reproach you' (Matt 5:11). This kind of reproach is not to be rejected; for it is good and will lead into the kingdom of heaven. But the reproaches of evil men are to be fled from. I was made mute and I did not open my mouth (Ps 39:21). Who is the foolish reproacher, or he is the sinner who stands against him, as...

"He became mute and did not open his mouth"? And here again the same thing is signified: "I became mute and did not open my mouth." He did not answer him regarding what he reproaches. This is often said by another power, as the apostle teaches this, saying: "Reprove not a contentious man for one exhortation" (Prov 9:8). Do not open the mouth to him at all. But so that you may have a defense and a word to say about yourself, "I have done this by myself," exhort him. If he does not submit to the exhortation, or "and a second"—for some manuscripts have "and a second"—overthrow him, "knowing that he sins." One who is "self-condemning" should not be set against.

10–11 For you are the one who made me, turn away your whips from me. Do not lash me; for I am your handiwork. "But he lashes every son whom he receives" (Heb 12:6), having it clear through which he is lashed. Therefore, leave these things to me; grant me a remission, for in this way I shall no longer be lashed. Now I am still liable for the lashings. 278 Therefore, he who has placed the Most High as his refuge (Ps 91:2) has no approaching evils nor a whip approaching his tent. Make me therefore such that I am no longer liable for the lashings; turn away the thing that punishes me. Since therefore I say, "Deliver me from all my iniquities" (Ps 51:2), when you deliver me, I am no longer liable for punishment.

He was lashing him in a certain way even through the thoughtless man, and says that the reproaches of the thoughtless are the lashes. Unless God delivers, one is not able even by opposing that which has not been delivered. 11 From the strength of your hand I have failed (Ps 31:9). The strength of your hand, the educational one, the striking one, the one subjecting to pains, presses upon me. Since therefore it has become strong against me, I have failed. I cast away my former life, I left my former state; for I did not fail so as to no longer exist, or to become weak, but so as to fail the state preparing to punish me. "I have failed." I, saying these things, confessing, saying, "You have given me reproach through thoughtlessness," have failed, having become outside of my former state. It is possible to fail praiseworthily, and it is possible to fail shamefully. "And Esau came from the field, leaving behind" (Gen 25:29), when he desired to eat a meal. The "leaving behind" here is instead of "having grown weak" and "longing for food." It is said often...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The distinction between fleshly, psychic, and spiritual states
english: spiritual

If one attempts things that are different—and one is true and the other is false—one knows from the attempt at opposites which is true and which is false. Indeed, the true itself appears by the showing of the false, because knowledge is of the opposites.

"And you searched out his soul like a spider" (Ps 90:8). You searched out his soul like a spider, his soul according to which he is psychic. Concerning someone bad it is said, "he was carried by the desires of his soul." When someone reshapes [things] from the soul, let it be said, as if they were prophecies or as if they were doctrines of piety, "he is carried by the desires of the soul"; he is not carried by the Holy Spirit.

In another book I have stated the difference: that man is fleshly, he who fights according to the flesh, he who follows the desires of the flesh, he who is driven by the flesh, he who has become fleshly and is driven by sin. But a man is spiritual who has ascended above the psychic state, when he carries everything by the Holy Spirit and by God-bearing, doing and practicing [them]. And psychic is he who is neither fleshly nor spiritual.

And perhaps all the wise of the world are such. They think themselves self-sufficient according to the movements and thoughts of their own souls. And because of this they do not receive the things of the Spirit; for they prefer their own and think their own understanding to be great, they do not receive the foolishness of the Spirit, regarding it as such. And indeed there are certain heresies established in their entirety, both among the Greeks and among the Christians, which say that allegories are foolishnesses, they are mere fabrications. And they say that the theorems concerning the intelligible are false, since they think all things to be bodies and sensible.

These, therefore, are psychic men, not receiving the things of the Spirit, regarding themselves as self-sufficient and capable of contemplating all things by themselves. His soul, then, such a soul—not the essence, but the state according to which it is a soul—you searched out like a spider. And the spider is very weak, as it is said, "they weave a spider's web; their web shall not be a garment" (Job 8:14). The fragility of the construction of the animal...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Prayer vs Petition and the Tears of Repentance
english: Regarding the one called a spider, he says there is an extension of the soul. When the soul is stretched out, this extension occurs for its own benefit; for the spider-like quality is weak in it, and moreover it is shown to be an external evil. Therefore, you have examined the soul of this man as a spider, he who is being reproved under accusations for lawlessness.

12 Moreover, every man is tossed about in vain. All men who are outside the instruction of God and the reproofs are tossed about in vain. But this one, even if he is tossed about while being reproved, even if his soul is stretched out like a spider, he does not suffer this in vain; for he receives a change toward better things. But if anyone were such a bare man, not being under instruction, not being under reproofs, he is tossed about in vain according to what was said previously: 'Indeed, man wanders in an image, but they are tossed about in vain' (Ps 94:11). He who does not wish to be tossed about, but has tranquility, becomes God, having received the word of God; for 'he called those gods, those to whom the word of God came' (Ps 82:6). And these are not tossed about in vain, but even if it happens that they slip or a passion occurs, they say: 'I was tossed about and I did not speak.' Their tossing stands only until passion.

Furthermore: do they toss about from themselves? — At times they toss about from themselves, at other times from those encountering them. 13 Hear, O Lord, my prayer and my supplication. It seems there is something else that is the supplication of the prayer. He sends up a supplication, the one who has known himself to be begging and lacking, so that he may be filled. But the one praying has this form as well, yet at times asks for the existence of good things from above. The one asking from God to receive something, that is, what he does not have, asks to receive it, or what he has, so that it may remain with him. Primarily this is prayer; it is a request sent up along with the one theologizing, the one wishing, to whom the prayer is sent up. When he says: 'Lord our God, give us peace, for you gave us all things' (Hab 3:2). 'The prayer of Habakkuk the prophet.'

He said: 'Lord, I have heard your voice and was astounded. Let him be known in the midst of two living creatures; when the years approach, he shall not be known' (Habakkuk 3:2). Behold, this is a prayer. When one asks for only those things which he lacks while being in need, it is a petition, being sent back like a wish. It is also possible to take it this way: those asking for more bodily things petition, such as health, wealth, and the others, as being in need, and many times they are worthy to receive these. But he who desires to have fullness, says: 'The prayer of Habakkuk the prophet: Lord, I have heard your voice and was astounded. Let him be known in the midst of two living creatures; when the years approach, he shall not be known' (Habakkuk 3:2). Behold, this is a prayer.

'Lord our God, give us peace, for you have given us all things' (1 Chronicles 29:14). Since even as one lacking, I ask that something might be given to me—for I am still at the peak of childhood—listen to my petition. But since I am about to come by chance to those things of which I am lacking, having become full, I ask for greater things; I ask for heavenly things and I say: 'Our Father who is in the heavens, hallowed be your name' (Matthew 6:9)—not as one lacking does he ask this. 'Let your kingdom come' (Matthew 6:10). Make it come. Then it comes, so that God may reign according to our energy.

Unite them with my tears. Seeing myself lacking, I weep, making that 'godly sorrow working repentance unto salvation' (2 Corinthians 7:10), regarding which I say: 'I will wash my bed every night, with my tears I will wet my couch.' And since he who is lacking perfection and the extremity of virtue—again he pours himself out saying: 'We who dwell in the tent groan' (Psalm 88:7), and again: 'I have poured out my tears before you according to your promise'—you see: 'as in the promise I have poured out my tears.' What tears are these, or those of the ones weeping so that they might laugh? For 'blessed' are 'those who weep now, that they may laugh' (Luke 6:21). These placed the tears as in the promise, so that they might laugh, so that they might be filled with joy.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Meaning of Non-Existence and the Patient Psalmist
english: unspoken and glorified. 'Do not disregard me, for I am a sojourner in this land.' Do not disregard me while I am praying, entreating, weeping, and bearing tears—such things as 'those who sow in joy shall reap.' Therefore, 'do not disregard me,' but having responded, give what I have requested; for disregard sometimes signifies delay and patience, and sometimes indeed patience, when it occurs regarding sins: 'having done these things, I was silent' (Psalm 39:8), instead of 'I have not repaid you.' If I were an inhabitant, I would not have dared to ask and to pray. For the inhabitants are those responsible for wickedness and impiety. For it is said in Jeremiah: 'from the face of the north shall the evils be burned upon those inhabiting the land' (Jeremiah 50:39), not 'upon those sojourning.' And in the Revelation of John, it is said three times: 'woe, woe, woe upon those inhabiting the land' (Revelation 18:7). If I were, therefore, an inhabitant, I would not have said, 'do not disregard me.'

And I am a stranger just as all my fathers were. The sojourner and the stranger are one and the same. For Paul, having made a list of all those who were well-pleasing through faith in the Epistle to the Hebrews, called them sojourners and strangers (Hebrews 11:13). None of them is an inhabitant, none is a native, but a stranger. He has come from elsewhere into this place; he was not born here. Therefore, all the fathers according to virtue were sojourners in the land and strangers, such as the patriarchs and others who produced according to divine instruction, such as prophets, teachers, and lawgivers.

Refresh me, so that I may find refreshment before I depart and no longer exist. Here, refreshment is called praiseworthy, being equivalent to 'delighting in the Lord.' 'I found refreshment for myself,' says Ephrem. And that refreshment is a slight thing. One refreshes praiseworthily when he enjoys virtue, when he 'delights in the Lord,' when he perceives and receives the understanding of the 'paradise of delight.' Since, therefore, much is lacking to me—for this is why I send up a petition, so that I may be filled of the things lacking—for this also he said at the beginning of the Psalm: 'Lord, make known to me my end and the number of my days, what it is, so that I may know what I lack' (Psalm 39:4). When he knows the things that are lacking and acquires these, he finds refreshment through such possessions. Therefore, he says: refresh me to remain in this life, so that having been instructed, I may [be refreshed]...

I shall refresh myself before I depart from this life and no longer exist. He does not say, 'I shall not begin to be,' but rather, 'I shall be such a person as I desire to be'; for the soul does not move into non-existence. Listen, accordingly, to what is said to people: one must take the words in their proper sense. If the righteous man or the wise man says according to God, 'I strive for all things so that I may become rich' (cf. Prov 28:20), do not take what is said to mean material wealth. But if someone else were a rhetorician or a physician—and this one is therefore a holy wise man—he says, 'I have no other endurance except the Lord and the subsistence from Him.'

Thus, if this wise man says, 'Let me live most hopefully in this only life, so that I may refresh myself having eaten and drunk according to: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (Luke 12:19), one must take the refreshment appropriately to the person, both the 'let me' and the 'no longer to be.' He who says this is immortal. Therefore, if he says, 'I shall no longer be,' he does not say, 'I move into complete destruction, I turn into non-existence,' but rather, 'I shall no longer be in the way that I desired to have been.' If a sinner says, 'Admonish me, discipline me, so that I may no longer be'—for it is not so that he may move into complete destruction.

1–2 unto the end; the Psalm of David: 'Waiting, I waited upon the Lord, and He attended to me' (Ps 40:1). The preceding Psalm could have been spoken by any saint who has lived his life with patience and magnanimity, and by the Lord's man; for the Apostle, taking words from it, has set forth in the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning Christ those things having been said. This is the whole: 'A sacrifice and an offering You did not desire' (Heb 10:5), until: 'It is written about me in the head of a book' (Ps 40:7). And the Psalm is single-personed. The same person who began announces and sings until the end of the Psalm. He therefore says thankfully to God: 'Waiting, I waited upon the Lord, and He heard my prayer.' The 'waiting, I waited' has such a meaning as if someone were to say, 'I healed medically, I wrote grammatically.' They are waiting, not in a manner of mere waiting, but either through much insensitivity or sometimes through ambition. For the Apostle says: 'I will not deliver my body so that I may boast' (1 Cor 9:27), because of praise.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Soul's Descent and Christ's Identification with Human Misery
english: He does not merely say 'having endured, I remained' as if to please the body and soul; rather, he endured with knowledge and as was necessary, not to receive a prize, glory, or praise from men. To endure thus is to say, as I might say, 'I acted wisely according to wisdom.' It was said in the preceding psalm that God is the endurance of the righteous: 'And now, what is my endurance? Is it not the Lord?' (Psalm 70:5). He who bears the heavy things falling upon him through this endurance says, 'Having endured, I remained with the Lord.' He bore the heavy things with an enduring disposition, for many, as I have said, bear the heavy things for some [other] reason. God is therefore the endurance of the holy. And in Jeremiah it is indeed said: 'A throne of glory rising, our holiness, endurance of Israel, Lord of Israel' (Jeremiah 33:16). He who is therefore established according to this endurance and is named from it says, 'Having endured, I remained with the Lord,' speaking as a slave. He who serves God calls him 'Lord' through his deeds, his mindsets, and his words. This one says, 'In the Holy Spirit, Lord Jesus'; for not everyone who calls Jesus Lord does so in this Spirit, but hypocrites indeed do this. Many will say to me on that day, 'Lord, Lord' (Matthew 7:21-23), and what does he say to them? 'I never knew you.' I never knew you having served me. And again: 'Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?' (Matthew 7:23). Therefore, he who calls Jesus thus Lord, doing the will of his Father in heaven, is the one who calls him 'in the Holy Spirit' Lord. The voice is therefore that of a slave.

And he heard my prayer. Being in distress, I cried out, and God, attending to my prayer, has fulfilled these things. For I 'having endured, I remained' [obeyed] the commandment concerning which the Savior said, 'He who endures to the end, this one will be saved' (Matthew 24:13). The 'I remained' is a state of having come to rest. And what kind of face did the Lord have? For we have not spoken out of necessity. If, then, you take it from the face of the Savior—for it has become a matter of pre-passion, it has not become a matter of passions—Jesus 'began to be amazed and distressed' (Mark 14:33). Such things happened to him until the beginning. We do not say that pre-passion occurs without disturbance; for we do not say that anyone other than the Trinity is without disturbance.

For the soul, which Jesus took up, is something other than the Trinity; it is of a nature to receive passion and the beginning of being terrified and distressed. And I say according to the apostles: 'Instead of the joy set before him, he endured the cross, despising shame' (Heb 12:2). If it had not become a victor in passion, it would not have been a feat or a contest.

Furthermore: the 'pay attention to me' [is] instead of 'he sighed'. And he brought me up out of the pit of misery and from the clay of matter. If each of the saints says this, 'the pit of misery' refers to the place concerning the earth; for a pit is a place where the waters falling from above gather. Often, in the divine writings, both the place concerning the earth and Hades are signified by this name; for when in the twenty-ninth [Psalm] it is said according to the man: 'You have saved me from those going down into the pit' (Ps 29:15), I do not myself go down into a pit. Because of others, I have been there. No one else brought me down.

Moreover, this appears more clearly from: 'I was counted among those going down into the pit; I became as a helpless man among the dead, yet free' (Ps 29:15). I am not one of those being led into the pit, but I 'was counted'. I counted myself among those. Therefore, I 'became' 'as a helpless man'. Not being helpless, he became as helpless; for when the Jews came to seize him, if he had not delivered himself, they would not have been able to take him. If he is 'free among the dead', he is not one of those becoming [members] of Hades by nature through choice and action, but he counted himself into this.

Therefore, he 'brought me up' 'from the pit of misery'. He who humbled his own body and enslaved it, and while still walking upon the earth, having acquired his citizenship in the heavens, he was lifted up from the pit of misery and from the clay of matter. And now indeed he was lifted up in power from the world and from matter and from the clay, from which the clay body has sailed. 'And God formed man from dust from the earth' (Gen 2:7). And even Job says: 'Remember that you formed me of clay' (Job 10:9). And Jesus will also say this according to the man: I have become into the pit of misery, I was counted, so that I might free them from misery and from the clay of matter; for because of them, I have become into the clay of matter.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The New Song and the Hope of the Lord
english: When this corruptible body is changed into incorruption, it is no longer held by the surrounding mud and distress, but has been rescued from these things. 'And he set my feet upon a rock.' Let this be said generally concerning the righteous. Regarding 'rock,' let the unbroken and indivisible Word of God be heard in these matters, which no storm or tempest moves. Often, indeed, the memory of a rock becomes a memorial of the holy words, not capable of being grasped by sensation; for when the saint says thankfully to God, 'Lift me up on a rock,' he does not say, 'He placed me suspended on a sensible rock,' but upon the unbroken and indivisible Word.

Paul interpreted this rock and said who it is, that it is Christ: 'for they drank from a spiritual following rock, and the rock was Christ' (1 Cor 10:4). And again this same hymnographer says with other things: 'their strong ones laid down the rock they were carrying.' Those of the Egyptians, approaching the rock, were seen as nothing. And just as 'Aaron's rod overcame the rods' (Exod 7:12) of the Egyptians who were singing, that is, he conquered them. When therefore it is said, 'Death is swallowed up' (1 Cor 15:54), 'Israel is swallowed up.' When those who think themselves strong—sophists, certain contentious men, or even evil spirits—approach the rock, they are swallowed up, proving themselves to be nothing.

Upon this rock, Christ, whom the approaching strong ones of the Egyptians are swallowed up by, the feet of the one being benefited stand, to be saved from shaking and tempest and having enemies. Endurance is produced. He does not always suffer these things when he is in the pit of distress, when he is in the mud of matter; endurance is produced. But he does not always suffer these things. When he comes out of these, the end of endurance having been received, the feet of the one having been benefited stand, therefore, upon the said rock. 'And he directed my steps' (Ps 119:133). And see how the Word leads us far into the history. No one standing walks, no one walking stands. When someone is therefore made firm according to Christ so as to be able to say, 'Who shall separate us from the love of God?' (Rom 8:35), his steps have directed paths; for he always hastens toward the higher things, toward the heavenly, being directed by God.

The steps of the runner: for it is 'not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy' (Ps 107:13). And he cast into my mouth a new song (Ps 40:9). 'Into the mouth' of the inner man, that is, into my word. 'A new song': often for us... regarding the new, how it is said. That which is uninterrupted is always new, while that which has been succeeded is old. And through many examples it has often been demonstrated.

A hymn to our God. He who was lifted up from the aforementioned circumstances of the pit of misery and the mire of matter obtained an uninterrupted victory. The victory of the uninterrupted is a new triumph. What is this new song? It explains: it is a 'hymn' 'to our God.'
