It is according to the imitation of another altar; for all things have been made according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain (Ex 25:40). A sacrifice of praise and that of righteousness is set forth; for 'sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God' (Ps 50:14) and 'sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness' (Ps 51:17). 'I will come' (Ps 51:18) therefore 'to the altar of God', then 'to the God who rejoices my youth' (Ps 51:19); for the one turning away from the shadow of the law and the exterior altar says: 'What multitude of your sacrifices to me? I am full' (Ps 50:6), he enters, 'according to the order of Melchizedek priest' (Ps 110:4) saying: 'I will come to the altar of God, better than the visible things'.

'I will come' therefore [away] from the sensible, from the literal, 'into the altar of God'. The one surpassing the 'oldness of the letter' which had preserved the shadow of the law and the old covenant, knowing these things, says: 'I will praise you, O God, with a harp' (Ps 108:2). Because I will enter into your altar having youth from the 'newness of the spirit' having been brought near, through this I will praise you gratefully with a harp. And the harp I have said many times that it signifies practical virtue or the body being struck by the inspired soul. Thus the confession...

Speech signifies thanksgiving, for the requests have come to pass. He desired to know the reason for being driven away and for walking in darkness; he desired that the light and the truth be sent to him, since they led him; he desired to enter the altar of God and to experience the tabernacles of God and the holy mountain. Since, therefore, of these good requests it has come to pass through experience by God having given them to him, and not by himself having found them, because of this he may gratefully confess to him, striking the senses, which are nerves or lyres, and various thoughts or members; for when each of the members is tuned toward virtue, it is a stretched nerve, so that it may be struck musically by the striker of truth.

“Why are you dejected, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall confess to him” (Ps 42:5). He asked if something belonged to him, and while he was still speaking of it, he sighed; moreover, before he receives, he has thus faithfully determined as if he had already received. Therefore he rouses his soul and says: “Why are you dejected, my soul?” Since, therefore, I have pre-decided to confess to him, hope in Him; accept that the things of thanksgiving shall belong to you. And the confession here signifies thanksgiving.

“God is the salvation of my face” (Ps 118:5). “You are the salvation of my true face” (Ps 118:14). The light is the salvation of your inner man, concerning which it is said: “The wisdom of a man makes his face shine” (Prov 15:13). And again the saint says to have “the eyes of the heart” (Eph 1:18) enlightened, and “with an unveiled face to reflect the glory of the Lord” (2 Cor 3:18). When the face is reflected by the appropriate and divine glory and is enlightened by wisdom, God is my salvation. Others, having been rescued from sickness, said: “My salvation is the physician”; and another, having been rescued from storm and sea, let him say: “My salvation is the pilot.

To the end: A psalm to the sons of Korah for understanding (Ps 147:1). Much has been said about the end, that the last thing is desirable, for the sake of which all other things come to be, but it is not for the sake of anything else... to have. He who knows the end knows also the poetic qualities of the end before...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Collective vs Individual Attributes
english: Of this. And as far as... again a transition through progress to ascend... it is not in the already existing desire.

It is therefore necessary to understand: 'God, in our ears we have heard, our fathers have declared to us' (Psalm 51:5). In their own ears, the saints say, we heard the words of God. An addition of ears occurs at the common hearing, when someone is able to hear intellectual words. The physician hearing medical words has a medical ear, but another does not. The one powerful enough to say, 'The instruction of the Lord opens my ears' (Psalm 51:6), does not speak about sensory hearing, but about that which is able to hear the intellectual words of God.

Thus, therefore, 'in our ears' must be heard, and it is not passing by; for it does not signify what is existing, but what is being added. And behold, how the saint says: 'The instruction of the Lord opens my ears.' He says: 'The Lord gives me a tongue of instruction to know when it is necessary to speak a word; He has placed for me first, He has added to me an ear for hearing; and the instruction of the Lord opens my ears.' The ear given according to addition is intellectual; it hears the words in a God-befitting way. And when this is added, His instruction then opens the ears—this thing which was added, the other ear, the intellectual one, the one hearing God-befittingly, the one able to say: 'I have heard unspeakable words'; for it is not possible for everyone to say this, but for the one having received the addition of an ear from God.

These things were in the mind of the Savior, having [them], He was saying: 'Let him who has ears to hear, hear' (Matthew 13:9). But not all had the hearing of the words of Jesus, the words being announced in parables. From this Porphyry learned, and in this: 'God, in our ears we have heard.' In our own [ears], not the common ones toward irrational animals, but in those joined toward the intellectual [words] of God.

Regarding words, this signifies in the dialects of the sensory things: the Egyptian among the Egyptians hears with his own ears; he hears with his own ear. Wherefore, what do we take from this according to scientific knowledge? —those who are concerned with teaching pretend for everyone; 'a people full of sins'; for it is not possible for each one to be full of those same sins, since there are also opposites and incompatible things. For instance, the same man cannot possess cowardice and boldness, but a whole people can possess them. And again, concerning things capable of coexisting, even if they do not coexist because of the multitude, if I say that the whole city has knowledge, not everyone has the same; for it is impossible for everyone to have [things] as is necessary. But it is possible to have them as rumors.

'Our fathers informed us' (Ps 78:3). Our fathers according to instruction. Wise are those who say this. In what way, then, are they wise, having been born from them? Not as men; for many are wise from the unwise, and many are not wise from the wise. 2 A work, which I worked in their days, in ancient days. In their own days, being ancient, ... our fathers informed us. And that it is necessary to hear scientifically ... those things that happened in the ancient days, such as in Exodus; it was impossible to learn that an exodus had occurred in Egypt without those announcing it, unless indeed those who wrote [it] ... for in every way it is necessary to tell all the things that happened, so that no one might come and say ... snatch [it] away. 'In days' therefore 'ancient', in first days. And what is this, having happened ... and of a heavy earth upon the saints and the ... having happened. But it is not strictly this that is signified previously, but it is said so that through this that thing might be viewed.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Right Hand and the Left Hand
english: God transfers men from the earthly place to the high heavens. If he says 'work', he does not mean it by number, but by kind or even by genus. In their light—for we take the fathers to be wise—we say that in the days which they had, being dazzled by the true light of the sun of righteousness, it became a work in the light of their life, which they were not envious to share with us.

He said, and he remembers: seven nations under the later called holy land he brought down (Ps 105:23). They were hidden, having been led in by God into that land. Moses, therefore, without neglect, prays to repeat the mystery: 'Having led them in, hide them in the mountain of your inheritance, O holiness, Lord, which your hands prepared' (Ex 19:4). See that no one living externally and hearing is able to enter into the holy mountain. The crowds in the parables, therefore, hearing and being outside, did not enter into the holy mountain, where the parables were made clear. It is necessary, therefore, to be led in first, and then thus to be hidden.

Your hand destroyed nations, and you hid them. Not of God in the ancient days. He was ancient of days (Dan 7:9), and we do not say that he was in ancient days, but he was ancient of days; for he was before days, before all time; and it is equal to the ancient of days to be existing before the ages, as it has been said: 'the one existing before the ages' (Rev 1:8). 'Your hand' therefore 'destroyed nations'. Your punishing power. Those who serve with punishments, angels, are able to be called hands of God, just as we say the hand of a king, and we do not mean the limb of the body of a hand.

And Job, concerning the punishing power—and he himself was the devil—was saying: 'withdraw your hand' (Job 2:3). This therefore he says: 'your hand', that is, the punishing power, or the active power of the persecutors, or your ministering power, 'destroyed nations'. And take the destruction of the nations by way of ascent as the death of men, by doing and the expulsion of life, according to which the nations were strangers to God. 'And you hid' our fathers. And the nations are destroyed because of the evil which they have; for their evil was a land and a city. And those are being hidden by no other than his right hand. But it is not the same...

One hand and the right hand: for the right is always a hand, but not every hand is right; for we have things to say that are performed by the right hand in a praiseworthy manner. Thus it is said in the Psalms: 'You held the right hand of me' (Ps 118:17). The right is the practical power of the good, but the left is the opposing one. And since things done happen from disposition and from thought, which is called 'heart,' it is said that the wise man has his heart to the right, but the fool to the left; here we do not take the places of bodies. But the wise man has a mind thinking rightly, having understanding concerning the intelligible things. But the heart of the fool is to the left, turning only toward the material.

Often the left is found in the writings not regarding pride, but regarding humiliation, as it says in the Song of Songs: 'His renown is upon my head, and his right shall embrace me' (Song 7:1). And concerning her wisdom it is said: 'For length of days and years of life are in the right' (Prov 3:16)—and the length is the immortal, the things not being destroyed—'but in her left, wealth and glory.' And it gives wealth that is sensible. And these gifts of the hand of wisdom on the left are not trivial.

3–4 You harmed the people and drove them out; for they did not inherit the land by their sword, and their arm did not save them. Those whom you drove out, you drove out having harmed them. But you brought harm upon them so that they might be disciplined. Often harm disciplines; for we do not speak here of harm from sin, but of harm from corrective discipline. Since, therefore, they did not attend to the corrective discipline as is necessary, they were moreover driven out and rejected. 'For they did not inherit the land by their sword' (Ps 106:11). Our fathers, having taken the history of those driven from the land, did not possess the land taken from them by their own war, nor by their own power; 'for not by their sword, nor their arm' prevailed over them, 'but your right and your arm and the light of your face' (Ps 106:11). There is the light, and the salvation.

Through which, therefore, the harm and the driving out happen, is simply a hand. Thus also in one of the Psalms concerning Christ it is said: 'And he shall put his hand in the sea and his right in the rivers' (Ps 74:3). There where there is salt and brine, the hand is simply placed against the evil powers; evil...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Horn as Strength and Divine Name
english: For the powers are now revealed through the sea. 'He said' 'rivers on the right.' For the prophets are rivers, streams flowing from the source of the water that is 'leaping into eternal life' (John 7:38). For 'he who believes' 'in me, as the scripture said, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly' (John 7:38). This indeed he was speaking concerning the Spirit whom the believers were about to receive.

These, being rivers, 'shall strike with the hand upon itself.' And it is a practice of harmony. See then, the hand, where the sea is, the saltiness, the dizziness. But your right hand and your arm and the light of your face. The right hand possesses and an arm suitable. You did not inherit the land by your own hand or by your own arm, but the arm of God and the right hand and the light of his own face provided this to you.

In one way, this is for tropology: that you were not liberated and became in the holy land by your own power or by your own deed. But if you take it with a higher allegory, both his arm and his right hand and the light of his own face are the Savior. Therefore, not in themselves, but in this you were saved, you were migrated from the land of bondage into the good one.

Having prepared, he triumphed, but with God having fought alongside, as the [scripture says]: 'not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of the God who shows mercy' (Romans 9:16). For you were pleased in them. You are yourself my king and my God (Psalm 146:5). For you are not only my God being my Creator and leading me toward my being, but also king, because by providence I rule, no longer being entangled in 'the affairs of life.' And indeed you are my God, I am a creation of God—and every creation has God as God—but as you rule.

He who commands the salvations of Jacob (Hebrews 1:5). To Jacob, who is fleeing from evil, the king and being God commands the salvations. And salvations are commanded to the spirits who minister the salvations, concerning which the apostle says: 'Are not all [of them] ministering spirits sent for the service of those who are about to inherit salvation?' (Hebrews 1:14). Not so that they might confirm and give it, but so that, having heard it, they might proclaim it beforehand.

"Say to the daughter of Zion, 'Behold, your savior is coming'" (Zephaniah 3:17). The 'salvations' of 'Jacob' may be the virtues according to kind, or the two virtues: the practical and the contemplative—the contemplation of truth and the productive [virtue] of praiseworthy works.

"We strike with horns our enemies in you" (Psalm 68:1). You see, we do not strike our enemies using physical horns; you are our horn and our defense. Therefore, you have that which is said in one of the Psalms by all the saints: "And in your favor our horn shall be exalted" (Psalm 92:10). It is not the physical [horn]; for the horn of those possessing it is again a defense. Through it, they will repel the approaching evils. Thus, those who have you as king and God do not have any other horn besides you. For instance, the word attributes something in one of the Twelve: "Those who say, 'We do not have horns in our strength'" (Psalm 75:10). Having a horn and having power, we strike our enemies with horns. Because of this, the horns of these are also crushed: "and all the horns of the sinner I will break" (Psalm 75:10). It is also possible for a king and a kingdom to receive a horn, as it is presented in Daniel: "the ten horns, ten kingdoms" (Daniel 7:24). Therefore, having you as king, we have you as a horn, and "we strike our enemies in you." And "in your name," since we have your designation upon ourselves, "we render powerless" all "those who rise up against us," having an invincible weapon: your designation. However, one must possess a designation, and not merely a hollow one. Not everyone who calls himself a Christian truly possesses the name of Christ, but rather he who is a Christian. "And in your name we rendered powerless those who rise up against us." And from this it is shown again that they rise up against us by premeditated will. They are not such by nature, nor are the [unjust/wicked] such by nature, as those who argue from natures say.

"For I do not hope in my bow, and my sword will not save me" (Psalm 118:95). I indeed have a bow and a sword, since I am clothed in "the full armor of God," but I do not hope in these; not the whole of my expectation is in these, using them. I wish to have God as an ally and a champion, so that I may have the strength to strike against those to whom I send my...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Confession and Divine Deliverance
english: arrows, and that my sword [be] timely... opposing ones. But these are invisible. Often the sword of those possessing the word is said: 'who have sharpened their tongues like a sword' (Ps 57:9); and 'sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp knife' (Ps 63:7). And another [saying]: 'his sword upon his thigh' (1 Sam 2:26). They possess swords not only 'in their hands', but also upon their thighs. And perhaps the discourses concerning temperance, which kill 'the members upon the earth' (Col 3:5), are swords upon the thigh.

Often also the things of generation are signified through the name of the thigh. For when it says in Ezekiel: 'and every thigh shall be moistened with moisture' (Ezek 47:9), this means: all are unrestrained, pursuing the moisture of pleasures. For you saved us from those who afflict us. Since you saved us also from those who afflict us, we knew that 'in you we gore our enemies' (Ps 118:145). Because of this, then, since this has surpassed us from you, we knew that one must not hope in the bow—to use it, indeed, but not as having shot through it irretrievably. And [you turn] those who hate us to shame.

Those who hate have a difference again from those who afflict, sometimes by the underlying substance and sometimes by the thought. Often the same ones both afflict and hate, and these are the same according to the underlying substance. Sometimes, however, the one hating is not able to be an enemy when he is weak; for the weak one is able to hate, but he is not able to act as an enemy from the manifest [action], for it would harm him. Moreover, even if they differ only in thought according to the underlying substance, even if they are different ones and others, God delivers and saves from these and puts them to shame.

'In God we shall be praised all the day long' (Ps 52:7). Of those being praised, some are praised for the beauty of the body, others because of strength. The stout ones are praised in strength, others in another skill, and others because of wealth, because of nobility; but in you we shall be praised. We have no cause for praise other than you; for even if we have hardship, since through you we have attained these things and 'in God we do power' (Rom 16:25), in you we have the praise. Often the day signifies the time of the life of those saying, as: 'for your sake we are dying all...' (Rom 7:24).

...the whole day, that is, through life. And we shall confess in your name forever. This calling of yours provides much power to us. For in it indeed we 'despise' all 'those who rise up against us'. Therefore 'in your name we shall confess forever'. The name of the confession here signifies thanksgiving: 'I will confess to you, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and have revealed them to infants' (Matt 11:25). In order that it may be a gift, it is possible to say thus: 'in your name we shall confess', because it has become to us a cause of salvation. And it is also possible to say this: in your name which has been invoked upon us, as if you are saying: in knowledge or in virtue I shall confess.

Psalm. But now you have saved and protected us, and you will not let go in the powers of our own. 'You are the same, my king and my God' (Ps 145:11). [Allusion to Ps 145/146] The voice to God; for those approaching and drawing near... God is king. 'He who commands the salvations of Jacob' (Ps 146:7). To those near... he commands the salvations and all good things. Concerning this he says: 'In you we shall be praised all the day and in your name we shall confess forever' (Ps 118:35), that is, we shall give thanks. And he says: 'But now you have saved and protected us, and you will not let go in the powers of our own'. When he went out in the powers of our own, his military power or by the power of our strength, we always prevailed. And everything contrary exists here for us.

And since I was saying—it is not necessary to speak the problematic things explicitly about them—Israel, sinning, was driven from Jerusalem to Babylon in the manner of captivity. And Daniel and those three and Joshua the son of Nun and Ezekiel and the others of the Twelve Prophets were there, Haggai and Zechariah. These were not taken into Babylon in the manner of captivity, but for the sake of being a participant, helping and healing those condemned there. God condemns someone with mercy, that is, he does not leave him without help. And he sends angels and makes holy men to fall and be harmed and in captivity, not because of their own sins, but for the sake of the salvation of others. On the contrary, they do not say that a change has occurred from...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Beneficial Shame and Divine Strength
english: Regarding the good [being abandoned] to the bad, it is not to provide help or to have a supporter so as to be left alone; rather, in a certain way they were left abandoned having become helpers to others, not so that they might be destroyed, but so that they might be useful and not allow the sins of the condemned to increase.

'I will send away' therefore 'us now' (Ps 118:7). And the 'I will send away' does not carry much mockery; 'Cain went out from the presence of the Lord the God' (Gen 4:16). God did not send him away, but with a self-commanding eagerness he embraced the evil, he rushed toward the wickedness.

Concerning Adam, it has been said regarding not falling entirely that: 'God expelled Adam' (Gen 3:24), acting in opposition, making it clear that those within did not want to go out. He was cast out of paradise because of Eve the woman; for because of her he transgressed the rule. For when God asks, 'Who told you?' (Gen 3:11) he says, 'The woman whom you gave with me' (Gen 3:12). He did not say, 'Whom you gave,' but 'with me you gave her.' And this is the purpose; and I also thought that, since she, having been deceived by the devil, as she herself confessed, is cast out of paradise, I thought to do the same to her, so that I too might be cast out of paradise; for if Adam had not been cast out together, the woman would not have entered into paradise.

Not everyone of the people was saying, 'God, in our ears we have heard, our fathers announced to us' (Ps 78:7). And with a few, 'But your right hand and your arm... and the light of your face' (Ps 44:3). Not all the people said this. I recall... what was said toward the Corinthians: 'I thank you, that in everything you have been enriched, in all speech and in all knowledge' (1 Cor 1:5). Then again: 'Fornication is heard among you' (1 Cor 5:1). It was not, therefore, concerning one [person]... among this people, some in their own way. These, therefore, did not stretch out hands toward a foreign god. 'Now I will send away and shame us' (Ps 118:7). No one sinning is shamed by God.
But by himself. And God is shamed in a certain way when the one not sinning is with the sinners; and the shame is beneficial and brings glory to the one being shamed.

He does not have a 'hidden shame' which must not be revealed according to the philosophy of the one saying: 'We do not reveal the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness.' The one saying: 'To the lawless I have become lawless' (1 Cor 6:9), was not shamed by himself, but the word of Christ, exhorting, persuaded him. Furthermore, does the one saying: 'I have become lawless,' not feel shame? As far as it reached human understanding, no one wanted to imitate the evil ones.

'And you will not go out in our powers.' Formerly you used to go out in our powers; you used to run ahead of us into the wars, and we were surrounded by those attacking. But this thing of not going out in the powers, he says: you help, but you do not help. You help us so that we may be shown to be athletes through being left behind and we may benefit others; for he did not say: 'You destroyed our powers,' but 'you will not go out in our powers.' You turned us back to the rear before our enemies. The enemies were behind them.

But they say praises of themselves: 'Upon my back' for 'the sinners have given birth' (Ps 69:6). In another way the enemies give these births; they will not be weak and they only persecute those who are about to surround them. The Savior therefore drives all the enemies and has hands upon their backs striking them, pursuing them. These therefore say: 'You turned us back to the rear before our enemies,' not strictly to be said concerning the one turning away according to a sect and imitating the enemies: 'God turned [us].' But the good thing happening through God is indeed praiseworthy. Behold, those concerning Daniel and the other saints who were in Babylon.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Teacher as Food and the Transformation of the Soul
english: They say: 'You turned us backward among our enemies' (Ps 44:23). And those hating us seized us for themselves (Ps 44:24). They would not have been able to take us by hand, if you had not turned us back among them for the sake of usefulness. They are enemies and haters; for to hate is to be an enemy. But we are neither enemies nor haters. And because of this we were far off; for what judgment... Lord, you turned us back among them, you have made us to be with those who are condemned. Therefore, those who were formerly in the form of God, having taken the form of a slave through compassion, say such a thing: that we have come to an earthly place not for ourselves, but for the sake of others, because you did not go out in our powers; for formerly you used to go out in our powers to bring us the victory against our enemies, and guarding us in the land of our fathers where we descended. Since therefore you did not go out in our powers, we were turned backward among those hating us. Those having seized us, to whom you gave—but with a bad intention... And you find many such things in the Scripture; from envy... him in action. But they did not crucify him with this intention. Again Judas betrayed the Savior, and the betrayal became useful for the removal of 'the sin of the world' (John 1:29). Again, those crucifying did not crucify him with this intention. 'Those hating us seized us for themselves' (Ps 44:24), they did not kill us. But if you say this, that they took our things for their own profit, and that the betrayal and the turning backward occurred timely. Therefore they bring forward: 'All these things came upon us, and we did not remember you' (Ps 44:26). You gave us as sheep for feeding (Ps 44:25). Formerly you helped openly so that our praise would be to you all day long and to confess in your name forever. But why now have we been delivered into captivity, suffering this not because of our wickedness or impiety? Those saying the psalm were such as Daniel... the one of Joshua and Ezekiel and Haggai and Zechariah and the three and others more. These are...

Not because of personal malice has one become in Babylon. But concerning those handed over to afflictions, and especially those in whom the choice is precarious because they rejoice over those handed over through malice, they were sent like physicians after wars, so that they might care for them, bringing aids that either preserve their existing health or dissolve disease and bring health.

For it is not, as some suppose, that they blame that day. Instead, they move toward other sayings: 'You have given us as sheep for food' (Ps 54:2). We were handed over for our own eating; lions and wolves are devouring us. However, even if we are being devoured, we do not cease to be sheep: 'Israel was a wandering sheep; lions drove him out; the first devoured him, the King of Assyria' (Hos 11:7, 10:6). It is a bad thing for what has happened to be praised, not to remain as it is, but to be resolved into another quality. The one eating bread, if he sends it down into the stomach, the bread does not remain. And those who have been cast down and have become the food of enemies have not ceased to be sheep.

It is often said that food becomes the disciple of the teacher, concerning whom he also says: 'My food is to do the will of Him who sent me' (John 4:34). The Samaritan woman was indeed a disciple, concerning whom he also said: 'I have food to eat which you do not know' (John 4:32). [Gaps in text] ... and again [Gaps] ... to be bread. And bread becomes nourishment. In a certain way [Gaps] ...

If, therefore, the man who preserves the image and the likeness, having become a teacher of God according to Jesus, eats a wild man through the process of training [Gaps] ... and having become food for the teacher, he shall not be a lion. For this reason, he is blessed and is called blessed, not because he is a lion, but because he has become a man. But if ever a rational man, moving rationally, were to be eaten by a violent wild man or an evil power, he becomes a lion and such a one is a terror; for 'woe to the man whom the lion eats' (Job 15:26). These therefore say: 'You gave us as sheep for food.' Having been eaten as sheep, they remained [sheep]. And among the nations you scattered us. According to the immediate sense of the word...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Bondage of Sin and the Substitutions of Sacrifice
english: They seem to say this: 'We have been sown among the nations, we have been dispersed in many places.' But they seem to have suffered this in Babylon and Assyria alone. Therefore, what he says is this: the sowing of these seeds, such as wheat or barley, is first useful in a Gospel-like way if they are sown in the earth; for this earth receives them into its own substance through a change and transformation. For from the earth, having changed, many came from one grain; they changed from the earth into harvests. It is animated... [gap]... into the adjacent earth, and it notifies it and transforms it into its own nature.

And he says 'seeds' regarding those saying these things, the saints, saying: 'In you we shall be praised and in your name we shall confess for ever' (Ps 111:3, 9). Behold, those saying: 'With you we horn our enemies' and the others, let them say: 'You have sown us among the nations' by way of seeds, so that the nations, in a certain way, if we are sown among them in a foreign land, we might change into ourselves, and one of us might become an ear of corn bearing many grains, benefiting many souls. And those being benefited are said to be different: sometimes children of those benefiting, when those are named fathers, sometimes sheep, when those have the state and conduct of a shepherd. These therefore, as seeds having been cast down, took into themselves those being benefited from being placed before them. Having been placed, the seeds changed the earth. The nations therefore are the earth, but the seeds are those cast down for the benefit of others. Let this also be simpler: that the Assyrians have become in Babylon, though they are not many nations and all the nations are. And let this also be toward my history.

13 You sent away your people without honor (Ps 79:2). Without honor... [gap]... sent away; for having been led into captivity, we were not led there with honor, but having been led by the law of captivity; for nothing is more dishonorable than this. 'Without honor' therefore [is] 'you sent away your people'. [gap]... the people whom they wished to hold. And it is possible also to call that people, for whom... [gap]... among the others. And since 'you sent away your people without honor', that is, not having received honor, 'you sent away', [gap]... them; for they were given over to their own sins. And it is possible also that 'without honor'...

And for this reason we have endured these things, to come into captivity and to be scattered among the nations, so that you might gather to yourself. He has done to himself through sin and has made himself a debtor.

Furthermore, the thing by which the enemy, the king of souls, holds [us], is called a handwriting. And a handwriting is something which someone has fastened with his own hands. Therefore 'he took it out from the middle,' so that it might no longer hold us by the handwriting with which we had fastened ourselves, having written ourselves down in it. And are they also being written down together with themselves? —that is, us being your people, you sent away without honor (Ps 79:9)—then we were honored—by the manner of the captivity; or they speak concerning the people, for whom they themselves went into captivity: 'You sent away your people without honor' (Ps 79:9). And for this reason we endure these things, because for the sake of their help you made the same things for them to draw from again, unpleasantly.

And there was not a multitude in our substitutions. Often, for the sake of certain things, safe and redeeming substitutions are given. For instance, it says: 'It is holy everything that opens a male womb.' And it says that, if it is a firstborn sheep or an ox or a goat, among those brought to the altar, it is necessary to perform the sacrifice itself. But if it is a firstborn donkey or something else [of the priests], it is not even brought to the altar; 'you shall change a sheep in its place.' Through a sheep its value is changed and it enters into the temple. He says therefore that, since there were many, 'there was not a multitude in their substitutions.' There were not so many substitutions so that... in this way that, since God is the one giving the substitutions in their place, the substitutions are given being changed. And through a few, he is able to nourish many-peopled multitudes. And so that I may speak from history, there were many people, and if ten righteous men were found there (Ezek 14:14)—for until they... there being no multitude of substitutions, they were being changed. No one will say, therefore, to Babylon, [but] few in number as the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Reproach and the Mustard Seed
english: Having been taken captive together... themselves and the people, and those others through sin, but the people through their own [sins] and the others through the [sins] of others. 'And there was not a multitude in their leaps' (Jonah 3:4). But few had become sufficient for... it would have happened, if they had turned back and known what evils they are in. 'Their sins are very great; I will go down and see if they have worked according to their cry coming toward me, but if not, so that I may know' (Jonah 4:2). How much [it reached] upon the cry of their wickedness and the... but if I do not find them such, but having repented like the Ninevites, I will know them. For those known by God are not trivial; 'the Lord knew those who were His' (1 Sam 2:30). 'But then, not knowing God, you served gods which are not gods by nature; but now, having known God, rather having been known by God' (Acts 17:29). When they were knowing, they were rather being known by the Benefactor.

14 A reproach has become to us from our neighbors. Regarding the history, the neighbors are the nearby ones... since therefore we were carried off into captivity, 'a reproach we have become to our neighbors' (Ps 147:2). They themselves have not suffered nor have they prevailed with the rising of wars, but we. And as for the thought of this: just as the cross of the Savior has become a reproach for the sake of salvation—for it has been said: 'counting the reproach of Christ a greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt' (Ex 12:33)—so also these have in a way fallen into reproaches, having been seized and having been led into captivity. 'Angels,' he says, 'who did not keep their own beginning, but having left their own habitation, fell into everlasting chains' (Heb 2:16). This reproach of the angels is not praiseworthy, because having been granted to dwell in heaven and being able to stand and remain beside God always praising, they became in wickedness so as to fall from heaven. This reproach is trivial. Behold, indeed, the [reproach] of Christ is not only praiseworthy, but is greater than treasures. And if there were no difference between these, the proverbist would not have said: 'Do not acquire the reproach of evil men' (Prov 22:1). When therefore the apostles [were] rejoicing...

They rejoice even while being reproached for Christ. Having done nothing [wrong], these reproaches of such people are not good. By becoming reproach itself, someone has established the practice of reproaching based on false accusations, not on truths. Thus also is the saying, 'We are without honor; for I think God has shown us the apostles to be the very last, as if marked for death' (1 Cor 4:9). This is the reproach in which they are placed. It is not a true reproach, nor is it from evil men, but from good men. Regarding the spoken word: that it is not earnest, nor God-fearing, and that those coming are our enemies, yet they did not drive us from their land.

14 They mock and deride us in our circle. The ones saying they have come not for their own sake, but for the sake of others, are holy. And they say: having been born, having held us and having drawn us into their land, being in our circle, they reproach us, mock us, and sneer at us; but the reproach, the mockery, and the derision do not touch us, but them. Just as if someone derides [another], so that they may have children by weaving themselves together, and enjoy [themselves]. Therefore, those who are being mocked by these are thought to be [such].

15 He made us a parable among the nations. Something hidden by a word is compared to something similar. That it may become clear, let us see from the Gospel (Matt 13:31): he compares the kingdom of heaven to a mustard seed, not saying 'it is like a mustard seed' while being a seed itself; for it was no longer a similarity, but an identity. He says 'hyper' [beyond/exceeding]. Therefore, the mustard seed has a power smaller in size than the seeds, capable of transforming and becoming such a plant. And the kingdom of heaven, thus revealing the teaching of the Scriptures, is something humble and small in its wording. If [one sees] it through the mustard seed, and that it becomes a greater plant, the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Life as an Age and the Covering of the Face
english: The Greek word is an evangelical word. For this reason, therefore, this parable was spoken: 'for a parable' thus 'us as a nation among the nations'. If anyone wishes to interpret the captives, they use us, saying: 'Behold, these ones having been led away well before... God, when the right hand of God and the light of his face were protecting them, they fell into a most evil leading away' (Ps 78:49). If anyone therefore wishes to show a falling away, they refer to us. And 'made us a parable' is not in [Israel], not in Israel, not in the Hebrew multitude, but 'among the nations'.

Those who are truly nations do not know the difference between good and evil, but they consider all pleasant things and all appropriate things to be good, and the opposites of these to be evil. And the name of the parable may be this: the rank of the saints has a certain superiority compared to the other ranks of men. Because of this, they have become a parable. See: men are often taken captive in different ways by enemies. One suffers the taking away of what he has possessed, while another has them remaining... in the winter and the storm of this life, they have their own... flows away into corruption. 15 A head-movement among the peoples. ... they observe [those] changing from prosperity into adversity, to move... those or perhaps grieving. 224 But a head-movement among the peoples we have become. 'Peoples' indeed all the coarsest men can be called, having nothing opened, not being afraid. These therefore, because of us, set a head-movement. We, having become toward the peoples, the coarsest men, moved their mind and their head. And the mind moves when... when it perceives the things being imposed upon it to be perceived. 16 All the day my trouble is against me.

It is. He says 'all the day' and 'through life'. A man's life is called that which is from birth until death, sometimes called one day, sometimes an age. Thus it is said: 'I will not eat meat for ever' (Gen 9:4), and: 'he shall be thy servant for ever' (Ps 18:25). I had trouble against me all this day which I endured for the sake of others (Ps 34:5); and the shame of my face covered me. The shame of the inner man covered me. For my face was not destroyed, but it was covered. And it is possible, having cast off the single covering, to bear his face naked, illuminated, as it is according to nature. And, so that I may phrase it this way, the ignorance that happens to other men destroys their face; for others become from others, from men serpents and wolves and foxes. But the holy man, even if he does not bear his own face naked, has it covered. And it is covered by the arrangement of the body, becoming a seeming ignorance from the incarnation. But when a change occurs into quality, I do not say that the fox, like Herod, had a covering, but his nature and disposition were such. When someone becomes foolish among the thoughtless, having cast folly upon himself, he has his face covered; when he becomes lawless among the lawless, he has his face covered.

From a voice reproaching and speaking idly. He says this: those are reproaching me and speaking idly. And those speaking idly are straying. So he says this: those who oppose us... as the rational [being] is accustomed to have, but rather they are straying. To speak idly is to say superfluous things. From the face of an enemy and one driving [me] away. When... I endured all these things. When the enemy appeared and was pursuing... shame of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Foreknowledge and Knowledge
english: To have the face covered. I do not have these things because of wickedness... [text gapped]... immediately indeed he brought [them]: 'all these things came upon us, and we did not remember you' (Psalm 78:22). [text gapped]... because not coming out in our own powers, it came upon us to turn backward toward our enemies; it came upon us that a reproach should be placed upon our neighbors and those around us, a mockery and to have the face turned down, to be covered in shame.

Because the voice is of holy ones. Many many times also from the pleasant things they forget God, not only from the unpleasant ones. For he says: 'take care of yourself lest, having eaten and being filled and having built fine houses... the Lord your God you forget' (Deut 8:12). Sometimes, having come into afflictions, it is said they forget God. All these things came upon us, and we did not remember you, and we did not act wickedly against your covenant.

Israel was captured from Judea both by chance and locally, and a chance and natural local displacement has happened; for they thought [text gapped] having [gone] there they did not keep [the laws] there and toward the laws there [text gapped] to Babylonize according to the soul. Often God hindered them, persisting in living thus. In order that they might know by trial that evil is that which they loved, he resettled them into Babylon. Along with this, he made a way to be captured, and holy ones like Ezekiel, Zechariah, Angel, Daniel, and those cast into the furnace, so that even being there they were not completely abandoned, so that they might experience [it] as if in war.

There is also a Jerusalem above. Those living according to the divine laws dwell in God. If they become apostates from the divine laws, they are resettled into the place concerning the earth, and this is the captivity according to allegory. And there are sent out to them again here for the sake of help: 'there came a man, sent from God, his name John. This came for a testimony, so that he might testify about the light' (John 1:6-7); for he did not come for the sake of another than to testify.

To the light. Again Jeremiah hears: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb I sanctified you, and I appointed you a prophet to the nations' (Jeremiah 1:5). Before coming forth from the womb he was sanctified, and as a prophet to the nations he was appointed. Again: 'Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world' (Ephesians 1:4). By 'foundation of the world' he means his coming-to-be. And Paul and those with him were chosen before the foundation of the world, and this election has become theirs from then until now, so that they might be sent out together with those who have been called and might be able to help them.

But did Paul speak according to foreknowledge? Foreknowledge is a theoretical viewing of what is coming to be. But according to kind, foreknowledge and knowledge are the same. They differ in time. For example, suppose I foreknow that tomorrow there will be thunder. When the thunder comes to be in the middle of the day, it is knowledge, no longer foreknowledge. And the knowledge of the thunder does not make it such, but what it is, that becomes the knowledge. Thus the known thing makes the knowledge, which does not receive the knowing from us. I use an image for the sake of the manner of foreknowledge: the one [child] is born so that he may demand, and the other, so that he may live in the house. What kind of justice is this of foreknowledge, if we take these things to happen according to foreknowledge? Foreknowledge both justifies and condemns. To foreknow and to know is also to condemn and to justify from the things being done and being thought.

Paul was foreknown in this life, both a traitor and a persecutor of Christ and an apostle. Was he not both foreknown? Foreknowledge therefore made him have both. Again, did he not become first an apostle and later a traitor? He was not foreknown by God. The foreknowledge of God made him at one time an apostle and at another time a traitor. And indeed it is sought: did he choose the apostles from among us? 'Did I not choose you, the twelve?' (John 15:16) and: 'Whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son' (Romans 8:29). He does not speak about existence, but about being conformed. Foreknowledge does not lead to existence. God has made [it so], having made [them] known; for the matter does not make the knowledge of God; for the knowledge of God is eternal. It is taken in relation to what is coming to be and is called foreknowledge; for that woman Susanna says again: 'He who knows the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Integrity of the Covenant and the Purpose of Affliction
english: All before their being. It is not foreknowledge that makes things such or such, but choice, the things chosen. I say: I foreknow that this person will give birth to a male and will have sons; this is not a matter of choice. But to become something trivial or important, or to have some other fitness, is a matter of choice. It does not come from foreknowledge, since God judges beforehand and justifies beforehand. And if He justifies beforehand, it was of His goodness to justify all.

Again, concerning Esau and Jacob, the apostle, as if speaking in a dilemma, says: 'What then shall we say to this? Is there injustice with God? May it never be!' (Romans 9:14). Because he had refuted injustice, he forced us to seek how there is not injustice with God. If it were so, as those who speak of foreknowledge say, we would rather find injustice in Him. 'I loved Jacob,' He says, 'but I hated Esau' (Romans 9:13). But one is hated or loved according to things done and according to things thought. How then does foreknowledge have room? Is injustice found with God? But he, refuting this, said: 'What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? May it never be!' Since there is no injustice, let the matter be sought in another way, how it has come to pass.

Many times we have also said that: if we have a correct assumption about someone, we understand everything about him accordingly; as we were saying concerning the king. And in all the ways of captivity, he said this in many pleasures and pains, and being wise in both pleasures and pains, it did not result in God being forgotten by them, but rather they were grieved, because they were men needing such things, just as concerning the captives, that they need captivity. Thus indeed some have demonstrated that in the one hundred and eighty-first and tenth psalm it is so: 'Despondency has taken hold of me from sinners' (Psalm 181:10). One becomes despondent when he sees men made in the image of God and in likeness having become sinners. And just as if someone is a father, when he sees his son suffering from fever and weakness, he strikes him, he is grieved, not because he strikes him, but because he has come into such a state; so also these, being noble and knowing that 'through many tribulations it is necessary to enter the kingdom of God' (Acts 14:22), they do not sink entirely into the afflicted. For they say: 'In all things we are afflicted, but not in anguish' (2 Corinthians 4:8).

Not being distressed is to bear the afflictions bravely. 'And we have not acted unjustly toward your covenant' (Ps 74:22). What has been decreed according to your will remains for ever, and all things according to your judgments, and therefore we have not acted unjustly. If anyone says, 'Why is this one a child and that one a child, and this one rich and that one poor?' he acts unjustly toward the covenant of God. Just as with these covenants which men establish, if anyone wishes to contradict and fight against one of those written, he unjustly acts against the covenant in vain. His own injustice seems to be an injustice against the covenant. If anyone handles the God-breathed [Scripture] differently, as the heretics do, they act unjustly toward the Gospel, toward the Divine Scripture.

And our heart has not turned backward (Ps 73:22). You see that there is a remaining straightness of following. 'Has not turned backward' means we have not become others, having a heart that is right and straight and looking straightly. And this thing of the unsettled and the uncertain happens to us; many, having come into affliction, turned their mind so as to grumble against providence. 'And you have turned our paths from your way' (Ps 119:176). This says that we ran your way well before we descended into this condition and conduct. 'You have turned our paths from your way,' because you have transferred us into another life and a way suitable to life. However, even if 'you have turned our paths' by handing us over to captivity, nevertheless our paths did not turn away from your way.

For you have humbled us in a place of affliction (Ps 102:19). Take the place of your humbling according to both the consequences of the deportation from Jerusalem to Babylon. Primarily this place is the earth, where the souls that are brought low are humbled, 'the body of humiliation.' It can also be handed over to the afflicted to bear the shame and the place of affliction, namely the land of Assyria or the land of Babylon. 'And you have covered us with the shadow of death' (Ps 23:4). Even if the death of affliction lay upon us, it did not consume us. His shadow covered us. Let it be like a heavy stone lifted up on high. Let someone be under this, but not necessarily fallen upon it. And let him see occasionally the shadow of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Sacrificial Death and Divine Slumber
english: Upon itself. And the shadow of the stone does not do what the stone itself has done, from which even God is delivered. It has been said: 'The rising sun appeared to those in darkness and the shadow of death' (Psalm 98:2).

If we have forgotten the name of our God and if we have stretched out our hands toward a foreign god, then these things are no longer said toward God himself. Previously, it was said toward God himself: 'You turned our paths from your way; you humbled us in a place of affliction' (Psalm 65:5). Therefore, they say to others that they have become in these things through sin and lawlessness, and they say: 'If we have forgotten the name of our God and if we have stretched out our hands toward a foreign god,' that is to say, if we have worshipped a foreign god. But all those called gods according to the Scripture who are falsely named should be considered foreign gods; for it has been said: 'All the gods of the nations are demons' (Psalm 95:5).

Not toward our own belly, nor toward mammon, did we stretch out our hands, which are allegorically called our deeds. [We stretched them out] toward a foreign god and toward the enemies who seem to have prevailed. God will not fail to seek these things. They were saying, in this way of reading: 'Will God not seek these things?' (Psalm 94:8) and they were saying, in this way of reading: 'Will God not seek these things?'

He says: do not think it a small thing to forget the name of God or to stretch out hands toward a foreign god. For God also seeks these things. And you know that some, especially in persecutions, were saying this: that it is possible to do things without acting with the heart. Indeed, many died saying this, and they silenced the name of God as if forgetting Him. He says, not even this [is enough to hide] God, who is invisible, and He seeks these things. For does He not seek? The following text does not permit this way of thinking. For He himself knows the secrets of the heart.

Let him who is ignorant of the secrets of the heart seek first whether he acted thus or like that. For instance, if someone, pretending to be wise, says: 'I did not stretch out my hands toward a foreign god,' I say: 'I, who am ignorant of the secrets of the heart, am examining these things.' But God does not seek; for He knows them. And He says, therefore, what He knows as secrets:

"Because of you we die all day, we were counted as sheep for slaughter" (Ps 54:3). Because of you we die all day, we were counted as sheep for slaughter. Those dying all day for God and counted as sheep for slaughter have no doubt whether they have come to the name of God or stretched hands toward a foreign god. Therefore, one does not seek these things from a heart that is manifest. "We were counted" then "as sheep for slaughter." Everyone who wishes to slaughter us can do so. And this is possible; even if some fight us, we consider ourselves as sheep being ritualized, as being sacrificed to God for a "pleasing sacrifice" (Ps 50:5). Indeed, in the Revelation of John, "the souls of those being persecuted for the testimony of Jesus" (Rev 6:9) appeared dancing under the altar of the heavenly God, clearly as victims having come there.

"Arise; why, Lord, do you sleep? Arise and do not cast us away to the end" (Ps 44:23). It seems that God sleeps when He is long-suffering toward the wrongdoing of His own holy men and the groaning of those made according to Him. Indeed, they send up a prayer saying: "Cast the hands toward their pride to the end" (Ps 54:5), and: "May the pride of those hating you ascend to you always" (Ps 54:6). And it seems God sleeps when He is long-suffering, when He overlooks His own being afflicted. "Arise and do not cast us away to the end" (Ps 44:23). For if even we have become captives and are being afflicted in the place of ill-treatment, being human, mortal, and liable to fall, we fear being cast away to the end. Israel was cast away in Babylon, when they worshiped Bel and had made the image of Nebuchadnezzar and other things of the Babylonians; they were cast away to the end. But those around Daniel, even if they were cast away locally, they were not cast away to the end; for they remained in the same godliness. It seems they were cast away, but they were not cast away to the end, the lions being silenced and him ascending unhurt.

"Why do you turn your face away, forgetting our poverty and our affliction? For our soul has been humbled into dust" (Ps 40:12-13). This is the same as sleeping and seeming to turn the face away. Appear to us, rescuing and saving us from the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Qualitative Change and the End
english: Because of an existing wickedness. Why then do you turn away? Will you then forget our poverty and our affliction? Because of you we are afflicted, because of you we are poor. But you do not forget these things. In which [things] one conquers, even if he is gloomy or even if he is joyless. It was said that the dust is more bodily. 'Our soul was humbled' therefore, of those saying these things, 'into the dust'. 'The body of humiliation' surrounds us, but we were not humbled by it. As if someone, for instance, receives a blow from a certain tyrant, he seems to have been humbled, but he was not humbled; for he still has the same pride, he still has the same joy. Because of this we are poor and are afflicted, because our soul, having been humbled into the dust, does not clearly possess its own resurrection, and 'our belly was stuck to the earth' (Ps 22:14).

But they do not say this about them in truth, but about their own members, about their own people. And there are two ways for the belly to have been humbled to the earth: when someone thinks of earthly things and seeks lower things, he does not produce heavenly offspring, he does not produce God-fearing thoughts, but all human things; and the soul saying these things becomes a mother, 'because our belly was stuck to the earth' (Ps 22:14). And according to a second meaning, the one being nourished by the heavenly bread, the belly receiving heavenly nourishment, was stuck to heaven. But those who eat the flesh of the dragon and carry the same food to the serpent, being earth, have the belly stuck to the earth. And just as it is said concerning the sensible [things]: 'the foods to the belly, and the belly to the foods; and God will destroy both this and these' (Lk 10:19), so also the belly and the stomach of the soul, when it is not nourished by heavenly things, when it does not receive from its divine bridegroom, has the belly stuck to the earth.
Arise, Lord, help us and redeem us for the sake of your name. We ask for help, lest the afflictions remaining for a long time might harm our soul which is turning. Ka-

And then, so that they may not boast in their own righteousness, trusting in it, he says: 'Arise, O Lord, help us and redeem us for the sake of your name' (Ps 3:7). We are enriched by you. For this reason we have come into these afflictions, because we are yours, and for the sake of help you have sent us into this hardship.

1 Toward the end, for those who are being changed; to the sons of Kore for understanding; a song for the beloved. Change is a movement and a transformation of something according to quality. Not every movement and transformation is a change. For there is a change according to becoming. I say, for instance, an egg becoming a bird and a grain of wheat a stalk. This movement and transformation is according to becoming. And there is another occurring according to corruption; when the body of a human decays and is dissolved into fluids and worms and the like, it is not said to be changed, but to have decayed. And there is also another movement and transformation according to increase, when an addition to the previous amount occurs; for when I am extended from a smaller to a greater size, I am said to have increased, but to have diminished when the amount is contracted and becomes less. Change, therefore, is a movement according to quality, such as from sickness to health and from health to sickness, from ignorance to knowledge and likewise, from unbelief to faith.

'Toward the end,' therefore, 'for those who are being changed.' We have often explained regarding the end, that it is that which is after all things, the last thing to be desired. Thus, 'toward the end, for those who are being changed.' When change reaches such a limit that it is no longer possible for it to be further extended, in the perfection of things, when 'God becomes all in all' (1 Cor 15:28), the quality can no longer be extended. Every knowledge and every virtue is a quality. It is possible, therefore, to begin virtue and to make progress in it, and it is always possible to receive [more] to that which already exists. But when someone possesses virtue perfectly as if nothing...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Transformation of the Right Hand of the Most High
english: To be transformed into something else until the end. The same applies to knowledge and wisdom; we say the same thing: there is one being introduced into wisdom who is subject to testing as one capable of sinning. For it is said, 'reprove the wise, and he will love you' (Prov 9:8). No one is reproved unless he possesses the things by which he is to be reproved. This wise person, who is subject to testing, is a newborn and, being just brought in, is able to make progress continually. But when he receives wisdom such that it is no longer possible to receive it as an addition, he has been transformed until the end.

And here, even if many saints were being influenced by 'the body of humility,' they receive 'out of His fullness,' not the fullness itself, nor each one out of the fullness, but 'all from the fullness.' And they receive here 'a pledge of the Spirit,' not the whole Spirit itself, so that I may phrase it this way. But when 'the partial' is abolished and the end remains, and 'face to face' is seen, and men become like God according to what has been said: 'when He is revealed, we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is' (2 Cor 5:17), here is the end of those being transformed. And it is well to say 'those being transformed' and not 'those having been transformed.'

No one is praised for knowledge and virtue if he merely became knowledgeable or virtuous, but when he is [actively] knowledgeable; for virtue and knowledge belong to the active, having their being in the act of being. Therefore, 'unto the end,' 'on behalf of those being transformed.' This blessedness, divine and superlative transformation, we have from the right hand of the Most High; for it is said concerning it: 'this is the transformation of the right hand of the Most High.' Just as it is said, 'being rich, He became poor for our sake, so that through His poverty we might become rich' (2 Cor 8:9)—and see: 'being rich, He became poor for our sake'—for having been transformed, He also made His presence felt. But remaining apart from His presence, He is the same, always possessing being as rich. 'For our sake' He became poor. Therefore, when having become poor for our sake, He makes us rich, we are being transformed in wealth and are coming unto the end, if we become rich as He is, as is possible, whenever we behold 'His glory, the glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth' (John 1:14). Thus, the saints receive 'out of the fullness.' No one receives the fullness, nor all...

In the same way with the words, 'I will pour out from my Spirit.' He did not say, 'my spirit'; for those who are spirit-bearers here receive a 'pledge' of the 'Spirit.' And the pledge is poured out from the Spirit. And the pledge is a part of a whole. Therefore, 'unto the end,' 'concerning those who shall be transformed.'

So, 'this is the transformation of the right hand of the Most High.' The right hand of the Most High is unshakeable and unchangeable. It always has and is the same; for we understand it as nothing other than the Savior. How then is it transformed, let us see: it descends along with [us] to instruct; and then, in reality, we were benefited if it descends along with us. But if it remains above itself, we are not benefited.

Therefore he says this: 'Will the Lord cast off forever or withhold his mercy?' (Ps 89:3) and 'Will he cut off his mercy from generation to generation or withhold his compassions?' (Ps 89:3) He says: 'And I said, Now I have begun,' when, through the descending [process], I received experience of the right hand. 'Now I have begun': it happened in the beginning to know the truth, in the beginning to know the works of providence, the creative mercies of God toward good. So I said, 'Now I have begun.'

He says: 'This transformation,' which I endured, 'of the right hand of the Most High' is. This transformed me. No one of the created things was able to transform me in this way; for all need one who leads toward progress, one who perfects. But speaking more popularly and for those speaking in the middle, we will say that this is the transformation of the Most High: being a blessing, it has become a curse, so that it may release the curse and demonstrate those who are blessed. Being righteousness, it has therefore become sin, but sin such as is a maker of righteousness. And 'in him' we become 'the creative righteousness of God.' It is not righteousness simply, but of God.

We have said many times that those who are renamed possess the names of the seven [gifts] when they are perfected according to them. In the same way, regarding the one perfected in love, as is possible in life, Paul calls it love; for 'love does not boast, is not rude, does not seek its own' (1 Cor 13:4) is not said concerning the virtue of love, the commandment which is greater than all, but concerning the one possessing it, concerning the one doing it. Therefore the Savior becomes for the sake of all of us. He becomes flesh, 'so that we might become the righteousness of God' (2 Cor 5:21); for having seen 'his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten' (John 1:14), [he...]
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Change through corruption vs. change of substance
english: We remain flesh, but we become gods according to those 'to whom the word of God became' (John 1:14). This 'alteration' is according to both, that is, both that which we others have been altered into and that which was undergone on our account; it is not a turning away, nor having been altered according to the divinity, but according to the economy, according to the humanization. 'Unto the end' therefore, 'for the sake of those who shall be altered'; these ones who are to be altered, while still being in the process of being altered, will one day reach the end of that alteration; for no one begins in order that he might not be perfected, but in order that after many progresses he might reach that very end of that quality according to which he is being altered.

And what is the end, or the becoming god-like, so that all might be? Some take this regarding the resurrection from the dead, saying that those being raised have an incorruptible instead of a corruptible body, and a spiritual instead of a psychic, and a strong and glorious instead of a weak and dishonorable. But Paul, saying, did not say: 'all shall be altered', but 'we shall be changed' (1 Cor 15:51), 'and the dead shall be raised incorruptible' (1 Cor 15:52), since the body is raised according to essence; for from a body an incorporeal thing does not become, but from such a body a certain kind of body becomes, having the change according to quality.

If we take it thus according to quality only, it is an alteration. But if, since the corruptible is not the same as the incorruptible, the corruptible becomes incorruptible, it is a change, a change according to transformation. I do not say that from a body an incorporeal thing has become, but from a corruptible body an incorruptible body. But does the body remain? The body remains, and just as a sinful soul, if it becomes righteous, the soul remains. But the change has happened according to alteration. If, therefore, a resurrection happens according to alteration, the flesh is flesh again, the corruptible is corruptible again; for I am not speaking of the quality of the corruptible or the flesh. It happens according to change.

If, for example, we change the colors of a vessel made from a shell either by painting or otherwise, this is altered; for the same thing remains. But if, having made a vessel from clay, we bring it to the fire and it becomes a shell, this is not an alteration, but a change, not because the clay was cast out and the shell was brought in, but because that thing has become shell-like. Again, the sand and nitre having been prepared by the glass-makers, glass is made...

It is a kind of [change], and I do not say that the sand has vanished as if it had departed, or the saltpeter, but rather those things have become natron. And listen to the fact that there is a change: when the saltpeter was saltpeter, it was dissolved upon the passing of moisture, but the natron having come from it is not dissolved. Again, the sand was seed upon the passing of moisture. But when it becomes natron, it is no longer seed. I say, therefore, that this is a change, not from one underlying substance into another underlying substance, but into something having come into being from that which has undergone corruption. The saltpeter and the sand undergo corruption and become natron. Yet the corruption of these does not destroy them into non-existence.

And the matter of the pottery, as I have said, the clay having become a pot through fire, does not cast the clay down into non-existence, but the pot becomes something else from it. Likewise, the bird comes from an egg; for the egg is not cast out from the outside so that the bird might be brought in; rather, that very thing transforms into this, yet it is no longer an egg; for it flies, and it has sensation. The egg has endured none of these things. And Paul has used the name of the seed: 'it is sown in corruption, it is sown in weakness' (1 Cor 15:43). I say: the seed of the animal, when it is a seed, is not an animal. But it transforms itself into the animal; for it is not that an animal comes from somewhere else after the seed has vanished, but the seed itself, first being turned into nature, then from nature into an embryo, and after the embryo, becoming an animal, undergoes birth. These, then, are changes, not alterations; for change does not occur by quality alone. And many such things are to be found.

And Paul himself, using the seeds: the grain of wheat is a grain before it is sown. But when it happens to be sown in agriculture, it becomes an ear; or, as others say, again wheat. But they did not know that what was said is an example. It has been said many times that examples are not made uniform, because they are no longer examples. Again, it is not the same thing to be an infant and a child. Nevertheless, the infant transforms into the child, and I do not say that the child entered from somewhere else after the infant had been turned into non-existence, but the infant itself, through growth and through another quality, became a child, without having reached maturity. And according to age, one is an infant and another is a child, but according to the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nourishment of the Heart
english: There is no difference in a man who is growing older; for there is one underlying subject to that infant and that age; having perished, he is again a man underlying the child. And if he changes from the child to an ox, the age has changed again. And this is a quality, and it is a non-substantial quality. And again, always growing older until he reaches old age. Therefore, qualities and ages are being exchanged; for he said that ages are qualities that are non-substantial. But the same man remains.

Even if the body receives ten thousand changes in the resurrection, it is a body, but not this body, not the one before the change. And Paul, therefore, was compelled to speak as one thing and another. He said: 'A natural body is sown, a spiritual body is raised' (1 Cor 15:44). He says: 'Not first the spiritual but the natural, then the spiritual.' And where there is the first and the second, identity is not signified. However, we do not take the first and the second as an exchange of substances, but an exchange of the same body, since it has become incorruptible from the corruptible and spiritual from the natural. So one thing is change and another is alteration. The change of the soul effects the alteration, which I call the praised or even the lied-about; for it is easier to undergo alteration, as it has been said: 'How shall the gold be darkened? How shall the good silver be altered?' (Ps 119:127). And he says: 'Children of Zion, the precious ones, overlaid with gold and silver, how were they counted as vessels of earthenware, the work of their own hands?' (Ps 12:6).

Again, allegory will show other things; for it is said that gold has been changed into earthenware vessels, not according to history, but according to anagogical ascent. 'Unto the end,' therefore, 'for those who shall be altered; to the sons of Kore for understanding.' And since the inscription itself and the whole psalm have mysteries hidden within them, for this reason understanding is needed for the one bringing this song; for it is 'for understanding.' And it was also said concerning the three hundred and first psalm, since it was spoken with an enigma: 'A song, therefore, for the beloved.' This very triumphal song became for the beloved; for he himself became the cause of the alteration; for he said that 'being rich, he became poor,' so that he might work us to be rich, not rich according to a fantasy, not sensually, but having...

"Every word and all knowledge." He said that having become cursed, he established a blessing. Therefore, the beloved has become the cause of this best of transformations. For this reason, the song is assigned to him; just as a victory song is sent to a general or a king, even though others, spear-bearers and soldiers, are accompanying him, yet the essence of the victory is inscribed to the king or the general.

What about "for the sake of the beloved"? Instead of "concerning"—for it is not always said "on behalf of something"; "so that the one against [him] may be entangled, having nothing to say something trivial concerning us"; for it is not said here "concerning us" instead of "gathering for us."

"My heart searched out a good word" (Psalm 63:3). Some take this psalm to be spoken from the presence of the Father and from the presence of the perfect man, the wise one. And you know that the eructation of previously eaten food brings forth its fragrance; for there is no eructation other than a proceeding of spirit from the stomach declaring the quality of the things previously eaten. If indeed anyone eats an apple, he has the eructation bringing forth the quality and fragrance of the apple.

When therefore a holy person eats the "bread of life" (John 6:35) and having Jesus' flesh as true food and the fruits of the "tree of life" (Genesis 2:9) and drinks the wine being harvested from the "true vine" (John 15:1), he has an eructation suitable to the foods previously eaten. He who has thus been fed and has eructated signifies: "the good man out of the good treasure of the heart brings forth the good" (Luke 6:45). And since it is concerning spiritual things, he was not hesitant to speak of a treasure instead of stomachs, namely the heart.

He who therefore has been fed on the blessed food and has enjoyed the flesh of Jesus and the "bread of life" (John 6:35), the bread of heaven, brings forth words suitable to that which he was fed and eructated: "my heart searched out a good word" (Psalm 63:3). We have therefore spoken fully concerning the man.

The sons of Korah, bringing the hymns with this same mind and the same spirit, bring them forth as one. Just as: "as the deer longs for the water springs, so my soul longs" (Psalm 42:1), so also here they say as one and in unison: "my heart searched out." And this refers to each of the wise; for if the wise man [brings forth] what he has in his heart and what he was fed, these [things]...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: God as Land, Source, and Radiance
english: He brings it forth by instructing, having searched out the good word. From this, the word again gathers this point: that if anyone wishes to bring forth a word without having been nourished, it is not a good movement. And again, just as a handler, having nourished himself on food, has a reason for instruction, so he says, 'I declare my works to the king.' My works are so boldly declared, and they bring me no condemnation nor any reproach. I say to him, to the king, to the judge.

My tongue is a scribe's pen, sharp-writing. My word is signified through the tongue. Often you will find the tongue used instead of the word. As if he says, 'The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the great-sounding tongue' (Psalm 12:2), he calls the word 'great-sounding'. It is a beautiful beauty according to the sons of men. And the sons of men—that is, the wise of the world and those who once promised teaching—seem to have beauty in their own words. Our word's beauty according to the sons of men is sent by God, is a gift from God, and is true wisdom. Therefore, it possesses something more than the sons of men who, speaking from their own hearts, gather words and lessons of their own zeal and learning.

For then listen: the Psalm is received from the face of the Father. And almost all those speaking to the common people receive it in this way. The transcendent and great things, which are above the intellects, are revealed only through many examples. Wishing therefore to say many times that God is one, we say ten thousand things. We say that nothing is joined to Him, that there is neither matter nor form in Him, that He is a Monad, He is a One, and only through a multitude of words do we make these things manifest. But when I wish to speak about wine, it is enough to say 'wine'; for they know what it is, it is said; and we signify only the concept through the word. The same is true concerning earth.
